#1. Dolly: A Childfree Inspiration for Us All

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted September 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Endowed as she was with the voice of an angel and a physicality she so adroitly applied for comedic purposes, Dolly Parton’s legacy will never be silenced. Dolly was not criticized for not having children. Instead, she’s heralded as a beacon of balance, generosity, and good humor.

With no children of her own, Dolly’s Imagination Library benefits over three million youth aged five and younger around the world. Each month they receive books at no cost, planting seeds for future literacy and love of reading. “The seeds of dreams are often found in books,” she said, “and the seeds you help plant in your community can grow across the world.”

Giving is often without show, and efforts are often woven into our very character. Like Dolly, many of us who are without children equivocate when grilled about why we don't have children. Part of the reason we don’t often tell our stories is that most involve the complexity and evolution included in living outside the mainstream of parenthood. Being non-parents is an element of our being, not a statement of our value.

Our crucial role in philanthropy and giving cannot be understated, though. Whether supporting lives on our family tree or giving to charities, many childless and childfree people contribute our time and treasures to support those in need. We make a mark that is not insignificant.

For example, those of us without children are much more likely to include a charity in our estate plans than parents. According to a study by Russell James, Professor of Charitable Financial Planning at Texas Tech from 1992 to 2012, 50 percent of childless decedents left money to philanthropic organizations versus 17.1 percent of those with children.

As childless and childfree adults, what we lack is a way to combine our giving to create lasting change. I’ve long thought if such a mechanism existed, together we could band together to balance disparities in intergenerational transfer of wealth, combat climate change, or nourish the hungry. But routes for unification of our demographic are few.

Before COVID-19, I was involved in planning my local community foundation’s event for women donors who don’t have kids. The event was packed, and participants clamored for future events tailored to our interests. Although the organization agreed, years later, another event has yet to come to fruition. No one can tell me why.

I can guarantee, though, that as a result of that first event, several new donor advised funds were established, and numerous liaisons and friendships were instigated. I have a small donor advised fund that will, upon my demise, support early childhood literacy.

After I cut back on my professional work life, I donated years of service to the primary grades, supporting children who struggled with reading and writing. Recalling the choruses of their greetings each time I entered the classroom nourishes me to this day; so do the drawings they put in a memory book when I moved away.

Those of us who are still star-struck may fail to see the the power of Dolly’s role in making the world a better place, not only for children but also by serving as a model for how we can better get along with one another. She offers inspiration for how to be thriving members of our communities who don’t happen to have kids. What more could one want as their life’s legacy?

#3. Your aging brain may be trading memory for something more valuable

Growing older is often associated with memory loss and declining mental abilities. However, scientists are questioning whether these changes tell the whole story. Rather than simply becoming less capable, the brain may be adapting to a new stage of life in which accumulated knowledge, wisdom, and understanding become more important than remembering every detail.

Researchers at the University of Arizona have proposed a different way of understanding cognitive aging. Drawing on findings from molecular biology and brain imaging, they suggest that the changes occurring in older brains may reflect a natural stage of human development rather than deterioration alone. Their work, published in Perspectives on Psychological Science, offers a new perspective on why thinking and memory change with age.

The researchers call their proposed explanation the adaptive aging hypothesis. It suggests that the brain gradually adjusts its priorities to make better use of a lifetime of accumulated experience. This could help explain why older adults often have valuable strengths in teaching, mentoring, storytelling, and passing knowledge to younger generations.

"If we look at normative aging as a story of just decline, we are really missing the boat," said study coauthor Fabian-Xosé Fernandez, an associate professor of cognition and neural systems at the University of Arizona. "The older brain is optimized for different things than the younger brain, predominantly the sharing of stored expertise and social relationships."

How the Brain Shifts From Memory to Meaning

Two brain regions play important roles in how people remember and interpret their experiences. The hippocampus helps preserve specific information about events, including their details and circumstances. The frontal cortex, meanwhile, is more involved in extracting broader meaning, recognizing patterns, and understanding the central message of an experience, sometimes called its "gist."

According to the researchers, the balance between these systems changes during healthy aging. As people grow older, the brain tends to place less emphasis on activity in the hippocampus and rely more on the frontal cortex. This shift may allow the brain to focus more on interpreting information through existing knowledge rather than recording every new experience in precise detail.

"The fact that you see this across people and animal models suggests there is an evolutionary driving force," Fernandez said. "One could argue you are developing your entire life, and development occurs in lockstep with the needs of your brain. When you're younger, the hippocampus turns on because you don't have a knowledge base or know how the world works. A kid absorbs information like a sponge because they are building an archive of information. In early life, the balance is tilted toward recollecting declarative memories with precision, detail, and context."

Young brains need to gather enormous amounts of new information because they are still building a foundation for understanding the world. By later adulthood, however, people have already developed extensive stores of memories, concepts, and experiences. Connecting new information to what they already know may become more useful than retaining every individual detail.

The researchers suggest that this changing balance reflects a shift in how the brain processes experience. Instead of concentrating primarily on collecting detailed memories, it increasingly emphasizes understanding relationships, identifying underlying meaning, and applying previously acquired knowledge.

Why Evolution May Favor Wisdom in Older Adults

Evidence of similar changes in animal models raises the possibility that this transition has an evolutionary explanation. Fernandez suggests that the aging brain may be adapting to help individuals preserve and share the knowledge they have acquired throughout their lives.

From this perspective, the ability to draw on decades of experience could be especially valuable for making judgments, guiding others, and transferring important information between generations. Older adults may therefore play a distinct role in supporting younger people through mentorship, teaching, and storytelling.

"Given those goals, it makes sense that you aren't interested in nitty-gritty details," Fernandez said. "You are interested in safeguarding the vast knowledge you already have. Evolution may be saying that if you make it long enough, there's a need to transmit this information, so we put into motion biological changes that enforce and protect your semantic and autobiographical memories."

Under this hypothesis, changes in memory and thinking are not necessarily signs that the brain is functioning less effectively. They may instead reflect a different set of priorities, with greater emphasis on preserving meaningful knowledge and using it to understand new situations.

Why Healthy Brain Aging Is Different From Alzheimer's

The adaptive aging hypothesis could also provide scientists with another way to examine the differences between normal cognitive aging and Alzheimer's disease.

Although both involve changes in memory, Fernandez emphasizes that Alzheimer's should not be understood as ordinary aging taken to an extreme. The biological processes involved are fundamentally different.

"When I was in grad school, people thought about Alzheimer's as a more intense version of cognitive aging, but that is just not the case," Fernandez said. "They are completely different."

During typical aging, the brain's gradual shift away from relying heavily on the hippocampus and toward greater involvement of the frontal cortex generally unfolds between the fifth and seventh decades of life. In Alzheimer's disease, however, abnormal processes involving proteins such as amyloid and tau may interfere with this transition.

One important distinction involves activity in the hippocampus. While healthy aging is generally associated with reduced emphasis on this region, Alzheimer's can involve unusually high levels of hippocampal activity. Rather than supporting the normal progression of cognitive development, disease-related changes may disrupt the brain networks responsible for memory and understanding.

"In normative aging, hippocampal activation is deemphasized, which is probably what should be happening in a 70-year-old. But in many cases of Alzheimer's, it turns out the hippocampus is hyperactive," he said. "This beautiful developmental transition is completely disrupted in Alzheimer's disease by pathological processes that mess with episodic memory and interfere with circuits that allow you to think about your own life, lexicon, and vocabulary."

These disruptions can affect the ability to recall personal experiences and access stored knowledge, including words and their meanings. Understanding how these changes differ from the adaptations associated with healthy aging may help researchers develop a clearer picture of normal brain development and neurodegenerative disease.

Embracing the Hidden Strengths of the Aging Brain

The researchers argue that society may need to reconsider what successful brain aging looks like. Encouraging older adults to process information exactly as younger people do may not always be the most productive approach.

Fernandez suggests that placing excessive emphasis on remembering precise details could work against the brain's changing priorities. "For many individuals, the weight of how you process information should probably not be so hippocampal-centric by the sixth or seventh decade."

Instead of judging older adults primarily by abilities that tend to weaken with age, the researchers encourage greater recognition of the capabilities that may become especially valuable later in life.

Creating more opportunities for social interaction could be one way to support these strengths. Relationships between older and younger generations may be particularly beneficial because they provide opportunities to exchange experiences, share expertise, and preserve knowledge that might otherwise be lost.

"People see older individuals and look at them as not being on par with younger individuals across a lot of metrics," Fernandez says. "The way I look at it is that you've got someone with a brain that has been active for several decades and has seen a lot. There is tremendous value there, and we don't do a good job of unlocking it."

The central message of the adaptive aging hypothesis is that growing older may involve more than a gradual reduction in cognitive abilities. Although some mental skills become less reliable with age, the brain may also be adapting to make better use of the knowledge and experience accumulated over a lifetime. Recognizing those strengths could change how society understands aging and the contributions older adults can make.

#5. The Thing Your Friends Don’t Tell You About Being Single

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

Time on your own can teach you steadiness, awareness, and self-compassion, so you bring your whole self into your next relationship.

I used to hear the phrase “you need to be single to work on yourself” and find it almost offensive, as if someone were saying I was too damaged or too complicated to be loved until I fixed myself.

Over time, I realized that wasn’t what people meant.

Being single isn’t about becoming more worthy of love.

Being single isn’t about becoming more worthy of love. It’s about finally having enough space to understand yourself without another person’s emotions, habits, and reactions constantly shaping the environment around you.

Because relationships don’t just connect two people. They connect two nervous systems.

The person you are closest to influences how you feel, how you respond, and how quickly you return to calm. Their presence can give you perspective, reduce uncertainty, or make difficult moments feel easier.

That comfort is real, but comfort and growth are not always the same thing.

Sometimes what feels like healing is actually relief. You feel better because someone else is helping you feel okay again, but you haven’t necessarily learned how to create that stability within yourself.

There is nothing wrong with needing connection. Humans are wired for it. The problem comes when we never learn the difference between being supported by someone and needing someone to feel whole.

Growth happens when you discover you can sit with discomfort and still find your footing.

Growth happens when you discover you can sit with discomfort and still find your footing. When you can experience fear, uncertainty, or sadness without immediately needing another person to make those feelings disappear.

That is one of the hardest things to learn while staying inside the same patterns you are trying to change.

Two people rarely grow at the same pace or in the same direction. One person starts setting boundaries while the other is used to having access. Someone begins to pause before reacting while the other is still waiting for the old response. As one person changes, the relationship has to decide whether it can change with them.

Sometimes it can, and sometimes it can’t. That is where solitude can become powerful.

Solitude is not about proving you can live without anyone…The purpose of that space is to hear yourself clearly.

Solitude is not about proving you can live without anyone. Independence is not the goal. The purpose of that space is to hear yourself clearly and understand what belongs to you before bringing that awareness back into connection with someone else.

You start noticing your own reactions more clearly. Old wounds become easier to recognize. You learn to separate what comes from within you from what was shaped by the dynamic you were in.

The advice to “be single for a while” isn’t a punishment.

It is an invitation to stop abandoning yourself while trying to build a life with someone else.

Because change is harder when you are still surrounded by the exact dynamics that shaped the patterns you are trying to break.

Being alone gives you the chance to learn that you can regulate your own emotions and make decisions from clarity instead of fear.

It is not impossible, but it does require more awareness, effort, and intention.

Being alone gives you the chance to learn that you can regulate your own emotions and make decisions from clarity instead of fear. It also gives you space to build a secure relationship with yourself, without relying on someone else to create that stability for you.

Then, when you do enter a relationship again, you’re not looking for someone to complete what is missing.

You are bringing a whole person into the room.

Catherine Swett is a writer exploring the intersection of lived experience, psychology, and human transformation. Through personal essays and reflective writing, she examines the nervous system, perception, relationships, and the ways internal patterns shape how we experience the world. Her work has been published in Divergent Magazine. You can reach her at thehumancartographer1991@gmail.com.

#6. Why AI Cannot Replace the Transformative Power of Human Creativity

As generative artificial intelligence masters the rapid synthesis of complex paintings, music, and literature, a new theoretical framework published in AI & Society re-evaluates the true essence of human creative cognition. The paper introduces the “decoupling thesis,” arguing that while AI can bypass decades of technical mastery to generate sophisticated outputs, it detaches production from the personal cognitive transformation traditionally required to make art. True creative value lies not in the finished artifact, but in the experiential journey that alters how humans perceive, interpret, and connect with reality.

Source: The Hebrew University of Jerusalem

Generative artificial intelligence algorithms can now assemble gallery-worthy oil paintings, orchestrate complex symphonic movements, write evocative poetry, and draft architectural blueprints in a matter of seconds. Across many metrics, these synthetic creations rival works that historically demanded decades of disciplined human apprenticeship.

As machines demonstrate the capacity to produce virtually any aesthetic artifact on demand, cognitive scientists, philosophers, and artists face a foundational dilemma: if algorithmic networks can generate sophisticated art instantaneously, what is the ultimate value of human creativity?

In a paper published in the journal AI & Society, Amit R. Zoran, PhD, an associate professor at the Rachel and Selim Benin School of Computer Science and Engineering at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, offers a conceptual framework to address this question.

Rather than engaging in circular debates over whether synthetic media meets the technical definition of “art,” Zoran argues that human creative cognition derives its significance not merely from the finished product, but from the neurocognitive and experiential transformations that mold artists, audiences, and human culture across time.

Historically, mastering an art form required years of intense deliberate practice, sensorimotor refinement, emotional maturation, and perceptual recalibration. A painter did not merely train their hand to mix pigments; they fundamentally restructured their visual processing systems and internal models of the physical world. A cellist did not simply memorize finger positions; they integrated acoustic feedback, fine motor control, and emotional regulation into a unified mode of expression.

Zoran formalizes how generative AI disrupts this historical unity through what he terms the “decoupling thesis.” The framework posits that AI tools now allow individuals to manufacture highly sophisticated aesthetic artifacts without undergoing the arduous cognitive and emotional maturation previously required to realize them.

“For centuries, creating art meant going through a process of learning, experimenting, and changing as a person,” explains Zoran. “Today, AI allows us to produce sophisticated works without necessarily undergoing that journey. But this doesn’t mean human creativity has lost its value. It means we need to rethink where that value lies. The real potential of AI is not simply to help us produce more images, music, or designs, but to open new possibilities for how we experience, understand, and engage with the world around us.”

By detaching technical output from personal development, AI strips away the traditional gatekeeping of craft. However, Zoran emphasizes that automated generation should not be mistaken for genuine creative cognition. When output becomes frictionless, the scarcity and ultimate value of human creativity pivot from technical execution to interpretive depth, philosophical inquiry, and relational engagement.

Rather than displacing human creative drive, algorithmic tools can be redirected toward deepening multisensory exploration and collaborative synthesis.

To illustrate this potential, the paper examines hybrid creative projects where computational systems serve not to flood digital feeds with synthetic imagery, but to enhance bodily and environmental awareness. In one featured installation, a living tree becomes the focal nexus of a shared, participatory encounter. The piece integrates olfactory stimuli, taste, environmental field recordings, adaptive AI-generated music, and spatial visual projections.

Instead of trapping the human participant inside an algorithmic screen, technology acts as a sensory amplifier, prompting visitors to engage with the natural environment and living systems in ways previously inaccessible to standard perception.

Zoran’s analysis presents direct challenges for computational design, software evaluation, and creative arts education:

Ultimately, the democratization and automation of aesthetic production may deliver an unexpected cognitive benefit. By relieving humanity of the necessity to treat technical execution as the sole arbiter of artistic worth, artificial intelligence provides a rare opportunity to rediscover the true core of creativity: an ongoing transformation of the human mind and its perception of the world.

More than we can make: Generative AI, artistic forms, and artistic becoming

Debates surrounding generative AI and creativity have largely focused on artifacts: who or what produced a given image or text, whether machine outputs qualify as art, and how authorship and value should be understood.

Drawing on aesthetics, craft theory, anthropology, human–computer interaction, hybrid craft, digital fabrication, and rematerialization, this article argues that art has historically involved two intertwined dimensions.

Artistic forms stabilize and transmit meaning through artifacts, whereas artistic becoming refers to the developmental and transformative processes through which new possibilities of perception, interpretation, and experience emerge, in makers, in recipients, and in cultures.

The article’s central claim is a decoupling thesis: for most of history these dimensions were contingently coupled, since producing sophisticated forms required the maker’s becoming, and generative AI loosens this coupling by enabling such forms to emerge without the specific developmental pathways that traditionally conditioned them.

Rather than signaling the disappearance of creativity, the decoupling relocates to new sites and makes visible dimensions of artistic practice that the demands of production long obscured.

The article situates generative AI within a longer history of hybridization and distributed creativity, develops the decoupling thesis across these three levels, and defends a normative orientation: under conditions of symbolic abundance, the creative practices most worth pursuing are those that route generative fluency back into embodied, situated experience.

#7. Ten TV Series That Highlight the Best in Humanity: 2026

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Every year, we invite staff and regular contributors to nominate TV series for Greater Goodies, the awards we give to stories that exemplify or illustrate kindness, community, empathy, and more keys to well-being. Here’s what we came up with this year: The Boroughs, Death by Lightning, Envidiosa, The Hawk, Heated Rivalry, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, Lucky, Murderbot, Pluribus, and Shrinking.

Name the last show you’ve seen that features a hero over the age of 60. Drawing a blank? It’s not your fault—the media’s modus operandi is to equate heroism with youthfulness. Netflix’s The Boroughs flips this stereotype on its head.

With a star-studded lead cast, all 70 or older, we follow Sam Cooper’s (Alfred Molina) experience as he reluctantly moves into a senior living community in New Mexico after the death of his wife. But a series of strange events suggests that this is no ordinary retirement community.

As Sam navigates grief, new friendships, and a new identity, he joins forces with his neighbors to solve and resolve the community mystery. Overcoming obstacles like age discrimination and self-doubts, the group peels back the layers of the strange occurrences. At the root of the mystery is a societal fear of aging.

The show highlights what researcher Margie Lachman calls “crystallized intelligence”: the culmination of life experience, memory, and know-how. In The Boroughs, that turns out to be just as heroic as super human strength or the ability to fly. — Shanna B. Tiayon

History has already told us how Death by Lightning ends: Charles Guiteau will assassinate President James Garfield in 1881. But why? That’s one of the questions explored by the series, and it finds motivation in a sense of purpose–how purpose forms and how people come to cross-purposes.

Garfield (Michael Shannon) is principled and drawn reluctantly into a presidential contest he entered to nominate someone else. Guiteau (Matthew Macfadyen), meanwhile, is disturbingly sympathetic: charming, articulate, and desperate to do something meaningful with his life. Despite failed ventures, including a stint at the Oneida free-love commune, he remains convinced greatness awaits him. Believing his campaigning secured Garfield’s victory, he expects a government position to confirm his worth.

As their stories converge, Garfield finds purpose in his presidency: fighting corruption while supporting education and equal opportunity. Guiteau pursues a reward he feels he deserves, an entitlement that leads to tragedy.

In these ways, Garfield and Guiteau offer sharply contrasting answers to what makes a life meaningful, and watching their stories unfold side by side, we see how differently the desire to matter can play out.

Who you really ought to be watching closely is Garfield’s Vice President, Chester A. Arthur (Nick Offerman). A comfortable beneficiary of the political machine, he becomes an unlikely source of hope as the story goes on. Offerman makes him funny, flawed, and increasingly affecting as the demands of office begin to collide with old loyalties.

In a political landscape that can leave us cynical–in both the 19th century and the 21st–the series makes room for something more hopeful: the possibility that even an unlikely person can rise to the occasion, if they know why they need to rise. – Aurelia Santos

When almost-40-year-old Vicky (Griselda Siciliani) breaks up with her long-term boyfriend, she is driven to embark upon a journey of self-discovery.

At first, Vicky is just looking for a replacement for her boyfriend—but the problem is that her compulsive comparisons with other women sabotage attempts to connect with other people. (Indeed, the name of this Argentinian show, Envidiosa, means “envious.”) Vicky is self-absorbed and yet at the same time she doesn’t have a strong sense of her own self.

We see this vividly in her hilarious sessions with her therapist. When, for example, she goes on an envious rant about a friend’s milestone, she is forced to confront the quiet, uncomfortable realization that she never once asked how her friend actually felt. In short, Vicky is not a polished role model—and over the course of four seasons, we see her empathy grow through the painful process of unlearning self-centeredness.

Personally, I see Envidiosa as an opportunity to question how we show up for others’ joys and struggles, and I take it as an invitation to reflect: How can I empathize with the ups and downs of those around me? Envidiosa is a funny and at times embarrassingly relatable story about trying to become a more empathic human being and friend. — Criss Cuervo

In The Hawk, washed-up professional golfer Lonnie “The Hawk” Hawkins (Will Ferrell) has made a miracle comeback into the PGA tour—this time around, facing a tough competitor in his son, Lance (Jimmy Tatro).

It’s a screwball comedy, full of dirty jokes and a rapid-fire rapport between Lonnie and his not-quite-ex-wife, Stacy (Molly Shannon). A makeshift-caddy he “picked up at Walmart” (while chatting up the parking lot, from his camper van) adds to the fun, serving up an unlikely duo that seem happy just to be alive.

Even when he’s pretty down and out, Lonnie is looking on the bright side of things. Everything is done with gusto—he chats up the golf ball before each swing, he devours plates of Buffalo Wild Wings, he plays mini golf with his son and makes it a full-on competition.

“Son, never play golf angry,” he tells Lance. For Lonnie, life is all about golf—and golf is all about fun. Why spend all your time on something if you aren’t doing it for the joy of it?

I especially love Lonnie’s adoration for his estranged wife, a firecracker in her own right. In episode four, when the Hawk crashes his son’s engagement party–yes, you read that right–and then attempts a getaway with his caddie in the van, Stacy hurls the cake at them, along with a string of expletives.

It doesn’t even faze him. “You gotta love the passion!” Lonnie gushes. “That is one hot tamale!” — Hope Reese

Heated Rivalry follows stick-crossed lovers Shane and Ilya as they figure out how to be intimate within the highly competitive, homophobic environment of professional hockey.

At first, Shane and Ilya swap fluids more readily than emotions. But over the course of six episodes, the two learn to love across gaps in culture, language, and experience. In one pivotal scene, Shane invites Ilya to speak vulnerably about family dynamics in Ilya’s native Russian—despite not understanding a word of it.

That works because Shane does not focus attention on himself. Instead, he stays present on the phone, serving as a witness to Ilya’s visceral emotions. Their connection lies in felt care, in hearing the texture of another’s heartbreak.

In similar fashion, Ilya grounds Shane in stressful encounters. He supports Shane through panic without wallowing in his lover’s fear and entices Shane to relish pleasures outside of straight standards. As a couple, they help each other explore complex parts of themselves. We see a similar process unfold in another couple in the show, as they learn to respect each other’s different needs.

People might tune into Heated Rivalry for locker room towel drops and HBO’s glossy cinematography. They should stay to see a couple learn to love each other’s differences. The show exemplifies how bridging differences, at its best, means supporting others to more fully encounter themselves, and how in the process our relationships can grow.

With plenty of additional homoerotic stick-and-ball games to pull on from the novels of Rachel Reid, the next season of Heated Rivalry is expected to air on HBO Max and Canada’s Crave in Spring 2027. — Luke Brown

The monstrously successful HBO series Game of Thrones famously tossed out a lot of good-and-evil fantasy tropes to tell a morally complicated story of how power corrupts even the best people. A prequel called House of the Dragon shares that worldview.

That’s why a new prequel called A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms came as something of a surprise to fans. Unlike the other two series, this is not a story about a struggle for power. Instead, it focuses on a rather naive, not-too-bright “hedge knight” named Duncan (Peter Claffey) seeking to be hired by whatever lord will take him. Though Duncan is taller and stronger than most, he’s touchingly childlike as he tries to find his place in the merry old kingdoms of Westeros.

The first two episodes are shockingly funny and charming, as Duncan acquires a squire in the form of a little bald boy going by the name Egg (Dexter Sol Ansell), and fumblingly tries to enter a jousting tournament. And then Duncan finds himself on a collision course with the great and powerful of Westeros. When violence finally comes, there’s nothing casual about it. We feel the force of every blow, the tragedy of every death, and the erosion of Duncan’s innocence.

I’m giving A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms the award for integrity, but I can’t tell you why without spoiling the ending. Let’s just say that the series turns out to be the story of how one simple young man discovers what is most important to him—and finds the courage to stick to that path even in the face of isolation, temptations, and threats. — Jeremy Adam Smith

How do you exit a life you were born into?

That’s the question behind Lucky, starring Anya Taylor-Joy. Lucky was raised by her con-artist father and taught the “family business” from a young age—but when we meet her, she navigating internal conflict with the life she’s been told to live and the life she wants for herself.

Her desire to quit is complicated by her marriage to Cary, the son of a ruthless mob leader, who was also socialized into a life of crime. The couple plan one final con as their exit strategy, but it goes terribly wrong. Lucky sets out to resolve the botched plan, reconcile her marriage, and protect both her life and her father’s.

Her intelligence is put to the test as she puts the pieces together, connects the dots, and outsmarts her rivals. In the process she discovers her own virtue—and that the intelligence which made her a successful con artist can also set her free.

Through the course of the series, she realizes that she does not have to pay for the sins of her father. Having never been given the opportunity for self-determination, she makes peace in the best way she knows how and chooses a new path. — Shanna B. Tiayon

The Murderbot Diaries are a series of science-fiction novellas by Martha Wells, about a genderless, robotic soldier who manages to achieve free will. Since discovery will result in deactivation and since it doesn’t like humans very much anyway, Murderbot conceals its freedom of mind and consumes a lot of human-made entertainment inside its own head, even as it externally follows every order given to it by the evil corporation that owns it. Murderbot even has a favorite TV show: the Star-Trek-like Rise and Fall of Sanctuary Moon.

As a result of this isolation, the novellas are built almost entirely around its memorable inner monologues, with a voice that is by turns snarky, vulnerable, cold-blooded, disgusted, and puzzled. One of the things that makes these books distinctive is that Murderbot is not Pinocchio—it has no wish to become a “real boy.” It doesn’t want a gender, or the same feelings and drives as people. It just wants to be itself—and to have that difference respected.

While the Apple TV show based on the books is not quite that original or interesting, Murderbot retains its focus on finding the balance between belonging and difference. When we meet Murderbot (Alexander Skarsgård), he’s been hired to protect a group of polyamorous hippie scientists who hail from a utopian colony that exists independently of the corporations that rule the rest of the galaxy.

They are Murderbot’s first encounter with humans not shaped by dehumanizing hyper-capitalistic values, and they observe Murderbot in a way the corporate humans cannot. Over the course of the first season, they begin to realize that there is more to Murderbot than meets the eye, and they learn to see and appreciate Murderbot on its own terms. But what’s crucial is not that they perceive the humanity in Murderbot—it’s that Murderbot sees the humanity (and the goodness) in them.

In time, it becomes an accepted part of their society—without becoming more like them. Even so, the first season concludes on a tough-minded, melancholy note, as Murderbot itself can’t quite feel like it belongs. Will it someday find a place among these crunchy idealists? Stay tuned: The second season is coming in 2027. — Jeremy Adam Smith

Have you ever been among people but you didn’t feel part of the crowd? Like they were in on a joke that you just couldn’t get?

Welcome to Carol Sturka’s world. The science-fiction premise of Pluribus is that an alien virus transforms humanity into one big happy hive mind—everyone except Carol and 13 other people who seem to have immunity.

Even among those remaining individuals, though, Carol stands out as a malcontent. We sense that she’s been a fish out of water for her whole life.

Indeed, not every viewer will find Carol relatable or likable. When we first meet her, she’s at a bookstore event promoting her highly successful romantasy series. With her fans, she’s charming, funny, and kind. When she gets into a limo after a big sendoff by readers, the drivers asks if she’s famous.

“That depends,” Carol replies. “Are you a big fan of mindless crap?”

In short, Carol hates herself, her work, and her readers. And as we discover, her personality is snarky, uptight, stubborn, and uncompromising. When the virus hits, it’s an apocalyptic event, but Carol doesn’t change one bit—and her traits become both a blessing and a curse. The whole world wants to be kind to her, but Carol can’t accept kindness. That drives her to fight back. And that’s what ultimately makes her the hero of the story.

In the end, Pluribus is a very Greater Good thought experiment. It takes prosociality to its limits and finds that a total togetherness, empathy, and cooperation to the exclusion of selfishness, crankiness, and boundaries is a self-destructive dystopia, not a utopia. The show seems to argue that humanity needs difficult people like Carol to survive, and so invites us to appreciate what the Carols of the world have to offer. — Jeremy Adam Smith

In Shrinking, talking and listening are the name of the game. Jimmy (Jason Segel) is a widowed psychotherapist who helps patients navigate anxiety, OCD, PTSD, and other ailments as he himself is floundering.

But he’s not alone. His teenage daughter, overbearing-but-lovable neighbors, and coworker-friends (with Harrison Ford as the curmudgeonly head of the practice) are all there to help him when his life goes off the rails after his wife was killed by a drunk driver.

In its three-season run, the series is heavy-handed with its use of therapy-speak among the whole gang, whether between therapist-to-patient, therapist-to-daughter, or therapist-to-therapist. Characters “feel seen.” More times than I can count, they tell each other “I hear you.” We witness, in detail, exchanges inside the therapy office—and outside of it, in a rogue practice known as “Jimmying,” where therapy takes place at such venues as, for instance, the boxing ring.

In other words, there’s a lot of “deep listening”: the practice of being present, open, and empathic with another person, in a way that goes beyond just hearing and understanding words. In his grief, Jimmy himself is not always a perfect deep listener. He tends to talk more than a typical therapist, and frequently injects himself into the discussion. Shrinking isn’t about perfection—it’s about struggling to connect and growing in the process. – Hope Reese

#8. How to Be Un-Dead: Notes on Waking Up from the Trance of Near-Living

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. “When you surrender, the problem ceases to exist,” Henry Miller wrote in his stunning letter to Anaïs Nin (February 21, 1903–January 14, 1977). “Try to solve it, or conquer it, and you only set up more resistance.”

But we, the controlling species, the conquering species, have a hard time with this notion of surrender; we, the conflicted species, spend our lives resisting it yet craving its liberations.

Nin herself — a woman uncommonly liberated from the common traps of convention, control, and self-consciousness — took up the spiritual mechanics of this paradox in her first published book, D. H. Lawrence: An Unprofessional Study (public library), composed when she was still in her twenties.

With an eye to D.H. Lawrence (September 11, 1885–March 2, 1930) and his “philosophy that was against division,” his “plea for whole vision,” she writes:

When the realization came to the moderns of the importance of vitality and warmth, they willed the warmth with their minds. But Lawrence, with the terrible flair of the genius, sensed that a mere mental conjuring of the elemental was a perversion… Lawrence believed that the feelings of the body, from its most extreme impulses to its smallest gesture, are the warm root for true vision, and from that warm root can we truly grow. The livingness of the body was natural; the interference of the mind had created divisions, the consciousness of wrong-doing or well-doing.

In a sentiment central to my own animating ethos, she adds:

Life is a process of becoming, a combination of states we have to go through. Where people fail is that they wish to elect a state and remain in it. This is a kind of death.

It was Lawrence’s own writing that awakened in her this awareness of ongoingness and the urgency of total aliveness — the way “livingness is the axis of his world, the light, the gravitation, and electromagnetism of his world.”

In his 1924 novel The Boy in the Bush, Lawrence makes a stunning case for the indivisibility of it all — the beauty and the sorrow, the ache and the astonishment:

All real living hurts as well as fulfils. Happiness comes when we have lived and have a respite for sheer forgetting. Happiness, in the vulgar sense, is just a holiday experience. The life-long happiness lies in being used by life; hurt by life, driven and goaded by life, replenished and overjoyed with life, fighting for life’s sake. That is real happiness. In the undergoing, a large part of it is pain.

This was the foundational philosophy of Lawrence’s worldview — the pulse-beat that makes his writing so resonant and eternally alive, the way all great spiritual texts are. He distilled this view in an especially beautiful passage from his 1923 novel Kangaroo, reckoning with the most universal reality of life — the reality we spend our lives fighting, yet the one that peeks through in all of our greatest works of art and highest triumphs of the creative spirit. Echoing Whitman’s defense of our inner multitudes, often at odds with each other, he writes in an era when every woman was a “man” purely as a matter of linguistic convention:

If a man loves life, and feels the sacredness and mystery of life, then he knows that life is full of strange and subtle and even conflicting imperatives. And a wise man learns to recognize the imperatives as they arise — or nearly so — and to obey. But most men bruise themselves to death trying to fight and overcome their own, new, life-born needs, life’s ever strange imperatives. The secret of all life is obedience: obedience to the urge that arises in the soul, the urge that is life itself, urging us to new gestures, new embraces, new emotions, new combinations, new creations.

In the same epoch when Hermann Hesse so beautifully defended the wisdom of the inner voice, Lawrence’s protagonist makes a passionate case for listening to the song of life as it reverberates through the singular cathedral of each self, yours and mine, as it did for Nin and Lawrence and every other great mind long sung out of existence:

I offer no creed. I offer myself, my heart of wisdom, strange warm cavern where the voice of the oracle steams in from the unknown; I offer my consciousness, which hears the voice; and I offer my mind and my will, for the battle against every obstacle to respond to the voice of life.

Complement with Mary Oliver on how to live with maximum aliveness and Henry Miller on the measure of a life well lived, then revisit Nin on the meaning of maturity and how reading awakens us from the trance of near-living.

#9. Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene

Some people carry one of the strongest genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease yet never develop it, remaining mentally sharp well into their 80s. For years, scientists have wondered what protects these individuals despite their increased genetic vulnerability.

Now, researchers at Columbia University have uncovered a biological mechanism that could help explain this remarkable resistance. Their findings point to a rare genetic mutation that protects the brain's blood vessels from damage, potentially opening a new path toward Alzheimer's treatments.

The discovery builds on research the team published two years ago involving APOE ε4, a gene variant strongly associated with Alzheimer's risk. The scientists found that some people carrying APOE ε4 also possess a rare protective mutation in the fibronectin (FN1) gene.

Fibronectin is a protein that helps support the structure of tissues. However, in people with APOE ε4, excessive amounts can accumulate around blood vessels in the brain, potentially compromising a critical protective system known as the blood-brain barrier. The rare FN1 mutation appears to limit this buildup and the damage associated with it.

That earlier discovery suggested an intriguing possibility: What if scientists could develop a treatment that recreates the protection provided by this rare mutation?

A new study published in Nature Aging brings that possibility closer by identifying how excess fibronectin damages the brain's protective barrier and revealing potential ways to interrupt the process.

"This new study takes us from a genetic clue to a disease mechanism," says Caghan Kizil, the study's corresponding author and professor of neurological sciences in the Department of Neurology and the Taub Institute for Research on Alzheimer's Disease and the Aging Brain at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.

"We knew that changes in fibronectin could protect against Alzheimer's, but we didn't know why excess fibronectin was harmful in the first place. This study gives us that detailed mechanism -- and with it, ideas for how to reproduce that natural protection."

How an Alzheimer's Risk Gene Weakens the Blood-Brain Barrier

The blood-brain barrier serves as a protective boundary between the bloodstream and the brain. Made up of tightly connected cells surrounding the brain's blood vessels, it carefully regulates which substances can enter brain tissue while helping maintain conditions necessary for removing potentially harmful waste.

When this barrier becomes damaged or excessively permeable, substances that would normally be kept out can enter the brain more easily. Such disruptions may contribute to inflammation and other processes involved in neurological diseases, including Alzheimer's.

To investigate the role of fibronectin, the Columbia team combined several advanced research approaches. They examined human brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid surrounding the brain and spinal cord, using genetic and epigenetic analyses to explore changes in DNA and gene activity.

Their investigation also included single-cell sequencing, which reveals the activity of individual cells, and spatial imaging to examine where biological changes occur within tissues. Additional experiments involved human stem-cell models, three-dimensional cultures of blood vessels, and studies in zebrafish and mice.

Despite the variety of methods, the findings consistently pointed to the same mechanism: APOE ε4 promotes the production and accumulation of fibronectin around the brain's blood vessels.

In mice engineered to carry human APOE ε4, researchers measured nearly twice as much fibronectin in the brain as in mice carrying APOE ε3, another common version of the gene. The greater accumulation was accompanied by evidence that the blood-brain barrier had become leaky.

Scientists Discover How Fibronectin Causes Brain Damage

One experiment provided especially important evidence that fibronectin does more than simply accumulate in damaged blood vessels.

The researchers increased human fibronectin specifically in astrocytes, specialized support cells that help maintain the blood-brain barrier and keep the brain functioning properly.

Increasing fibronectin in these cells was enough to disrupt the barrier, allowing it to become more permeable. Conversely, reducing fibronectin improved the barrier's ability to function normally.

These results provided experimental evidence that excess fibronectin can directly contribute to blood-brain barrier damage rather than merely appearing alongside it.

"The animal experiments allowed us to move beyond association," says co-first author Prabesh Bhattarai, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. "When we increased fibronectin in astroglia, the barrier became permeable. When we reduced fibronectin, barrier function improved."

The team then investigated the molecular events responsible for the damage.

They found that excessive fibronectin interferes with communication between cells by activating abnormal signals through integrins, proteins that help cells sense and respond to their surroundings, and an enzyme known as focal adhesion kinase.

These abnormal signals disrupt a network of growth factors called VEGF, HBEGF, and IGF1. Although growth factors are often associated with cell development and repair, these particular signaling molecules also help astrocytes and blood vessel cells coordinate their activities to maintain a healthy blood-brain barrier.

When their communication becomes disrupted, the barrier can lose its integrity, potentially leaving brain tissue more vulnerable to damage.

"Single-cell analysis allowed us to examine this pathway in the different cells that maintain the brain's blood vessels," says co-first author Elanur Yilmaz, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. "We observed the same biological pattern across experimental models and human Alzheimer's tissue, making the mechanism especially compelling."

Evidence From Human Brains Strengthens the Alzheimer's Connection

Importantly, the researchers found signs of similar biological disturbances in human samples, suggesting that the process identified in laboratory experiments may also contribute to Alzheimer's disease in people carrying APOE ε4.

Analyses of brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid showed that elevated fibronectin levels were associated with inflammation in astrocytes.

Genetic and gene-regulation analyses also connected FN1 to blood vessel disease and changes involving VEGFA, a growth factor that plays an important role in maintaining healthy brain blood vessels.

Together, these findings provide multiple lines of evidence linking excess fibronectin to the vascular damage associated with APOE ε4.

"The convergence of these independent human datasets strengthens the case that fibronectin is part of the APOE ε4-related vascular disease process," says Badri Vardarajan, associate professor of neurological science in the Department of Neurology, Gertrude H. Sergievsky Center, and Taub Institute, who collaborated on this discovery of the FN1 mutation.

A Rare Genetic Defense Could Inspire New Alzheimer's Treatments

The potential implications are significant because APOE ε4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Approximately one in five people carries at least one copy of this gene variant.

Although carrying APOE ε4 does not guarantee that someone will develop Alzheimer's, it increases their likelihood of developing the disease. Understanding why certain carriers remain unaffected could reveal new opportunities for prevention and treatment.

The latest findings suggest several possible approaches.

One strategy would be to prevent harmful amounts of fibronectin from accumulating around the brain's blood vessels. Another would involve blocking the abnormal cellular signals triggered by excess fibronectin. A third possibility would be to restore the growth factor signaling that allows astrocytes and blood vessel cells to maintain the blood-brain barrier.

Researchers are already investigating these possibilities through laboratory experiments.

However, translating the discovery into a treatment will require considerable care. Fibronectin performs essential functions throughout the body, including supporting tissue structure and helping damaged tissues heal. Any future therapy would therefore need to target its harmful accumulation or effects without disrupting these beneficial activities.

By identifying the molecular mechanisms involved, scientists now have a more precise framework for designing such treatments. The findings may also help researchers determine when interventions would be most effective and how to measure whether they are successfully protecting the brain.

"By showing how fibronectin contributes to early vascular damage, this study gives us new therapeutic targets and potential ways to measure whether treatments are working," says Richard Mayeux, chair of the Department of Neurology and a collaborator on the project. "Clinically, it connects a major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's to an early disease process that may be possible to modify."

Although these potential therapies remain experimental, the discovery offers a promising new direction in Alzheimer's research. Rather than focusing only on the damage that develops as the disease progresses, scientists may eventually be able to reproduce a natural genetic defense that helps protect vulnerable brains before significant damage occurs.

#10. Lessons on Healing 25 Years after 9/11

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted September 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

Cherie Castellano, CSW is Vice President for Survivor Services at TAPS and was a member of the New York Emergency Services 9/11 Delegation to England and Ireland

Lisa Zucker, MSW is Senior Director of Education at TAPS

Bonnie Carroll is the Founder and President of the Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors (TAPS) and recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Barack Obama in 2015

George S. Everly, Jr., PhD, MA is on the faculty of The Johns Hopkins School of Medicine and served on the NYPD and Columbia University initiatives at Ground Zero post 9/11

The pain of loss surely extends to time immemorial. It is safe to say that the experience of grief is a universal human experience extending far prior to written records. Societal and religious traditions of lamentation are legion. The earliest written records in Western civilization are replete with mentions of grief. Evidence from the Old Kingdom of Egypt (2600 BC) suggests the mourning of a loss was a public experience involving great pomp and circumstance, especially in the case of the wealthy and ruling class. The 5th-century Greek tragedies were large‑scale public rituals for the cathartic expression of loss and trauma. The tragedies made grieving a civic experience, if not an obligation. The Nordic and Germanic traditions continued the theme of grief as a civic responsibility, but in these cases, grief was expressed in public mythological storytelling and ritualized remembrances such as funerals. With the rise of Christianity and other religions, organized public funerals spread in popularity. Grief was one of the centerpieces of the birth of psychology in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Freud’s Mourning and Melancholia (1917) marked the first formal psychological theory of grief, emphasizing the importance of “letting go” of that which was lost.

But more recently, Freud’s notion of letting go has been challenged. Reformulating the connection in a different manner (reattachment) with that which was lost is favored more than the detachment advocated by Freud (Klass, Silverman, & Nickman, 1996). So, we see the process of grieving loss has been characterized by public displays and rituals throughout history. Grieving has been understood as a process that is best shared rather than denied or hidden away. If there was one relatively recent watershed moment that concretized the notion of never forgetting, it may well be the events of September 11th, 2001.

As we approach the 25th anniversary of September 11th, we reflect on the thousands of lives lost that day, the thousands more affected by illness, and the families forever changed by the subsequent wars and military service. For example, the Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors (TAPS) has provided support for over 100,000 bereaved family members since its inception, with 14,858 9/11-related bereaved military family members served since 9/11/2001. In order to fulfill such a mission, the approach of providing psychological support through the exclusive use of licensed mental health clinicians had to be abandoned. Peer support models were adopted instead.

Peers may be defined as two or more people who share some common denominator, typically shared lived experiences. Individuals who have successfully navigated challenging life experiences can, with proper training, effectively serve in a peer support capacity. These peer supporters can harness the bond of shared experience to create credibility, perceived empathy, and hopefulness (SAMHSA, 2015). Peer support is recognized and endorsed by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Administration (SAMHSA). In the wake of September 11, 2001, peers were trained and mobilized to provide support to military families, but in order to harness the power of peer support, those peer supporters were those who had experienced the pain of similar losses, but had healed.

In the TAPS approach, peers were trained in a simple three-step non-linear bereavement model:

Decades of walking alongside bereaved families confirms that peer support can be profoundly therapeutic. These same principles are now being applied in the Ukraine. So, as we find ourselves looking back, we see a three-fold revelation: 1) grief is a process best seen as a journey, 2) the journey is best undertaken with companionship, and 3) the best companions are those who have made a similar journey before. There is healing in being able to sit with someone who does not need grief explained, who understands that there is no timetable for mourning, and who can offer living proof that it is possible to survive devastating loss while continuing to carry love forward.

Twenty-five years after 9/11, and in the case of TAPS, a core promise remains unchanged: no one who is grieving the death of someone who served our nation should ever have to walk that road alone. Survivors caring for survivors has been at the heart of helping from the beginning, and it remains one of the most powerful expressions of healing, hope, and the enduring bonds of love. This promise can be made to all survivors of loss regardless of its origin. So, it seems the ancients got it right. They understood that healing from loss should never be a solitary experience. The support of others, especially peers, teaches the essential lessons of love and hope.

Klass, D., Silverman, P. R., & Nickman, S. (1996). Continuing Bonds: New Understandings of Grief. Washington, DC: Taylor & Francis.

Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. (SAMHSA, 2015). Core competencies for peer workers in behavioral health services. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

#12. Macrophages Settle in the Brain After Sepsis, Driving Memory Loss

A study led by the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences reveals that peripheral immune cells infiltrating the hippocampus during acute sepsis take up permanent residence, driving long-term neuroinflammation and cognitive impairment. These long-lived monocyte-derived macrophages signal through the pleiotrophin (PTN) pathway to provoke resident microglia into abnormally engulfing myelin. Blocking this initial cellular infiltration with the clinical drug natalizumab prevented chronic memory deficits in mice, identifying a critical therapeutic window.

Source: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences

Severe systemic infections such as sepsis can be successfully managed in intensive care units, yet millions of survivors are left with debilitating long-term consequences. Months or years after the primary infection resolves and systemic inflammation subsides, patients frequently suffer from persistent cognitive impairment, characterized by brain fog, compromised memory, and reduced learning capacity.

While clinicians have long recognized post-sepsis cognitive decline, the precise cellular mechanisms that sustain chronic neuroinflammation after the blood-brain barrier heals have remained a biological mystery.

Now, a comprehensive study led by Professor Qi Xu at the Institute of Basic Medical Sciences, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, uncovers the cellular culprit behind this chronic damage.

Publishing in the journal Immunity & Inflammation, the research team combined single-cell transcriptomics, bone marrow chimera lineage tracing, functional cellular assays, and post-mortem human brain tissue analyses to demonstrate that peripheral immune cells entering the brain during acute infection establish a permanent, destructive niche.

Using a clinically relevant mouse model of sepsis (cecal ligation and puncture), the researchers evaluated brain function six months post-infection, long after the initial systemic crisis had resolved and blood-brain barrier permeability had returned to normal. Despite physiological recovery, the surviving mice showed persistent deficits across spatial learning, working memory, and novel object recognition.

Single-cell RNA sequencing of the hippocampus revealed an altered immune microenvironment populated by two distinct myeloid classes: resident microglia exhibiting hyperactive phagocytic states and foreign, CCR2-positive monocyte-derived macrophages.

To trace the precise origin of these cells, the researchers generated green fluorescent protein (GFP) bone marrow chimeric mice. Tracking these bone marrow-derived cells at 3 days, 1 month, and 6 months post-sepsis confirmed that peripheral macrophages breaching the hippocampus during the acute surge did not clear away. Instead, they down-regulated inflammatory markers like MHCII and Ly6C, adapted to the neural tissue, and embedded themselves as a permanent resident population.

Dual-color bone marrow transplantation confirmed this dynamic: the brain almost exclusively retained green-labeled cells that entered during the acute phase, showing zero recruitment of red-labeled cells from later stages. The chronic population was established entirely during the initial infection window.

Once embedded, how do these long-lived peripheral cells disrupt cognition?

Ligand-receptor communication modeling identified intense cross-talk between the persistent CCR2-positive macrophages and neighboring microglia. At the center of this signaling was pleiotrophin (PTN), a neurotrophic cytokine heavily enriched in the invading macrophages, and its receptor, the integrin alphabeta2 (CD11b/Itgam), which was strongly upregulated on resident microglia.

Under inflammatory stimulation, macrophage-derived PTN bound to microglial CD11b, driving downstream expression of stress and activation genes, including Jun, Atf3, and Ccl3. This abnormal signaling cascade provoked microglia to excessively engulf and degrade nearby myelin sheaths—the protective insulation coating neural axons.

High-resolution tissue imaging verified the consequence: persistent macrophages were situated directly alongside activated Iba1-positive myeloid cells showing significantly increased internalization of myelin basic protein (MBP).

Because these long-lived macrophages enter during the acute crisis, the researchers investigated whether blocking their initial entry could protect the brain long term.

The team administered natalizumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting alpha4 integrin-mediated extravasation, on days 0, 3, and 6 following sepsis induction. Mice were then monitored for six months without further treatment.

The early, short-course therapy delivered lasting neuroprotection:

To confirm whether these findings translate to human pathology, the team evaluated hippocampal tissue from 24 human autopsy cases.

Brain tissue from patients with a documented history of severe systemic infection exhibited a significantly higher density of CD74-positive, TMEM119-negative cells compared to uninfected controls. These cells were clustered tightly around CD31-labeled cerebral blood vessels, exhibiting the identical phenotypic and spatial characteristics of infiltrating peripheral macrophages observed in the mouse models.

“This study links acute infection to long-term brain functional changes through a population of persistent peripheral immune cells, providing a new cellular basis for understanding post-infection cognitive impairment,” the authors concluded.

By defining the acute temporal window when peripheral leukocytes establish residency, the findings demonstrate that protecting the brain during severe infection may require early, targeted anti-migratory interventions to prevent lifelong cognitive decline.

Acute sepsis seeds long-lived brain-resident macrophages that drive microglia-dependent chronic neuroinflammation through PTN signaling

Early-life severe infection is increasingly recognized as a cause of persistent cognitive impairment; however, the mechanisms by which peripheral immune cells drive and sustain chronic neuroinflammation remain poorly understood. Although infiltrating peripheral myeloid cells are generally considered transient populations that are rapidly cleared upon disease resolution, their long-term fate and contribution to chronic neurological sequelae remain undefined.

Here, using a murine model of polymicrobial sepsis, we demonstrate that central nervous system (CNS)-infiltrating macrophages can establish long-term residence and persistently remodel the hippocampal immune microenvironment.

Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed a distinct MHCIIlow/Ly6C+ macrophage subpopulation that infiltrates the brain following sepsis and persists for at least six months. Dual-color bone marrow chimera experiments demonstrated that this infiltration is strictly restricted to the acute inflammatory phase, thereby seeding a long-lived resident population.

Mechanistically, these macrophages drive microglial phagocytic activation and subsequent myelin damage via the pleiotrophin (PTN) signaling pathway. Importantly, blocking CNS macrophage infiltration during the acute phase of sepsis with a monoclonal antibody targeting alpha 4 beta 1 (α4β1) integrin substantially prevented chronic neuroinflammation and late-stage cognitive impairment.

Consistent with these murine findings, a phenotypically similar population of CD74+/TMEM119− infiltrating macrophages was identified in postmortem hippocampal tissues from individuals with a history of severe systemic infection. Collectively, this study redefines the fate of brain-infiltrating macrophages following systemic infection, revealing them not as transient effectors, but rather as a long-lived cellular substrate that perpetuates chronic neuroinflammation.

These findings provide a novel mechanistic framework for postinfectious cognitive decline and highlight acute-phase α4β1 integrin blockade as a viable therapeutic strategy for preventing long-term neurological sequelae.

#13. Attention Is Our Original and Shared Vocation

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

A reflection on the late poet Mary Oliver, and what her work modeled for us and asks of us now.

We’ve lost a handful of visionary writers in recent months and years: Mary Oliver, Wendell Berry, and Annie Dillard come to mind for me, among others. These are people who not only inspired me as a writer in my formative years but who also shaped my moral imagination. In each case, learning about their deaths was like watching a giant redwood crack and list and crash into the forest below. Something regal and ancient disappeared from the skyline.

These writers were unafraid to be close to things I also longed to be close to: the natural world, the rich loam of a quiet inner life, Mystery itself.

I understand why it’s a little silly to feel like I knew them, or to experience their loss as personal somehow, but their writing offered an intimacy that felt like kinship. They were unafraid to be close to things I also longed to be close to: the natural world, the rich loam of a quiet inner life, Mystery itself.

When I read them, huddled under pooled lamplight in my dorm room bed, I was both witnessing and learning about what arises when we give our whole selves over to simply noticing and loving the world. I was responding to the writing, yes. But ultimately my response was much more visceral. It happened long before I even clocked the craft—the shimmering language, the rhythm, a wise insight, or a brilliant turn of phrase.

#14. How to Grow Old without Letting Life Become a Parody of Itself

For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. We live in a culture that dreads the entropic inevitability of growing older, treats it like a disease to be cured with potions and regimens, anesthetizes it with botox and silence, somehow forgetting that to grow old at all is a tremendous privilege — one withheld from the vast majority of humans populating the history of our young species (to say nothing of the infinite potential humans who never chanced into existing).

“For old people,” Ursula K. Le Guin wrote in her sublime meditation on aging and what beauty really means, “beauty doesn’t come free with the hormones, the way it does for the young… It has to do with who the person is.” Another way to say this, to feel it, is that to become a person worthy of old age is the triumph of life. Henry Miller, in his reflection upon turning eighty, located the triumph in remaining able to “fall in love again and again… forgive as well as forget… keep from growing sour, surly, bitter and cynical.” Grace Paley instructed in what remains the finest advice on the art of growing older: “The main thing is this — when you get up in the morning you must take your heart in your two hands. You must do this every morning.”

Life is largely a matter of how we hold ourselves — our hearts, our fears, our forgivenesses — along the procession of the years. Hardly anyone has furnished a more elegant and robust banister for the holding than Simone de Beauvoir (January 9, 1908–April 14, 1986) in her 1970 book La vieillesse, published in England as Old Age and in America as the characteristically cottoned The Coming of Age (public library).

Two years before she came to consider how chance and choice converge to make us who we are, De Beauvoir observes that contemporary Western culture winces at old age as a “semi-death.” With an eye to the biological privilege of getting to grow old, she writes:

Old age is not a necessary end to human life.

A particular value has sometimes been given to old age for social or political reasons. For some individuals — women in ancient China, for instance — it has been a refuge against the harshness of life in adult years. Others, from a pessimistic general outlook on life, settle comfortably into it… The vast majority of mankind look upon the coming of old age with sorrow and rebellion. It fills them with more aversion than death itself.

And indeed, it is old age, rather than death, that is to be contrasted with life. Old age is life’s parody, whereas death transforms life into a destiny: in a way it preserves it by giving it the absolute dimension.

Only one thing can keep the final chapter of life from becoming a parody of itself. Growing old, she cautions, is not a project — not something one can endeavor to do industriously, to ace. It is a fact — something to be met on its own terms, something for which we spend our whole lives practicing as we learn to control for surrender.

Growing, ripening, aging, dying — the passing of time is predestined, inevitable.

There is only one solution if old age is not to be an absurd parody of our former life, and that is to go on pursuing ends that give our existence a meaning — devotion to individuals, to groups or to causes, social, political, intellectual or creative work… In old age we should wish still to have passions strong enough to prevent us turning in on ourselves. One’s life has value so long as one attributes value to the life of others, by means of love, friendship, indignation, compassion.

Complement with Bertrand Russell on how to grow old and Thoreau on the greatest gift of the winter years, then revisit Simone de Beauvoir on the ultimate frontier of hope and the artist’s task to liberate the present from the past.
