#15. What a Fictional Robot Can Teach Us About Care

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

This essay contains mild spoilers for the novel Klara and the Sun.

The baby, my baby, was to be named Josie. Josie Joy.

But when she was born, she was decidedly not a Josie. The name was too soft, too ethereal for such a sentient, wide-awake, bird-like baby. I knew that I had to find a new name. Who are you? I whispered into the swirls of her astoundingly warm, circulated, and singularly perfect ear. I couldn’t wait to get to know her.

In another story, a girl named Josie is dying. In Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel Klara and the Sun, Josie has an unknown illness and a prognosis that haunts the pages. Her life exists in the shadow of her sister, Sal, who has already died of the same unarticulated illness, likely caused by an elective genetic alteration procedure known as “lifting.”

In Josie’s world, being lifted is the new social currency; those who are lifted are expected to have greater access to both intellectual and economic success. The procedure does not, however, come without risk. When we meet Josie’s mother, she is tasked with the impossible: coping with the impending death of her only remaining child. A death likely resulting from a choice she made as a parent. The ultimate consequence.

Klara is a robot purchased by Josie’s mom to be her companion, in part (it is implied) to assuage the guilt she feels. I first read Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun shortly after its debut. Despite being disturbed by some aspects of the dystopian world depicted within, my memory of the novel was poignant. I recalled Klara with particular affection.

Now, the distance between Ishiguro’s dystopian world and our current reality is rapidly collapsing. With the much anticipated film adaptation set to be released this Friday, October 23, and the sudden ubiquity of artificial intelligence in our day to day lives, Klara and the Sun is now repositioned as a mirror. If we look closely enough, we might discern what remains uniquely human during this moment of profound technological and social change.

We are introduced to Klara, the story’s narrator, when Josie’s mom takes her to find an artificial friend, or AF for short. In the novel, AFs confer social standing, but also offer practical assistance—tutoring, companionship, monitoring an ailing child—not unlike the benefits purported by artificial intelligence companies today.

Klara has been patiently waiting, alongside several other AFs, to be chosen. Josie’s mother is the final decider. In a foreboding scene, Josie’s mother commands Klara to reenact Josie’s gait—a test, of sorts—before agreeing to purchase her. It’s the precision of Klara’s mimicry that convinces “the Mother” (as she’s called in the novel) that Klara is the right model for Josie.

All of this, we learn through Klara. Ishiguro’s choice to position the reader within Klara’s perspective allows us to bypass the quagmire question of whether or not Klara is conscious and instead project our own consciousness onto her. In doing so, we view the human world through her sometimes malfunctioning robot eyes, as she nonjudgmentally conveys the complexities of the very flawed and sometimes desperate human behaviors she seeks to understand. In one particularly moving scene, Klara witnesses the vulnerability of caring for another human being:

I saw before me, on the near edge of the bed, a large shifting shape, made additionally complex by the patches of blackness and moonlight moving over its surface. I realized the shape was the Mother and Josie embracing… As well as their limbs, their hair had become mingled, and then their shape began gently to rock, in a way not unlike when their goodbyes became extended.

“Don’t want to die, Mom. I don’t want that.”

“It’s okay. Okay.” The Mother’s voice was soft, at just the same level mine had been.

Prior to this moment, Klara—steadfast and ever-available—had offered her presence to comfort Josie. Yet, despite their far more complicated and at times strained relationship, it is the Mother that Josie calls for.

When I first became a parent, I confided to a friend that when my not-Josie was born, I felt like a new sun had burst into my solar system, and I was now orbiting around her. I couldn’t quite articulate the “before,” in my metaphor. I didn’t feel like I was previously my own sun, nor did I feel like I was a planet untethered to others. But there was something distinctly different when she arrived, a whole new consciousness, a space and force and awareness created within me. Her pull was intoxicating, undeniable, sometimes terrifying, and my awareness and attention seemed to expand overnight to now include not only my own experiences, but also to track, perceive, anticipate, and accommodate her own.

If Klara had turned to psychological theory and research about the complexity of parent-child bonds, she would have found a great deal of it. Consider Winnicott’s “Good Enough Mother” or research indicating that parents and infants are rarely, if ever, perfectly attuned, and the growing body of evidence suggesting that the navigation of the ruptures and repairs themselves reinforce attachment. It has become increasingly clear through evolving applications of experiments such as Edward Tronick’s now famous “still-face” experiment that the imperfect dance between caregiver and child lays the groundwork for resilience and emotional regulation.

In The Philosophical Baby, developmental psychologist and philosopher Alison Gopnik says, “It’s not so much that we care for children because we love them, as that we love them because we care for them.”

Beyond Gopnik’s own research, there is an abundance of data to back this up. Studies I have long been familiar with, such as those demonstrating that in same-sex, non-carrying male couples, fathers who act as primary parents show changes in similar brain regions to women who carried their pregnancies and go on to parent their children. Yet, there was something profound about the simplicity of Gopnik’s statement, about love being something we cultivate within ourselves and, more precisely, about care being the means through which we build love, not merely a necessary byproduct.

In a separate interview, Gopnik jokes that spending time with a three-year-old gives you a small taste of sainthood. Not in the sense that the demands are so extreme that you inherently become a saint (though there is a real argument to be made here for any parent who weathers the storm of a parking lot tantrum), but in the actual felt-sense of the divine, the experience of feeling so acutely and utterly in love with this being, so in awe of their singularity, their specialness, their openness to experience, their brilliance.

Gopnik continues on, teasing, about our tendency to claim the uniqueness of our three-year-old, in her case her grandchild, but gently affirms the truth beneath: that there is something numinous, universal, pure within all three-year-olds, a near-magical vitality that we sometimes make contact with when we intimately care for one. Something primal, or perhaps primary, is awoken when we re-experience the world through the eyes of a three-year-old.

My not-Josie is now three. In many ways she is more unknowable, separate, than she was when she was a newborn, so physically attached and dependent on me. Now, she has her own relationships—with teachers, classmates, family members—that are entirely her own. And yet, she occupies and orients so much of me, continually changing my experience of the world, my access to play, to awe, to unadulterated, intoxicating adoration.

This past summer, I was sitting by a lake, relaxed but hawk-eyed as I watched my not-Josie from the shore. I felt a familiar presence by my side, the barely-perceptible shadow in my peripheral vision of a small body sitting down, and soon thereafter, the unselfconscious weight of a small hand on my leg. I looked down to see a head covered in feathery blonde hair, not the dark, curly brown of my own child.

The wispy tufts belonged to another small child who had clearly mistaken me for her mother. In that brief moment before she looked up, before we both acknowledged our separateness, I felt overcome with the awareness—as though received through the touch of her hand on my leg—that her mother loved her in the way that I love my child, and that, despite how unbelievably special my not-Josie is, my love for her is not. It is precious, but also universal.

Intellectually, of course, this is not a profound realization. Emotionally touching into it is, on the other hand, equally as brutal as it is beautiful. Next to this small child, healthy and safe, I felt her preciousness, but also that of all the children flooding my news feed every day who are not healthy and safe, and whose parents must live with this love and that devastation.

On the back cover, Klara and the Sun is described as a story about love, which it undeniably is. But I think it’s perhaps more fundamentally about care.

Care is arguably more tangible than love, but also more complex, friction-prone, messy. It’s the gaps, the mistakes, the harms, the repairs, the precarity, the forgiving, that make care so deeply painful and so deeply nourishing. Nourishing enough to sustain the vulnerability of love.

It is care that drives Josie’s mother to have her “lifted” in an age-old attempt of desperation to give her child what she perceives as the best chance at a full life in a rapidly reorganizing world. It is care that sends the Mother down the path of trying to find a way to have Klara “continue” Josie’s life, even though she has already tried and failed to recreate her first child’s consciousness in an artificial intelligence through the work of an artist and scientist named Capaldi.

It is care that allows the Mother—despite her cold exterior—to fearlessly comfort her child as she confronts the possibility of her own death, enveloping her, rocking her, soothing her through the unimaginable. It is the Mother’s human care, not her cowardice, that makes her love true.

There is so much in Klara and the Sun that is undeniably relevant in this particular social, cultural, and technological moment, so many ways in which Ishiguro’s Josie and my not-Josie’s world are suddenly uncomfortably proximate, but it is what Klara herself affirms about humanity that is most resonant.

At the end of the novel, Klara reflects on what she’s learned. She did not have to become a Josie 2.0, for Josie survived. Klara is glad for this, of course, believing that it was her bargain with the Sun (which she sees as a kind of god) that saved Josie. Sitting discarded in a junk yard, Klara is increasingly convinced that the desperate plan to turn Josie into a digital consciousness wouldn’t have worked:

Mr. Capaldi believed there was nothing special inside Josie that couldn’t be continued. He told the Mother he’d searched and searched and found nothing like that. But I believe now he was searching in the wrong place. There was something very special, but it wasn’t inside Josie. It was inside those who loved her. That’s why I think now Mr. Capaldi was wrong and I wouldn’t have succeeded.

It is what happens within us and between us when we care for another being that differentiates us as humans. In other words, it’s not so much what’s there but what’s not there—the space between the person in front of us and how we perceive, imperfectly care for, and ultimately love them—that makes us human.

Through Klara’s eyes, I was able to see more clearly what connects the Mother and her Josie to me and my not-Josie. It is the very fact that we can so wholeheartedly love another being, without being them, having them, solving them, knowing every bit of them. It is the fact that still, we carry them in our hearts, and somehow we are not heavier for it.

#16. "Mind-blowing" Alzheimer’s breakthrough: Two hours of sleep restored without clearing brain plaques

Scientists have discovered an unexpected reason why Alzheimer's disease disrupts sleep, and their findings suggest that the problem may be reversible. In experiments involving mice with Alzheimer's-like brain changes, researchers restored more than two hours of sleep per day without removing the amyloid plaques associated with the disease.

The surprising discovery points to an overlooked culprit: the brain's own immune cells. Rather than simply protecting the brain from damage, these cells can trigger inflammation that interferes with healthy sleep.

Researchers at the University of Kentucky found that temporarily eliminating most of these immune cells allowed the mice to sleep longer and spend more time in the deep, restorative stages of sleep. The results suggest a potential new approach to treating one of the most disruptive symptoms of Alzheimer's disease.

The findings, published in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, were reported by a team led by Shannon L. Macauley, Ph.D., an associate professor of physiology at the University of Kentucky College of Medicine, and first author Nicholas J. Constantino, Ph.D., a recent doctoral graduate.

Macauley described the discovery as "paradigm-shifting" because it challenges the prevailing understanding of why people with Alzheimer's often experience severe sleep problems.

How the Brain's Immune System Can Disrupt Sleep

To understand what the researchers uncovered, imagine a small fire breaking out in a kitchen. Instead of containing the flames, the building's sprinkler system activates everywhere, flooding the entire house and causing widespread damage.

Something similar may happen in the brain during Alzheimer's disease.

Amyloid plaques are deposits of sticky protein fragments that accumulate between nerve cells. They are one of the characteristic features of Alzheimer's and have long been investigated for their role in the disease.

The brain also contains specialized immune cells known as microglia. These cells normally protect the nervous system by removing debris, responding to injuries, and helping maintain a healthy environment for neurons.

However, when microglia detect amyloid plaques, their defensive response can become excessive. Instead of simply addressing the threat, they release inflammatory signals that may interfere with normal brain activity.

Scientists have traditionally linked sleep problems in Alzheimer's primarily to damaged neurons or the accumulation of amyloid plaques. The new findings suggest that the immune system's reaction to those plaques plays a major role.

"Basically, we showed that it is not the plaques themselves, or solely dysfunctional neurons, that cause sleep loss but actually microglia," said Macauley. "Microglia are immune cells that, when they respond to plaques, kick off this elaborate cascade of inflammation, as if the microglia are partying all night, and keeping the brain awake."

In other words, the brain's response to Alzheimer's pathology may create additional problems beyond those caused by the plaques themselves. The researchers compared this widespread reaction to a "whole house response," in which a defense mechanism ends up causing more disruption than expected.

Tracking Alzheimer's Sleep Changes Inside the Brain

To investigate the connection between microglia and sleep, the scientists studied two groups of mice. One group was genetically predisposed to develop amyloid plaques, while the other consisted of normal "wild-type" mice that experienced typical aging.

The researchers examined the animals at two ages: six months, when plaques first appeared in the genetically modified mice, and 18 months, when the disease model showed more advanced pathology.

Comparing these groups helped the scientists distinguish changes associated with Alzheimer's pathology from those that naturally occur as the brain ages.

The team used several advanced technologies to measure sleep and examine what was happening inside the brain.

Each mouse was fitted with a small device that recorded electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG).

EEG measures the brain's electrical activity, including the patterns and rhythms produced when networks of neurons communicate. These electrical signals change depending on whether the brain is awake, dreaming or experiencing deep sleep.

EMG measures electrical activity in muscles. Combining the two techniques allowed researchers to identify different sleep stages and determine how long the animals remained in each one.

The scientists also wanted to visualize the relationship between amyloid plaques and immune cells throughout the brain.

For this, they used light-sheet microscopy, an imaging technique that makes biological tissue transparent and illuminates it with a thin layer of laser light. The resulting images can be assembled into detailed three-dimensional maps, allowing scientists to examine structures that would otherwise be difficult to see.

This approach revealed the distribution of plaques and microglia across the brain, helping researchers understand where immune cells were responding to Alzheimer's pathology.

Scientists Temporarily Remove 87% of Brain Immune Cells

To determine whether microglia were actually responsible for disrupted sleep, the team conducted an experiment designed to temporarily eliminate most of these cells.

The researchers administered a drug called Pexidartinib (PLX3397), which was originally developed for cancer research. It blocks a cellular signal that microglia depend on for survival.

After the mice received the medication in their food for 14 days, approximately 87% of their microglia had been depleted.

This allowed the scientists to test whether sleep would improve when the cells driving the inflammatory response were largely absent.

The researchers also performed a detailed analysis of the animals' brain activity using a mathematical method called Fitting Oscillations and One Over Frequency (FOOOF).

This technique separates electrical signals into periodic activity (the rhythmic waves we usually think of as brain waves) and aperiodic activity (the background electrical noise).

By examining these different components, the team could identify changes in how the brain was functioning, including whether it remained unusually active during periods when it should have been resting.

The process is somewhat like monitoring a car engine to determine whether it continues running at high speed even when the vehicle is supposed to be idle.

A Surprising Discovery About Alzheimer's Brain Plaques

Macauley called the results "mind-blowing and unexpected."

One of the most surprising findings was that sleep problems did not continue worsening as amyloid plaques accumulated.

The researchers initially expected that increasing plaque buildup would lead to progressively more severe sleep disturbances. Instead, the mice developed substantial sleep problems relatively early, and those problems remained largely unchanged even as plaque levels increased dramatically.

"I expected that as plaque burden became more severe, sleep disruption would also worsen," said Constantino. "The disruptions in sleep and cortical EEG activity that occur at 6 months, when plaques first emerge, did not worsen by 18 months, despite more than double the amount of plaque burden."

The team described this pattern as a ceiling effect. Essentially, sleep disruption appeared to reach a certain level early in the disease process rather than increasing in direct proportion to the amount of amyloid in the brain.

This suggests that the initial inflammatory response triggered by plaques may be particularly important. Once microglia become activated and disrupt sleep, additional plaque accumulation may not necessarily produce an equivalent increase in sleep loss.

The discovery offers an important clue as to why sleep disturbances can emerge relatively early in Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's Disrupts a Different Type of Sleep Than Normal Aging

The study also revealed a notable difference between sleep changes caused by normal aging and those associated with Alzheimer's pathology.

Sleep is not a single, uniform state. Throughout the night, the brain moves through several stages that perform different functions.

Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is strongly associated with vivid dreaming and plays an important role in processing memories. The researchers found that normal aging primarily reduced this type of sleep.

Alzheimer's pathology, however, had a different effect. It selectively disrupted non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, which includes the deepest and most physically restorative stages of sleep.

During NREM sleep, the brain performs essential maintenance functions that support learning, memory, and recovery. Deep sleep is also associated with processes that help clear metabolic waste products from the brain.

"That restorative sleep is super important for physical repair, learning and memory and washing out the toxins of the day," Macauley said.

Losing this important stage of sleep could have consequences beyond daytime fatigue.

Because healthy sleep helps maintain the brain's internal environment, disruptions may interfere with processes that normally remove potentially harmful waste. Researchers suspect this could contribute to a self-reinforcing cycle in which Alzheimer's pathology disturbs sleep, and inadequate sleep may further aggravate the disease.

Breaking that cycle could therefore become an important treatment strategy.

More Than Two Hours of Sleep Restored Without Removing Plaques

The most striking result emerged after the researchers temporarily removed most of the microglia from the brains of mice with Alzheimer's-like pathology.

The animals gained more than two hours of sleep per day.

They also experienced longer periods of restorative NREM sleep, giving them more opportunities to transition naturally into REM sleep, which is important for memory formation.

Even more surprisingly, these improvements occurred without any reduction in amyloid plaque levels.

The plaques were still present, but the mice were sleeping substantially better.

This finding provides evidence that the inflammatory response driven by microglia contributes directly to sleep disruption and that suppressing this response can reverse at least some of the associated sleep problems.

It also suggests that researchers may not need to eliminate amyloid plaques to improve sleep in Alzheimer's disease.

Although these findings are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice, and the same benefits have not yet been demonstrated in people. Temporarily removing most of the brain's immune cells is also not an established or practical treatment for Alzheimer's patients.

The researchers are now interested in whether the beneficial effects can be reproduced by adjusting microglial activity rather than eliminating the cells themselves.

If such an approach eventually proves successful in humans, it could provide a way to improve sleep and potentially reduce some of the additional stress that poor sleep places on the brain.

The work was conducted in Macauley's laboratory in the Department of Physiology at the University of Kentucky's Sanders-Brown Center on Aging.

Macauley credits the achievement to a "beautiful partnership" with students and researchers who were willing to challenge established ideas about Alzheimer's disease.

"I love people who take initiative, find their passion, are curious, and keep pushing to find an answer," Macauley said.

She encourages members of her laboratory to be "calculated risk-takers," emphasizing that meaningful discoveries often require scientists to investigate possibilities that may initially seem unlikely.

A quote from hockey legend Wayne Gretzky hangs in her office: "You miss 100% of the shots you don't take."

Constantino, who recently completed his doctorate at the university, said the laboratory's collaborative environment encouraged him to pursue questions that crossed traditional scientific disciplines.

"Dr. Macauley has also taught me to embrace uncertainty and failure as part of the scientific process," Constantino said. "Some of the most interesting studies I have been a part of emerged because our original hypothesis was wrong."

Macauley reinforces this mindset with a simple instruction to her team: "Follow the data, ask better questions, and figure out what is actually happening."

That approach helped the researchers move beyond the traditional emphasis on neurons and amyloid plaques to examine the broader role of the brain's immune system.

Could Existing Medications Help Restore Sleep in Alzheimer's?

The research team is now exploring ways to translate these findings into treatments and diagnostic tools that could eventually benefit people with Alzheimer's disease.

One promising direction involves calming overactive microglia without removing them.

Because microglia perform essential protective functions, eliminating them is not an ideal long-term strategy. Instead, the researchers hope to modify how these immune cells respond to amyloid plaques and regulate inflammation.

The laboratory is investigating existing medications, including the diabetes drug Metformin and the anti-seizure medication Stiripentol.

These drugs are being studied for their potential to alter how microglia produce and use energy, a process known as cellular metabolism. Changing that energy use could potentially reduce excessive immune activation and its harmful effects on sleep.

The hope is to prevent the brain's inflammatory response from becoming so intense that it disrupts normal sleep activity.

Researchers are particularly interested in whether intervention during the earlier stages of Alzheimer's could improve sleep and quality of life before substantial memory loss develops.

"If we can target that process, it might help with quality of life, attention, cognition and confusion," Macauley said.

The proposed drug strategies remain experimental for this purpose, and additional research will be necessary to determine whether they can safely produce similar benefits in humans.

A Simpler Way to Detect Early Alzheimer's Changes

Beyond identifying a potential treatment target, the study uncovered electrical activity patterns that may help distinguish Alzheimer's pathology from normal brain aging.

The researchers believe these patterns could eventually make EEG a useful tool for detecting and monitoring changes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Unlike more expensive imaging procedures, EEG records electrical signals through electrodes placed on the scalp. It is relatively affordable, does not require surgery, and can be repeated to follow changes over time.

The team envisions EEG becoming a "readily accessible, affordable and longitudinal biomarker of Alzheimer's disease."

A biomarker is a measurable biological sign that provides information about a person's health or a particular disease. A longitudinal biomarker can be tracked repeatedly to monitor how a condition develops or changes.

"Portable EEG systems could allow us to monitor people in their home environments and potentially screen for changes associated with an Alzheimer's disease, without the initial need for expensive or invasive tests," Macauley said.

If future human studies confirm the usefulness of these electrical signatures, portable EEG devices might eventually help doctors identify people who need additional testing.

This could be particularly valuable in rural communities across Kentucky, where patients sometimes must travel long distances to reach specialized medical centers.

Instead of requiring every potentially at-risk patient to undergo advanced testing immediately, local clinics might use simpler monitoring tools to identify individuals who would benefit from further evaluation.

Although this application still requires validation, it offers a possible path toward more accessible Alzheimer's screening and monitoring.

Ultimately, the study suggests that treating Alzheimer's may require looking beyond the plaques themselves and examining how the brain responds to them.

By identifying the immune cells responsible for much of the sleep disruption in their mouse models, the University of Kentucky researchers have uncovered a potential way to restore an essential brain function without first removing the underlying amyloid deposits.

The next challenge is determining whether calming these cells can deliver similar benefits in people, potentially improving sleep, cognition and quality of life long before the most severe symptoms of Alzheimer's develop.

#17. Focused Ultrasound Calms Delusions in Schizophrenia

A pilot clinical trial led by NYU Langone Health psychiatrists and biomedical engineers reveals that non-invasive transcranial ultrasound stimulation directed at the globus pallidus interna safely reduces delusions in individuals with schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder. A single 10-minute session produced a clear, statistically meaningful decrease in delusion severity that persisted for up to one week compared to sham treatment, without significant adverse effects.

Schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder are chronic, complex neuropsychiatric conditions that severely impact daily functioning, often causing auditory and visual hallucinations alongside fixed, false beliefs known as delusions. While antipsychotic medications serve as the standard frontline treatment, an estimated 30% of patients experience persistent, treatment-resistant symptoms, and existing pharmacological options frequently carry heavy metabolic and neurological burdens.

Now, a pioneering cross-disciplinary study by psychiatrists and engineers at NYU Langone Health shows that acoustic waves can safely reach deep into the brain to alleviate these symptoms non-invasively.

Publishing October 20 in the journal npj Acoustics, the research team evaluated transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) in 10 patients with chronic schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder who experienced persistent psychotic symptoms despite ongoing drug therapy. The trial provides the first clinical evidence that focused acoustic neuromodulation can quiet psychotic delusions by precisely “tuning” subcortical circuits.

Transcranial ultrasound stimulation uses gentle, low-intensity focused sound waves to excite or suppress neural firing in targeted subcortical structures. While transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and direct current stimulation (tDCS) are established clinical tools, their electrical and magnetic fields disperse rapidly, making it difficult to modulate structures buried deep beneath the cerebral cortex without affecting overlying tissue.

“Unlike other emerging techniques that modulate brain circuits, transcranial ultrasound stimulation offers a unique opportunity to precisely target very small regions that affect thinking and behavior,” said co-senior author Shy Shoham, PhD, professor of neuroscience and ophthalmology at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and director of the Tech4Health Institute at NYU Langone.

The investigators targeted the globus pallidus interna (GPi), a key subcortical structure within the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop that coordinates movement, cognition, and emotional processing. Prior work by lead author Wei Qi, MD, demonstrated that pathological hyperactivity and network dysregulation within this specific basal ganglia node are closely tied to delusion severity and medication non-responsiveness.

In the double-blind, sham-controlled crossover trial, each participant received two experimental sessions spaced one week apart in randomized order: one active ultrasound treatment and one sham control. During the sham visit, the transducer device was positioned identically on the scalp and powered on, but acoustic transmission was physically blocked.

Guided by high-resolution structural MRI scans, the clinical team delivered ultrasound waves directly to the globus pallidus interna for 10 minutes using 30-second on/off pulsing cycles.

The results showed a clear divergent clinical response:

Adverse events, including transient headaches, mild fatigue, and brief fluctuations in psychotic distress, were minor, self-limiting, and showed no significant difference between the active and sham conditions.

“Our results offer early evidence that a single session of transcranial ultrasound stimulation can safely ‘tune’ a brain circuit linked to psychosis and lead to a noticeable drop in delusions,” said lead author Wei Qi, MD, clinical assistant professor in the Department of Psychiatry at NYU Grossman School of Medicine.

The study opens new possibilities for treating psychiatric illnesses that have historically resisted therapeutic innovation.

“These promising early findings suggest that further work is needed to establish whether targeted ultrasound could one day supplement or even replace standard medicines for schizophrenia,” said senior author Donald C. Goff, MD, the Marvin Stern Professor of Psychiatry, vice chair of research in the Department of Psychiatry at NYU Grossman School of Medicine, and director of NYU Langone’s Schizophrenia Research Group. “This work also demonstrates that focused ultrasound can be used to examine brain circuits relevant to psychiatric illness.”

Building on these early results, the NYU Langone psychiatry and biomedical engineering teams are designing expanded clinical trials to assess whether multi-session ultrasound regimens produce deeper or more durable symptom remission. Future trials will also incorporate personalized acoustic modeling to calibrate sound-wave intensity to individual skull thickness and brain anatomy, optimizing target engagement in the deep brain.

Funding: Funding for the pilot study was provided by the Doris Duke Foundation Fund to Retain Clinical Scientists, the Brain & Behavior Research Foundation, and the Max G. Schlapp Mental Hygiene Fund.

Along with Drs. Qi, Goff, and Shoham, NYU Langone researchers involved in the study were Alon Gilad, ME; Michele Santacatterina, PhD; Spencer Brinker, PhD; Gillian Capichioni; and Fumika Ando.

Transcranial ultrasound stimulation of the right globus pallidus interna in schizophrenia: A randomized, sham- controlled pilot study

Functional abnormalities of the globus pallidus interna (GPi) are linked to psychosis severity and treatment response in schizophrenia. Transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) is a noninvasive method for precisely targeting deep brain structures.

The effects of GPi-targeted TUS on psychosis had not been examined. We conducted a random-order, sham-controlled, crossover pilot study assessing safety, tolerability, and preliminary efficacy of right GPi TUS for psychotic symptoms.

Ten outpatients (mean age 37.5; 50% female) with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder and persistent psychosis received one TUS and one sham session, one week apart. TUS was MRI-guided, targeting right GPi with a 350 kHz transducer (100 Hz pulse repetition frequency, 5% duty cycle, in situ Ispta 400 mW/cm²). Outcomes—delusion experience sampling assessment (DESA) and auditory hallucinations rating scale (AHRS)—were measured before, during, and immediately, 1 h, 1, and 7 days after stimulation.

DESA scores decreased significantly more after TUS than sham (p = 0.002, Cohen’s d = 0.68); AHRS and cognition changes were not significant. Mild transient adverse effects occurred in both conditions; none were serious. GPi-targeted TUS was safe, well-tolerated, and associated with a preliminary reduction in delusional severity, warranting further study in larger, randomized trials.

ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05643196, registered 21 November 2022.

#18. The Mysterious Mushroom That Makes You Gulliver's Companion

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted September 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

For most people, the world around them appears certain and obvious beyond any doubt. We have sensory receptors that perceive information from the external world. However, the brain's perception of reality is not as simple as we think. The objects and events we face daily, even though they appear very real to us, might not be real at all. This time, not only philosophers but also neuroscientists are in consensus on this complexity. Modern neuroscience suggests that the brain uses sensory signals to make predictions about external information that favor our survival rather than fitting with reality. We can give many examples of errors in visual, auditory, and other sensory systems.

Lisa Feldman Barrett provides a compelling example at the opening of her book, Seven and a Half Lessons About the Brain. She says that a soldier in the civil wars of southern Africa, while doing drills in the forest, suddenly spots what appears to be a line of camouflaged fighters armed with AK-47s. His heart pounding, he raises his rifle and flips off the safety, until a comrade grabs his arm and says, "Don't shoot, it's just a boy." He looks again and sees a ten-year-old herding cows with a stick, not a rifle. The writer tells this story to show how predictive processing works: The soldier's brain had built a strong prior perception from past combat experience and imposed it on ambiguous sensory input, nearly overriding what was actually there. It has been suggested that the brain uses sensory input just to correct these predictions [1].

Perhaps many people, like me, have become familiar with a mysterious Chinese mushroom, Lanmaoa asiatica, recently studied by researchers at the University of Utah. Researchers investigated two kinds of mushrooms by sequencing DNA samples from Yunnan, China, and the Philippines. They found that both mushrooms are the same species, despite having different names in the two regions. They also confirmed that these mushrooms do not contain any known hallucinogenic compounds, such as ibotenic acid or psilocybin. However, people in southwestern China and the Philippines knew hundreds of years ago that consuming this mushroom raw or semi-cooked causes them to see tiny people jumping, climbing, and running around them. The condition is named “Lilliputian hallucination” [2].

Hallucinogenic mushrooms are not unusual, as seen in Amanita and magic mushrooms. Additionally, other compounds, such as psychedelics, can produce profound hallucinations. Common hallucinogenic substances, such as psilocybin, produce hallucinations that differ from person to person depending on their mindset, culture, and experience. They include mostly color-shifting patterns, warped geometry, and changing visual textures. However, this particular mushroom induces a completely different effect.

The name of this condition, Lilliputian hallucination, was first coined by the French psychiatrist Raoul Leroy in 1909, inspired by Jonathan Swift's tiny islanders in Gulliver's Travels. It has been observed during alcohol withdrawal, in certain stages of dementia, Alice in Wonderland syndrome, schizophrenia, and even in macular degeneration, where the eye itself is failing rather than the mind. Leroy himself personally experienced these visions and noticed the same pattern in his patients. The main characteristic of this condition is a relatively consistent experience: seeing fantastically small humans within a real environmental background, occurring across a wide range of conditions.

Some neuroscientists argue that everything we call perception is really an inference, the brain's best guess built from fragments of sensory signal about what's out there. Anil Seth, a neuroscientist at the University of Sussex, calls this a "controlled hallucination": What we experience as a solid, stable world is a prediction the brain generates and only occasionally corrects with the senses, rather than a direct readout of reality [3]. If that's true, then the line between a hallucination and ordinary perception isn't as sharp as we'd like to think—both are constructions, and the only real difference is how tightly one is anchored to incoming sensory data. So how do we ever get close to the "real" at all? Perhaps the answer isn't philosophical but statistical: When enough people construct the same illusion, independently, without communicating with one another, we stop calling it a hallucination and start calling it the truth.

A mushroom that produces a shared hallucination — shared not in the sense of two people perceiving the same scene together in the same room, but in the sense that unrelated individuals, across cultures, eras, and continents, arrive at the identical vision independently — apart from its biological appeal and the nature of its psychoactive compound, raises important philosophical questions. First, why is it that most people who consume this mushroom raw, or who experience Lilliputian hallucinations for other reasons, see small people a few centimeters tall? Why don't they see, for instance, aliens? Do all these afflicted people carry some prior belief about little people, or does the brain inherently contain this fantasy? Are there regions in the brain where the elements of hallucination, dream, and imagination reside, and does our mysterious chemical compound use this reservoir of memory to produce hallucinations? And most importantly of all, does this mushroom teach us that even when a perception is the same among a population of people, we should still doubt whether it is real?

Previously, strange claims by individuals about witnessing supernatural phenomena were easily attributed to hallucination. Now, we must also doubt collective experiences of strange events. If a hallucination can be shared independently by so many people, the line between "subjective error" and "objective reality" becomes blurrier than we ever imagined. Someone once said, half-jokingly, that maybe these little people are real, and under ordinary conditions we simply do not see them, but this mysterious mushroom opens our eyes to them.

1. Barrett, L. F. (2020). Seven and a Half Lessons about the Brain: Houghton Mifflin Harcourt.

2. Domnauer C, Dentinger BTM. Phylogenomic systematics of Lanmaoa (Boletaceae) reveals cryptic diversity, resolves global evolutionary relationships, and suggests a novel psychoactive lineage. Mycologia. 2026 Jul-Aug;118(4):732-742.

3. Seth, A. K. (2021). Being You: A New Science of Consciousness: Faber & Faber.

#19. Are you in a “friends-with-benefits” relationship? 6 tips worth knowing

A friendship has turned physical, but everything else seems to be staying the same. You grab dinner, send memes, and share inside jokes, all with the understanding that it’s just casual. And yet, you can’t help but wonder where things are headed.

Friends-with-benefits relationships sit in the gray area between friendship and romance. These arrangements work out well for some people, but for others, they slowly become a source of anxiety or hurt.

Whether you're already in one or just curious what you'd be signing up for, here's a closer look at what a friends-with-benefits relationship involves — the risks and the rewards, plus how to navigate one with grace and self-awareness.

A friends-with-benefits relationship (often shortened to FWB) is when two friends are also physically involved with each other, without the commitment or expectations that come with a romantic partnership. There's no exclusivity agreement (unless discussed), no defined future together, and usually none of the relationship milestones that come with dating.

The idea is that the friendship stays intact while you enjoy the physical side of a relationship, no strings attached. It may sound straightforward, but in practice, it usually takes more communication and honesty than people expect going in.

Every FWB relationship looks different. Some see each other regularly, while others keep it more sporadic. What they generally have in common is a mutual understanding that neither person is looking for something more serious.

Not sure if you’re in one? Here are some signs that point toward a FWB dynamic:

You skip the things typical couples do, like meeting each other's families or planning trips together.

You haven’t talked about exclusivity or where the relationship is headed.

You call each other “friends” when describing your situation to others.

You’re dating, or open to dating, other people.

The relationship stays undefined, and one or both of you is comfortable keeping it that way.

Like any relationship structure, being friends with benefits has its upsides and its risks. If you're deciding whether to start a FWB relationship, this list is a good gut check for whether the upsides outweigh the risks for you.

Physical intimacy without the pressure of commitment

Closeness and companionship that come from an existing friendship

More freedom to focus on other priorities, like your career, personal growth, or social life

Low-stakes exploration if you’re not ready for something serious

Clarity about what you want (or don’t want) from relationships

One-sided feelings that go unnoticed or unspoken

Ambiguity about what the relationship actually is, even as time passes

Jealousy, especially if one of you starts dating someone else

Damage to the friendship if it ends badly

Lack of communication about needs due to unclear expectations

FWB relationships don't come with a rulebook — but there are common threads among the ones that work: honesty, self-awareness, and ongoing communication. These tips follow those threads.

FWB tension often comes from mismatched expectations that were never discussed. Before you get physically involved—or as soon as possible if you already are—have an open conversation about what you both want.

Get clear about what “casual” means to each of you, and make sure you're both comfortable with it. Talking through this early beats untangling confusion later.

💙 For more guidance, here’s how to set healthy boundaries in relationships.

Unless you've agreed otherwise, friends-with-benefits arrangements are usually non-exclusive, meaning either of you could be dating or getting involved with someone else. It's worth discussing up front how you'll handle that — will you tell each other when someone new is in the picture?

Your feelings about a FWB setup might shift over time. Take a moment every so often to check in on how you're feeling about the situation.

A few minutes of reflection, or a short meditation, can help you notice any uncomfortable feelings you've been avoiding.

💙 Try Checking In With Yourself with Prof. Megan Reitz on Calm.

Without active effort, the friendship side of FWB can slowly fade into the background until only the physical side is left.

Make it a point to spend time together without getting intimate. Ask about different parts of their life. Show up for each other the way you would have before your dynamic changed.

💙 Learn more about Mindful Friendships with Jay Shetty on Calm.

A FWB arrangement that works one month might not work the next. People's feelings and circumstances naturally evolve with time. The key is speaking up when you notice a change, whether it’s on your end or theirs.

This is where these relationships often get complicated. One of you has a change of heart, but stays silent, afraid of disrupting the dynamic or losing the other person.

Being upfront can be uncomfortable, but it’s one of the most respectful things you can do for yourself and your friend.

💙 Press play on Say What You Need to Say with Jay Shetty on Calm.

Any friends-with-benefits relationship could end at some point, and thinking ahead about how you'd handle it can reduce the fallout. Think about whether preserving the friendship matters to you. Either way, expect some awkwardness afterward.

It can be hard to end things with care and honesty, but it does less damage to the friendship than silence or avoidance.

Knowing what to do in a FWB situation matters, but it’s equally important to be aware of what can trip you up.

Don't assume you're on the same page without checking. Shared silence isn't shared understanding.

Don't use the arrangement as a way to stay close to someone you have feelings for. That's a recipe for getting hurt.

Don't ignore your feelings because they feel inconvenient. Feelings that get dismissed tend to resurface louder later.

Don't skip the conversation about seeing other people. Assumptions here can turn this arrangement messy fast.

Don't stay in it if you’re consistently left feeling worse. A casual relationship isn't worth more than your peace of mind.

Don't expect the friendship to survive constant unspoken tension. Even close friendships have limits, and unspoken hurt can gradually erode them.

Friends with benefits means you and your friend are physically intimate without the commitments of a romantic relationship. There's no assumed exclusivity and no defined future — just a dynamic that exists somewhere between friendship and romance.

Friends-with-benefits relationships get complicated when feelings become one-sided. One of you may develop deeper feelings while the other doesn't. It can also get tricky when expectations shift without a conversation, when one of you starts dating someone else, or when the physical side starts overshadowing the friendship.

There's no set timeline for a FWB relationship. Some arrangements last a few months, while others go on for years. How long yours lasts depends on whether you’re both comfortable with it, communication stays open, and your feelings stay compatible over time.

Friends with benefits may be a good idea if you and the other person are aligned on what you’re looking for. It can be a comfortable, low-pressure arrangement, or a source of confusion and hurt if expectations aren't discussed. Open communication and regular self-reflection tend to give the relationship the best shot at working.

Yes, some FWB arrangements do evolve into committed relationships, particularly when both people develop feelings around the same time and are open to more. That said, staying in the arrangement in hopes that it'll turn into something more comes with a risk. You may end up hurt if the other person doesn't feel the same way.

Jealousy is a normal reaction, even in FWB arrangements that are meant to be casual. This happens because intimacy can naturally lead to attachment. If you’re feeling this way, it might be a sign the situation no longer fits what you want.

The best way to end a friends-with-benefits relationship without ruining the friendship is to be direct and honest. Ghosting or avoiding the other person usually does more damage than an open conversation. Be clear about why things have changed, share appreciation for what you had, and give each other some space afterward.

#20. Mapping the ADHD Brain: How Neurotransmitters and Medication Work

The unique structures, wiring, and functionality of neurodivergent brains, according to science.

Why do one person’s ADHD symptoms differ from another’s? The answer lurks inside the structural and chemical differences of the ADHD brain.

No single brain region is the source of ADHD. However, subtle variations in brain structure, function, connectivity, and neurochemistry shape the neural networks that govern attention, motivation, reward, emotion, and self-control.

The regions involved in ADHD traits include:

[Get This Free Download: Unraveling the Mysteries of Your ADHD Brain]

The brain comprises billions of nerve cells called neurons. These neurons work in circuits, passing signals to each other that allow our bodies to think, move, remember, manage emotions, and control impulses.

Between neurons is a tiny gap called a synapse. To get messages across, neurons release chemical messengers called neurotransmitters into the gap. The neurotransmitters cross the gap and attach to receptors on the next neuron to help the message continue. Afterward, the brain clears neurotransmitters away in a process called reuptake.

The neurotransmitters dopamine (DE) and norepinephrine (NE) help the PFC hold goals and instructions in mind, filter distractions, and guide behavior. They also help reward circuits decide what feels interesting, urgent, or worth doing.

In ADHD, these signals don’t support those circuits and processes as strongly or consistently as they should. Task-relevant information may fade too quickly, while distractions, impulses, emotions or immediate rewards may pull more strongly. This is why ADHD is sometimes described as a “signal-to-noise” problem: the useful signal is there, but it may be drowned out by competing noise.

ADHD is linked to differences in how brain networks communicate and coordinate attention, motivation, emotion, and self-regulation.

ADHD medication can optimize brain signals by slowing the reuptake of DE or NE, increasing their release, or activating receptors that strengthen signaling. All of this helps guide attention, motivation, and self-control.

COMPARING THE IMPACTS OF ADHD MEDICATIONS

New insights: Functional connectivity data show that stimulants enhance performance by increasing vigilance and perceived task value.11 In other words, stimulants help the ADHD brain stay motivated and engaged with non-preferred tasks.

In addition to dopamine and norepinephrine, a third critical neurotransmitter is serotonin, which helps to regulate mood and emotion, both deeply relevant to the ADHD experience.

Emotional dysregulation is a core feature of ADHD, and many people with the condition also live with mood disorders. Almost half of adults with ADHD are also prescribed selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) – medications that increase serotonin levels to regulate mood, emotion, and sleep.

Viloxazine, a non-stimulant, became the first ADHD medication in the U.S. to also modulate serotonin. Beyond targeting ADHD symptoms, the medication was shown to improve co-occurring depression and anxiety in adults with all three conditions.12

Centanafadine (Simtriyo), a stimulant ADHD medication recently approved for children aged 6 years and older and adults, is a norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin reuptake inhibitor (NDSRI). Trials show that the medication improves symptoms in both groups and in adults with ADHD and co-occurring anxiety.13

Untreated ADHD impacts neural connectivity.14 Unstable brain connections increase risk for the development of anxiety, depression, insomnia, emotional frustration, and other challenges. ADHD medication enhances neural connectivity, but there are other ways to promote neural growth, protect the brain, and decrease risk for secondary issues.

Greg W. Mattingly, M.D., is an associate clinical professor at Washington University School of Medicine.

#22. My Journey to Mindfulness

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

October’s Teacher of the Month is a new voice to Mindful: musician Thaddaeus Washington. As a Toledo-based artist and founder of MIND Music, Thadd sees music as medicine and offers his original compositions as meditative practices.

My journey to mindfulness started long before I knew what the word meant. I was born to two wonderful parents, Lenny and Linda, and from the very beginning I was a kid full of vigor, energy, spontaneity, and deep curiosity. Eclectic, you could say.

I’ve always loved people: getting to know them, wondering what makes them tick, and figuring out what makes things move.

When I was four, my parents divorced. It affected me and my sister, Esther, but I can only speak for myself, and for me the effects were major. I blamed myself because my parents couldn’t stay together. I loved them both equally, but I was a momma’s boy, and the divorce changed how my mom showed up. The emotions she carried toward my dad came out in the way she spoke about him to me.

I was always in trouble for something: too much energy, too curious, too many questions. It seemed like just being Thaddaeus was the problem.

That, among other things, was the beginning of my anger and isolation. I felt like I could never do anything right. I was always in trouble for something: too much energy, too curious, too many questions. It seemed like just being Thaddaeus was the problem.

After the divorce, Esther and I bounced back and forth between Philadelphia, where my mom is from, and Toledo, Ohio, where my dad is from. I remember so many moments from those years of feeling like the problem, misunderstood, alone, like I never fit in, like something was wrong with me. My energy was different, my parents were apart, and there was plenty of tension around it. That was a recipe for a bumpy road.

Then came the labels. At age eight I was diagnosed with ADHD. The reports said I had trouble staying on task, that I was disruptive and couldn’t focus like “normal” kids. I was put on meds to help me focus and sleep. I remember the first time the Ritalin set in. I felt like a totally different person. My natural energy was gone. Straight zombie mode, no appetite. But it made my mom, the doctors, and the people at church say, “That’s Calm Thadd. Look at him. That’s a good boy.”

I was a kid full of energy, trying to process the fact that my parents just weren’t together anymore.

I was a kid full of energy, trying to process the fact that my parents just weren’t together anymore. I would go to the doctor, see the therapist, and throw the pills in a trash bag that I emptied every week, acting as if the meds were the reason I was getting better. All the while, I wasn’t taking anything. Instead I was taking the time to process my choices before I made them. Eventually, they decided I didn’t need the meds anymore, though I had stopped taking them two years before.

I’m thankful for my mother, just as I am for my father. They did the best they could to raise me. Are there things I wish had been handled differently? Of course. But I’m grateful, and I carry no bitterness.

I was raised in church. We went more than anything else: Wednesday night service, Friday night service, Sunday morning, and Sunday night. We were taught to trust in God because He knows all and can handle all. I am very much a Christian, but living life has shown me that there are things we’re equipped to do ourselves, like taking care of ourselves and prioritizing our mental and emotional well-being, when we have the proper tools. Many of us aren’t given those tools, and many don’t have access to them. That’s why I have great respect for doctors, therapists, and everyone in their respective roles who do the real work of helping those who feel helpless.

From elementary school through my sophomore year of high school, “Bad Thadd” followed me. That’s what I was called. I remember being expelled from my regular school and sent to an alternative school for kids with extreme behaviors. It no longer exists, but at the time it was called Mayfair Achievement Program , on Bennett Road. I remember it like it was yesterday. I had to catch two buses, the 27 to downtown Toledo and then the 17B to the school, and most days we were lucky to make it there without a fight. Getting patted down on the way in was part of the daily routine, because plenty of kids had weapons, cell phones, or sometimes drugs. My vice was my phone.

Through all the trouble, the bumps and bruises, music was the one thing that stayed consistent in my life.

Every student had what was called a mainstream assessment: goals to set, good behaviors to work on, and assessments to pass so we could be mainstreamed back to our regular school. We had to set goals for what we wanted to do with our lives, and one thing I knew was that I wanted to play guitar. Drums were my first instrument, and I learned them in the basement of the Church of the Living God. But my father was an amazing guitar player, and he was my inspiration. When it finally clicked for me at 13 that I wanted to play guitar, I asked my dad to teach me.

Through all the trouble, the bumps and bruises, music was the one thing that stayed consistent in my life. So that became my big goal, and to make a long story short, I hit it. I was mainstreamed, made it out of Mayfair, and got back into the regular school system, though I still had some behavior classes.

It was my junior year when a conversation with my Granny Doris changed everything. The odds still seemed against me, and I might not graduate if I couldn’t stay out of trouble.

She said to me, “Thadd, it’s time to make a choice. Either you’re going to keep going left, or you’re going to go right.” She reminded me of who I was and what I was capable of. I had plenty of support. My dad would always tell me, “Thadd, stay in control. Control your emotions, don’t let them control you, and don’t allow people to push your buttons.” But that conversation with Granny was the game changer.

I finished high school and went on to do some college. I tried for Mom and Dad’s sake, because that’s what they wanted, but it just wasn’t for me. I wanted to do music and travel, so I did. It took me to so many amazing places. I’ve done some great things with music, played for some great artists, and met many great people along the way.

But after years of playing and traveling, I realized that even though I had found what I loved, I still wasn’t settled within.

In late 2019, shortly before the COVID-19 pandemic, a mentor introduced me to mindfulness and meditation. I was apprehensive at first, because sitting still with my thoughts was foreign to me. I thought it was impossible. I believed I would just pray and everything would work itself out. She helped me understand there was more I could do. I thought I’d have to become a monk to be still and practice meditation, and she assured me that wasn’t it.

We started with breathing exercises and affirmations, and as I stayed consistent, I began to see the benefits in my life. I felt better. I felt clearer in how I thought about myself and others and how I processed my emotions.

We started with breathing exercises and affirmations, and as I stayed consistent, I began to see the benefits in my life. I felt better. I felt clearer in how I thought about myself and others and how I processed my emotions. It was life-changing. I could actually sit still for 60 seconds and focus on my breath, and if my mind wandered or thoughts came, I learned that was completely normal. It became a daily practice, and then a deeper one, and I started finding creative ways to meditate. Music, of course, and sound came naturally, whether it was through the sounds of nature, in my studio, or with my guitar. I began playing with different sounds and music for my practice, never knowing it would grow into what it is today: MIND Music.

I started creating the music out of necessity. It was something I needed, and for over a year I used it for exactly that. Then, after sharing it with my inner circle and my brother D, I felt it could help others. I released my first meditation album, MIND in November 2022, and the rest has truly been history. From students to staff and teachers, to working with principals, live experiences, and projects, MIND Music has grown into a movement.

This path has led to projects I’m proud of, including Mindful Meetup with the Metroparks Toledo, and the Common Ground albums, Common Ground 1 and now Common Ground 2, recorded on-site in the Metroparks. Each one is another way of doing the same thing: meeting people where they are.

So many people feel  tired, overwhelmed, anxious, and unwell in ways they don’t always have words for. I know that feeling, because I lived it long before I had any tools to name it.

We are living in a world full of distractions. We have countless ways to connect, and yet loneliness and disconnection remain very real. We’re more plugged in than ever and somehow lonelier than ever. So many people feel  tired, overwhelmed, anxious, and unwell in ways they don’t always have words for. I know that feeling, because I lived it long before I had any tools to name it.

That’s why I believe in what MIND Music can be. For me, it’s become a source of calm and brain food for a mind that’s running on empty. It’s one more tool to meet people exactly where they are and gently guide them back to themselves. I don’t see that as a product. I see it as service for all.

The goal is simple: to make mindfulness accessible to everyone. For me mindfulness is about the ability to be present in the moment, judging nothing, just being, taking time to reset. We do it through music, transparency, rawness, and storytelling.

I don’t come from a place of being an expert. If I’m an expert at anything, it’s staying the course, because life has always been hard, and life will life. My goal is to share my story and help others find their purpose and live and lead better lives, one mindful moment at a time.

Thaddaeus Washington is a musician, singer, songwriter, and founder of Mind Music—a company dedicated to making mindfulness accessible through music and immersive experiences.

#23. The Constitution of the Inner Country: Leonard Cohen on Language and the Poetry of Presence

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. “We die. That may be the meaning of life,” Toni Morrison asserted in her spectacular Nobel Prize acceptance speech. “But we do language. That may be the measure of our lives.” We do language not merely with our words — which are themselves events — but with the lived and living presence behind them. “Words mean. Words point. They are arrows. Arrows stuck in the rough hide of reality,” Susan Sontag wrote in contemplating the conscience of words. If words are the arrow, we ourselves — our interior landscapes, our outward actions, the authenticity of our lives — are the bow.

The elusive, essential art of not mistaking one for the other is what Leonard Cohen (September 21, 1934–November 7, 2016) explores in a prose poem from his out-of-print 1978 book of poetry, Death of a Lady’s Man (public library).

In consonance with James Baldwin’s insistence that “it is experience which shapes a language; and it is language which controls an experience,” Cohen — who began his career as a poet — writes:

Take the word butterfly. To use this word it is not necessary to make the voice weigh less than an ounce or equip it with small dusty wings. It is not necessary to invent a sunny day or a field of daffodils. It is not necessary to be in love, or to be in love with butterflies. The word butterfly is not a real butterfly. There is the word and there is the butterfly. If you confuse these two items people have the right to laugh at you. Do not make so much of the word. Are you trying to suggest that you love butterflies more perfectly than anyone else, or really understand their nature? The word butterfly is merely data. It is not an opportunity for you to hover, soar, befriend flowers, symbolize beauty and frailty, or in any way impersonate a butterfly. Do not act out words. Never act out words.

Speak the words with the exact precision with which you would check out a laundry list. Do not become emotional about the lace blouse. Do not get a hard-on when you say panties. Do not get all shivery just because of the towel. The sheets should not provoke a dreamy expression about the eyes. There is no need to weep into the handkerchief. The socks are not there to remind you of strange and distant voyages. It is just your laundry. It is just your clothes. Don’t peep through them. Just wear them.

Four decades before poet Elizabeth Alexander contemplated “the revelatory and unguarded and surprising self in language,” Cohen writes:

The poem is nothing but information. It is the Constitution of the inner country. If you declaim it and blow it up with noble intentions then you are no better than the politicians whom you despise. You are just someone waving a flag and making the cheapest kind of appeal to a kind of emotional patriotism. Think of the words as science, not as art. They are a report. You are speaking before a meeting of the Explorers’ Club of the National Geographic Society. These people know all the risks of mountain climbing. They honour you by taking this for granted. If you rub their faces in it that is an insult to their hospitality. Tell them about the height of the mountain, the equipment you used, be specific about the surfaces and the time it took to scale it. Do not work the audience for gasps and sighs. If you are worthy of gasps and sighs it will not be from your appreciation of the event but from theirs. It will be in the statistics and not the trembling of the voice or the cutting of the air with your hands. It will be in the data and the quiet organization of your presence.

Complement with Virginia Woolf’s love letter to words in the only surviving recording of her voice, then revisit Cohen on creativity, the art of stillness, and democracy and its redemptions.

#24. Should We Look to Hunter-Gatherer Societies as Models of Equality?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

On the shores of Lake Eyasi in Northern Tanzania, a small number of people still hunt and gather their food. Today a Hadza hunter has taken down an animal—a kudu. He can’t carry it by himself, so he cuts his poisoned arrow from its flank, covers the carcass in dry grass to hide it from hyenas, and heads home to enlist help.

News spreads like wildfire across the camp. Everybody rushes to the kill. They divide up the carcass, carry it back, then divvy it up some more. Every family gets some, and after the meat is cooked, there’s more sharing still. On a good day like today, the hunter and his family retain half, but sometimes they keep much less. People may even walk from other camps, and almost everyone, from miles around, is entitled to a share.

The post-hunt scene above is idyllic. It paints a quintessential picture of egalitarianism and equality. But our experience as anthropologists working with the Hadza people of Tanzania and with the Tsimane people of Bolivia’s Amazon rainforest is that inequalities are part of even the most equal of societies. Furthermore, the equalities that do exist often emerge from selfish motives.

Insights like ours are revising researchers’ understanding of both the past and how people operate today, as inequality grows globally. Hunter-gatherers are often at the center of heated academic battles about what it means to be human, including debates over gender, war, and peace and whether humans are, by nature, egalitarian or hierarchical.

Sometimes these debates oversimplify. So we pulled together hundreds of different sources covering more than a century of ethnography to find out just how egalitarian hunter-gatherer and other subsistence societies really are.

Anthropologists have called hunter-gatherers such as the Hadza “egalitarian societies,” with equalities of power, wealth, and social status. And it’s true that the traditional subsistence communities we work with successfully limit many inequalities.

Most families have similar, modest possessions and store little material wealth. When leaders do emerge, they are highly constrained in how they can direct other people. People often make decisions via consensus, and, if they cannot reach agreement, families will move away.

While the same anthropologists also emphasize that some hunter-gatherers are very unequal and that equality takes deliberate effort, the prevailing impression is that equality characterizes hunter-gatherers, past and present.

A quick trip to your local bookshop will reveal grand claims, including that past hunter-gatherer societies had no permanent leadership and no hierarchy, inequality only spread with the development of agriculture, and humans are noble by nature.

Some scientists are pushing back against these utopian portrayals. The popular bestseller, The Dawn of Everything, calls egalitarianism a “Garden of Eden narrative” that lacks substance. Other scholars have called egalitarian societies a scientific origin myth.

So where does the truth lie? Probably somewhere in between.

In our recent wide-ranging review of the evidence from the early 20th century onward, we found that no society lacked inequality.

Like the Hadza, the Ju/’Hoansi of the Kalahari desert in southern Africa had little property and widespread food-sharing, yet certain families controlled valuable hunting territory surrounding waterholes. The Bayaka of the central African rainforest had little material inequality, yet they bought, sold, and hoarded ritual knowledge. The Philippine Agta controlled and arranged their children’s marriages, hugely discriminating against orphans.

Gender inequalities were commonplace. The Tanzanian Hadza keep certain cuts of meat exclusively for older men, and give more respect to better hunters. Across societies, women have universally done more direct parenting, and men have participated more frequently in community-level decision making.

No society lacks informal leadership. Age was another source of inequality. In many Australian societies, older men controlled ritual secrets and had power over the marriage choices of younger relatives.

Our study also found that although hunter-gatherers are frequently generous, the processes limiting inequality often do not require any generosity. Instead, equality often results from people’s self-interested motives to acquire resources, status, and autonomy.

A great example of this is food-sharing. Although each Hadza family gets a cut of kudu meat, it often happens not because the hunter’s family prioritizes total equality, but because other families request it vociferously. It can involve more taking than giving, often through strongly stated demands or complaints.

Another example is ridicule and mockery of stingy or braggadocious individuals, which keeps greed and bravado in check. Paradoxically, status-seeking can also promote equality, when cooperating to gain status diffuses status throughout the community.

Many of these inequality-reducing processes are familiar to people everywhere.

Ridicule and mockery are ubiquitous in industrialized societies, from political cartoons to social media. Lampooning authority is even common in autocratic societies where governments spend large sums of money suppressing speech. Demands and complaints form the basis of strikes and collective bargaining. And key to social mobility is cooperation among people of different social strata.

Like many great debates, the truth is complex: Our ancient hunter-gatherer ancestors didn’t reach the giddy heights of inequality seen in other societies over the last 6,000 years, but putting hunter-gatherers on a pedestal as paragons of equality is a mistake. Sweeping statements about equality in the past blind us to the tools that probably allowed ancient hunter-gatherers to combat inequality, just as they and people in all societies do today.

Egalitarianism, then, is best seen not as perfect equality but as a set of tools that people use to secure their own autonomy and access to resources. Equality along one dimension or another might be the outcome, but it doesn’t rely on people being amazingly noble or completely lacking in greed or status-seeking. If you consider egalitarianism as equality-creating processes, you can see that it is a widespread reality among hunter-gatherer societies, and beyond.
