#25. Modern neuroscience is rediscovering a surprising idea freud had 130 years ago

What if the human brain works in ways that Sigmund Freud began describing more than 130 years ago? A new scientific analysis suggests that some of his ideas about the mind share surprising similarities with one of the most influential theories in modern neuroscience.

Published in the scientific journal Entropy, the paper explores connections between Freud's original theories, later developments in psychoanalysis, and a modern approach to brain research known as the prediction paradigm.

This approach describes the brain as a prediction machine. Rather than simply responding to information from the outside world, the brain is constantly anticipating what will happen next. It then compares those expectations with incoming information from the senses and works to reduce any differences between what it predicted and what actually occurred.

Scientists believe this ongoing process plays a central role in how people perceive their surroundings, make decisions, behave, and regulate emotions.

Researchers Erik Stänicke, Bendik Hovet, and Line Indrevoll Stänicke, together with colleagues, argue that this modern understanding of brain function has important parallels with ideas that psychoanalysts have been developing for more than a century.

"For over 130 years, psychoanalysis has developed psychological theories about how predictions take place at a subjective level, which cognitive neuropsychology is now studying at a physiological level."

How Freud's Ideas Connect to the Predictive Brain

Although neuroscience and psychoanalysis approach the mind differently, the researchers suggest that both may be describing related processes.

Neuroscience examines the physical mechanisms behind thought and behavior, often using mathematical models to explain how the brain processes information. Psychoanalysis, which grew out of Freud's work, focuses more on unconscious mental processes, emotional experiences, and the ways past relationships influence present behavior.

In other words, one field investigates what happens inside the brain, while the other explores how those processes are experienced by the individual.

A particularly interesting connection involves the psychoanalytic concept of projection and the neuroscientific concept of prediction.

In psychoanalysis, projection involves attributing feelings, intentions, or qualities to someone else. The researchers suggest that this resembles how the brain uses previously learned expectations to interpret new experiences.

"When we attribute qualities, intentions or feelings to other people, our brain shapes our experience of the world in line with established expectations," says Stänicke.

For instance, someone who has repeatedly experienced rejection may become especially sensitive to signs that other people are rejecting them. Even an ambiguous remark or facial expression might be interpreted negatively because past experiences have shaped what the person expects.

Over time, these expectations can influence how someone approaches unfamiliar situations and forms new relationships.

"This corresponds to the neuroscientific distinction between changing one's own predictions, perceptual inference, and the attempt to make the world conform to them, namely active inference."

Perceptual inference refers to the way the brain interprets sensory information and updates its expectations in response. Active inference, by contrast, involves taking actions that help bring experiences into line with predictions or reduce uncertainty.

Together, these concepts help explain why people do not always experience the world as it objectively is. Their expectations can influence what they notice, how they interpret events, and how they respond.

Why the Brain Holds On to Negative Expectations

The researchers believe the similarities between Freud's ideas and modern neuroscience could offer valuable insights into mental health disorders, particularly those involving deeply established patterns of thinking and behavior.

Both approaches portray the mind as constantly seeking stability and predictability. This tendency is related to homeostasis, the process through which a system maintains a relatively stable internal state.

In the predictive brain model, reducing uncertainty is an important part of maintaining that stability. The brain relies on familiar expectations to make the world easier to understand, even when those expectations are inaccurate or no longer helpful.

"Psychoanalysts refer to the tendency in the mind to recreate familiar relational patterns, even when these are poorly adapted," says Stänicke.

This could help explain why people sometimes repeat harmful patterns in relationships or continue interpreting situations negatively despite evidence that challenges their assumptions.

"Rigid and persistent symptoms, such as paranoid ideas or an internalized critical voice, may be stable but not very flexible prediction models," says Stänicke.

"For example, there may be people who automatically expect criticism, rejection or hostility from others, and therefore interpret situations through this filter despite the fact that reality does not warrant it."

Such expectations can become deeply entrenched because they make experiences feel familiar and predictable. Even when the resulting interpretation is distorted, maintaining an established mental model may feel less uncertain than changing it.

According to Stänicke, this offers a possible explanation for why some psychological symptoms can persist for years and why changing longstanding patterns of thought and behavior often requires considerable time.

The connection is particularly interesting because it suggests that some mental health difficulties may involve more than consciously held beliefs. They may also reflect deeply learned expectations that automatically shape emotional responses and interactions with others.

How Psychotherapy Could Help Change Deeply Rooted Patterns

The researchers also highlight an important distinction between what people consciously believe and what they have learned through experience.

"In addition, both models give us insight into how parts of our expectations of the outside world are not only anchored cognitively, but in procedural memory that is expressed in relational ways of being," he says.

Procedural memory is a type of long-term memory involved in learned habits and skills. It allows people to perform familiar actions without consciously thinking through every step.

In the context of relationships, the researchers suggest that a similar form of learning may help explain why certain emotional reactions and patterns of interaction become automatic.

Someone might intellectually understand that other people are not necessarily hostile or critical, for example, yet still instinctively respond as though rejection is inevitable.

These expectations are not simply thoughts that can be changed through reasoning. They can also be embedded in habitual ways of reacting to people and navigating relationships.

This distinction may help explain why psychotherapy sometimes needs to address personal relationships and emotional experiences rather than focusing only on conscious thoughts.

"Therefore, psychotherapy sometimes has to work relationally. For example, new experiences in the relationship between therapist and patient can gradually help to change entrenched relational patterns."

Through repeated experiences that challenge familiar expectations, patients may gradually develop different ways of interpreting situations and relating to other people.

Bringing Freud's Psychoanalysis and Neuroscience Together

The researchers argue that connecting psychoanalysis with modern predictive brain theory could benefit both fields.

Neuroscience may provide a biological framework for understanding processes that psychoanalysts have long described through subjective experience. At the same time, psychoanalytic theories may offer more detailed explanations of how expectations are experienced emotionally, interpreted personally, and expressed through relationships.

The proposed similarities do not establish that Freud's broader theories were correct. Instead, they suggest that two very different traditions of studying the mind may offer complementary ways of understanding some of the same psychological processes.

By examining both the brain's physical mechanisms and the individual's inner experience, researchers hope to develop a more complete understanding of human behavior and mental health.

"Bringing these two fields together can open up for a more holistic psychology, in which both neurological mechanisms and subjective experience are included. In this way, we can understand subjectivity in a more scientific manner."

#26. Abnormal Astroglia Linked to Fluid Intelligence Decline

Researchers at USC examining living human brain tissue surgically resected from epilepsy patients discovered that higher numbers of abnormal, immature astroglia in the hippocampus correlate directly with poorer fluid intelligence, the ability to reason, solve novel problems, and adapt. The finding provides rare direct human cellular evidence that non-neuronal glial cells actively influence complex human cognition, identifying a potential cellular target to treat accelerated cognitive aging.

Fluid intelligence, the fundamental capacity to think logically, solve unfamiliar problems, identify patterns, and adapt to novel circumstances independent of acquired knowledge, inevitably declines with advancing age. It is also among the first cognitive domains to disintegrate in neurodegenerative conditions such as frontotemporal dementia, Parkinson’s disease, and multiple sclerosis.

While neuroscientists have conventionally attributed cognitive reasoning deficits to synaptic dysfunction and neuronal death, the potential contribution of glial support cells has remained difficult to evaluate directly in living human tissue.

Now, a team led by researchers from the USC Stem Cell laboratory of Michael Bonaguidi, PhD, and the USC Neurorestoration Center has revealed that non-neuronal support cells play an active role in human problem-solving capacity.

Publishing in the journal Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience, the investigators established that older adults harboring an increased abundance of abnormal, immature astroglia in the hippocampus perform significantly worse on clinical evaluations of fluid intelligence.

Studying cellular dynamics in the living human brain presents severe technical barriers. Standard non-invasive neuroimaging tools like magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and electroencephalography (EEG) lack the cellular resolution necessary to differentiate distinct glial phenotypes. Conversely, post-mortem brain donations often suffer from tissue degradation and lack recent, standardized cognitive testing prior to death.

The USC team overcame these limitations through a rare clinical opportunity: examining hippocampal tissue surgically removed from 29 patients undergoing therapeutic resections for drug-resistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.

Prior to surgery, each patient completed comprehensive neuropsychological batteries measuring reasoning, working memory, attention, language, and fine motor skills. Immediately following resection, the researchers microscopically examined and quantified the exact distribution of immature astroglia within targeted anatomical zones of the hippocampus.

Astroglia—the star-shaped cells of the central nervous system, have long been viewed primarily as metabolic and structural caretakers that nourish neurons, regulate the blood-brain barrier, and recycle neurotransmitters.

However, the tissue analysis revealed that older patients had a disproportionate burden of abnormal, arrested immature astroglia. When cross-referenced with pre-surgical cognitive performance, a distinct relationship emerged: greater numbers of these immature cells tracked directly with lower fluid intelligence scores.

“We found that older patients tended to have more abnormal immature astroglia, and that higher numbers of these cells were also associated with poorer performance on tests of fluid intelligence,” said first author Aswathy Ammothumkandy, PhD, assistant professor of research in the Department of Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. “These findings suggest that astroglia could be a shared therapeutic target for accelerated age-related cognitive decline in people with epilepsy, as well as for seizure control, as indicated by our previous research.”

Because the cells were arrested in an abnormal, immature functional state, they may fail to properly support local synaptic plasticity within the hippocampus, impairing the dynamic network synchronization required for complex problem-solving.

“Aging is something we’re all familiar with and all impacted by, it’s a matter of when, not if,” said co-corresponding author Michael Bonaguidi, PhD, associate professor of stem cell biology and regenerative medicine, gerontology, biomedical engineering, and neurological surgery, and assistant director of the USC Neurorestoration Center. “What this study provides is a new therapeutic target that could someday help us slow down or potentially even reverse age-related declines in our ability to solve new problems.”

The research group is currently screening for specific molecular markers that distinguish these abnormal immature astroglia from healthy mature cells. Identifying these transcriptional and metabolic signatures could enable the development of small molecules designed to drive astroglial maturation or selectively eliminate dysfunctional cells.

Additionally, the investigators plan to test whether targeted neuromodulation, using precise electrical or magnetic stimulation to alter hippocampal network states, can encourage healthy astroglial physiology and preserve fluid reasoning across the lifespan.

This research was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grant R01AG076956), , the , the Cure Alzheimer’s Fund, The Eli and Edythe Broad Foundation, the USC Neurorestoration Center, the Rudi Schulte Research Institute, the American Epilepsy Society, the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine (grant EDUC4-12756), and CURE Epilepsy Taking Flight.

An age-related decline in human fluid intelligence corresponds with immature astroglia prevalence

Age-related cognitive decline remains a daunting health challenge, and targeting neuronal cells alone has been insufficient to halt its progression. Astroglia are emerging as key players in cognitive function and dysfunction, yet their relevance to age-associated cognitive decline in humans remains unclear. Epilepsy patients undergo age-amplified progressive cognitive decline.

Our prior research in Mesial Temporal Lobe Epilepsy (MTLE) patients identified pathological stellar Dcx + immature astroglia in epileptic, but not healthy hippocampus. In this study, we combined histology data with pre-surgical neuropsychology tests to assess (1) age-associated cognitive decline in MTLE patients (N = 40), (2) age-related changes in Dcx + immature astroglia (N = 29), and (3) the association between Dcx + immature astroglia and cognitive decline (N = 19).

We observed a strong decline in fluid intelligence, visuospatial reconstruction, and memory with age. An increase in Dcx + immature astroglia positively correlated with age, whereas negatively associated with nonverbal abstract reasoning and fluid intelligence as measured by the Raven’s Progressive Matrices test.

These findings reveal an interplay among aging, fluid intelligence decline, and immature astroglia prevalence in epilepsy patients. Our study suggests immature astroglia represent a new cellular target to consider for altering age-associated cognitive decline.

#27. How to dream more: 6 tips to increase how often you dream

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA

We all know that one person who says, “You’ll never believe what I dreamt last night!” Many people who dream can become obsessed with the stories their minds show them at night. Some people believe their dreams provide insights into their subconscious, while others say they inspire creativity. And those who aren’t into the deep dream interpretation simply like the fantasy world that their minds create when they’re asleep.

If you’re fascinated by your dreams for any of these reasons, you might want to learn how to dream more and make your dreams more vivid. And while you can’t control everything—like the inevitable falling nightmare everyone has had at least once—you can do things to dream more frequently and to make those dreams easier to recall. Here are a few simple techniques and lifestyle changes you might want to try to make the most of the time you spend asleep.

When you sleep better, you’re more likely to enter the rapid eye movement (REM) part of your sleep cycle, when most dreaming occurs. This sleep cycle may increase the chances of having more frequent and vivid dreams, so here are a few tips to encourage deeper sleep.

Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day to help regulate your sleep cycle and increase the likelihood of dreaming. To get enough REM sleep, aim for 7–9 hours of sleep each night.

💙 Try relaxing an hour before bed with Soften Into Sleep, a meditation that can help you release tension at night.

Read, take a warm bath, or practice mindfulness to ease into rest and create an environment for dreaming. Avoid screens for at least an hour before bed, as the blue light can disrupt your body’s natural sleep-wake cycle. If you must use devices, try a blue light filter or dim your screen.

💙 Explore these nine tips to help you build a better bedtime routine.

To improve sleep quality and increase your chances of dreaming, keep your bedroom dark, quiet, and cool. The ideal temperature is about 60–67 degrees Fahrenheit (or 15–19 degrees Celsius). Use blackout curtains to block light, earplugs or a white noise machine to drown out noise, and invest in a comfortable mattress and pillows to support your posture.

Lastly, keep your bedroom tidy and use it only for sleep and relaxation if you can. This can help you create a mental association between your bedroom and restful sleep.

💙 Press play on one of our relaxing Soundscapes, like White Noise Ocean Surf, to help you drift off to sleep.

Practice meditation, yoga, or deep breathing exercises to help decrease anxiety so you can get a good night’s sleep, which may promote more vivid dreaming. Regular exercise can help too, but remember to avoid vigorous activity too close to bedtime.

💙 Keep stress at bay by tuning into 7 Days of Managing Stress, a stress reduction series hosted by Tamara Levitt.

Heavy meals, caffeine, or alcohol before bed can disrupt sleep and decrease dream frequency. Opt for light snacks if you're hungry, and avoid caffeine or alcohol close to bedtime.

💙 Add mindfulness to mealtime with our session on the Benefits of Mindful Eating.

Drink water throughout the day to support sleep quality, but try to limit water intake about an hour before bed to prevent trips to the bathroom in the middle of the night.

During your wind down routine, you can sip teas like chamomile or valerian root. These are thought to have calming effects that may promote relaxation and improve sleep quality, which may lead to more vivid dreams.

💙 Listen to a relaxing Sleep Story before bed, like Why Do We Sleep, while sipping tea as part of a new nighttime ritual.

Sleep is divided into several stages that cycle throughout the night, typically lasting about 90 minutes per cycle.

Stage 1 (light sleep): This is a transitional phase where you drift in and out of sleep.

Stage 2 (deeper light sleep): Your body temperature drops and your heart rate begins to slow.

Stage 3 (deep sleep): Known as slow-wave sleep, this stage promotes physical recovery and health.

REM sleep: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, where your brain activity increases and your eyes move rapidly under your eyelids, is when the most vivid dreams occur.

Melatonin is a hormone your body naturally produces that helps to regulate your sleep-wake cycles. Levels rise in the evening to help you feel sleepy and decrease in the morning to help you wake up. Some people take melatonin supplements to help with sleep issues like insomnia, jet lag, or other sleep disorders, but it may also affect your dreams.

Some studies suggest that melatonin may enhance REM sleep. This might lead to more frequent and vivid dreams, and some people who take melatonin report more intense and memorable dreams.

Melatonin may also help with dream recall by enhancing overall sleep quality.

The effect of melatonin on dreams can vary from person to person. Remember to always consult a medical professional before you take any supplement, as they can interact with other medications or simply not be right for you.

People like remembering their dreams for a number of reasons. Perhaps it sparks their curiosity about what they could be feeling on a subconscious level or could provide them with an escape from reality. Whatever your reason for wanting to remember your dreams may be, dream recall can become easier and more natural with time and practice.

Keep a dream journal: Write down your dreams as soon as you wake up, even if you can only remember bits and pieces of them. Over time, this can train your brain to pay more attention to your dreams. Review your dream journal during the day to help reinforce your memory and increase your chances of remembering future dreams.

Set an intention: Before you go to sleep, reinforce your desire to remember your dreams. Repeating a phrase like "I will remember my dreams" may increase your chances of recalling them when you wake up.

Stay still upon waking: Moving too quickly when you wake up can cause you to forget your dreams, so before you get out of bed, lie still for a few moments and try to focus on your dream. Sometimes a single image or emotion can trigger the memory of the entire dream.

Reflect on your day: Before bed, think about your day and journal about it. This can help create a connection between your waking and dreaming life and associate both with memories and self-reflection. Thus, this practice may make it easier to remember your dreams.

Practice mindfulness: Regular mindfulness and meditation practice can improve your overall awareness and attention, including your ability to remember dreams. Meditate before bed to clear your mind and prepare for a restful night’s sleep. These six tips for meditating in bed can help you get started.

Wake up naturally: Waking up suddenly can startle you into thinking intensely about the here and now, making it harder to remember dreams, so try to avoid using an alarm clock if you can. Pay attention to your body's natural sleep cycles and try to go to bed early enough to wake up naturally. If you need an alarm, set one that wakes you gently, perhaps with soft sounds or a sunrise effect.

Vivid dreams can be more engaging and memorable than other forms of dreaming that are less detailed.

Before falling asleep, visualize a recent dream or imagine a scenario you’d like to dream about in as much detail as possible. This can help stimulate your mind and lead to more vivid dreams.

Experiment with different sleeping positions to see if they influence the vividness of your dreams.

Get natural light during the day and reduce light exposure before bed to help regulate your sleep cycle and improve the quality of your REM sleep. Improving your sleep cycles and natural circadian rhythm may lead to more vivid dreams.

Creative activities like drawing, writing, or playing music can stimulate your imagination and enhance your dreams.

Meditate before bed to help calm your mind and prepare for a restful night’s sleep. This may increase the chances of having vivid dreams. As you’re releasing stresses from the day, you may create space for your subconscious mind to flourish as you rest. These 10 mindful activities can help you release stress quickly at the end of the day.

Some people use supplements like galantamine, choline, or vitamin B6 to try to enhance dream vividness. Consult a healthcare provider before using any supplements, as they can have side effects and interactions with other medications you’re already taking.

Once you’re remembering your dreams most mornings, you might get curious about steering them. That’s lucid dreaming: knowing you’re dreaming while it’s happening, which can let you look around, change the scene, or just enjoy the ride.

It takes practice, and it doesn’t happen for everyone. The good news is that things you may already be doing, like keeping a dream journal and setting an intention before bed, are also how many people start learning it.

If you’re curious, our step-by-step guide can help you learn how to lucid dream, with techniques like reality checks, MILD, and wake back to bed.

Certain foods and nutrients may influence your dreaming patterns. For example, foods containing tryptophan, like turkey and dairy products, can promote sleepiness and may impact the quality of your dreams. Foods rich in vitamin B6, like bananas, chickpeas, fish, and fortified cereals, may help with recall.

Eat a balanced diet with a variety of nutrients to support your overall sleep health, and avoid heavy meals and caffeine close to bedtime, as they can disrupt sleep and reduce dream frequency.

Several factors can affect your ability to remember dreams.

Poor sleep quality, such as disruptions in your sleep cycle, can hinder dream recall.

Stress or anxiety can interfere with sleep and make it harder to remember your dreams.

Sleep disorders like insomnia, sleep apnea, and restless leg syndrome disrupt sleep and impact dream recall.

Some medications, particularly those that affect the central nervous system, can interfere with dreaming.

Alcohol and drugs can alter sleep patterns and reduce the likelihood of remembering dreams.

A lack of interest in dreams can mean the brain doesn’t focus on retaining them.

Sleep disorders can significantly impact dreaming. Insomnia, which makes it difficult to fall or stay asleep, can reduce the amount of REM sleep you get, leading to fewer dreams and poorer dream recall.

Sleep apnea causes repeated interruptions in breathing during sleep, disrupting REM sleep cycles and reducing the frequency and vividness of dreams. Treatments like CPAP therapy for sleep apnea may improve sleep quality and dreaming.

Restless leg syndrome can also interfere with falling and staying asleep, which can impact dream frequency and recall.

Narcolepsy is marked by excessive daytime sleepiness and fragmented nighttime sleep. It may lead to vivid (and sometimes bizarre) dreams or dream-like hallucinations.

Generally, there are few risks to trying to dream more. Supplements like melatonin or galantamine may cause side effects or interact with other medications, so talk to your doctor before taking them.

Paying more attention to your dreams can sometimes lead to more vivid nightmares, especially if you have underlying anxiety or stress.

Understanding your dreams may reveal hidden thoughts, fears, and desires, and can help process emotions, particularly those you may not fully address during waking life. This may help in emotional healing.

Dreams can also offer creative solutions to problems or provide new perspectives for challenges you face in waking life.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

#28. Inside the Belly of the Beast

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated September 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina

I began writing professionally in 1985, something that feels like a lifetime ago. I was a young copywriter, and the pencil was still very much a tool of my trade. The Macintosh was new, and so was I. In a curious way, we grew up together, and I don't think that's inconsequential.

I watched the tools of writing change around me. Pencil and paper gave way to point and click, and eventually the internet and search became integral to the mechanics of writing. I embraced most of those changes. But the basic relationship remained rather mechanical and the graphical user interface was a tool to write something. That's what I thought.

But Large language models changed that relationship, almost overnight. Here was a technology that could work directly with an unfinished idea and do something with it. I could offer the machine a bit of a thought and get something back that might actually move the thought forward.

I jumped in headfirst, not realizing that my head (brain) was at the heart (soul) of this transformation.

I used LLMs a lot. From the exploration of ideas to a timely debate, I found something that I'd never experienced before. And I wasn't particularly interested in defending the ownership boundaries around writing. More importantly, I wanted to understand what happened when AI entered the process, with me, for me, and at times, without me.

Let me be blunt. In the beginning, I was a techno-optimist and maybe even one of those "tech bros" that populated social media. I became fascinated with an LLM's ability to move across tremendous bodies of information to bring distant concepts to my screen (and mind).

I eventually described this as the Corpus Cognitionis Humanae. I described how human knowledge was becoming accessible through a conversational interface. Suddenly, we could engage with knowledge rather than searching for it. From there came iterative intelligence, the back-and-forth process through which a person and an LLM can develop an idea. The back-and-forth process, for me, became sort of cognitively hypnotic or even meditative.

I still find this one of the most compelling and fascinating aspects of our interactions with LLMs. We begin with a prompt that is incomplete—by design. Now, what matters next is enlightening. Iteration builds insight and new thinking that can often take us on a journey where neither the path nor destination was previously known

AI didn't just hand me an answer, it put an unexpected idea in front of me that changed the direction of my thinking.

I'll argue that this is important and it's why I'm skeptical of those who reduce AI to just a tool for intellectual outsourcing. My experience doesn't support that conclusion at all. And after spending enough time inside that cognitive loop, I began to reject this over-simplification. In fact, I've recently become more interested in what was happening to the (my) thinking itself—the cognitive addition and subtraction and how that was potentially changing me.

Think about it. When an idea develops through many iterations with an LLM, it becomes difficult to determine where that thought really lives. I may start with the idea, but what comes back changes what I think next. And there you have a loop in the spirit of Douglas Hofstadter.

I've recently described this as thought losing its address. It pushes on the idea that thought has a biological home—there was a thinker somewhere in the process. Now, the recursive relationship with an LLM, particularly agentic AI, makes that address less obvious, if not downright invisible.

My long career as a writer gives me a unique comparison. I distinctly remember what it was like to have an idea that couldn't find its way to paper. There was no "second intelligence' waiting in the wings with a logical and coherent completion. So, I had to force ahead, often bound to a deadline.

However, some of that cognitive friction was pointless, and appropriately, technology got rid of it. But I'm no longer convinced that all this friction is something you just throw away in the pursuit of efficiency. The rub of the unfinished sentence against that unfinished thought is the friction of progress. And while LLMs are extraordinarily good at shortening that path, I'm not sure we understand everything that disappears when they do.

The "displacement" of thought brings me to the common claim of cognitive surrender. The phrase defines itself, but what makes this unusual and powerful is that we often don't notice it happening.

Less cognitive participation can exist along with better cognitive output.

This also connects to another idea I've written about, ghost thought. A traditional (and well-accepted) ghostwriter writes for you, but the underlying thinking is generally considered to be yours. Ghost thought pushes that construct further. The machine can become the thinker as well as the writer, even presenting the finished idea for our approval. At that point, we haven't just shortened the cognitive journey but abdicated it.

The unsettling part about ghost thought is that the result can still feel like yours.

Do you sense a struggle here? I hope so. And I guess what I'm trying to articulate here is that the human engagement with AI might be as complicated as the technology itself. I still remain a big fan of AI and I'm sure it has helped me think thoughts that I might never have had. I'm equally certain there have been times when I defaulted to AI's output too quickly. And when that happens, I precariously allow the machine to do the heavy lifting that I should (must) be doing.

After several years of working this way, I'm still not sure where the tool ends and my own cognition begins. And that's the question that keeps me up at night. I started writing when a pencil was still part of my working day. Today I work with a technology that can enter an unfinished thought and help determine where it goes. And I'm still trying to understand what that change means.

#29. The Lies We Heard (and Told Ourselves) About ADHD

The world is largely aware of ADHD, but does it truly understand? Jessica McCabe sees lots of room for improvement. Here, the founder of “How to ADHD” reflects on the persistent misconceptions, knowledge gaps, and threats facing people, especially mothers, with ADHD today.

Along the way, McCabe has become a certifiable ADHD spokesperson, a New York Times bestselling book author, and a mother. She has also contributed significantly to the growing de-stigmatization of ADHD and to a still-broiling conversation about how to better recognize and support women with ADHD.

“The more we talk about it, the more shame dissipates,” McCabe said during her recent ADDitude webinar, “The Lies We Were Told About ADHD: An ADHD Awareness Month Conversation.”

When McCabe posted her video, there was no YouTube #ADHD channel and TikTok did not yet exist. Today, social media is bursting with research, analysis, and validation. It’s also wrong more than it is right.

According to a 2025 study, more than half of the claims made in the Top 100 TikTok videos on ADHD were false. Almost 90% of videos were created by non-experts, and only about 20% of ADHD content was deemed clinically useful by trained professionals.1

[Get This Free Download: Fight Misinformation with These 11 Facts About ADHD]

“The [videos] that are validating and make you go ‘Yeah, that’s me,’ are not necessarily the ones that are accurate,” McCabe said.

She cited a claim circulating on social media that individuals with ADHD lack object permanence, as an example. Object permanence is the understanding that objects, people, and places continue to exist even when they cannot be seen. People with ADHD experience inattention and executive function challenges such as poor working memory, which may contribute to forgetfulness, but that is distinct from poor object permanence.

McCabe recommended checking sources on any health information found on social media. “Google Scholar it,” she said.

From a young age, people with ADHD hear that the frequency and intensity of their emotions are a problem. They’re told they are “too much,” and that their feelings overwhelm and distract others. McCabe says she grew up suppressing her emotions in hopes of combating that narrative. Now, she is working to actively “unlearn” that negative perception of her feelings, and she hopes others can do the same.

“Some of us have forgotten it’s okay to feel. It’s okay to have emotions when you have ADHD,” she said. “The emotions are not actually the problem. What you do with those emotions might be problematic, but by trying not to feel things, that actually creates other issues.”

Acknowledging and creating space for your emotions keeps them from exploding and/or festering — neither of which is healthy.

Executive dysfunction carries a lot of shame and guilt for people with ADHD. Society generally doesn’t recognize that challenges with working memory, organization, and prioritization, for example, are part and parcel of ADHD. Criticism is a constant, and many people add to the pressure by berating themselves with negative thoughts.

“When you don’t have an explanation, you accept the ones that are handed to you by society,” McCabe said. “It looked like I was flaky. It looked like I was uncommitted. It looked like I didn’t actually care about things.”

Executive functioning often fluctuates. Sometimes you can complete a task; other times, that same task feels impossible. In those moments, you may beat yourself up by saying, “I should be able to do this. Why can’t I do this?”

As McCabe shared, sleep quality, personal interest, support systems, and other factors influence a person’s ability to manage ADHD challenges in the moment. Not all of those factors are obvious, or within your control.

“A lot of those things are invisible, so unless you pick it apart and look at it, you don’t know why you’re struggling. You’re just like ‘I shouldn’t be,’” McCabe said. “Anytime I’m like ‘I should be able to do this,’ [I ask] what’s the evidence for that? Have you ever in your life been able to do this without help consistently? No? Then you shouldn’t.”

The effect of childbirth on the ADHD brain is largely unknown due to a critical research gap. What we do know is that women with ADHD are six times more likely to experience postpartum anxiety and five times more likely to experience postpartum depression than their neurotypical peers.

McCabe, who welcomed her daughter in 2024, suffered from postpartum depression. The supports she relied on during pregnancy stopped working and postpartum hormonal changes brought her to a very dark place mentally and emotionally. She was admitted to a partial hospitalization program for postpartum depression, where she received treatment while caring for her child.

As critical research slowly takes shape, McCabe believes strongly in normalizing this experience for mothers and entire families by talking openly about it.

“I think [the outcome] would’ve been different if I didn’t understand this wasn’t my fault that I was struggling,” she said. “Because the idea of what a mom is supposed to look like and what I looked like were so different that I could have piled so much shame on myself. And I think that shame would have made it so much worse. I wouldn’t have reached out for help. I wouldn’t have wanted to tell anybody I was having these thoughts or struggling with these things.”

“For so long we’ve been asking, ‘How do we get people with ADHD functional?’” she said. “Now I think we can ask a new question: How do we get them happy? How do we make it so they can live a good life? What does a good life with ADHD look like?”

Maybe the objective shouldn’t be to never struggle with focus, time management, memory, or emotional regulation ever again, but to use the tools you’ve developed to build a life that looks good and feels comfortable to you.

“Success and happiness to me with my ADHD is like having this powerful stallion that I know how to take care of, ride, accomplish incredible things, have excitement and adventures, handle the rough and challenging moments, while not getting bucked off, trampled, or left behind in the dust,” Katherine, an ADDitude reader, commented during the live event. “It’s still now working to unlearn all of the suppressive things taught through school that wanted to teach me to break the spirit of the stallion, whip it into submission, and then lock it in the stable and feel ashamed of it and what it needs instead of learning how to work and thrive with it.”

#30. How to Stop Waiting and Start Living: A Jolt from Henry James

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. “The things we want are transformative, and we don’t know or only think we know what is on the other side of that transformation,” Rebecca Solnit wrote in her exquisite Field Guide to Getting Lost.

The wanting starts out innocently — awaiting the birthday, the new bicycle, Christmas morning; awaiting the school year to end, or to begin. Soon, we are awaiting the big break, the great love, the day we finally find ourselves — awaiting something or someone to deliver us from the tedium of life-as-it-is, into some other and more dazzling realm of life-as-it-could-be, all the while vacating the only sanctuary from the storm of uncertainty raging outside the frosted windows of the here and now.

It matters not at all whether we are holding our breath for a triumph or bracing for a tragedy. For as long as we are waiting, we are not living.

If we are not careful enough with the momentum of our own minds, we can live out our days in this expectant near-life existence.

That is what Henry James (April 13, 1843–February 28, 1916) explores in his 1903 novella The Beast in the Jungle, found in his collection The Better Sort (public library | public domain) — the story of a man whose entire life, from his earliest memory, has been animated by “the sense of being kept for something rare and strange, possibly prodigious and terrible,” something fated “sooner or later to happen” and, in happening, to either destroy him or remake his life. He calls it “the thing,” imagines it as a “beast in the jungle” lying in wait for him, and spends his life lying in wait for it, withholding his participation in the very experiences that might have that transformative effect — leaping after some great dream, risking his life for some great cause, falling in love.

It is, of course, a dramatized caricature of our common curse — the treacherous “if only” mind that haunts all of us, in one way or another, to some degree or other, as we go through life expecting the next moment to contain what this one does not and, in granting us some mythic missing piece that forever keeps us from the warm glad feeling of enoughness, to render our lives worthy of having been lived.

Since it was in Time that he was to have met his fate, so it was in Time that his fate was to have acted; and as he waked up to the sense of no longer being young, which was exactly the sense of being stale, just as that, in turn, was the sense of being weak, he waked up to another matter beside. It all hung together; they were subject, he and the great vagueness, to an equal and indivisible law. When the possibilities themselves had accordingly turned stale, when the secret of the gods had grown faint, had perhaps even quite evaporated, that, and that only, was failure. It wouldn’t have been failure to be bankrupt, dishonoured, pilloried, hanged; it was failure not to be anything.

When the protagonist meets a woman to whom his entire being pulls him, he begins spending time with her but ultimately keeps her heart at arm’s length, too afraid to love her, telling himself that he is protecting her from his fatalistic fate, failing to recognize that love itself is that great force of self-annihilation and transformation, “rare and strange” even as the most commonplace human experience.

When Time forecloses possibility, as Time always ultimately does, he arrives at his final reckoning at her tombstone:

The escape would have been to love her; then, then he would have lived. She had lived — who could say now with what passion? — since she had loved him for himself… The Beast had lurked indeed, and the Beast, at its hour, had sprung; it had sprung in that twilight of the cold April when, pale, ill, wasted, but all beautiful, and perhaps even then recoverable, she had risen from her chair to stand before him and let him imaginably guess. It had sprung as he didn’t guess; it had sprung as she hopelessly turned from him, and the mark, by the time he left her, had fallen where it was to fall. He had justified his fear and achieved his fate; he had failed, with the last exactitude, of all he was to fail of; and a moan now rose to his lips… This was knowledge, knowledge under the breath of which the very tears in his eyes seemed to freeze. Through them, none the less, he tried to fix it and hold it; he kept it there before him so that he might feel the pain. That at least, belated and bitter, had something of the taste of life. But the bitterness suddenly sickened him, and it was as if, horribly, he saw, in the truth, in the cruelty of his image, what had been appointed and done. He saw the Jungle of his life and saw the lurking Beast; then, while he looked, perceived it, as by a stir of the air, rise, huge and hideous, for the leap that was to settle him. His eyes darkened — it was close; and, instinctively turning, in his hallucination, to avoid it, he flung himself, face down, on the tomb.

Complement with Anaïs Nin on how reading awakens us from the trance of near-living and Mary Oliver on the key to living with maximum aliveness, then revisit Henry James’s equally brilliant sister Alice on how to live fully while dying.

#31. How Do You Raise Kids to Be Emotionally Mature?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Raising a teen is one of the last chapters in parenting. During these years, it’s easy to prioritize your child’s grades, sports, and other accolades, especially as they inch toward leaving the nest.

While achievement is one marker of success, there’s another (often overlooked) skill that shapes your teen’s well-being and development: emotional maturity.

According to clinical psychologist Lindsay Gibson, emotional maturity develops through deep emotional connections, beginning with a child’s parents and primary caretakers. Research shows emotional maturity is the ability to accept and express care, temper big feelings, and make wise choices. Without it, teens are more likely to feel lonely and less satisfied with life, one study found.

In her latest book, How to Raise an Emotionally Mature Child, Gibson points out that “the quality of humanity’s future depends on the emotional maturity of coming generations.”

Juli Fraga: In your book, you mention that humanity’s future will depend on emotional maturity. Why does this matter so much right now?

Lindsay Gibson: Emotional maturity is critical to our well-being as individuals and to the smooth, productive, and innovative aspects of society. When you’re emotionally mature, you can think and anticipate consequences. You can also look back and learn from what you’ve done before. So, you can rely on your thinking to help you deal with reality. Emotional maturity also means tuning into your inner world, including your emotions, imagination, hopes, dreams, connections to other people, and sense of belonging.

JF: Our society places a lot of emphasis on achievement, and less importance on emotional intelligence. How can parents help their teens balance the two?

LG: There’s a real cultural pull in society to prize intelligence and achievement. But when parents get too fixated on these qualities, a child may feel like performance matters more than their thoughts, feelings, and sense of safety.

Kids need to be safely held and supported through the growing-up process. It helps them feel resilient, secure, and confident—qualities they need to take out into the world to function independently. If you get too fixated on the intelligence and achievement parts, you’ve got someone who’s very powerful in one area, but whose emotional side may be underdeveloped. It’s the balance between the two that matters.

JF: In your book, you mention why it’s so important for parents to help their kids develop a sense of self. Can you explain why this matters, especially during the teen years when kids are individuating?

LG: One way teens find out who they are is by discovering who they’re not. Teens might push a limit or break a rule, and it’s all par for the course. What’s important for parents is to be able to recognize and imagine that their child has a separate heart and mind from theirs—a process called “mentalization.”

A self is that inner spark that speaks to us. It says “don’t do that” or “now’s the time to go for it.” It guides you toward what’s most compatible with your individuality and who you are meant to be.

Our sense of self comes from our relationships with people we love and who love us. To feel secure, kids need solid, dependable, connected, and deeply resonant relationships with their parents and caretakers. They need parents who are curious and reflect something back that’s meaningful about who the young person is. When they have that foundation, they have a sense of being a real person inside.

JF: Parents are so busy these days, and overloaded—mentally and emotionally. Raising emotionally mature kids may feel like another big to-do on an already long list. What advice do you have?

LG: Taking time to pause and take your child seriously as a real person will work wonders for their self-confidence and future resilience.

Slowing down takes practice because by the time you’re old enough to have a family, you’ve probably been very goal-directed; parents can be pretty hard on themselves because our culture is so fixated on achievement.

But pulling yourself away from your goal for even a second to tend to your child is something worth practicing because that’s what children’s needs are all about. Kids also develop confidence when they know they matter just as much as anybody else.

JF: What are some behaviors that are normal for teens but that parents might misinterpret as pushback or misbehavior?

LG: Sometimes teens experiment with saying or doing things that clash with their socialization up to that point, such as the language they use or the clothes they wear. These are things that the parent can feel like, “Whoa, I’m uncomfortable with this…”

Here are two meaningful ways to navigate these moments.

Ask your teen questions about what they’re into, such as the styles they like or what they admire about someone they idolize. Try showing interest, not intrusive interest, but just interest in what they like, or why they are experimenting with different things.

Keep in mind that when your teen snaps at you, is in a bad mood, or slams the door, their emotional centers are activated in a way that will probably never be repeated in their life because their brains prioritize emotional development first during this stage.

JF: Can you share more about why a teen’s development follows this trajectory?

LG: Yeah, I know it’s easy to ask, “Why in the world would nature do it that way?” It’s because that’s how important the emotional self and relationships are to our real success as independent adults.

As adults, we have to know ourselves inside and out and use our feelings to guide us. Teens are still trying to work this out. Learning how to handle these emotions takes a lot of practice. They’re finding out what it’s like to feel rage, or what it’s like to be in love, or to feel disappointed. And they’re feeling them in the most intense way they ever will, because the brain is taking on the job of developing them into a really deep, complete human being.

JF: What advice do you have for parents when their teen’s emotions push their own buttons?

LG: Keep in mind that when your teen responds in an adamant, emotional, defiant way, or calls you names, they’re not really in command of those emotions yet.

Instead of coming down hard with words that suggest they’re not a good person, try to respond with: “I’m really interested in how you feel about this. I want to hear your arguments, but when you call me a name, it makes it impossible for me to be available to you. It just doesn’t work. We don’t call each other names in this family. That won’t work when you’re an adult, either.”

The interaction then becomes an education about how people respond to different kinds of approaches. Harshness that stops a teen cold shuts down their impulse to communicate their feelings to other people, which isn’t good for resilience or honest relationships.

JF: What are two things that parents do to foster emotional maturity that can actually backfire?

LG: One is the importance of achievement, of having a good resume. Of course, parents know how hard life is as an adult. We feel it’s our duty to convey these realizations to our kids. But when it becomes something that feels like everything else will fall into place if you do these things first or achieve X, we are not helping our kids with the emotional or interpersonal side of life. We’re creating a one-dimensional kind of person.

Sometimes parents also think that if they don’t give their child severe consequences or punishments, the child won’t learn and mature. When you try to convey information through punishment, you actually teach a child to defer to other people’s anger and control. Of course, we want them to be aware of consequences, but sometimes we can go too far. You can’t have a full, right life if you’re always anticipating that somebody might be mad at you.

#33. Restless Legs in Pregnancy Triples Depression Risk

A prospective study of more than 2,400 pregnant women reveals that developing restless legs syndrome (RLS) during pregnancy is tied to a threefold increase in the risk of perinatal depression. The vulnerability peaks during the third trimester, when severe evening leg discomfort and sleep disruption compound emotional strain, highlighting late-pregnancy RLS screening as a vital opportunity for early maternal mental health intervention.

Source: American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) / University of Tokyo

Perinatal depression, encompassing major depressive episodes occurring during pregnancy or across the vulnerable first months postpartum, affects millions of new mothers worldwide, impairing maternal health and early infant bonding. While biological, hormonal, and psychosocial stressors are well-known contributors, sleep-related movement disorders have largely flown under the diagnostic radar.

Now, a prospective investigation led by researchers from the University of Tokyo Graduate School of Medicine points to restless legs syndrome (RLS) as a substantial clinical warning sign for perinatal mental health decline.

Publishing in the Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine, the official publication of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, the team followed 2,435 pregnant women in Japan to trace the connection between gestational RLS onset and subsequent depressive episodes through three months after childbirth.

Restless legs syndrome is a sensorimotor neurological disorder defined by an irresistible urge to move the legs, typically driven by unpleasant creeping, crawling, or pulling sensations deep within the limbs. Because these symptoms emerge during rest, peak late in the evening, and temporarily resolve only with active movement, RLS causes severe sleep fragmentation, prolonging the time it takes to fall asleep and destroying restorative slow-wave rest.

In the general adult population, individuals with RLS experience depression and anxiety at approximately four times the national average. During pregnancy, physiological shifts, including fluctuating dopamine levels, surging estrogen, and transient maternal iron deficiency, frequently trigger or unmask dormant RLS symptoms.

The Tokyo study tracked women across gestation: 1.6% (40 participants) screened positive for RLS during their second trimester, while prevalence climbed to 3.5% (60 participants) by the third trimester. Following delivery, 69 women across the broader cohort developed full clinical perinatal depression.

The statistical modeling delivered a stark correlation: pregnant women with RLS were three times more likely to experience perinatal depression and twice as likely to report clinically meaningful depressive symptoms.

“We found that pregnant women with restless legs syndrome had about three times the risk of developing perinatal depression,” said lead author Kazuhide Tezuka, MD, PhD, a visiting researcher in the Department of Mental Health at the University of Tokyo Graduate School of Medicine. “This association was seen for restless legs syndrome identified in the third trimester, but not in the second.”

Crucially, this vulnerability held firm after adjusting for confounding variables including maternal age, education level, socioeconomic indicators, partner support, number of prior children, and pregnancy intention.

The finding that risk concentrates in the third trimester reflects the cumulative biological strain of late pregnancy. As fetal growth peaks, physical discomfort and insomnia are already pronounced; the sudden onset of persistent nocturnal leg agitation can push an already strained neurobiological system into severe affective distress.

Currently, routine prenatal intake forms assess sleep and movement complaints predominantly in the first trimester, if at all. Because gestational RLS predominantly manifests as the third trimester approaches, standard clinical evaluations frequently miss the disorder entirely.

“Because restless legs syndrome often develops later in pregnancy, asking about its symptoms again in the third trimester, not just at early prenatal visits, may help healthcare providers identify women at higher risk of perinatal depression,” emphasized Tezuka.

The researchers noted several study caveats: the observed RLS prevalence in this cohort was lower than typical Western cohorts, the overall count of depressive episodes among RLS-affected mothers was modest, and measures relied on validated self-reported instruments.

Nevertheless, recognizing RLS as an early biomarker provides clinicians with a concrete, actionable intervention point. Future research will explore whether non-pharmacological RLS treatments, such as targeted iron supplementation, stretching regimens, and specialized sleep hygiene, can directly lower subsequent rates of postpartum and perinatal depression, protecting both mother and child during the transition into parenthood.

Time-varying restless legs syndrome and risk of incident perinatal depression

Previous studies have reported associations between restless legs syndrome (RLS) and perinatal depressive symptoms. However, no study has used diagnostic instruments to examine changes in RLS status during pregnancy in relation to the incidence of perinatal depression. This study aimed to investigate whether time-varying RLS status is associated with an increased risk of incident perinatal depression.

This prospective cohort study analyzed data from 2435 Japanese pregnant women in the control group of a randomized controlled trial on perinatal depression. Time-varying RLS status was assessed using data obtained in the second and third trimesters with the short form of the Cambridge–Hopkins diagnostic questionnaire. Incident major depressive episodes and depressive symptoms from the second trimester to 3 months postpartum were assessed using the self-administered World Health Organization Composite International Diagnostic Interview 3.0 and the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS), respectively. Associations were examined using Cox proportional hazards models with time-varying covariates.

The prevalence of RLS was 40 (1.6%) in the second trimester and 60 (3.5%) in the third trimester. During a mean follow-up of 6.5 months (SD, 3.2), 69 participants developed perinatal depression. Time-varying RLS status was significantly associated with an increased risk of incident perinatal depression (hazard ratio [HR], 3.04; 95% CI, 1.22–7.58) and depressive symptoms (EPDS ≥ 13; HR, 2.12; 95% CI, 1.28–3.51). These associations remained robust after adjustment for potential confounders.

RLS, modeled as a time-varying condition, was associated with an increased risk of incident perinatal depression, suggesting the importance of screening for RLS during pregnancy for the prevention of perinatal depression.

RLS is common during pregnancy and has been linked to depressive symptoms, possibly through shared pathophysiological mechanisms such as sleep disturbances and iron deficiency; however, longitudinal evidence using diagnostic instruments remains limited. This study examined whether time-varying RLS status is associated with incident perinatal depression.

Pregnant women with RLS, particularly in the third trimester, had an increased risk of perinatal depression, suggesting the clinical importance of routine RLS screening to support timely treatment and potentially prevent perinatal depression. Increased awareness of RLS among pregnant women and healthcare providers may promote early identification of individuals at higher risk. However, whether RLS treatment can reduce perinatal depression risk requires further investigation.

#34. Why Can’t We Rest Anymore?

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

We have more technological assistance with daily tasks, more self-care, and more sedentary hours than any previous generation. So why are we still so exhausted? And what do we actually need to help us feel restored?

When I was a student at Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism in 2016, I thought it would be a good idea to write about the appropriation of mindfulness by corporate America for my Master’s project. What I discovered during the course of my reporting was a paradox.

When I spoke to those who understood Buddhism, they referred to mindfulness as a way of life where simplicity and slowness are important. When I spoke to those who used it at their corporate jobs with multi-national companies, they felt it helped them meet their targets, respond to rude emails with courtesy, or even let go of their employees in a gentler way. Finally, there were those who built a business around it, earning their livelihood in New York City by selling mindfulness as a productivity tool to manage workplace stress.

To me, all of these stories felt inherently at odds with each other.

In 2023, John Mark Comer, a young American pastor, shot to fame when he published his book, The Ruthless Elimination of Hurry, which was an instant hit even amongst secular millennials. Comer’s book is written like a really long social media post and is devoid of research, prose, or narrative depth. It’s tough to know if that was a deliberate strategy to target younger audiences, but some of his tips such as shutting off smartphone notifications, turning screen devices to grayscale display, and basically adopting a more offline life resonated with many young burnt-out Americans. Today, he is a veritable celebrity with almost 300,000 followers on Instagram.

In his book, The Burnout Society, the South Korean philosopher Byung-Chul Han illustrates how our society today is a fundamentally “achievement-society” which prizes the object of achievement over everything else. As the pace of life increases, our sprint towards achievement becomes more frenetic. He explains, “[T]he capitalist economy absolutizes survival. It is not concerned with the good life. It is sustained by the illusion that more capital produces more life, which means a greater capacity for living. Concern about living the good life yields to the hysteria of surviving.”

In this worldview, rest is absent, yet somehow physical health becomes more important than ever before, because it is only through a healthy body that the ego can go on amassing more and more.

All the great wisdom traditions of the world emphasize stillness as the doorway to not just the divine but also rest. But rest from what?

He also makes the startling observation that it is an illusion to believe that being more active means being freer. So even when we think we are resting—travelling the world, preparing an aesthetic Buddha bowl, enjoying copious amounts of alcohol, processed food and loud music (partying, in other words), or simply scrolling through social media at the end of a hectic day—we are still only laboring under the illusion of rest. Our minds and bodies are just as much at work in this form of rest, perhaps even more than our regular routines. We keep chasing rest but never manage to feel rested enough.

All the great wisdom traditions of the world emphasize stillness as the doorway to not just the divine but also rest. But rest from what?

In the first book of the Torah, for instance, it is rest from the work of creation of the world. It is not fatigue but an intentional withdrawal from life to absorb the creation itself, which is best done in stillness rather than a raucous celebration. This is where the idea of Sabbath comes from, derived from the Hebrew Shabbat, which meant “ceased” or “came to a stop,” with the implication that intentional rest was taking place.

Comer, too, encourages his followers to practice Sabbath, including fasting, and it is in this context that his popularity becomes relevant. Millennials are not necessarily looking for a higher power but rather a near-total rest from the unceasing busyness of their lives.

But here’s another paradox: human life today is the most sedentary it has ever been, thanks to technological developments which would have seemed God-like to our ancestors only a few generations before us. So why are we so tired, and why do we seek rest?

In order to understand this better, it might be more insightful to look at a potential meaning of rest. In his book Consolations, the Irish poet David Whyte writes of rest as “the conversation between what we love to do and how we love to be.” He meditates on the topic further, writing:

What Whyte outlines here is life as a constant attempt at aligning our inner and outer worlds. Rest, then, is the moment where that alignment becomes manifest. The poet, who has worked with corporate America and is also a Zen practitioner, opens up a whole new possibility of what it means to be at rest when he makes the case that it may manifest at any time, be it joy or sorrow. It is rest because it takes us from being at war with reality to a reconciliation with it.

Rest is not mere ceasing of tiresome physical or mental activity, as we commonly believe today, but a sense of acceptance about who we are, what life in this world is, and our place in it.

Rest is not mere ceasing of tiresome physical or mental activity, as we commonly believe today, but a sense of acceptance about who we are, what life in this world is, and our place in it. Rest is letting go of our desire to control our lives and the world.

While I don’t know if most people would agree with this definition of rest, it does make you wonder if our inability to find true rest today goes beyond the training of the mind. Meaning: Is it really a spiritual and existential crisis in disguise? We are so accustomed to turning to consumerism as the one-stop solution to our problems that it seems almost gob-smacking that our answers may lie in not just our ability to turn away from consumerism,  but in developing the ability to converse meaningfully with our inner and outer spheres of reality.

When I started researching for my long-form story about mindfulness as a grad student, the first relevant material I came across was the idea of Slow movement. As someone who enjoys slowness in life, it seemed perfect. But the more I dug into it, the more the paradox emerged.

The movement began as a sort of a protest in none other than Italy, the land of la dolce vita, or the sweet life. As one of the countries with the best life expectancy, there are things older Italians do differently than their counterparts in the Western world. They take longer to finish their meals, spend time with their friends and family members daily, eat lots of fat and drink as much wine, and perhaps most importantly, do not chase consumerism as an end goal of life.

They also take immense pride in their cultural inheritance and are not distracted by foreign influences. Which is why it is little wonder that Carlo Petrini protested against the opening of a McDonald’s outlet in Rome in 1986. It was the birth of Slow Food movement which eventually gave way to many other Slow movements such as art, fashion, education, media, economy, parenting, and even travel.

Many of these movements had their heart in the right place, but in some cases the mind took over quickly enough. The movements often turn into books, podcasts, courses, and businesses where the core message of slowness slowly becomes lost on their progenitors. When I tried to get in touch with a prominent American journalist who had written a book about mindful work, I had a hard time fixing an interview appointment with him as he was busy traveling, delivering talks, and giving interviews. Eventually we could not schedule an interview at all. I was amused but also perplexed as to why he wasn’t taking his own advice.

The question remains: Why can’t we truly slow down to the point of stillness?

For one, it is because the world around us is accelerating at an increasing speed. To not keep up would be to fall behind.

What the wisdom traditions define as stillness is a reservoir for receiving the life that is meant for us. But too often, we think of that stillness as emptiness that must be filled up with anything and everything until it quiets our inner discomfort.

But if we probe deeper, something slightly more disturbing reveals itself. What the wisdom traditions define as stillness is a reservoir for receiving the life that is meant for us. But too often, we think of that stillness as emptiness that must be filled up with anything and everything until it quiets our inner discomfort.

The result is a constant state of panic and dissatisfaction at not being able to achieve the imagined life. In this scenario, rest not only becomes impossible but in fact, it becomes an affront to the personal ego. To rest would be to allow the ego to be defeated, and modern culture does not make space for that kind of an experience. When this becomes the pathology of a global collective, it becomes an acute existential crisis for the entire world.

This collective pathology ensnares all of us in its desire for speedy accumulation, which can only lead to increasingly intense conflicts amongst each other.

As distressing as this is, is there a remedy?

For Byung-Chul Han, the insight lies in the observation that the “late-modern ego has no character” and is extremely flexible. This flexibility makes it suitable for rapid technological and economic changes, because it makes us all more efficient cogs in the wheel. But what this means is that this ego rejects conflict resolution, whether internally or externally, due to modern emphasis on ideas of freedom, deregulation, and self-absorption. It either tends towards extreme expression or extreme repression, neither of which facilitate in us that “living conversation” that Whyte nudges us towards.

Conventional advice around rest tends to follow predictable narratives. It asks us to limit our exposure to screens, reduce our social media usage, spend time in nature, share meals with loved ones, sleep better, or pursue a hobby. While all of this is good advice, it only helps our minds and bodies feel rested.

For the deepest parts of us—what so many writers, thinkers, poets, and teachers might call our souls—to experience genuine restoration, we might benefit from heeding the higher call for rest. In fostering stillness within, we might even find it in ourselves to extend that rest to the world outside of us.

Garima Garg is a New Delhi based journalist and author. Most recently, she published her debut non-fiction book, Heavens and Earth: Story of Astrology Through Ages and Cultures, with Penguin Random House India in 2022. She writes about culture, with an emphasis on how modernity interacts with religion and spirituality.
