#46. 7 types of anxiety disorders (and how to deal with each one)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Your heart starts racing the moment you walk into a crowded room. Even when nothing’s wrong, worry looms in the back of your mind. The thought of a specific fear, like snakes or needles, makes you feel sick. If any of that sounds familiar, anxiety might be part of the picture.

Anxiety doesn't look the same for everyone, which is sometimes why it can be so hard to name. The term "anxiety" covers several disorders, each with its own signs and triggers — though they often overlap, both in how they show up and in what helps.

Anxiety disorders affect roughly 1 in 5 U.S. adults every year. The good news is, they’re typically quite treatable. Let’s break down the seven main types of anxiety listed in the DSM-5 (the manual used for clinical diagnosis), and how to find some relief.

The seven anxiety disorders below share a general thread: they’re rooted in fear or worry that sticks around and gets in the way of daily life. They’re also the most common types, though a few related conditions are worth knowing too (covered further down).

GAD is a persistent, hard-to-control worry that spans multiple areas of your life and shows up more days than not for at least six months. Everyday stress usually has a clear cause and fades once the situation resolves. By contrast, generalized anxiety moves from topic to topic and rarely lets up, because your mind treats any uncertainty as a threat.

This disorder often comes with physical and mental symptoms such as restlessness, muscle tension, fatigue, trouble concentrating, irritability, and disrupted sleep.

What helps: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is widely used for GAD. It helps you spot and shift the thought patterns that fuel your worries. A regular mindfulness practice can also ease tension by training your attention to stay in the present instead of running through what-ifs.

💙 Start with Calm’s Tools for Stress and Anxiety series.

For a more detailed overview, check out our GAD guide.

A panic attack is a sudden rush of intense fear that brings on physical symptoms—racing heart, tight chest, dizziness—and usually peaks within minutes. A single panic attack doesn't mean you have panic disorder — plenty of people experience one and never have another.

Panic disorder is defined by what comes after the attack, such as ongoing dread about when the next one might hit and routine changes made to avoid triggering one.

This fear response tends to feed itself in a cycle. A normal body signal, like a fast heartbeat, gets misread as danger. That triggers more fear, which leads to more physical symptoms.

What helps: CBT can help you learn to read these body signals as harmless rather than dangerous. It’s often paired with interoceptive exposure, where you deliberately bring on mild versions of those same sensations until they stop feeling threatening. During this process, slow breathing can signal safety to your nervous system.

Discover 5 mindfulness tools to calm you down during a panic attack.

Social anxiety disorder is a strong fear that you’ll be negatively perceived in social or performance situations, often severe enough that dread sets in days before the event itself.

It's much more than being shy. At its core is a belief that you'll do something embarrassing and be judged for it. That belief may lead you to avoid those situations altogether, which can bring short-term relief but reinforces the fear over time.

What helps: Exposure-based CBT has the strongest evidence. It gradually builds your comfort in the situations you've been avoiding by facing them in small, manageable steps. Self-compassion can also make a real difference. Since social anxiety tends to run on harsh self-judgment, practicing kindness toward yourself can help quiet that inner critic.

Not sure if you have social anxiety? Here are signs to look out for.

A specific phobia is a fear of one particular thing—like heights, flying, needles, dogs, or tight spaces—out of proportion to the actual danger. A fear becomes a phobia when it impacts your behavior, whether that’s rerouting a drive to avoid a bridge or skipping a checkup because of needles. Even thinking about the trigger can set off anxiety, so avoiding it becomes your default.

Phobias often start with a scary experience or a fear picked up early in life. Avoidance keeps the fear alive, since your brain never learns that the trigger is safe.

What helps: Exposure therapy is the leading treatment, shown to outperform placebo and other therapies. Pair each step with grounding and breathing techniques to make the process feel more manageable.

Explore the most common phobias and how to deal with them.

Agoraphobia is a fear of being somewhere you couldn't easily escape or get help if panic or embarrassing symptoms hit. This can include public transit, open spaces, crowds, lines, or long stretches away from home alone. Many people with agoraphobia avoid those places altogether.

The DSM-5 classifies it as its own diagnosis. Left untreated, this avoidance can shrink your world, sometimes making it hard to leave the house at all.

What helps: CBT with step-by-step exposure is the first-line treatment, and it helps you return to avoided places gradually. Since agoraphobia and panic often overlap, treatment usually addresses both. To build confidence, try calming techniques at home first, then in triggering places.

Learn 8 evidence-backed ways to manage agoraphobia.

Separation anxiety disorder is an excessive fear about being away from people you're close to. Once seen as a childhood condition, it’s now known to affect adults too. It can show up as real distress when a partner travels or constant worry that something bad will happen to a loved one.

Underneath it is a fear of loss: of the person or of your own ability to cope without them. You may find yourself seeking reassurance or checking in repeatedly, but these responses tend to feed the anxiety rather than calm it.

What helps: CBT can help you reduce your need for reassurance and build comfort with time apart. Mindfulness encourages you to pause when an anxious thought arises and let the worry pass. For severe cases, a doctor may suggest therapy alongside medication.

💙 Practice riding out anxious thoughts with Calm’s Letting Go of Anxiety course.

Selective mutism is an inability to speak in certain social settings where talking is expected, like school or work. It's rare, affecting under 2% of people, and it usually shows up in childhood, though it can last into later years.

This isn't stubbornness or a speech problem — it's fear. You may want to speak, but hold back because of it in those environments.

What helps: Behavioral therapy that slowly builds up speaking in those settings, often involving family or school staff, is the main approach. Early intervention tends to lead to better outcomes, so it’s worth seeking professional guidance as soon as symptoms appear.

While the disorders above are what most people mean by "anxiety," a few related conditions are helpful to understand for the full picture.

Two more fall under the DSM-5's anxiety chapter:

Substance or medication-induced anxiety disorder: This anxiety is caused directly by a substance, whether that’s too much caffeine, a prescription drug, or withdrawal from alcohol. It can be overlooked, which is why a doctor will often ask what you're taking before making a diagnosis.

Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition: A physical illness—such as an overactive thyroid or a heart or lung problem—can cause anxiety. A checkup can rule out this possibility early on, and treating the underlying illness often eases the anxiety too.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) get grouped with anxiety disorders a lot, as they also involve overwhelming fear and distress. But the DSM-5 classifies them separately: OCD centers on unwanted thoughts and behaviors, while PTSD comes after a traumatic event.

If either sounds closer to what you're dealing with, our OCD guide or our complex PTSD guide is a good place to start.

Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and panic disorder differ mainly in how the worry builds and shows up. GAD involves a slow-burning worry about many areas of life that rarely fades. Panic disorder centers on sudden, intense attacks and the fear of having another one. It’s possible to have both, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) works well for either.

Curious about CBT for anxiety? Here are 5 techniques to try.

The difference between having social anxiety and being introverted comes down to preference versus fear. Introversion is a preference about how you recharge — social time drains your energy, but it doesn't fill you with dread. Social anxiety, meanwhile, brings a fear of judgment or embarrassment, often strong enough to make you skip things you'd enjoy.

It’s not unusual to have more than one anxiety disorder at the same time, and they can show up alongside other conditions including depression. A doctor can help you sort out which ones you’re dealing with, and treatments like CBT can target several disorders at once.

A specific phobia and agoraphobia differ in what the fear is tied to. A specific phobia is about one clear trigger, such as spiders or flying. Agoraphobia is broader: it's a fear of being somewhere you couldn't easily escape or get help, like a crowd or public transit.

The most common types of anxiety in adults are specific phobias, social anxiety disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder. Altogether, anxiety disorders affect close to 1 in 5 U.S. adults each year and are the most prevalent type of mental health condition.

Anxiety disorders can ease on their own for some people, but many stick around or return without treatment. Fortunately, treatment can meaningfully improve your quality of life. Most people find that therapy, medication, or a combination makes a noticeable difference.

The most well-supported therapy for anxiety disorders is cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), often paired with gradual exposure work. Medication is another option with strong evidence, either used alone or alongside therapy. The right fit depends on your specific disorder and its severity, so it's important to consult a professional.

There are several natural ways to manage anxiety, though they aren’t a replacement for clinical treatment. Regular exercise, quality sleep, and cutting back on caffeine and alcohol can all help alleviate how anxious you feel day to day. Mindfulness practices (like breathing exercises or grounding techniques) are especially well-supported, since they teach you to notice anxious thoughts or sensations without getting swept up in them.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

#47. The Power of the Pause: A Simple Way to Begin Your Practice of Not Reacting

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

One of the core principles of mindfulness is learning the practice of not reacting to everything that's going on inside and around us. But where do we begin?

Our days are made up of countless small reactions to the outside world. A short email from a colleague can put us in a bad mood for the afternoon, a criticism from a partner can linger for days, or an ordinary disappointment can suddenly make us question everything.

We tend to think the problem is whatever has happened to us: the difficult person, the frustrating job, the argument, the mistake, the uncertainty about the future. But what if some of our suffering comes not only from what happens to us, but also from how we react to it?

We tend to think the problem is whatever has happened to us: the difficult person, the frustrating job, the argument, the mistake, the uncertainty about the future. But there is another way to look at these experiences. What if some of our suffering comes not only from what happens to us, but also from how we react to it?

This perspective draws on Buddhist teachings about the relationship between craving, attachment, and suffering, and it offers a surprisingly practical way to approach the stresses of modern life. Behind every problem is a reaction of the mind. The goal isn’t to eliminate difficult emotions or convince ourselves that everything is fine. It’s to understand what is happening in the mind so we have more choice in how we respond.

Everyday annoyances, disappointments, pressures, regrets, and anxieties can all become overwhelming when we get caught in cycles of reacting to them. Pausing before we respond doesn’t mean suppressing emotions, brushing things off, or pretending not to care. It means recognizing our automatic reactions and creating space to choose what happens next.

You can be angry without lashing out. You can be disappointed without getting caught in a cycle of replaying what happened. You can feel anxious without following every worried thought into the future. The feeling itself isn’t necessarily the problem. What matters is how we relate to it and what we choose to do next.

Buddhism often points to attachment—the inability to let go—as a source of suffering. We cling to desires, regrets, anger, fears, and expectations.

Closely connected to this attachment are the habitual ways our minds react to experiences. We get annoyed when things don’t go our way. We worry about what other people think. We replay mistakes and wonder what we should have done differently. We overthink and convince ourselves that we aren’t good enough. These reactions can spill directly into our lives, sometimes leading us to lash out at people we care about, buckle under pressure, or remain trapped in regret.

One thought produces another, and soon the original event is buried beneath an entire chain of reactions.

Think about how this works in everyday life. Maybe your boss gives you feedback that feels dismissive. The event itself takes only a few seconds. But afterward, the mind gets to work. They don’t respect me. Maybe I’m bad at my job. Why did they say it that way? I should have said something back. One thought produces another, and soon the original event is buried beneath an entire chain of reactions.

The same thing can happen in relationships. Someone doesn’t text back. Your partner seems distracted at dinner. A friend makes a comment that lands badly. Before you have all the facts, your mind has already constructed an explanation. You may feel rejected, angry, unappreciated, or defensive—and then respond to the story in your head as though it were established reality.

One way to apply the Buddhist mindfulness teachings is to begin by noticing that process. Instead of immediately asking, How do I fix this situation? We might first ask, What is happening in my mind right now?

Rather than being carried away by the reaction, pause and observe what is happening. Bhuddism’s approach is to look beneath the individual incident and examine the pattern.

Suffering is connected to tanha, or craving—the underlying current of wanting that shapes how we think, feel, and act. The mind is continually moving toward something: safety, comfort, pleasure, rest, intimacy, ease, or recognition.

We want something. We don’t get it. We react. Or: we get what we want. For a moment, we feel satisfied. Then the mind wants something else.

While we can’t necessarily eliminate every desire, recognizing our habitual patterns of craving may help us change how we relate to them.

In Buddhist teachings, craving is sometimes compared to a river’s current, carrying us along even when we may wish to move in another direction. In this view, much of our emotional life can involve being pushed and pulled by changing desires.

While we can’t necessarily eliminate every desire, recognizing our habitual patterns of craving may help us change how we relate to them.

We often assume that the next thing will finally make us feel complete. A new job. A better relationship. More recognition. A different home. More money. A more exciting life. And there is nothing inherently wrong with wanting things or trying to improve our circumstances. But the Buddhist insight is that getting what we want does not guarantee lasting satisfaction. The mind can simply move on to the next desire.

Instead of “I need this to be different,” we can begin with “I notice that I want this to be different.“

Once we understand this, the feeling of wanting doesn’t necessarily have to become an emergency.

Instead of I need this to be different, we can begin with I notice that I want this to be different.

Naming the desire can help us recognize the feeling without becoming completely caught up in it. That moment of awareness may create space for a more intentional response.  Here’s how you can incorporate this practice into your daily life.

First, put your experience into words. If you’re irritated, say, “I feel irritated.” If you’re anxious, “I feel anxious.” If you’re angry, “I feel angry.” If you’re overwhelmed, “I feel overwhelmed.” If your mind is racing, “My mind is racing.”

For now, there’s no need to analyze the feeling, try to explain it, or decide whether it’s justified. Just name what’s happening.

There’s a difference between “I am angry” and “I feel angry.” The latter can serve as a reminder that anger is an experience you’re having, rather than something that defines you.

This kind of labeling is a basic mindfulness practice. By giving your current mental state a simple name, you may begin to create a little space between yourself and the emotion. You might find it helpful to use  the word “feel” to describe your emotional states. There’s a difference between “I am angry” and “I feel angry.” The latter can serve as a reminder that anger is an experience you’re having, rather than something that defines you.

The practice can be even simpler than that. When you catch yourself reacting emotionally, try saying, “This is anger,” or “This is anxiety,” or simply, “Something is happening in my mind right now.” Do not argue with the feeling or attempt to shoo it away. Instead, see if you can pause and notice what’s happening before responding. . Make this kind of labeling a regular practice, even with ordinary activities: “I am walking,” “I am working,” “I am washing dishes.” The point is to practice observing your experiences rather than moving through life entirely on autopilot.

Once you’ve named the emotion, bring your attention into your physical experience. Where do you feel the reaction? Maybe your shoulders are tight, your jaw is clenched, your chest feels constricted, or your stomach has tightened. Maybe your hands feel clammy or sweaty. Maybe you notice your heart beating faster.

You can say, “My shoulders feel tight,” or “My chest feels tense,” or “My breathing is shallow.” The sensation may not go away, and that’s OK. Remember, we’re just noticing and naming.

This is useful because thoughts can pull our attention toward the past or future, while physical sensations can offer an anchor in the present. If you’re replaying an argument from three hours ago, your thoughts can make the argument feel as though it’s happening again. But when you bring your attention to the physical sensation of your feet against the floor, the movement of your breath, or the tension in your hands, you have an opportunity to notice what’s happening in your body right now.

Try this the next time you’re upset: if it’s comfortable, stop and feel your feet inside your shoes or the weight of your body in the chair. Feel the air moving through your nose. Notice your chest rising and falling. You don’t need to breathe in a particular way or achieve some special meditative state. You’re simply becoming aware of physical sensations you might ordinarily overlook. This can help bring your attention back to what’s happening in the present, even as thoughts and emotions continue to arise.

Once you’ve named your physical and emotional states, you can begin to notice what your mind is saying, and recognize that a thought is not necessarily a fact.

Imagine you receive a short text from someone you care about: “Can we talk later?” Your mind immediately responds: They’re mad at me. I must have done something wrong. This is going to be a disaster.

Notice what has happened. There was an event: you received a text. Then your mind created an interpretation. Whether or not that interpretation will turn out to be true is irrelevant. It is merely an interpretation.

A thought can feel convincing without telling the whole story.

Try saying: “I’m having the thought that they’re upset with me.”

This small change in language creates some breathing room. You can do the same thing with almost any recurring thought: “I’m having the thought that I’m failing.” “I’m having the thought that everyone is judging me.” “I’m having the thought that I’m not good enough.” “I’m having the thought that I need to fix this immediately.”

Rather than arguing with these thoughts, you’re simply seeing them clearly for what they are: mental experiences that may or may not accurately reflect what’s happening around you. A thought can feel convincing without telling the whole story. Learning to recognize that distinction can give you more room to decide how to respond.

Let’s say you receive a frustrating email at work. Your first impulse is to fire back. Instead, pause.

Then, feel it: notice your clenched jaw, the tension in your shoulders, or the shallowness of your breathing.

Finally, see it: “I’m having the thought that this person is deliberately disrespecting me.”

Then, wait. Don’t respond immediately, suppress the anger, or try to convince yourself that the situation isn’t so bad after all. Take a beat and give yourself the space to separate your emotions and thoughts from reality.

Maybe you decide that the email does require a response. Maybe you wait ten minutes. Maybe you realize you misunderstood it. Maybe you’re still angry but decide to address the issue calmly. The point is to create a little more room to choose how you respond, rather than acting automatically on your first impulse. With practice, that pause may become easier to recognize and use in everyday situations.

One of the best ways to develop this skill is to practice when you’re relatively calm, rather than waiting until you’re already overwhelmed.

Set aside a few minutes each day. Sit comfortably and close your eyes if you’d like. Then ask yourself: “What am I feeling right now?”

Give the feeling a simple name: tired, restless, calm, anxious, bored, content.

Then ask: “What am I noticing in my body?”

Feel your hands. Feel your feet. Notice your breath. Notice any tension.

Perhaps it’s planning, remembering, worrying, judging, comparing, rehearsing a conversation, or wishing something were different. Instead of ruminating or trying to fix anything, just practice seeing.

This is an important part of mindfulness: learning to recognize what’s happening in your mind without immediately getting pulled into it. This kind of observation allows for emotional reactions to settle so we can see clearly.

By returning your attention to direct experience instead of automatically following every thought that appears, you can restore peace and balance to your life.

The next time something gets under your skin, try asking yourself one simple question:

“What is happening in my mind right now?”

Not, “Why does this keep happening to me?”

Just: “What is happening in my mind right now?”

Then name what you find. Notice how it feels in your body. Notice the thoughts without immediately treating them as facts, and give yourself a moment before deciding how to respond.

The practice of not reacting, at its core, is about taking the time to pause, notice, and differentiate between thoughts and realities.

Life will always surprise you. People will sometimes disappoint you. Plans will go wrong. Your mind will become anxious, irritated, restless, and afraid. You won’t be able to eliminate hardship in your life, but you may be able to lessen some of the additional suffering that comes from getting caught in automatic reactions.

The practice of not reacting, at its core, is about taking the time to pause, notice, and differentiate between thoughts and realities.

With practice, this pause may begin to feel more familiar.. A moment that once led to anger might offer an opportunity for awareness. A familiar negative thought might pass without pulling you along with it. And little by little, you may discover that you have more freedom in the space between what happens and how you respond. You don’t have to eliminate difficult emotions to develop a different relationship with them. Sometimes, simply noticing what’s happening is where that change begins.

These steps are drawn from the book The Practice of Not Reacting, written by Buddhist monk and scholar Ryushun Kusanagi and edited by Megan Wenerstrom.

Megan Wenerstrom is an associate editor at Portfolio, an imprint of Penguin Random House. She is passionate about books that spark curiosity and solve problems for readers.

#48. Four Paths the Brain Takes After Trauma

A longitudinal study tracking 1,035 adults for six months following the October 7 attacks in Israel identifies four distinct psychological trajectories after mass trauma: resilience (54%), natural recovery (27%), chronic distress (18%), and delayed onset (2.5%). Researchers found that the dynamic trajectory of symptoms over time predicts long-term PTSD risk far more accurately than any single point-in-time clinical assessment, while also revealing that high emotional empathy can increase vulnerability to persistent distress during collective crises.

Source: Hebrew University of Jerusalem / Columbia University

Following large-scale terrorist attacks, warfare, or community disasters, psychological strain is nearly universal. Yet individuals exposed to the same traumatic shock respond in profoundly different ways. While many experience transient acute stress that resolves naturally, others develop debilitating, persistent psychological conditions.

A prospective longitudinal study led by researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Columbia University, and Pace University demonstrates that psychological adaptation after mass trauma follows distinct, identifiable trajectories.

The findings, tracking 1,035 Israeli adults across three systematic intervals for six months following the October 7 attacks, reveal that tracking how distress evolves over time provides far greater diagnostic accuracy for long-term post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) than single-point mental health screenings.

Using longitudinal trajectory modeling, the research team tracked participants at approximately two weeks post-attack, seven weeks later, and six months into the ongoing conflict. The analysis mapped four distinct psychological courses:

“One of the most important messages from our findings is that early distress does not necessarily mean someone is on a path toward long-term psychological difficulties,” said lead author Dana Katsoty, PhD, of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and Columbia University. “Many people who initially experienced severe distress recovered over time. At the same time, a single assessment cannot identify everyone who will need support. Following how symptoms change over time allows us to distinguish natural recovery from patterns that may require clinical intervention.”

Crucially, the investigators discovered that a person’s symptom trajectory over time predicted long-term PTSD severity above and beyond their distress level at any single evaluation. Even when controlling for distress scores at the six-month mark, the specific developmental curve of how an individual arrived at that score remained a robust, independent predictor of post-traumatic stress.

This finding challenges standard disaster mental health protocols that rely on one-time triage screenings immediately after an event. Single-snapshot assessments risk overtreating individuals undergoing natural, adaptive recovery while entirely missing delayed-onset cases whose vulnerabilities emerge weeks or months later.

The researchers also evaluated demographic, psychological, and behavioral factors that shaped trajectory membership:

While empathy is conventionally celebrated as a protective prosocial virtue, the data revealed an emotional cost during acute national crises. Unregulated “empathic distress” absorbed collective suffering without providing psychological protection. In contrast, “empathic concern”, a more regulated, externally oriented compassion, was linked to proactive volunteering, suggesting that empathy can act as both an emotional burden and a social asset during prolonged crises.

Surprisingly, initiating volunteer work or receiving social support after the conflict began did not predict improved trajectories. Only pre-existing, long-standing volunteering habits prior to the crisis conferred protection, suggesting that pre-established cognitive and community frameworks build resilience far more effectively than reactive coping behaviors.

As prolonged geopolitical conflicts, natural disasters, and mass casualty events increase globally, the researchers emphasize that mental health infrastructures must shift away from rigid, early single-point screenings.

Implementing repeated, longitudinal tracking allows health systems to conserve specialized psychiatric resources for individuals exhibiting chronic or delayed distress trajectories, ensuring timely interventions for those truly at risk of enduring psychological harm.

Psychological-Distress Trajectories and Posttraumatic-Stress-Disorder Symptoms Following Continuous Trauma: Empathy, Positive Emotions, and World Beliefs After the October 7th Attack

Using a large, representative sample (N = 1,035), this study examined trajectories of psychological distress during the first 6 months following the October 7th terrorist attack. Four adjustment patterns were identified: resilience (54.5%), recovery (29.1%), chronic distress (13.9%), and delayed onset (2.5%).

Trajectory membership significantly predicted posttraumatic-stress-disorder (PTSD) symptoms beyond final distress levels, highlighting the value of a longitudinal perspective. Key predictors of more adaptive trajectories included demographic factors (e.g., male gender, older age), level of exposure to the events of the war, world beliefs (e.g., perceiving the world as safe), and early positive emotions.

Empathic distress and empathic concern were associated with distress levels, elevated PTSD symptoms, and more severe trajectories, although empathic concern also related to social support and volunteering. Social support and wartime volunteering were not associated with distress or trajectory membership.

Findings highlight the value of ecological and longitudinal approaches to understanding adaptation during continuous mass trauma.

#49. How Artificial Intelligence Can Help With Critical Thinking

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers, and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity, and problem solving. Ironically, perhaps, recent research shows that people who interact with generative AI for work tasks can end up not thinking critically. They can surrender to AI’s quick and confident answers, which can lead to speedy but low-quality solutions.

Scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as cognitive offloading. And they are showing that it can erode the very skills that make knowledge workers valuable.

My research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however. In one study, my colleagues and I interviewed 45 knowledge workers at a U.S. public university. They all were using generative AI applications in their core tasks: generating new ideas, solving complex problems, and designing novel solutions. We also analyzed the prompts and outputs from their iterative AI chats.

We found that when knowledge workers intentionally use AI to challenge their ideas—to generate friction—they can significantly improve their performance. Previous research on human-AI collaboration for loan evaluations had similar results.

Using AI to find information that contradicts your own can reveal unlikely perspectives that disrupt your familiar logic and spark new insights. This is particularly important because AI models quickly become familiar with how a user prompts the model and interprets its output, and the model presents information according to these patterns.

For example, a marketing professional in our study asked AI to create virtual customers with personas that would lead them to dislike a product under development, which was an accounting certificate program. The contrary feedback from the AI model revealed customer preferences that the accounting professional designing the program had not considered, such as using multiple cases from different industries to illustrate a principle, rather than cases from the same industry.

An attorney used AI to find obscure legal loopholes and to consider how companies might exploit them. That exposed surprising but realistic scenarios of hard-to-detect unethical behavior in employees.

Exploring unlikely and opposing ideas presented by AI can feel disorienting. To help, knowledge workers should lean on their own expertise to question surprising information that an AI system might provide.

An operations research scientist who works with supply chains described adapting unfamiliar computing programs from other fields suggested by AI, such as signal processing and wireless communication, which helped him create a stronger program of his own. Although the programs were new to him, his strong understanding of supply network modeling helped him see how he could apply them.

A study I was not involved with found that creative writers produce better copy when they use AI as a sounding board rather than to ghostwrite.

Knowledge workers can also use AI’s outputs to examine topics from multiple viewpoints, deepening their knowledge.

A research scholar in our study probed an AI system for journal papers that used a concept he was using, but in contrasting settings, which helped him understand the concept from different angles. A lawyer followed up on legal citations suggested by an AI model by asking for different types of illustrative cases. That helped her fully understand the original case and write a strong legal brief.

Leaders of organizations can encourage knowledge workers to develop friction-generating queries of AI models.

A straightforward approach is to use prompts that challenge rather than agree with a person’s thinking. People can also draw on their own knowledge, work experiences, and professional ethics to scrutinize AI outputs. Sometimes people realize that a response lacks originality, even if it is factually correct.

Organization leaders can also create programs for knowledge workers to share their experiences and insights. Regular sessions—led by cross-functional AI task forces or AI champions—can also help knowledge workers keep up with rapidly evolving AI tools.

Providing resources for knowledge workers is important, as well. Internal AI bootcamps and workshops led by AI experts or experienced users can help workers understand what AI tools can and cannot do.

A professor leading an initiative about AI use in teaching described how she developed internal competitions with prizes for professors who successfully completed AI bootcamps. Organizations can also offer AI sandboxes—safe, private environments where employees can experiment and learn how to use AI tools.

In these efforts to support knowledge workers, an important detail is pointing out that adding friction can appear to make an AI system work against you, but—as new research shows—it actually helps it work for you.

#50. When Relationships Change: Anne Morrow Lindbergh on Embracing the Intermittency and Mutability of Love

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If it makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider aiding its sustenance with a one-time or loyal donation. Your support makes all the difference.

For an act of resistance to the tyranny of algorithms, try the Marginalian newsletter—undistracted notes on the search for meaning, free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human since 2006. (Here is an example.)

“God is Change,” Octavia Butler wrote, channeling in poetic truth the fundamental scientific fact of the universe.

We know this. And yet to be human is to long for constancy, to crave the touchingly impossible assurance that what we have and cherish will be ours to hold forever, just as it is now. We build homes — fragile haikus of concrete and glass to be unwritten by the first earthquake or flood. We make vows — fragile promises to be upheld by selves we haven’t met in a future we can’t predict.

The dearer we hold something, the more tightly we cling to the dream of constancy, the more zealously we torture ourselves with the belief that any change is loss. Naturally, it is in our intimate relationships that we most come to fear change and most suffer when it comes — a fear not at all groundless, given what relationship rupture does to our limbic system.

The salve for this singularly discomposing suffering comes not from ossifying change but from changing our beliefs about it. Such salutary recalibration is what the aviator and writer Anne Morrow Lindbergh (June 22, 1906–February 7, 2001) offers in Gift from the Sea (public library) — a book I found in a Little Free Library and felt immediately speaking to my soul, drawn from the diaries Lindbergh kept during two weeks of solitude on the ocean shore “searching for a new pattern of living” as she was entering the second half of her life, that vital “period of second flowering” when one is “free for growth of mind, heart and talent.”

Reflecting on the natural trajectory of intimate relationships, she writes:

The pure relationship, how beautiful it is! How easily it is damaged, or weighed down with irrelevancies — not even irrelevancies, just life itself, the accumulations of life and of time. For the first part of every relationship is pure, whether it be with friend or lover, husband or child. It is pure, simple and unencumbered. It is like the artist’s vision before he has to discipline it into form, or like the flower of love before it has ripened to the firm but heavy fruit of responsibility. Every relationship seems simple at its start. The simplicity of first love, or friendliness, the mutuality of first sympathy seems, at its initial appearance — even if merely in exciting conversation across a dinner table — to be a self-enclosed world. Two people listening to each other, two shells meeting each other, making one world between them… It is free of ties or claims, unburdened by responsibilities, by worry about the future or debts to the past. And then how swiftly, how inevitably the perfect unity is invaded; the relationship changes; it becomes complicated, encumbered by its contact with the world.

While this is true in most relationships, Lindbergh observes, the pattern is most pronounced — and most painful — in our most intimate bonds. And yet the pain we experience as a relationship exits this early stage of unselfconscious mutual elation is not evidence of loss — it is evidence of our misshapen ideals of closeness as a static pattern of attachment. She offers an alternative orientation to the inevitability of change:

We mistakenly feel that failure to maintain its exact original pattern is tragedy. It is true, of course, the original relationship is very beautiful. Its self-enclosed perfection wears the freshness of a spring morning. Forgetting about the summer to come, one often feels one would like to prolong the spring of early love, when two people stand as individuals, without past or future, facing each other. One resents any change, even though one knows that transformation is natural and part of the process of life and its evolution. Like its parallel in physical passion, the early ecstatic stage of a relationship cannot continue always at the same pitch of intensity. It moves to another phase of growth which one should not dread, but welcome as one welcomes summer after spring.

At the heart of this dread is our unwillingness to relinquish the polished self-image we see in the light-filled eyes of the other in those early stages of mutual infatuation, before we have touched each other’s darkness, before we have met the hungry ghosts of each other’s unmet needs. We long for that image, perfect and haloed with adoration, to become our identity, seeking to make of love a flattering mirror in which to find our best selves, tasking the other with the emotional brunt of bearing the parts we don’t want to look at. Lindbergh pulls back the curtain on the most damaging myth handed down to us by the Romantics:

Certainly, one has the illusion that one will find oneself in being loved for what one really is, not for a collection of functions. But can one actually find oneself in someone else? In someone else’s love? Or even in the mirror someone else holds up for one? I believe that true identity is found… in creative activity springing from within. It is found, paradoxically, when one loses oneself. One must lose one’s life to find it… Only a refound person can refind a personal relationship.

The twin root of our suffering in a changing relationship is the expectation — the demand, even — that the other’s love be total and permanent, reserved for us alone, unshared with other priorities and passions, those natural constituents of a fully developed personality and a fully inhabited life. Lindbergh writes:

We all wish to be loved alone… Perhaps, as Auden says in his poem, this is a fundamental error in mankind.

For the error bred in the bone Of each woman and each man Craves what it cannot have, Not universal love But to be loved alone.

Lindbergh recounts discussing this verse with an Indian philosopher, who made a striking observation — while mutuality is the essence of love and therefore it is natural for us to wish for it, it is in the time-sense that we err. “It is when we desire continuity of being loved alone that we go wrong,” he told her.

The fear of change dissolves when we come to see love not as a vector of constancy but as a rosary of nows, its core promise not that of permanence but of presence. Hannah Arendt would affirm this a generation after Lindbergh in her superb meditation on love and the fear of loss, insisting that “fearlessness is what love seeks [which] exists only in the complete calm that can no longer be shaken by events expected of the future… Hence the only valid tense is the present, the Now.”

Only by meeting each now on its own terms, Lindberg argues, can we allay the reflexive ache of perceiving change as loss, reframing it instead as fertile evolution:

One learns to accept the fact that no permanent return is possible to an old form of relationship; and, more deeply still, that there is no holding of a relationship to a single form. This is not tragedy but part of the ever-recurrent miracle of life and growth. All living relationships are in process of change, of expansion, and must perpetually be building themselves new forms. But there is no single fixed form to express such a changing relationship.

Those able to configure their relationships with such fluidity of form, Lindbergh notes, are “pioneers trying to find a new path through the maze of tradition, convention and dogma.” Auden was one himself — his relationship with the young poet Chester Kallman, like that of Virginia Woolf and Vita Sackville-West, shape-shifted from friend to lover and back again over the last quarter century of Auden’s life.

Ultimately, our fear of change is a trap of self-limitation, keeping relationships from deepening and broadening to encompass the full range of who we are as complete human beings, as dynamic processes in continual state of becoming, which in turn makes possible the thrill of continual mutual discovery. Lindbergh writes:

One comes in the end to realize that there is no permanent pure-relationship and there should not be. It is not even something to be desired. The pure relationship is limited, in space and in time. In its essence it implies exclusion. It excludes the rest of life, other relationships, other sides of personality, other responsibilities, other possibilities in the future. It excludes growth.

With an eye to the best kind of pure-relationship — “the meeting of two whole fully developed people as persons” — and with the recognition that “the light shed by any good relationship illuminates all relationships,” she considers the core dynamic of such a relationship:

A good relationship has a pattern like a dance and is built on some of the same rules. The partners do not need to hold on tightly, because they move confidently in the same pattern… To touch heavily would be to arrest the pattern and freeze the movement, to check the endlessly changing beauty of its unfolding. There is no place here for the possessive clutch, the clinging arm, the heavy hand; only the barest touch in passing. Now arm in arm, now face to face, now back to back… Because they know they are partners moving to the same rhythm, creating a pattern together, and being invisibly nourished by it.

The joy of such a pattern is not only the joy of creation or the joy of participation, it is also the joy of living in the moment. Lightness of touch and living in the moment are intertwined. One cannot dance well unless one is completely in time with the music, not leaning back to the last step or pressing forward to the next one, but poised directly on the present step as it comes.

With this, she returns to the correct time-scale of love — not constancy but intermittency, measured out by the metronome of presence:

When you love someone you do not love them all the time, in exactly the same way, from moment to moment. It is an impossibility. It is even a lie to pretend to. And yet this is exactly what most of us demand. We have so little faith in the ebb and flow of life, of love, of relationships. We leap at the flow of the tide and resist in terror its ebb. We are afraid it will never return. We insist on permanency, on duration, on continuity; when the only continuity possible, in life as in love, is in growth, in fluidity — in freedom, in the sense that the dancers are free, barely touching as they pass, but partners in the same pattern. The only real security is not in owning or possessing, not in demanding or expecting, not in hoping, even. Security in a relationship lies neither in looking back to what it was in nostalgia, nor forward to what it might be in dread or anticipation, but living in the present relationship and accepting it as it is now.

Complement these fragments of Gift from the Sea — a revelatory read in its entirety — with philosopher Martin Buber on love and what it means to live fully in the present, then revisit Thich Nhat Hanh on the four Buddhist mantras for turning fear into love.

#51. Scientists uncover 3 key brain pathways linked to lasting depression relief

Scientists at Mount Sinai have identified three important brain connections associated with long-term improvement in patients receiving deep brain stimulation (DBS) for severe depression that has not responded to conventional treatments. The discovery could help researchers make this experimental therapy more precise and effective.

Published October 1 in the American Journal of Psychiatry, the research examined the largest group of patients assembled across multiple independent cohorts to date who had received subcallosal cingulate deep brain stimulation (SCC DBS) for treatment-resistant depression.

The researchers found that lasting improvements were consistently associated with electrical stimulation reaching three specific white matter pathways: the cingulum bundle, forceps minor, and medial uncinate fasciculus/ventral amygdalofugal pathways.

These findings strengthen the case for using detailed maps of the brain's connections to determine exactly where electrodes should be implanted, rather than choosing their positions based primarily on anatomical landmarks. Known as connectome-based targeting, this strategy has already helped shape the ongoing Abbott TRANSCEND clinical trial, a randomized, controlled study that uses individualized brain connectivity maps to guide SCC DBS treatment.

"This study underscores the importance of individualized surgical targeting for achieving optimal outcomes with deep brain stimulation for depression," said Helen Mayberg, MD, Mount Sinai Professor in Neurotherapeutics and founding Director of the Nash Family Center for Advanced Circuit Therapeutics at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. "In any randomized controlled trial of a neuromodulation treatment, precise lead placement and confirmation that the intended brain target has been engaged are essential first steps. We still have much to learn about which patients are most likely to benefit from stimulation of this particular target, but developing imaging-based signatures that can match patients to their optimal treatment remains a central goal of our research."

How Deep Brain Stimulation Targets Severe Depression

For people with treatment-resistant depression, standard therapies have failed to provide adequate relief. Researchers are investigating deep brain stimulation as a possible treatment for individuals living with severe, persistent symptoms.

The procedure involves surgically placing electrodes inside the brain to deliver controlled electrical signals to circuits involved in depression. However, positioning the electrodes correctly remains one of the greatest challenges.

Electrical stimulation does not simply affect the brain tissue closest to an implanted electrode. It can also influence larger networks through the white matter pathways that connect different brain regions. As a result, two patients with electrodes implanted in nearly identical locations may experience very different outcomes depending on which connections are actually stimulated.

Earlier research from Mount Sinai and Emory University helped establish the importance of these networks. In studies published between 2014 and 2023 in Biological Psychiatry, Molecular Psychiatry, and Nature, the teams identified white matter pathways associated with successful SCC DBS treatment and developed a method for planning electrode placement using brain connectivity maps.

The latest investigation sought to determine whether those connections were also important in patients treated at other research centers. Scientists also wanted to understand whether differences in the pathways reached by stimulation could help account for patients who did not benefit.

Three Brain Connections Linked to Lasting Improvement

To investigate, the researchers examined information from several clinical studies, including the BROADEN trial and a patient cohort at the University of Toronto, where SCC DBS was originally developed.

They used computer models of the electrical fields generated by implanted electrodes alongside maps of brain connectivity. This allowed them to estimate which pathways received stimulation and compare those patterns across different patient groups.

The results showed a consistent relationship between sustained improvement and stimulation of the cingulum bundle, forceps minor, and medial uncinate fasciculus/ventral amygdalofugal pathways.

One finding was especially notable. Across the study sites, patients who had not responded to treatment after two years showed a lack of stimulation engagement with the left cingulum bundle.

The researchers did not investigate whether moving electrodes to reach this pathway would improve those patients' symptoms. Nevertheless, the pattern offers a possible explanation for why apparently similar electrode placements can produce different results. An electrode might be positioned in the correct general region but still fail to activate all the connections associated with lasting improvement.

"This study addresses an important question in DBS: not simply which area of the brain to stimulate, but which connections within that area need to be engaged," said Brian Kopell, MD, Director of the Center for Neuromodulation at Mount Sinai. "For a network disorder such as depression, millimeters can determine whether stimulation reaches the pathways we intend to modulate. Identifying and reproducibly engaging those pathways gives us a more precise surgical target and a framework for understanding why otherwise similar electrode placements may produce different clinical outcomes."

Toward More Personalized Depression Treatments

Although reaching these three pathways appears important, the researchers emphasize that electrode placement alone is unlikely to determine whether a patient improves.

The investigation concentrated on identifying the brain connections that should receive stimulation. Additional studies are needed to determine which individuals are most likely to benefit from SCC DBS and how electrical stimulation should be adjusted as treatment continues.

There were also limitations to the brain imaging data. Individual diffusion MRI scans, which can provide information about a person's white matter connections, were not available for every participant. Consequently, much of the analysis used generalized maps of brain connectivity rather than maps created specifically for each patient.

For the Emory patient group, the researchers were able to compare results obtained from generalized connectivity maps with those based on individual diffusion imaging. Both approaches produced consistent findings, providing further support for the importance of the identified pathways. However, more research is needed to establish the value of patient-specific imaging.

Future investigations will explore whether additional brain imaging measurements, including white matter integrity and functional connectivity, can help identify suitable patients, improve electrode placement, and guide treatment settings.

"Our findings show precisely engaging these white matter pathways is a critical first step toward sustained response," said Ki Sueng Choi, PhD, Associate Professor, Imaging Core Leader at the Center for Advanced Circuit Therapeutics at Mount Sinai, and corresponding author of the study. "The next step is to characterize abnormal functional and structural brain states along these pathways to build more detailed models for setting patient-specific stimulation parameters, including amplitude, frequency, and pulse width, for precision medicine."

By combining increasingly detailed brain maps with personalized stimulation settings, scientists hope to better understand why some people experience lasting relief while others do not. The findings represent another step toward developing more targeted treatments for severe depression, although further clinical research is necessary to establish how much these approaches can improve outcomes.

The research received support from the National Institutes of Health BRAIN Initiative through grant UH3NS103550, the Hope for Depression Research Foundation, and the DANA Foundation.

Abbott's Neuromodulation business supplied data from the BROADEN clinical trial but did not participate in designing or analyzing the current study.

Conflict of Interest Disclosures: Dr. Brian Kopell serves as a paid consultant to Abbott Laboratories.

Dr. Helen Mayberg is a named co-inventor of a method that uses deep brain stimulation (DBS) in a particular brain region (the subcallosal cingulate area) to treat treatment-resistant depression. The method was licensed to Abbott Laboratories. Dr. Mayberg has received royalty payments from Functional Neuroscience related to this technology and is eligible to receive additional payments in the future. She also serves as a paid consultant to Abbott Laboratories in connection with its clinical trials involving DBS for depression.

Dr. Ki Sueng Choi and Dr. Martijn Figee are also paid consultants to Abbott Laboratories.

#52. Rethink Your Drink: How Real People Cut Back on Alcohol

Research confirms that reducing alcohol use improves sleep quality, reduces health risks, and saves money and relationships. Still, it is hard to stop drinking. Here are the reasons ADDitude readers shared for drinking less and their strategies for doing so.

More than a third of young adults with ADHD meet the criteria for alcohol use disorder.1 At least a quarter of all patients seeking treatment for alcohol and other drug-related problems also have ADHD.2 And we know that drinking alcohol has detrimental effects on sleep, relationships, and overall health — with many studies showing links to liver disease and cancer.3

Everyone has their own reasons for engaging with alcohol the way they do – but people with ADHD may have extra incentives and challenges related to cutting back.

So, we asked ADDitude readers who’ve curtailed their drinking to share their motivations for making a change. Their answers ranged from curbing negative emotions to preventing or reversing overdrinking, and saving money. Here, they share the details and the creative strategies they used to make this habit change.

[Self-Test: Could You Have a Substance Use Disorder?]

“[I was able to cut out alcohol by] finding the right doctor who took the time to get to the root of why I was self-medicating with alcohol too much for anxiety, helping me find that balance through the proper medication and a very supportive wife. I can honestly say that it’s a thing of the past.” – An ADDitude Reader

“I realized I needed to cut back because I was drinking every evening. Giving myself a specific day to drink helped at the time: only on Fridays after work, only with my friend, and only two drinks. Giving it a structure and an association really helped. I rarely drink any more, and when I do, it’s usually one or two drinks. I feel them the next day, so I try to save drinks for fun or celebration.” – Cecily, Idaho

“I like scotch and wine, but assorted ancestors were alcoholics, so I’ve always been careful. And maybe genetically lucky. My only proactive rule has been never to drink as a reaction to stress, anger, or other emotional issues. When I’m upset, the scotch bottles stay closed.” – Chris, Ontario

“Alcoholics Anonymous (AA), prayer, and therapy helped. Alcohol use made my life unmanageable, and I behaved in ways that led to self-loathing and suicidal ideation, resulting in an attempt where I was in intensive care for few days; then, a mandatory psych ward for a week. After that, drinking scared me because I didn’t know if I’d make another attempt when drunk. That was 36 years ago, and I’ve been sober ever since.” – Renée, Alberta

[Read: ADHD Teens at Risk for Alcohol Abuse]

“I’m currently abstaining altogether for health reasons (silent reflux). I quit another time because it really disrupted my sleep, but I also found I was in less pain when I didn’t drink alcohol.” – An ADDitude Reader

“I stopped drinking 17 years ago. I was acting out impulsively, feeling ill most mornings, craving wine, spending too much money on alcohol, and having angry outbursts. A counselor recommended attending AA, so I did. I attended several times a week for several months and avoided being around temptation, where others were drinking or alcohol was being sold. Since then, I am much more relaxed, healthy and make better choices.” – Michelle, Virginia

“I didn’t really have a problem with alcohol consumption, but using a calorie tracker app has helped me realize how wasteful drinking alcohol is to my daily macros.” – McKenna, Colorado

“I’ve found the best strategy is replacing [alcohol] with some other ‘treat’ drink… The complex acquired flavors and sensations in alcoholic beverages are tricky to replicate, but I’ve discovered hibiscus has tons of tannins in it, which meets that sensory-seeking need very nicely. I created a tea bar with all the other ingredients I like, and I will make a custom cup based on other factors like anxiety level or time of day.” – Maria, North Carolina

“I never really drank a lot, but I cut back because of my need to lose weight and lower my A1C (pre-diabetic).” – Sharon, Ontario

“I stopped drinking altogether following the death of a co-worker, who died in a drunk driving accident. I also worried I might have a predisposition to addictive behavior and figured it’s best if I don’t try drugs or try to develop a taste for beer or wine. Easy decision and easy to follow.” – Kay, California

“25 years ago, I hit rock bottom and declared I would never have another sip of alcohol. And that is exactly what I did. It was a pledge I made to myself or the universe, and somehow, I just stuck to it. That doesn’t mean it was easy. My life shifted drastically. I lost friends, or rather drinking buddies I thought were friends. I became distanced from my siblings, who were both big drinkers (though they would not say they had an issue with alcohol, it is a constant in their lives).

“I uncovered my anxiety, depression, and social challenges but was finally forced to work through them and get to a better place… eventually seeking and receiving an ADHD diagnosis, which I now know to be AuDHD. There was work to do after that last drop of alcohol, but my life was immediately better.

“I finally finished college (with straight As my final semester), I started drawing again instead of going drinking after work. I figured out who my real friends were (and they are my closest friends to this day), I fell in love with baseball and practically lived at the ballpark watching my team win the World Series. I stopped dating losers. I found love, got married, had two beautiful children and have an amazing life. At 50, my life is beautiful; at 25, it was a disaster.

“How did I do it? I just did it. I said no more and I did what it took to change my life. I do not crave or miss alcohol, and I do not take it ‘one day at a time.’ Alcohol is not top of mind. I replaced drinking/partying with art, ice skating, baseball, reading… living a true and beautiful life.” – Beth, Colorado

#53. Risk-Taking Spikes Before Alcohol Bingeing

A longitudinal study utilizing gamified smartphone tasks has demonstrated that shifts in risky decision-making precede increases in alcohol consumption in people with mild to moderate alcohol use disorder (AUD), rather than occurring as a consequence of drinking. By tracking monthly cognitive-behavioral fluctuations, researchers identified that changes in risk tolerance and information gathering forecast subsequent surges in alcohol intake, paving the way for real-time digital warning systems.

Source: Elsevier / University Hospital Würzburg

Alcohol use disorder (AUD) represents a leading contributor to global disability, chronic illness, and preventable mortality. While decades of cross-sectional clinical research have established that individuals with AUD often display impaired cognitive control and elevated risk-taking, scientists have faced a fundamental “chicken-or-egg” question: do neurocognitive impairments precede and trigger hazardous drinking, or does chronic alcohol exposure degrade executive decision-making?

Now, a pioneering one-year longitudinal study published in Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging has resolved this question of temporal order.

By tracking individuals with mild to moderate AUD via gamified smartphone tasks, researchers from University Hospital Würzburg and Technische Universität Dresden demonstrated that subtle escalations in risky decision-making precede surges in alcohol consumption, not vice versa.

Evaluating natural variations in cognitive control and decision-making has historically presented significant methodological hurdles. Traditional clinic-based self-reports and retrospective questionnaires fail to capture dynamic shifts in executive function as they occur in daily life.

To capture these real-world fluctuations, the investigators developed gamified, smartphone-based decision-making tasks administered monthly over the course of a full year. Participants with mild to moderate AUD—a population characterized by meaningful fluctuations in drinking volume rather than fixed dependence—completed mobile tasks assessing cognitive control, risk tolerance across different reward/loss scenarios, and information sampling behavior.

The longitudinal data uncovered a clear predictive timeline:

“We found that monthly fluctuations in aspects of decision making predicted subsequent alcohol consumption,” explained co-lead investigator Hilmar Zech, PhD, postdoctoral research fellow at University Hospital Würzburg and Technische Universität Dresden. “Specifically, participants shifted to higher monthly alcohol consumption when their risk-taking was higher in a mixed gambling context and lower in a loss context in the preceding month. Further, when information sampling biases decreased, participants consumed more alcohol in the subsequent month.”

Importantly, the relationship was entirely unidirectional. Prior alcohol intake did not forecast subsequent deterioration in cognitive control or decision-making on subsequent monthly tests.

Furthermore, general measures of impulse control, such as working memory capacity and motor response inhibition, remained stable and did not track drinking shifts. This indicates that relapse vulnerability is driven by specific computations regarding risk evaluation and evidence accumulation rather than generalized executive failure.

“This temporal direction was specific and was not observed vice versa, even after accounting for the amount of previous drinking,” noted co-lead investigator Lorenz Deserno, MD, PhD, Principal Investigator of the Computational and Developmental Psychiatry Lab at University Hospital Würzburg. “The findings also showed that fluctuations in self-control and reward-driven behavior were not associated with fluctuations in drinking.”

By validating smartphone-based behavioral assessments as objective predictors of real-life drinking surges, the study lays the groundwork for digital phenotyping in addiction medicine.

“Decision making and cognitive control cannot be accurately examined through interviews or self-reports and instead require experimental tasks,” said Cameron S. Carter, MD, Editor-in-Chief of Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging and Professor at the University of California, Irvine School of Medicine. “The findings of this longitudinal assessment suggest that smartphone-based gamified tasks show promise in identifying periods of heightened risk in people with AUD, paving the way for mechanism-based, real-time interventions.”

While clinical applications require further validation, passive or micro-gamified mobile monitoring could eventually power “just-in-time” adaptive interventions, alerting users or their clinical care teams when cognitive risk markers signal an impending binge before the first drink is consumed.

Fluctuations in Real-Life Drinking in Alcohol Use Disorder: A 1-Year Longitudinal Study Using Gamified Tasks of Decision Making and Cognitive Control

Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a major contributor to global disability and mortality. Cross-sectional studies have linked AUD to reduced cognitive control and heightened risky decision making. However, the temporal direction of these effects remains unknown: are cognitive-behavioral alterations a consequence or a precursor of changes in drinking?

We deployed a battery of smartphone-based, gamified tasks in a 1-year longitudinal ecological momentary assessment study of 603 participants diagnosed with mostly mild-to-moderate AUD. Tasks measured cognitive control (working memory, response inhibition) and decision making (risk-taking, information sampling). Participants completed tasks monthly and reported alcohol consumption every 2 days.

We found that monthly fluctuations in aspects of decision making predicted subsequent consumption. Specifically, participants shifted to higher monthly alcohol consumption when their risk-taking was higher in a mixed gambling context and lower in a loss context in the preceding month. Furthermore, when information sampling biases decreased, participants consumed more alcohol in the subsequent month. This temporal direction—that within-subject fluctuations in task outcomes preceded changes in monthly drinking—was specific, was not observed vice versa, and survived correction for autocorrelation in drinking, indicating risky decision making as a precursor to subsequent drinking. Fluctuations in cognitive control and risk-taking in a win context were not associated with fluctuations in drinking.

Our findings offer novel insights into the cognitive-behavioral forces driving changes in alcohol consumption in AUD: specific alterations in decision making precede changes in consumption. These findings suggest that smartphone-based gamified tasks show promise in identifying periods of heightened risk, paving the way for mechanism-based, real-time interventions in AUD.

#55. How Do We Agree on Anything?

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted September 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

Say you need to tell someone over the phone how long something is in your room. It’s easy: You take a ruler, measure the thing, and read the number to the person on the other end of the line. Scientists and much of the world use the metric system for this sort of thing.

This all sounds very precise, but how does anyone know how long a meter is?

Initially, the definition of a meter was tied to the Earth’s circumference. In the 1790s, the French defined it as exactly one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole. That’s about as objective as it gets, but is almost entirely useless in daily life: A tailor cannot triangulate the globe every time they need to cut a piece of fabric.

To make this whole measuring thing more practical, expeditions spent several years surveying the Earth, did the math, and forged a literal metal bar to represent that distance. For over a century, that was the “meter”: a platinum-iridium bar locked in a vault in France. If your wooden ruler matched the metal bar in Paris, you had a meter.

But a metal bar isn’t perfect either. It can expand in heat, contract in cold, and sustain microscopic scratches. As industrial technology and global communications demanded a higher degree of uniformity, the definition of a meter had to change again. First, it was pegged to the radiation emitted by krypton-86 atoms. Today, it is tied to the speed of light. A meter is officially the distance light travels in a vacuum, or exactly 1/299,792,458 of a second.

Practically speaking, these definitions are once again not super useful for everyday people. If a tailor needs to measure something, they will simply buy a tape measure at the hardware store. But when they do, they are participating in a massive, invisible chain of trust. The tailor trusts the hardware store, the store trusts the factory, the factory trusts the national laboratory’s calibration, and the laboratory aligns its equipment with the physical constants of the universe.

At the very foundation of this social chain of trust is a long history of human institutions having to agree on where the ruler starts, and where it ends. Which brings us to the surprisingly difficult question: How do we agree on anything?

When addressing a complex problem, we might assume people will naturally gravitate toward the most accurate or efficient solution. But in reality, we rarely settle on an option solely because it is the “truest.”

Instead, as game theorist Thomas Schelling observed, humans are quite desperate for coordination. We land on an agreement, fundamentally, because the cognitive and social costs of disagreeing are too high. And to do so, we look for focal points, or a default answer that stands out just enough for people to expect everyone else to think of that answer. (For example, if you ask someone in North America to name a fruit, did they say “apple”?)

Once that agreement is locked in, a psychological shift happens: the very human habit of treating our abstractions as though they were a natural feature of the world. The sociologists Peter Berger and Thomas Luckmann called this “reification.” Once a decision is made, it’s water under the bridge. Our “objective reality” today is a bunch of these coordination problems. Once we solve one, we no longer need to think about it.

Time is humanity’s ultimate coordination problem. We tend to experience it as an absolute—a universal metronome ticking steadily in the background. But for most of human history, time was intensely local. Before the 19th century, it was “noon” whenever the sun reached its highest point overhead in your specific town. If you traveled from New York to Boston, you had to adjust your pocket watch upon arrival. There was no need for perfect synchronization because we just couldn’t travel fast enough to make the 12-minute difference matter.

Then came the railroad, moving people and goods across large distances on complex schedules. You cannot run a continental railway system when every station operates on its own local solar time, so standardized time emerged. But how did we end up with Greenwich Mean Time, and not Your-Hometown Mean Time? When delegates from 25 nations met in 1884 to base global time zones around the Greenwich meridian, that decision was a matter of geopolitical power as much as it was a matter of astronomy.

Even today, we treat time and the calendar as facts, but they regularly yield to economic convenience. This is why the International Date Line doesn’t drop straight down from the North Pole to the South Pole; instead, it zig-zags around political alliances. In 2011, the nation of Samoa literally erased Friday, December 30th, from their calendar, shifting their entire country across the Date Line because being a day behind their biggest trading partners—Australia and New Zealand—was bad for business.

In their research on how categories shape society, the scholars Geoffrey Bowker and Susan Leigh Star observed that every successful infrastructure becomes invisible. We only notice systems when they break down

Standardized time is a perfect example of invisible infrastructure. The irony is that only a few decades after the world’s governments decided to synchronize everybody’s clocks and create a universal, objective “now,” Albert Einstein proved that a universal “now” doesn’t actually exist: time is entirely relative, bending and stretching depending on speed and gravity. But by that point, people didn’t even blink—at the scale of human movement, Newtonian mechanics worked just fine, and the social infrastructure was already too valuable to abandon. And so, we keep using our clocks like there’s no tomorrow.
