#70. IBS, Stomach Pain, and Other GI Symptoms Strongly Tied to ADHD: New Review

People with ADHD are up to four times more likely to experience certain gastrointestinal symptoms, according to a large-scale meta-analysis that offers possible explanations for the link.

People with ADHD are 48% more likely than their neurotypical peers to experience gastrointestinal (GI) issues, including irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), encopresis, dyspepsia, and constipation, according to a large scale review published in the Journal of Attention Disorders.1

Data from 1.9 million individuals with ADHD aged 2 to 65 was included in the review of 23 studies. While past studies have explored the association between ADHD and intestinal diseases, such as celiac disease and peptic ulcers,2 this is the first review to examine the association between ADHD and GI symptoms, broadening the scope of the investigation to include those without a formal diagnosis of a GI disorder. The findings, wrote the study’s authors, suggest that past studies “may have underestimated the burden of functional bowel dysfunction in people with ADHD and highlights the importance of analyzing symptom-level data.”

The study found that people with ADHD face increased odds of experiencing GI symptoms investigated, including the following:

A recent ADDitude survey exploring readers’ experiences with inflammation found similarly high rates of gastrointestinal disorders.

The study’s authors offered several possible explanations for the demonstrated association between ADHD and GI symptoms.

Traits characteristic of ADHD, including impulsivity, emotional dysregulation, sensory sensitivities, and poor interoception, may disrupt digestion and lead to behaviors that contribute to GI symptoms.

ADDitude readers observed many of these connections between ADHD symptoms and digestive challenges.

“My IBS gets bad when my ADHD keeps me from doing basic things like taking my probiotics or drinking my fiber supplement every day and remembering to renew the medications,” wrote Alex from New Jersey.

“I’ve had SIBO before, and I’m trying very hard not to get it again,” wrote Jennifer from Texas. “Between fructose malabsorption and a delayed stomach, I can’t eat most foods, so every meal involves prep — and prep is exactly the thing executive dysfunction makes impossible!”

“The irritable bowel issue is made worse by stress and anxiety, which is a part of my ADHD,” explained Sarah, an ADDitude reader in the United Kingdom. “When my stomach feels bad, I can’t think as clearly, and my ADHD is worse. They both affect each other.”

Building on past studies that have found differences in the microbiota of those with and without ADHD,3 the study’s authors posit that gut microbiome may be a key player. “There is a clear link between gut health and the brain, yet the exact mechanism of the gut-brain axis is not yet clear,” they write. “One theory is the vagus nerve acting as a bidirectional pathway of communication between the brain and the gut.”

This communication was explored in a 2025 ADDitude webinar titled “The Surprising Association Between ADHD & Inflammation,” with James Kustow, BMedSci, BMBS, MRCPsych. “Problems with the digestive system frequently occur in people with ADHD, impeding gut motility and nutrition, and causing chronic pain and discomfort,” Kustow said. “The autonomic nervous system is responsible for the peristaltic movement through the gut, so dysautonomia causes sluggish gut. Mast cells in the gut that get activated cause swelling, which limits flow. The combination of poor peristaltic movement and inflammation causes the contents of the gut to stagnate, leading to gastrointestinal problems.”

“What happens in the gut does not stay in the gut,” explained Miguel Toribio-Mateas, DProf, MSc, BSc (Hons), CBiol, in the 2026 ADDitude webinar, “How Gut Health Impacts ADHD Symptoms: New Insights on Food, Microbes, and Inflammation.” “The gut will contribute to conditions such as ADHD as well as other coexisting conditions… in the neurosphere — anxiety, depression, and so on.”

Stimulant medications used to treat ADHD often suppress appetite, which can impact digestive processes, and may cause nausea and abdominal pain.4,5 “ADHD medications have given my daughter a lot of upset stomach, leaky gut, inflammation with her skin, and other problems processing the medication,” said Sandra, an ADDitude reader from Canada.

Since the studies included in the review did not segment the data by medication status, the authors could not assess the influence of medication side effects. They explained, however, that several of the GI symptoms most prevalent among ADHD patients — constipation and encopresis — are not common side effects of stimulants, suggesting that non-pharmacological explanations are at play.

The study’s authors hope their findings will raise clinicians’ awareness of a complex and under-recognized association. “Healthcare workers should be aware of this increased risk of GI symptom presence and should actively ask about GI symptoms during consultations… ensuring that these issues are not overlooked,” they wrote.

Understanding the relationship between ADHD and somatic conditions, including GI disturbances, has been highly instructive for Rebecca, an ADDitude reader from Chicago. “It’s been a tiny relief to learn that some of the things that trip me up, like GI issues that make me late to work might not be just a failure of my willpower or my ADHD meds,” she said. “Pulling apart more strands of what’s happening to me makes it a little clearer which challenges might be treated differently than just throwing the ADHD meds at them. This gives me hope that I might be able to access a whole other set of tools and treatments.”

#71. Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness

Even when a person is fully unconscious under general anesthesia, their brain may still be doing something remarkable: processing language, recognizing patterns, and even anticipating which words will come next.

Researchers at Baylor College of Medicine have discovered that the brain retains surprisingly sophisticated abilities during anesthesia, despite the absence of conscious awareness. The findings, published in the journal Nature, challenge traditional assumptions about the relationship between consciousness and thinking. They could also provide new insights into how the brain processes memories and language, potentially leading to advances in technologies that help people communicate after neurological injuries.

"Our findings show that the brain is far more active and capable during unconsciousness than previously thought," said Dr. Sameer Sheth, professor and Cullen Foundation Endowed chair of neurosurgery and a McNair Scholar at Baylor. "Even when patients are fully anesthetized, their brains continue to analyze the world around them."

Recording Brain Activity During General Anesthesia

To investigate what happens inside the unconscious brain, Sheth, who is also a neurosurgeon at Baylor St. Luke's Medical Center, and his colleagues studied patients undergoing epilepsy surgery while under general anesthesia.

These procedures offered an unusual opportunity to examine the hippocampus, a brain structure deeply involved in learning and memory. Located within the brain's temporal lobe, the hippocampus helps organize information and plays an important role in forming new memories.

The researchers used advanced recording devices called Neuropixels probes to monitor electrical signals from hundreds of individual neurons in the hippocampus. These tiny probes can detect activity from many nerve cells simultaneously, providing a detailed picture of how groups of neurons respond to information.

According to the researchers, this technology had not previously been used to investigate this particular brain region in this way. It allowed the team to examine how the hippocampus responds to sounds and language while patients are unconscious and unable to report what they experience.

The first experiment involved playing a series of repeating tones, occasionally interrupted by a sound that differed from the others.

Although the patients were under anesthesia, neurons in their hippocampus responded differently to the unexpected sounds. Even more surprisingly, the brain cells became better at distinguishing these unusual tones as the experiment continued.

This improvement suggested that the hippocampus was showing signs of neural plasticity, the brain's ability to change its responses through experience. In other words, some of the basic processes associated with learning appeared to remain active even without conscious awareness.

The Unconscious Brain Can Process Language and Predict Words

The researchers then tested whether the unconscious brain could handle something more complicated than simple sounds.

They played short stories to the anesthetized patients while continuing to record activity from neurons in the hippocampus.

The results revealed a surprising level of language processing. Distinct patterns of neural activity contained information about different categories of words, including nouns, verbs, and adjectives. This suggested that the hippocampus was responding to meaningful features of language rather than simply detecting that sounds were occurring.

But the most intriguing discovery went a step further.

The researchers found that neural activity also carried information that could be used to predict upcoming words in a sentence. Even though the patients were unconscious, their brains appeared to anticipate how the language unfolding around them might continue.

"The brain appears to anticipate what comes next in a story, even without conscious awareness," said Sheth, who is also Director of The Gordon and Mary Cain Pediatric Neurology Research Foundation Laboratories within the Duncan Neurological Research Institute at Texas Children's Hospital.

This ability is related to a process known as predictive coding. Rather than passively receiving information, the brain continually uses patterns and previous experience to anticipate what might happen next. When listening to someone speak, for example, the brain can use the words already heard to form expectations about what is likely to follow.

Scientists have typically studied this kind of sophisticated prediction in people who are awake and paying attention. Finding evidence of it during general anesthesia suggests that at least some of the underlying neural processes can operate independently of conscious awareness.

"This kind of predictive coding is something we associate with being awake and attentive, yet it's happening here in an unconscious state," said Dr. Benjamin Hayden, professor of neurosurgery at Baylor.

What Does This Discovery Mean for Consciousness?

The findings raise important questions about what consciousness actually contributes to the brain's ability to process information.

Consciousness is generally associated with subjective awareness, including the experience of hearing, thinking, and understanding the world around us. Yet the study suggests that some neural processes involved in interpreting language and predicting future information can continue even when that awareness is absent.

This does not necessarily mean that the anesthetized patients consciously understood the stories being played to them. Instead, it indicates that the brain can carry out surprisingly complex aspects of language processing without a person being aware of doing so.

The distinction could help researchers better understand how consciousness emerges.

One possibility is that awareness depends not simply on whether individual brain regions remain active, but on how information is coordinated and shared across larger networks of brain regions.

Under this view, a structure such as the hippocampus might continue analyzing information even when the broader communication between brain regions needed for conscious experience is disrupted.

A Surprising Connection Between the Brain and Artificial Intelligence

The discovery also highlights an intriguing similarity between human brain activity and artificial intelligence (AI).

Large language models, the technology behind many modern AI chatbots, generate text by using patterns learned from enormous amounts of language data to predict what should come next.

The researchers observed a related predictive ability in the hippocampus, where neural signals reflected information about upcoming words even during unconsciousness.

Although biological brains and AI models operate in fundamentally different ways, both can use patterns in language to anticipate future information. Studying these similarities may help scientists better understand how prediction works in natural and artificial systems.

The findings could also have practical implications for brain-computer interfaces, which use signals recorded from the brain to communicate with external devices.

One potential application involves speech prosthetics, technologies designed to help people communicate when injuries or neurological conditions have impaired their ability to speak.

If scientists can reliably identify meaningful language signals in the brain, those signals might eventually be used to support communication technologies for patients who have lost speech abilities.

"Can we use these signals to deploy and run a speech prosthetic for some of the parts of the brain that are damaged by stroke or injury? These are questions that we can now consider in relation to this part of the brain," said Dr. Vigi Katlowitz, first author and a neurosurgery resident with Baylor.

Scientists Are Rethinking the Limits of the Unconscious Brain

Despite the striking results, the researchers emphasize that several questions remain unanswered.

The experiments were conducted under one particular type of general anesthesia, so the findings cannot automatically be extended to other anesthetic methods or states of unconsciousness.

It is also unclear whether similar language processing occurs during sleep or coma, two conditions that differ significantly from medically induced unconsciousness.

Another important limitation is that the researchers focused on the hippocampus. Further studies will be needed to determine whether comparable abilities persist in other brain regions and how these areas interact when consciousness is absent.

Nevertheless, the results provide compelling evidence that unconsciousness does not necessarily mean the brain has stopped performing sophisticated information processing.

Instead, the brain may continue analyzing patterns, responding to unexpected events, and anticipating language even when a person has no conscious awareness of the surrounding world.

"This work pushes us to rethink what it means to be conscious," said Sheth. "The brain is doing much more behind the scenes than we fully understand."

#72. Celebrating 20 Years of The Marginalian and the Search for Meaning: Free Livestream This Friday

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If it makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider aiding its sustenance with a one-time or loyal donation. Your support makes all the difference.

At the dawn of my twenties, lonely, destitute, and disoriented by the demands of making a new life in an alien world, I started keeping notes on my search for meaning while working four jobs to pay my way through college. On October 23, 2006, I began sharing my discoveries — passages from books, links to neuroscience studies, reproductions of 16th-century Japanese woodcuts — in an office email to seven colleagues. They in turn began sharing it with friends, who began sharing it with friends. The fractal spread and, within a few years, the Library of Congress had included it in its permanent digital archive of culturally valuable materials. It changed shape (the essays grew longer, the questions deeper) and name (Brain Pickings became The Marginalian) but continued beating with the same heart, reckoning with the ongoing bewilderment of being alive — sometimes through science and philosophy, sometimes through poetry and children’s books, always through the lens of wonder, always offered freely: no advertising, no AI, not even an assistant, a thoroughly one-woman labor of love sustained by the love of strangers.

To celebrate twenty years of it, I am inviting friends from various walks of life — poets and physicists, musicians and actors, artists and historians of science — to read fragments of the writings, poetry and prose, that have most touched me over the years as I introduce each with a short reflection on its resonance to the eternal questions we live with: what do we make of our suffering, why did the world have to be beautiful, how do we see more clearly and love more purely.

With the format of The Universe in Verse and the feeling-tone of my Marginalian essays, the evening will feature live appearances and special contributions across spacetime by a constellation of beloved humans who have made my own life more livable over the years, among them Debbie Millman, Joan As Police Woman, Krista Tippett, Marie Howe, Diane Ackerman, James Gleick, Natascha McElhone, Sophie Blackall, Stephon Alexander, Natalie Batalha, Willow Defebaugh, Wendy MacNaughton, Zoë Keating, Nick Cave, Paola Prestini with the Young People’s Chorus of New York City, and surprise guests.

If you aren’t attending in atoms at breathtaking Saratoga Performing Arts Center — a state-of-the-art outdoor amphitheater in Upstate New York, surrounded by waterfalls and hot springs, awned by an old-growth forest in full autumnal glory — you can join us virtually via this free livestream:

#73. For How Long Do You Need to Meditate?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Picture this: 71 adults signed up for a study comparing brief to longer mindfulness practice. Many had never meditated, while others had dabbled years before.

Participants were divided at random into three groups: One group got 20 minutes of mindfulness meditation, a second group got five minutes, and the control group relaxed with audiobook excerpts from Bill Bryson’s A Short History of Nearly Everything, Bryson’s soothing recounting of the cosmos and our place in it.

In studies like these, “mindfulness meditation” typically means sitting quietly, eyes closed or softened, resting nonjudgmental attention on your breath or bodily sensations, gently noticing when your mind wanders (as it will), and just as gently bringing it back.

Now, you might expect that longer meditations would deliver greater benefits. After all, we’re conditioned to believe that more is better—especially when it comes to self-improvement. But this research and many other studies find that more minutes don’t necessarily mean more benefit: Shorter practices can work just as well—and sometimes better—while consistency may matter more than duration.

In this first study, each participant attended four 25-minute sessions over two weeks. In every session, the time not spent on audio-guided mindfulness-of-breath practice was filled by Bryson’s eloquence. To ensure the results reflected only the study activities, participants were asked to avoid any formal mindfulness practices outside these sessions.

After those two weeks, the five-minute meditators actually showed greater improvements in stress and mindful awareness (the tendency to stay present in daily life with less judgement) than the 20-minute group. Even depression and anxiety improved just as much—if not more.

Was the extra time with Bryson the magic ingredient for those five-minute meditators? The control group, who luxuriated in 25 uninterrupted minutes of his charm, showed no meaningful improvement. So while his voice may soothe, it wasn’t what moved the needle.

One five-minute meditator put it this way: “I always thought that to do mindfulness, I’d need a long time to dedicate to this, which seemed too challenging to even start. But I’ve learned that five minutes can help!” In contrast, a 20-minute participant admitted, “I think a shorter one would be better for me to learn mindfulness.”

There’s more. The facilitator observed that participants in the 20-minute meditation sessions more often fidgeted, shifted in their seats, and peeked through half-closed eyes, as if tranquility were just out of reach. Meanwhile, the five-minute meditators appeared more at ease and less prone to these signs of discomfort. Five of them even requested recordings to continue at home. The 20-minute group? Not a single request. For these beginners, less really did seem to be more.

Now, before you dash off to cancel that meditation retreat, remember that this study focused on people with little to no meditation experience. So if you’re a seasoned meditator, those longer sessions might still pack more punch for you, as we’ll explore later. And both the five-minute and 20-minute groups showed improvements in mindful awareness, depression, anxiety, and stress compared to the control group. The five-minute meditators just improved more when it came to mindful awareness and stress.

The takeaway? For beginners, a quick dip into mindfulness might be more refreshing than a long soak.

You might be wondering, Isn’t this just one study? Could it be a fluke? But multiple randomized controlled trials have explored how the length of meditation shapes its impact.

I join Christine Carter, Ph.D, in a webinar next week to talk about my book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick

In the largest of these studies, researchers recruited 372 adults online—about half of them new to meditation—to see how the “dose” of mindfulness meditation affected mindful awareness and emotional well-being. Participants were randomly sorted into one of four groups: Some meditated for 10 minutes, others for 20, and the rest listened to a 10- or 20-minute National Geographic article on sequoia trees. (Because nothing soothes stress like a deep dive into bark thickness.)

What did the researchers find? The 10-minute meditators showed greater improvements in mindful awareness than those who listened to the 10-minute sequoia lecture. Surprisingly, the 20-minute meditation group didn’t outperform any group—not even the tree enthusiasts. In fact, the 10-minute group showed slightly greater improvements in mindful awareness than the 20-minute meditators, although the difference wasn’t statistically significant, meaning it could have occurred by chance. Still, it suggests that for boosting mindful awareness right after practice, 10 minutes might be at least as effective as 20.

But that was just one session. What happens with consistent practice? In another study, 77 college students were randomly assigned to meditate daily for 10 or 20 minutes. After two weeks, both groups showed similar improvements in stress and, again, mindful awareness. But those assigned to the 20-minute group experienced a slightly greater boost in self-compassion, the skill of meeting your own struggles with the kindness you’d offer a dear friend.

So if you’ve poured hours into longer meditations, you can rest easy—it wasn’t for nothing. The evidence suggests that whether your sessions are short or sustained, they can offer meaningful benefits.

Another notable finding is that the 10-minute group practiced more consistently, logging about 82 minutes total. The 20-minute group missed more days and didn’t always finish, ending up with just 103. Double the goal, barely a quarter more practice.

If you’ve ever tried meditating, you might be nodding along. Some sessions are bliss, while others are a tug-of-war with time. Maybe you’ve battled that nagging frustration, trying to keep your mind steady for more than a fleeting moment. Or felt the magnetic pull of distraction, your mind wandering just when you need it to stay put. As the minutes crawl, doubt can creep in: Am I even doing this right? Is it worth it? These tough moments can teach you a lot, but they can also make meditation feel intimidating—and make you less likely to stick with it, especially when you’re just starting out.   Another study looked at even longer sessions, comparing 10 minutes of meditation to 30 minutes. This experiment split 161 adults into four groups: 10 or 30 minutes of daily sitting meditation, or the same amount of mindful movement. The mindful movement was a stretching practice that brings mindful awareness into motion—less stillness, same presence.

After two weeks, everyone saw benefits: Mindful awareness increased, well-being improved, and distress levels dropped. But there were no significant differences among the groups. Whether they meditated for 10 minutes or 30, sitting or moving, all the groups seemed to benefit equally.

So, here’s the bottom line: One study found that longer sessions more strongly boosted self-compassion. Another showed that shorter ones more effectively reduced stress. But across studies, most of the key benefits—mindful awareness, mental health, well-being—weren’t tied to how long people practiced.

Why? Because as we’ll keep exploring, the nervous system learns through repetition, not duration. It’s consistency that reshapes patterns. Not heroic efforts once in a while, but showing up, again and again, however you can.

The benefits of consistency over length show up in observational studies, too, where people choose how often and how long to meditate. While observational studies can’t pin down cause and effect, they offer a richer view of how shorter practices play out in the real world.

Imagine it’s early morning. You reach for your phone and open Insight Timer, a free meditation app. Before your meditation, it asks, “How are you today?” You tap an icon—maybe “OK,” maybe “great”—capturing a snapshot of your mood in seconds.

Now imagine doing this regularly, for 14 months straight. That’s exactly what 10,409 people from 103 countries did in a groundbreaking study. Many were new to meditation, using the app to track their emotional ups and downs in real time. It’s like taking your emotional temperature—not with a thermometer, but with a single tap that sums up how you feel.

The findings? Consistency (four to seven days a week)—not duration—was the strongest predictor of better mood, resilience, and equanimity, the ability to stay cool under pressure. Think of it like watering a plant: A little each week keeps it happy and growing. Forget all month and drown it after four weeks? It wilts anyway.

For beginners in the Insight Timer study, short sessions—five to 10 minutes—outshone longer ones in improving mood over time. But after 20 sessions? Longer practices—21 to 30 minutes—began to take the lead in mood improvement. It’s like your brain needs to build its meditation muscles before longer sessions feel better than short ones—like a marathon that only gives you the high once you’ve earned it.

But do shorter sessions lose their impact as you gain experience? Not at all. They might just become your secret weapon. After 80 sessions, shorter practices make a late-game comeback, boosting equanimity and showing that even seasoned meditators can benefit from briefer sessions.

The idea that consistency beats duration is backed by a meta-analysis challenging the belief that longer equals better. Think of a meta-analysis as a “study of studies,” combining data from multiple research papers to uncover clearer, big-picture insights.

When researchers analyzed 203 randomized controlled trials totaling 15,971 participants, they found no association between meditation session length and better outcomes. In fact, a trend emerged in favor of shorter practices for reducing depression symptoms, although it wasn’t statistically significant. Still, shorter sessions were at least as effective as longer ones, calling into question the assumption that more minutes always mean more benefits.   So what’s the takeaway? When you’re starting out, don’t sweat the long stuff. Quick sessions might do more to lift your mood early on. As you settle in, longer practices might bring deeper emotional gains. But even if you’re a pro, short sessions don’t lose their value—they just shift their superpower, helping you stay steady when life throws you curveballs. Different strengths, different stages. And who doesn’t love a shortcut that actually works?

Eli Susman, Ph.D., is a UC Berkeley-trained psychologist, former Harvard researcher, and author of Micropractice: A Science-Backed Approach for Calm, Clarity, and Joy in 30 Seconds or Less, forthcoming in 22 languages.

Using animal characters, educators can help children navigate big feelings with mindfulness and self-compassion.

A study of 38,000 people around the world finds that people who feel connected to nature are more hopeful, purposeful and resilient.

Whether we’ve been trying to improve our exercise, eating, sleep, or happiness, self-reflection is one of the most practical tools we have.

What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.

#74. ADHD Linked to 70% Higher All-Cause Mortality Risk

A massive meta-analysis spanning nearly 16 million individuals across three continents reveals that people diagnosed with ADHD have a 70% higher rate of death from all causes compared to those without the condition. The increased mortality is driven by heightened risks of suicide, accidental injuries, and natural causes, though preliminary evidence suggests that ADHD medication is associated with a 25% reduction in overall mortality risk.

Source: University College London (UCL) / University of Liverpool

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is widely recognized as a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by challenges with sustained attention, executive function, and impulse control. While its cognitive and educational consequences are well established, emerging epidemiological data shows that its health ramifications can be far more serious.

In a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis published in JAMA Network Open, researchers from University College London (UCL) and the University of Liverpool analyzed data from 19 longitudinal cohort studies encompassing close to 16 million participants across three continents. In some included cohorts, individuals were monitored for more than two decades.

The findings deliver a sobering look at the long-term health inequalities associated with the neurodivergent condition: individuals with an ADHD diagnosis had a 70% higher rate of death from all causes compared to those without the diagnosis.

The elevated mortality associated with ADHD spanned both unnatural and natural causes, reflecting a mix of behavioral, psychiatric, and physical health challenges:

“We have previously found that people with ADHD have reduced life expectancies, so here we are adding to our understanding of what drives this very concerning statistic,” said senior author Joshua Stott, PhD, professor in UCL Psychology and Language Sciences. “We found that people with ADHD face an increased risk not only of death by suicide and injury, but also of deaths by natural causes, adding to evidence that health inequalities faced by people with ADHD are broad and wide-ranging.”

The researchers noted that excess natural-cause mortality is frequently compounded by lifestyle risk behaviors, including tobacco, alcohol, and substance use, as well as systemic barriers to healthcare engagement, difficulty scheduling appointments, and reduced adherence to chronic disease regimens.

Despite the stark mortality statistics, the researchers found a promising signal when examining treatment interventions. Among individuals diagnosed with ADHD, those who were prescribed ADHD medication exhibited an estimated 25% reduction in all-cause mortality compared to untreated peers.

While promising, the investigators caution that this protective effect was drawn from three of the 19 studies that specifically tracked medication status, meaning further targeted investigation is needed.

“Our findings provide early evidence to suggest that medication may play an important role in supporting the health of people with ADHD, but this is based on a small number of studies and further research is needed to clarify this link,” said first author Lucy Corrigan of the University of Liverpool. “And medication is just part of the story; many people with ADHD benefit from comprehensive, long-term treatment and support.”

The research team stressed that ADHD itself is not inherently fatal, and that the elevated mortality risk largely reflects modifiable environmental, societal, and treatment deficits.

“ADHD is not by definition a life-limiting condition as the right support and treatment can help people with ADHD to live long and healthy lives,” emphasized Stott. “Our findings underscore the importance of ensuring that everyone who may have ADHD has access to accurate diagnosis and treatment. While ADHD diagnosis rates have risen in recent years, they may still lag behind actual prevalence, particularly for older age groups where mortality risk may be most pertinent.”

Senior author Amber John, PhD, of UCL and the University of Liverpool, added that addressing systemic healthcare disparities must remain a central public health priority: “Many people with ADHD face challenges throughout their lives, so equitable access to evidence-based assessment and treatment is vital to ensure they can live long, healthy lives.”

Mortality among people with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with adverse life outcomes and increased mortality. Clarifying the magnitude of mortality risks using international data and the potential association between medication and mortality is essential to inform clinical care and motivate public health strategies to address mortality.

To examine the association between ADHD and all-cause and cause-specific mortality and to assess whether mortality risk differs according to ADHD medication use.

A comprehensive search of PubMed, Web of Science, PsycINFO, EMBASE, MEDLINE, and CINAHL was conducted from database inception to July 8, 2025.

Eligible studies included quantitative research across all age groups reporting all-cause and/or cause-specific mortality in individuals with ADHD, defined via diagnostic criteria, self-identification, trait measures, or ADHD polygenic risk scores. Exclusion criteria were nonoriginal research, qualitative studies, non–peer-reviewed publications, and studies not reporting mortality outcomes.

Data extraction was conducted independently by 2 reviewers. Study quality was assessed by 1 reviewer. Summary data were extracted from published reports, and pooled hazard ratios (HRs) were calculated using random-effects model meta-analysis.

The primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and cause-specific mortality (suicide, unintentional or intentional injury, and natural causes), measured using HRs with 95% CIs.

Nineteen studies including 15 920 970 participants (36.1% female) were included. ADHD was associated with increased all-cause mortality (HR, 1.71; 95% CI, 1.31-2.24; P < .001). Significant associations were also observed for suicide (HR, 1.89; 95% CI, 1.21-2.95; P = .005), unintentional or intentional injury (HR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.22-2.00; P < .001), and natural-cause mortality (HR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.16-1.38; P < .001). ADHD medication use in people with ADHD was associated with reduced all-cause mortality (HR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.64-0.87; P < .001). Substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies.

In this systematic review and meta-analysis of ADHD and mortality, ADHD was associated with increased mortality across multiple causes; and ADHD medication was associated with a decreased all-cause mortality risk, underscoring the importance of timely diagnosis and treatment. However, the heterogeneity observed across studies highlights the need for standardized methods and improved control of confounding factors to better characterize mortality risk among individuals with ADHD.

#75. Struggling with impulse control? Try these 7 tips

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

You send the text before you finish thinking it through. You put in an online order before asking yourself whether you really need it. You eat three bites of the snack before you realize you’re not even hungry.

Impulsive moments like these aren't signs of a character flaw. They reflect your brain's tendency to act before it fully evaluates the consequences. For some people, that tendency shows up during a stressful stretch and eases once life calms down. For others, especially those with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), it's more of a constant struggle. Either way, impulse control is a skill you can improve.

So, what does this mean for you? Let’s break down what drives impulse control, and what you can do about it.

Impulse control is your ability to pause before you act on an urge, thought, or emotion — that split second where you decide whether to follow through.

Your prefrontal cortex, the part of your brain responsible for planning and thinking ahead, mostly handles this. When it's working well, it helps catch an impulse before that impulse becomes an action.

If your impulse control feels shaky at times, that’s not necessarily a willpower problem. It usually means your brain is under strain from stress, poor sleep, or emotional overload.

Most people who act impulsively on occasion don’t have a diagnosed disorder. For others, though, struggling to resist harmful urges is a persistent pattern. Impulse control disorder covers conditions like intermittent explosive disorder (sudden, disproportionate anger), kleptomania (compulsive stealing), pyromania (compulsive fire-setting), and compulsive gambling. These conditions may respond well to professional support, such as therapy or medication.

Your brain relies on two systems that don't always agree. The limbic system reacts fast, driven by emotion and instinct. The prefrontal cortex works slower, weighing your options before you act.

When you're calm and rested, the prefrontal cortex can keep impulsive urges in check. When your brain is pushed past its capacity, the limbic system takes over instead. Impulse control shifts throughout the day depending on how you're feeling, which is why the same urge can feel manageable to sit with one moment and impossible to resist the next.

A few factors can make impulse control harder:

sleep deprivation, which weakens your brain's ability to regulate behavior

chronic stress, which keeps your brain in a heightened, reactive state

strong emotions that feel too intense to ignore or resist

substance use, which affects your brain's decision-making centers

ADHD and other neurodevelopmental conditions, where pausing may be a challenge throughout daily life, not just under pressure

Like any skill, impulse control strengthens with practice. The tips below work at different layers: some help in the moment, while others ease the mental strain that makes urges harder to resist in the first place. Feel free to start with one or two that feel relevant to you.

Impulsive urges can feel pressing, but they don’t have to dictate what you do next. Often, just pausing for a moment is enough to break the pull.

Try: Counting to ten, taking a slow breath, or naming what you're feeling out loud. Some people find a go-to phrase useful, such as "not yet" or "wait and see" to delay their response. Over time, this habit starts to feel more natural.

💙 Learn how to Resist Emotional Urges with Dr. Julie Smith on Calm.

Most impulsive behavior follows a pattern. It tends to spike around conflict, boredom, overwhelm, hunger, or fatigue. Once you learn your triggers, you can work with them instead of reacting in the moment.

Try: Keeping a brief log for a week or two. Note when impulsivity shows up, what leads to it, and how you feel. Once you spot a pattern—say, you're most reactive before meals or after a difficult conversation—you can plan around it.

Eat before that difficult conversation. Save demanding tasks for your sharper hours. Take a breath before responding to messages that tend to trigger a reaction.

💙 Discover Dr. Judson Brewer’s Breaking Bad Habits masterclass on Calm.

Under pressure, your brain defaults to what's fast and familiar. If-then planning gives it a prepared response instead, so you're not improvising when emotions are running high.

Try: "If [situation], then I'll [response]." For example, "If I feel the urge to reply right away, then I'll wait 10 minutes first." Or "If I'm about to make an unplanned purchase, then I'll add it to a list and revisit it in 48 hours." The more specific the plan, the harder it is to talk yourself out of it later.

💙 Walk through this process with Calm’s If-Then session with Jay Shetty.

Impulse control runs on limited fuel: sleep, stress, and mental bandwidth all shape how much of it you have on a given day. That's why impulsive urges tend to show up most at the end of a long day or after a stretch of bad sleep.

You can't eliminate every source of strain, but you can cut down on low-stakes daily decisions. Try prepping meals or laying out clothes the night before — that way, you're not making choices when you're already running on empty.

It’s also worth protecting what restores you, including sleep, movement, time away from screens, and nourishing meals.

Struggling with too many decisions? Here are 8 tips for when your mental energy is low.

Regular mindfulness practice builds your ability to pause as an ongoing habit, not just in the moment an impulse hits. Start with a few minutes a day, and keep at it on a schedule that works for you.

Try: Focusing on your breathing during practice. When you notice an urge come up (to shift position, check your phone, stop early), gently return your attention to your breath instead of acting on it.

💙 Start with the Basics of Mindfulness from the 7 Days of Calm series.

New habits can be tempting to abandon in the moment. Outside structure, like asking someone to check in on you, gives you accountability beyond your own willpower.

Try: Telling someone about the pattern you're trying to change. Even saying it out loud can make it harder to slide back into old habits.

If you’d rather handle this on your own, here are 6 ways to hold yourself accountable.

If your impulsivity is a constant pattern that impacts your relationships, work, and daily life, self-directed strategies may not be enough.

A therapist trained in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can help you identify what's driving your behavior and develop more effective responses. If ADHD is part of the picture, an assessment can open the door to options like medication.

If you're not sure where to start, your primary care provider is a good first stop.

Poor impulse control can look like interrupting people mid-conversation, buying things without thinking it through, snapping in anger, or acting on cravings without a second thought. It tends to show up most when you're under pressure, drained, or emotionally overwhelmed.

If you have ADHD, tools such as if-then planning give your brain a prepared response before the moment of temptation arrives. Consistent mindfulness practice can also help you build the capacity to pause in those moments.

If impulsivity is getting in the way of your work, relationships, or daily life, it's worth talking to your doctor or an ADHD specialist. For some people, medication can meaningfully help.

Impulse control disorder may involve anger that feels bigger than the situation calls for, compulsive stealing, or gambling that's negatively impacting your life. If resisting an urge feels out of your control, that's worth bringing to a doctor — this condition is treatable.

Stress puts your brain into threat-response mode, which interferes with the part of your brain that handles careful decisions. That heightened stress state is useful in an actual emergency, where speed is more important than reflection. But in everyday situations, it makes thoughtful decision-making harder.

Mindfulness trains the same skill impulse control relies on: noticing an urge without immediately acting on it. Regular practice improves attention and emotional regulation, which makes it easier to find that pause in tempting situations. This can be especially useful if you have ADHD or you’re working on substance-related impulsivity.

Check out how a regular mindfulness practice can support your overall mental well-being.

The amount of time it takes to improve impulse control depends on your situation and your approach. Tools such as if-then planning or pausing before big decisions can help within a few weeks, while mindfulness and therapy tend to take longer — often several months of consistent practice.

Self-control is broader than impulse control: it covers habits like managing emotions and staying on task. Impulse control is more specific: it's about what you do in the gap between having an urge and acting on it. You can have strong self-control overall and still struggle with impulses in the moment, or be quick to pause in the moment while your broader self-control could use work.

#77. Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger

Stress does more than influence how we feel. It can also change what we remember, particularly when an experience is emotionally intense or personally meaningful. Scientists have long known that cortisol, a hormone released during stressful situations, can strengthen emotional memories. What has been less clear is exactly how this happens inside the brain.

Researchers at Yale University have now uncovered important clues. Their study reveals that cortisol strengthens emotional memories by changing how brain networks involved in emotion and memory function and communicate with one another. The findings offer a deeper understanding of why certain experiences leave such powerful impressions while others quickly fade.

"We all experience stress, and my lab is interested in understanding how stress can be helpful," said corresponding author Elizabeth Goldfarb, an assistant professor of psychiatry at Yale School of Medicine and of psychology in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences.

The findings were published in the journal Science Advances.

Previous research involving both humans and rodents has shown that stress and cortisol can improve memory for emotional events. Scientists also know that certain brain regions, including the amygdala, play an essential role in this process. The amygdala is particularly important for processing emotions and identifying experiences that may be significant.

However, understanding precisely how cortisol strengthens memories has been challenging. Many brain regions participate in several mental functions, making it difficult to determine whether the hormone is influencing emotional responses, memory formation, or both.

"Forming memories for emotional experiences involves different processes in the brain: first, perceiving an experience as emotional or intense, and second, encoding that experience into long-term memory," said Goldfarb, who is also a member of Yale's Wu Tsai Institute, an interdisciplinary research initiative that explores cognition.

The researchers wanted to examine these processes separately to determine how cortisol affects the brain's ability to recognize emotional significance and preserve an experience as a lasting memory.

Watching the Brain Form Emotional Memories

To investigate, the Yale team conducted an experiment in which participants took a pill containing either hydrocortisone, a form of cortisol, or an inactive placebo. They then viewed a series of pictures while undergoing functional MRI (fMRI) scanning.

This imaging technique measures changes in blood flow and oxygen levels associated with brain activity, allowing researchers to identify which areas of the brain are more active during different tasks.

As participants examined the pictures, they reported their emotional reactions to each image. The following day, researchers tested how well they remembered what they had seen.

Each person completed the experiment twice, once after receiving hydrocortisone and once after receiving the placebo. The study used a double blind design, meaning neither the participants nor the experimenter knew which substance had been administered during a particular session.

This approach allowed the scientists to compare how the same person's brain responded with and without the additional cortisol.

A Five-Second Look at Brain Network Activity

One of the study's most important advances came from the way researchers analyzed the brain scans.

Scientists often study a measurement called functional connectivity, which describes how closely activity in different parts of the brain fluctuates together. When two regions show synchronized patterns of activity, it can indicate that they are participating in related processes.

Traditionally, examining these relationships requires several minutes of brain imaging data. The Yale team instead analyzed functional connectivity during individual trials lasting only around five seconds.

Using these brief snapshots, the researchers tested whether patterns of brain activity could predict two different outcomes: how emotionally intense participants found a picture and whether they would remember that picture the following day.

The approach worked for both. By identifying patterns associated with emotional intensity and memory formation separately, the scientists were able to examine how cortisol influenced each network and the interactions between them.

This gave the researchers a more detailed picture of the changing brain activity associated with emotional memory formation.

Cortisol Changes How Brain Networks Work Together

First, cortisol improved participants' ability to remember emotionally significant experiences, confirming what earlier research had suggested.

Second, and more importantly, the hormone strengthened emotional memory through distinct changes in the brain networks responsible for processing emotion and forming memories.

In networks associated with emotion, cortisol produced more consistent patterns of activity and increased their engagement. This suggests that the hormone helped the brain respond more strongly and reliably to the emotional significance of an experience.

In memory networks, cortisol had a different effect. It made their activity patterns more specialized for emotional information, suggesting that the brain was adjusting how it encoded emotionally meaningful experiences.

The hormone also increased coordination between the networks involved in emotion and memory. In other words, cortisol appeared to help these different brain systems work together more effectively when processing experiences that carried emotional weight.

Together, these findings suggest that stress strengthens emotional memories through several interacting brain mechanisms rather than through a single region or process.

Why Emotional Experiences Can Be So Memorable

The results help explain why stress does not necessarily improve memory for everything. Instead, its benefits appear to be selective, making experiences that feel particularly intense or meaningful more likely to be remembered.

The researchers believe this reflects the brain's ability to adapt to stressful situations by prioritizing information that may be important.

"Stress responses are fundamentally adaptive and can help you form strong memories -- but this is specific to experiences that you find to be emotionally intense or meaningful," Goldfarb said. "This is in part related to your brain increasing engagement of networks that track emotional intensity. So, if you are stressed out and trying to learn something new, it might help to think about exciting elements or strong feelings connected to what you are learning."

The findings also point to a potentially useful insight about learning. Connecting information to something exciting, personally important, or emotionally engaging could make it easier to remember, particularly during stressful situations.

Rather than simply disrupting memory, stress can sometimes help the brain identify which experiences deserve special attention and strengthen the networks involved in preserving them.

Other Yale researchers involved in the study include Rajita Sinha, the Foundations Fund Endowed Professor in Psychiatry and professor in the Child Study Center and of neuroscience at Yale School of Medicine (YSM), and Todd Constable, the Elizabeth Mears and House Jameson Professor of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging and professor of neurosurgery at YSM.

The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health.

#78. Why House Mapping Can Save the ADHD Home

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated September 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

People believe that homes are supposed to look a certain way. Our counters, closets, desks, and dining tables all have to have a certain order; otherwise, it is chaos.

Instead of trying to shape your home to fit a perfect picture of what you think a space should look like, house mapping—which means intentionally following the way you live when you design your home—follows your natural rhythms as a family and individual. The goal is to reduce the amount of work your brain must do.

Where do you put things when you are not thinking about it? Why do you put them there? How do you move around your space? When working well, the house map acts as an executive function by reducing demands rather than continually forcing you to override your natural behavior. Less decision-making means less mental fatigue.

As an ADHD specialist and creator of the W-CAT Model—a women-centered ADHD treatment—I once spoke with a woman who was frustrated because her family kept leaving their shoes scattered near the entry doorway. They were partially onto something, as they put their shoes in the right location, but they lacked the contextual cue of the rack, which, surprisingly, was hidden right behind the door they opened to enter.

That is the thing with house mapping: Most of us are not far off from systems that could actually work for our families. Instead of doing what looks best, is most expected, or is most socially acceptable, we can shift toward how we move throughout our homes to curb the chaos without putting more pressure on our family. Something as simple as moving the shoe rack two feet to where everyone already took off their shoes worked for that woman. Their floor is now mostly shoe-free, but on days the shoes do not make it onto the rack she practices compassion, because reshaping habits—and even gendered expectations for housekeeping—takes time and adaptation.

1. Nervous system first. Your home should help lower activation rather than continually adding to it. Visual chaos, harsh lighting, and sensory discomfort can create moments of stress throughout the day. Research shows that parenting in an environment with clutter and material disorganization, alongside noise and unpredictability, can increase salivary alpha-amylase (sAA), a marker of activation in the body’s stress-response system.

2. Follow the path of least resistance. The more steps a system requires, the harder it may be to sustain. A hook may work better than a hanger, and a visible basket can work better than a container stacked inside a closed closet. Every extra step adds mental load. You can also use friction intentionally. If you want to interrupt an automatic pattern, place something directly in its path. For example, put a small table and lamp where you usually throw dirty clothes. By changing the physical space, you interrupt the habit and cue a different choice. This makes desired behaviors easier and unwanted patterns slightly harder to continue automatically.

3. Choose function over appearance. Much like the French culinary concept mise en place, meaning everything in its place—where ingredients and tools are made visible and accessible before cooking begins—our home should function similarly. Open storage, clear bins, and unconventional landing zones can offer ADHD brains the visible cues they need. Take inventory of whether what you need is visible and within reach—and if it is not, remap it.

4. Contain where possible. Our environments interact with our mood, energy, and attention. In feng shui, each piece of clutter is thought of as an unmade decision, meaning every visible object is another thing for the brain to process. Containing items can help with this. When multiple objects are grouped inside a basket, the brain can visually register them as one organized unit rather than many separate items competing for attention.

5. Map as a team. A house map affects everyone who lives within it, so creating and maintaining it should not be one person’s burden. Explain what is changing, why it matters, and what each person can do to support it. Family habits do not change instantly, so expect repetition, reminders, and adjustments. The goal is a shared system that becomes easier and more natural to use over time.

House mapping does not require reorganizing your entire home all at once. Begin with one space that repeatedly creates friction and notice where things naturally land, where tasks tend to stall, and what small change might make the next step easier. Sometimes an ADHD-friendly home just needs one manageable adjustment that helps action happen more naturally.

Here is what that can look like in practice:

The Entryway: A typical entryway may rely on a closed coat closet, hangers, and a small decorative table. An ADHD-friendly house map uses open hooks at eye level, a sturdy floor bin, and visible places for shoes, bags, and keys. Mail is another high-friction task in this space. Try immediately ripping up and recycling junk mail, then placing anything requiring attention into one visible container. In my home, we put these items on the coffee maker because we use it every morning and must see and physically move the mail to use it. The landing zone should be where people naturally interact with cues so they cannot easily overlook it.

The Kitchen: When food and utensils disappear behind doors, they can also disappear from working memory. Wire baskets, accessible shelves, visible produce, or frequently used tools kept within reach can create reminders without requiring someone to search where things are hidden. Remain aware that if everything is visible, too much input can also be overwhelming. The map should help you see what you most often use without turning the entire room into noise. Bonus tip: If you are right-handed, these items may work best to the right of your workspace. Every inch matters.

The Living Room: A single overhead light may be too intense for some nervous systems. Multiple lower-level lamps give family members more control over stimulation and can help families transition toward rest in the evening. A basket with fidgets, headphones, or blankets helps keep regulation supports within reach. If you are a “living room family” and this is the space where the kids play, consider decorative bins that slide easily into the furniture and feel soothing within the room. Invite children to return their toys “home” each night. Their favorites may naturally stay near the top, making it easier to identify forgotten items at the bottom that can be donated or discarded.

The Bedroom and Laundry: Deep drawers and highly specific clothing categories can become an ADHD bottleneck. One option is three accessible baskets: one for clean items that do not need folding, one for dirty clothes, and one for clothes that have been worn but are not ready to be washed. This gives the in-between clothes a home and reduces the shame of the familiar “floordrobe” or chair piled with clothing. Also consider whether your bedroom is solely for sleep and rest or whether it serves another purpose, such as a home office. If it's the latter, bring some of the living-room house-mapping principles into this space and follow what is actually happening in a room rather than forcing the space to conform to expectations.

When you live with neurodivergence, are overcoming trauma, are postpartum, menopausal, burned out, or overwhelmed, everything, including clutter, is input. Over time, house mapping can make this input feel more predictable and less stressful. The space may not make sense to anyone else, and that is okay if it follows the map of how you and your family move and live. Don't try to house-map every procedure in your home at once and turn this into a mission for failure. Pick one map at a time: the counter, the mail, the dining table, or the laundry. And if and when systems fail—as they often do—return to the principles with a growth mindset, curiosity, and the willingness to try again.

Portions of this article were adapted from Wired and Worthy’s podcast episode House Mapping for ADHD: Organize Your Home Around How Your Brain Works.

#79. “How Did They Not Notice? Confronting My Parents After My Late ADHD Diagnosis.”

“This is where the real ADHD burnout hits. It’s the constant second-guessing, the masking. It’s the outbursts I’d have as a child toward my parents, after acting perfect all day at school.”

If you were diagnosed with ADHD later in life like I was, you likely felt a sense of grief and confusion after receiving the news.

So you’re telling me that everything — from my constant burn out and mortifying tendency to overshare with strangers to my nonsensical impulse buys — boils down to a four-letter acronym? That I’ve had a medical condition all this time that necessitated treatment, yet I was forced to rawdog life with ADHD? That my family didn’t notice, or didn’t think my struggles were enough to act on?

As a child I was very energetic. My mom enrolled me in multiple hobbies and activities a day just so she could get some peace. While I don’t remember much from my childhood, I remember being unable to sit still. (That was torture!) Boredom was always an entirely overwhelming feeling — I constantly needed something to do, even if that meant painting the walls of my bedroom, which obviously pleased my mother.

In school I focused on my studies. I was terrified of my teachers and authority figures, so I ensured I was a perfect, grade-A student. I only achieved this by studying well past midnight, only getting about three to four hours of sleep most nights.

I was not like my accomplished peers, on the other hand, who completed homework during “after-school club” with such ease. Their minds were not unfocused by the birds outside the window or the click-clack sound of a teacher’s heels. “Good for her; I could never wear those heels,” I thought. And then suddenly the history essay I needed to finish was overcast by my stress of not being able to remember what was needed to finish the damn thing.

[Read: “You Are Way Too Hard on Yourself” Unspoken Truths About Women with ADHD]

ADHD came up in other ways, too. I was constantly fixated on what others thought of me. I picked up on everything — like the annoyed expression on my local barista’s face when I was indecisive about what to order, or the car honking directed my way due to my excellent driving skills. A dirty look, or a less-than-favorable impression of me would have derailed my whole day. It would utterly consume how I saw myself.

This is where the real ADHD burnout hits. It’s the constant second-guessing, the masking. It’s the outbursts I’d have as a child toward my parents, after acting perfect all day at school. On edge all day, I would get irritated and explosive over the smallest inconveniences, like having my sleeve catch on the door. (I found out during my ADHD assessment that bumping into things and having no spatial awareness is very common. I feel for all of you who have experienced the same challenges with proprioception.)

Now I am not saying ADHD is all bad. I strongly disagree with the sentiment that “ADHD is a superpower,” but it does offer moments of superhuman focus and flow. I found this out while in university, when I thought I had cracked the code to my brain. Being in a flow state felt safe. I would forget to eat, forget to message friends back, and spend up to 14 hours on a project. I would produce amazing results and then, of course, burn out the very next day.

Sometimes I’d abandon projects altogether. This still happens from time to time, as is the case with my garden. I mounted bamboo on the walls, added brickwork, YouTubed every new DIY skill needed for the project, and after cutting wooden planks with a chainsaw-type machine (very scary, would not recommend), I just left it, half done. Now I avoid looking at it.

[Read: “What It Feels Like Living with Undiagnosed ADHD”]

After my diagnosis, I asked my parents directly: How did you not notice?

I asked because I felt I missed the opportunity to find clarity and peace within myself a lot earlier in life. But my parents didn’t have much of an answer. The conversation ranged from, “But you seemed OK, you just had too much energy” to, “You sang that song over and over for 15 days straight to annoy us and because you loved it.” All of that screams ADHD to me, yet I was overlooked.

It did feel bad that my parents showed very little interest in my diagnosis, even going so far as saying things like, “It just means you can’t concentrate, right?” and, “But you have a master’s degree, you surely needed to concentrate for that!” I held back my disappointment and hurt rather than spew. Sure, I got an advanced degree, but I paid the price of burning out every other weekend and holding myself to impossible standards. Somewhere in the process of grieving a life that could have been, I found myself getting a bit petty about it. I sent and reposted Instagram reels that poked fun at parents who never clocked the signs of neurodivergence. I call it coping.

I am glad that the how-could-you-not-notice phase is over. I am diagnosed, my parents know, they don’t care to research or understand ADHD, and that is OK. I cannot control the actions of others.

My diagnosis has taught me a lot about myself. It has helped me build trust in myself and empathize with that little girl who just kept thinking “Why am I so different? Why can’t I be normal?”

I am genuinely glad I am not “normal.” I realize now there is no such thing. There are so many not-normal people out there who are wonderfully brilliant and living life on their own terms. I am not quite there yet, but I know I will be.

#80. Increase Your Agency By Responding, Instead of Reacting

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

Ever wonder why your emails tend to be better when you wait a little before replying? Choosing to take a pause before we act may sound simple, but it yields powerful results. Longtime mindfulness teacher and author Andrew Safer shares a few ways we can practice pausing, both at our job and everywhere in our life.

You are sitting at your desk, working on a project summary that has to go out by end of day. In order to get to this, you had to put two other priorities in hold. This is a critical deliverable, and you’ve just sat down with a fresh cup of coffee to dig in. Your manager appears. “I know you’re planning on turning in that report later today,” he says, “but there’s something else that you need to look at by the middle of the afternoon.” Plunking a folder on the only clear section of your desk, he vanishes.

“No problem,” you valiantly blurt out, immediately wishing you hadn’t said that, considering you will have to turn your day upside down. Now, your boss will have no idea what contortions you have to go through to satisfy his request. Your stress response kicks in, and you start on the new file. Part of you wants to race through it, and part of you wants to be thorough, so you read it unevenly. With a partial understanding of the contents, you do a half-assed job writing your comments.

Mindfulness can bring a different mindset if we begin to practice pausing and responding instead of reacting, and we can start with small inconveniences. At any point during our day, we can use the STOP method of pausing, described by David Gelles, a New York Times reporter and author of Mindful Work.

No longer at the mercy of habit, we have agency, and with that comes improved decision-making.

It’s not about a happy ending so much as interrupting the reactions that come automatically. Each time we bring ourselves out from under the thumb of emotional pressure, we experience a sense of freedom. We also momentarily break a habitual pattern. We see that it’s possible to “keep our head” and proceed. No longer at the mercy of habit, we have agency, and with that comes improved decision-making.

When there is a sense of urgency, the last thing we want to do is pause. We want to take care of it! Often when something feels urgent, it’s actually not. Take an itch, for example. In sitting meditation, suddenly, our nose itches. Our arm reflexively goes up with one finger extended, we give it a good scratch, and that’s that! Scratching is automatic. Since it’s not a life-or-death emergency, an itch becomes an opportunity to practice pausing and seeing the bigger picture.

If you don’t feel an itch during this practice session, keep this in mind and apply this approach when you do, either while practicing or in everyday life.

Practice provides a safe environment for a “dry run.” We see that we can be aware of the itch, without necessarily having to scratch right away. Our habitual pattern takes us from the first sensation of the itch to immediately scratching. If you think of how many times you have scratched an itch, this automatic response is very well established! It might take some practice before we are able to interrupt our reactivity.

General Mills is a Fortune 500 company that began providing mindfulness training for its employees in 2006. Sandy Behnken, General Mills’ Continuous Improvement Internal Consultant, coordinated 25 IT leaders in a seven-week mindful leadership course and participated in the learning herself. “Within a couple of weeks of the course starting,” she recalls, “I could see how my mindfulness practice impacted my interactions at work. I became more aware of the many stimuli impacting me and was better able to decide how I was going to respond versusreact to them.”

We spend a great deal of our waking hours in our heads: thinking a step ahead, planning, strategizing, rehearsing, worrying, remembering. Of course, some of this can be productive, but we can become oblivious to where we are! All of this mental activity can go on whether sitting in our office or standing on beach sand. Being grounded means feeling our connection to Earth, which is fundamental, and which helps us transition from reactivity to reasoned response.

We practice grounding ourselves in meditation. In the beginning of a practice session, we place our attention on our feet on the floor, our breath, or another anchor, and then during the session we might touch back there a number of times.

During the workday, another way we can ground ourselves is through mindful walking. If you have a few minutes in between meetings, a little mindful walking may be your only chance to refresh before working again.

The transition from reactivity to reasoned response comes down to awareness. With reactivity, we are trapped in stimulus-automatic response mode—ensconced in that system, with no way out. In that mode, we don’t have a chance to do something different. There is only one playbook. So how do we go from choicelessness to options? We allow a gap. Taking a break, we challenge the premise that a stimulus necessarily leads to a reaction. Instead, there is an opening for awareness; the next move is up to us.

“Between stimulus and response there is a space,” writes neurologist, psychologist, and Holocaust survivor Viktor Frankl. “In that space is our power to choose our response. In our response lies our growth and our freedom.”

When you hear the chime alerting you to the email that just landed in your inbox, if you’re like me, you’re curious: who’s it from? What’s it about? The anticipation produces a hit of dopamine and the feeling of pleasure that goes along with it, which brings you to 1) want to see who it’s from, and 2) possibly open and read the message now. It could be good or bad news, important or junk, priority or not. The problem with sending an immediate answer is we’re feeding the stimulus-response loop, and overriding a considered response. I might miss context and tone, because panoramic awareness is absent.

Taking a break, we challenge the premise that a stimulus necessarily leads to a reaction. Instead, there is an opening for awareness; the next move is up to us.

Recently, I received an email from the mother of a youth who was suffering from psychosis in a mental hospital. She wanted to know if I could see him, and possibly, continue to see him over time. While I was delighted to hear from her, I found her email frustrating. Since email has become the norm for this type of communication, I felt duty bound to email her back, but didn’t think I could adequately address her questions that way. I let that message sit for several hours. Then I thanked her for getting in touch and asked if we could have a conversation. We proceeded to set up a telephone call. There was much in our conversation that could not have been covered in an email. Pausing and re-engaging when I was ready helped pave the way for a fruitful exchange.

Peter Bregman, founder and CEO of Bregman Partners, coaches CEOs and senior leaders internationally. A long-time meditator, he reflects on responding instead of reacting. “Our ability to resist an impulse determines our success in learning a new behavior or changing an old habit,” he writes. “It’s probably the single most important skill for our growth and development. As it turns out, that’s one of the things meditation teaches us. It’s also one of the hardest to learn.”

Republished with permission from Mindfulness in the Workplace: Cultivating Well-Being at Work. 2nd Tier Publishing: 2024. Copyright Andrew Safer.

Andrew Safer is a mindfulness instructor and trainer, and author based in St. John’s, Newfoundland, Canada. With a 55-year practice and 30 years as a mindfulness instructor, he presents applied mindfulness training programs for mental health (anxiety and stress, ADHD, depression, suicidal thoughts, and addictions) and the workplace.
