#81. What Bystanders Can Do to Stop Sexual Violence

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

As an undergrad student decades ago, I attended a dorm presentation describing the importance of giving and receiving sexual consent. The workshop leaders explained that if your partner said “no” or “stop” but you proceeded to have sex anyway, it was considered rape.

A high-profile athlete on campus raised his hand and said, in utter disbelief, “That can’t be right. By that definition, everyone I’ve ever had sex with I’ve raped.”

I was horrified by his comment, but most students laughed. He clearly saw nothing wrong with the view he’d expressed, presumably believing it was widely shared.

I immediately thought of this experience when I heard about the alleged sexual assault committed by seven fraternity members at Cornell University. As a social psychologist, and the author of a book examining why so-called good people stay silent in the face of problematic behavior, what I find most tragic about the events at Cornell is that reportedly over 50 men on a group chat learned about the assault as it was happening. Yet there’s been no public report that any of them tried to stop the assault, help the victim, or contact campus or local police departments.

This type of inaction is very common. In about one-third of sexual assaults, at least one other person is present who potentially could intervene but in most instances chooses not to. Why?

Data suggests a minority of men actually commit sexual assault. Researchers estimate about 6.5% of male college students in the United States and Canada have committed rape. Yet many men who find sexual violence offensive mistakenly believe that other men do not.

Undergraduate men in one study reported their beliefs about common rape myths, such as “If a girl doesn’t physically fight back, you can’t really say it was rape,” and “If a girl goes to a room alone with a guy at a party, it is her own fault if she is raped.” Researchers then asked participants how they thought both their close friends and average male college students would answer these same questions.

The results provided clear evidence that college men have skewed views of what those around them are thinking. Most students saw their classmates and friends as more supportive of rape myths than they themselves were.

Unfortunately, believing that other men generally accept sexual violence—even when this belief is wrong—inhibits their willingness to intervene to stop such behavior when they encounter it. In fact, men’s beliefs about their peers’ attitudes are a stronger predictor of their willingness to intervene than their own stated attitudes about sexual aggression.

Men who underestimate their peers’ discomfort with sexually aggressive behavior often fear the consequences of calling out problematic views or intervening in the face of inappropriate behavior. The most common reason male college students give for failing to intervene in situations involving sexual violence is a fear of being laughed at or ridiculed—in particular, a desire not to appear weak to other men.

Men who actually commit assault also tend to overestimate support for such behavior. Not surprisingly, men who report having committed sexual assault believe that other men are more accepting of such behavior and have engaged in such behavior themselves.

This assumed support leads them to feel comfortable describing problematic behavior, which leads other men to believe that sexual violence is more common, and more accepted, than it actually is.

Given the consistent evidence that men wrongly believe that most men are more comfortable with sexual violence than they themselves are, the challenge is not to change the social norm. It’s getting people to see what it actually already is.

Correcting such misperceptions can go a long way toward reducing sexual violence. First-year male college students who participate in a 90-minute sexual assault prevention program—focused on refuting rape myths, increasing awareness of the importance of consent, and correcting misperceptions about other men’s attitudes and behaviors—report reduced levels of sexual aggression themselves four months later.

These programs work in two ways. First, men who receive accurate information about what other men actually believe are less inhibited about speaking out and intervening. Second, men who are at risk of engaging in sexual aggression may change their intentions after learning that their peers do not support such behavior.

At the same time, men in tight-knit groups feel considerable pressure to show loyalty to other group members, which may lead to ignoring bad behavior committed by their peers.

But the underlying dynamics of peer influence can help shift group norms from protecting group members by staying silent to stepping in to prevent bad behavior. One college football player described looking out for his teammates, even if that meant interrupting a potential sexual encounter: “Maybe you don’t get the girl, but you’ll keep your scholarship and still be on the team.”

Another approach for preventing sexual assault is to learn strategies for intervening. Bystander intervention programs emphasize the importance of stopping bad behavior before it escalates, teach specific skills for intervening, and remind people that everyone has a responsibility to prevent sexual violence.

Students who participate in such programs are more confident in their ability to intervene and more willing to do so. Most importantly, rates of sexual violence are markedly lower on campuses that have implemented these programs. For example, one study found that experiences of sexual harassment and stalking were 11% lower and that instances of unwanted sexual activity with women who were too drunk or high to stop them were as much as 17% lower.

It’s tempting to read about the Cornell case and assume the apparent inaction in the face of problematic behavior is uniquely a problem at one college, or only with members of fraternities, or only with college students. But the reality is that pretty much everyone has been in situations where they’ve seen potentially problematic behavior and failed to speak up.

Understanding the very normal psychological factors that lead people to misperceive what others are actually thinking and feeling—and learning specific strategies for intervening—can make a real difference.

#82. Resetting Interneuron Timing Rescues Memory in Alzheimer’s

Researchers at Gladstone Institutes have decoded how parvalbumin (PV) interneurons generate gamma oscillations—the fast brain waves essential for attention and memory—by firing in precise, successive waves rather than all at once. In Alzheimer’s disease models, this coordinated turn-taking breaks down into hypersynchrony; however, restoring the sodium channel Nav1.1 resets cellular timing, repairs gamma rhythms, eliminates epileptic spikes, clears amyloid plaques, and rescues cognitive function.

Whether focusing on a complex calculation, mastering a new skill, or retrieving an autobiographical memory, the mammalian brain relies on rapid, rhythmic electrical pulses known as gamma oscillations. Cycling between 30 and 90 times per second, these high-frequency background rhythms synchronize distant brain regions to facilitate high-level cognitive processing.

For decades, neuroscientists have recognized that gamma oscillations are severely degraded in patients with Alzheimer’s disease. Yet how individual cells naturally coordinate to generate these rhythms, and why that choreography collapses in disease, remained an enduring biological question.

Now, a study led by researchers at Gladstone Institutes, in collaboration with the Allen Institute and UTHealth Houston, has uncovered the precise cellular dynamics behind these cognitive waves.

Publishing in the journal Neuron, the research team revealed that specialized inhibitory cells called parvalbumin (PV) interneurons generate gamma rhythms by firing in precise, successive relays. Crucially, the researchers demonstrated that this relay breaks down in Alzheimer’s disease, and showed that restoring the sodium channel Nav1.1 resets cellular timing and rescues cognitive function.

Previous research into gamma rhythms relied heavily on optogenetics, stimulating all PV interneurons simultaneously with light. While this proved that PV cells can drive gamma frequencies, mass stimulation obscured how single cells interact naturally in an awake, behaving animal.

“Turning on all the cells at once shows you what they can do, but not how they naturally work together or how they’re recruited to generate spontaneous gamma oscillations,” said lead author Keran Ma, PhD, who spearheaded the project as a postdoctoral scholar at Gladstone and is now an assistant professor at UTHealth Houston. “Until now, no one has actually been able to image these cells and look at gamma oscillations at the same time in an awake animal during natural behavior.”

To observe their natural behavior, the team combined high-speed in vivo electrical recordings with live optical imaging. Tracking mice running on treadmills, a behavior that naturally engages attention-related circuits, the researchers engineered PV interneurons to glow fluorescently each time they fired an action potential.

The imaging captured a dynamic cellular relay: during each gamma burst, PV cells fired in organized, progressive waves rather than a uniform pulse. The earliest responding cells exhibited powerful activity, followed by subsequent cohorts with progressively lower firing rates, while roughly 30% of the population remained completely quiet.

“The relationship between the PV cells and the gamma oscillations was much more dynamic and complex than we expected going into this,” said senior author Jorge J. Palop, PhD, an investigator at Gladstone Institutes. “Rather than all the cells contributing to the rhythm at once, each cell contributes for just a brief moment, and those small contributions add up to create the larger brain rhythm. It’s less like a military lockstep march and more like a flock of birds in the sky, each responding to the others, shifting turns and trajectories, yet together creating a remarkably coordinated pattern.”

When the investigators examined mice genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer’s-like pathology, this coordinated relay was completely disrupted.

Instead of orderly turn-taking, early-responding PV cells became sluggish, late-stage cells fired excessively, and the inactive subset failed to stay silent. This loss of temporal segregation forced the cells into an abnormal hypersynchrony, firing simultaneously rather than sequentially, which paradoxically weakened the overall gamma rhythm.

“The important thing here is that more activity is not always going to produce better oscillations or better cognition,” Ma explained. “The dynamics of the cells are most important.”

This rhythmic breakdown provides a molecular explanation for a known clinical phenomenon: over 25% of Alzheimer’s patients exhibit subclinical epileptic-like brain activity. In the experimental models, epileptic spikes emerged directly after sudden drops in PV interneuron activity, illustrating how the breakdown of inhibitory timing destabilizes whole networks.

Looking for a way to repair the timing deficit, the team turned to Nav1.1, a voltage-gated sodium channel essential for generating fast electrical spikes in PV interneurons. Palop’s lab had previously demonstrated that Nav1.1 levels are significantly reduced in both Alzheimer’s mouse models and post-mortem human patient tissue.

To test whether replenishing the channel could fix the network, the researchers engineered Alzheimer’s mice to overexpress Nav1.1 within PV cells using cross-species viral delivery vehicles developed by Boaz P. Levi, PhD, and Jonathan T. Ting, PhD, of the Allen Institute.

“We still don’t know why interneuron dysfunction happens early in Alzheimer’s disease,” Ma noted. “But this is another study underscoring that a lot of the pathology of the disease could arise downstream of disrupted interneurons and the abnormal brain rhythms this disruption produces.”

The research team is now developing small-molecule Nav1.1 enhancers designed to selectively boost interneuron firing fidelity in humans, opening a therapeutic avenue to restore brain rhythms and protect against neurodegeneration.

Funding: The work was supported by the Ray and Dagmar Dolby Family Fund, the Cure Alzheimer’s Fund, the Simon Family Trust, the Alzheimer’s Association (24AARG-1247332), the Texas Alzheimer’s Research and Care Consortium (1271368), and the National Institutes of Health (AG094667, AG092683, AG082147, AG062629, AG073082, UG3/UH3 MH120095, R35 NS097976, R35 NS143067, RF1AG064926, K99/R00AG062776).

Parvalbumin cell state dynamics regulate gamma oscillations and are disrupted in Alzheimer’s disease

Gamma oscillations are fundamental for cognitive processing, but the cellular and circuit dynamics that generate them remain poorly defined.

Establishing a method for simultaneous calcium imaging and electrocorticography recordings in awake mice, we found that spontaneous gamma oscillations are accompanied by dynamic transitions between parvalbumin (PV) interneuron states.

Rather than acting as a uniformly synchronized population, PV interneurons showed sequential recruitment, transient inactivation, and frequent transitions between activity states, indicating the formation of dynamic functional networks.

In J20 Alzheimer’s disease mice, these state transitions became dysregulated, leading to abnormal PV recruitment, impaired coupling between PV activity and gamma oscillations, and network hyperexcitability. Increasing interneuron excitability through expression of the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.1 restored PV cell dynamics, gamma oscillations, and network stability.

These findings reveal dynamic PV cell states as an organizing feature of gamma oscillations and identify their disruption as a circuit mechanism of network dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease.

#83. The Map to the Route of Your Life

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If it makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider aiding its sustenance with a one-time or loyal donation. Your support makes all the difference.

You can also become a spontaneous supporter with a one-time donation in any amount:

Partial to Bitcoin? You can beam some bit-love my way: 197usDS6AsL9wDKxtGM6xaWjmR5ejgqem7

Need to cancel a recurring donation? Go here.

For an act of resistance to the tyranny of algorithms, try the Marginalian newsletter—undistracted notes on the search for meaning, free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human since 2006. (Here is an example.)

No one will map for you the path by which you must cross the wilderness of your own life — not your parents or your teachers, not your heroes or your lovers, not the self-help books or Shakespeare’s sonnets. Some may give you signposts, some may become turning points, but it is a path you ultimately make by walking. Along the way, you mistake dreams and desires for destinations, only to find that they have been way-stations — as soon as you attain them, you begin longing for something else. This Möbius strip of longing is the root of everything we suffer in the fangs of the Wanting Monster, but it is also the root of our creative vitality: the restless urge to make, to leave a mark that says “I AM,” a monument to having been. It is our incompleteness that maps the territory of the possible in us. It is our existential wanderlust that makes us what we are — pilgrims of mortality, forever coming home to the horizon of tomorrow.

Mario Benedetti (September 14, 1920–May 17, 2009) captures this paradox, with subtlety that doesn’t offer an answer but whispers the living question back to you, in an unedited poem found among his papers after his death, beautifully read in the original Spanish by my Patagonian friend Manuel Gutiérrez — a communicator of wonder through theater, music, and humor, whose hospitality made the serpentine birdworlds possible and who is always teaching me how to navigate the terrain of life with an open heart for a compass.

Music: “Sun Will Set” by Zoë Keating, with the artist’s permission; image: my father walking through the sunflower fields of Bulgaria merged with the first image captured by the Vera Rubin Observatory — 678 exposures of the Trifid and Lagoon Nebulae taken over the course of seven hours.

La encontré en mi bolsillo / era una ruta no sabía hasta dónde me llevaba pero igual la seguí en un merodeo con todas mis nostalgias en la mano

era un atlas del alma / la conciencia de lo que cometí y lo que me espera en el suelo vi huellas que eran propias así que era una senda ya corrida

el piélago de antes ya no estaba todo era más fuerte más seguro de pronto me encontré con la ribera de ese río que siempre fue mi anhelo

sólo entonces me aconsejé a mí mismo en el bolsillo volví a poner la ruta y allí quedó esperando otro mañana

ROADMAP by Mario Benedetti      translated by Maria Popova

I found it in my pocket / it was a roadmap I knew not where it led but I followed it anyway in aimless wanderlust with all my nostalgias in hand

it was an atlas of the soul / of consciousness of what I have committed and what awaits me on the ground I saw footprints that were my own and so it was a path already trodden

the vastness of before had vanished everything was stronger, surer suddenly I landed on the riverbank the river that had always been my longing

only then did I heed my own advice I tucked the path into my pocket once more and there it remained, awaiting another tomorrow

Couple with Benedetti’s clarion call to stop waiting and start living, then revisit C.S. Lewis on what we long for in our existential longings.

#84. 63 Christmas card messages, wishes, and greetings for all

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Christmas is almost here, and it’s time to put together your family's holiday card. You’ve already done the work of choosing the perfect photo and selecting the design you like best, but now comes the hard part: writing the perfect message.

Even though you know how much a thoughtful greeting can brighten someone’s day, it’s not always easy to find the right words. It can be tough to strike the right balance between meaningful, caring, and sincere — but not too cheesy. (Okay, maybe a little cheesy!) Coming up with the right words to express your feelings can feel a little overwhelming. After all, every person in your life—your family, friends, coworkers, or even that special someone—deserves a message that feels meaningful and personal.

We know what you’re facing, so we’ve gathered together our favorite Christmas greetings to inspire you to write the perfect note for everyone on your list.

For many people, family is at the heart of the holiday season. It’s a great time to reflect on the love and memories you’ve shared and let your relatives know just how much they mean to you. Here are some ideas to help you express your gratitude as you wish your family members a very merry Christmas.

Have your parents been there through it all? Take a moment to show your appreciation in a way that feels natural and true to your relationship. Maybe your message will be lighthearted and jokey, or deep and moving — whatever suits the situation best.

“Merry Christmas, Mom and Dad! Thanks for always making the holidays feel magical — and for putting up with my crazy Christmas wish lists over the years. (There’s still time to get me those rollerskates, by the way!) You’re the best, and I hope you know how much I appreciate you.”

“Hope you’re ready for another Christmas where I eat most of the snacks and do none of the cooking. Love you both — thanks for everything you do to make the holidays special.”

Whether your relationship with your siblings is built on laughs, bickering, or a little of both, a Christmas message is the perfect way to show your love in a way that’s true to your bond.

“Merry Christmas to my partner-in-crime (and occasional sparring partner). Thanks for keeping life interesting and for always having my back. Love you!”

“Christmas wouldn’t be the same without you. Thanks for being the person who knows all my embarrassing moments and still chooses to hang out with me — although I guess you have to, because I know all your secrets, too! Hope your holidays are as awesome as you are.”

“Wishing you a Merry Christmas full of love, laughter, and minimal family drama. Here’s to another year of surviving the holidays together!”

For grandparents, aunts, uncles, or cousins, a thoughtful message can remind them how much you value them.

“Merry Christmas to my wonderful [grandma/grandpa/aunt/uncle/cousins]. You’ve always made the holidays so special, and I’m so lucky to have you in my life. Hope your Christmas is full of everything you love!”

“Wishing you all the joy and laughter the season can bring. You’re the heart of our family, and I’m so grateful for you this Christmas and every day.”

“Merry Christmas to the family who always knows how to keep things fun—and occasionally chaotic. (This year, I'm going to win our Christmas game of Monopoly — so don’t help [another relative] cheat!). Love you all, and I hope your holidays are amazing!”

When you can’t be together in person, a warm and heartfelt greeting can help bridge the distance.

“Even though we’re not together this Christmas, you’re always in my thoughts. Wishing you a holiday full of love, laughter, and all the little things that make the season special. Miss you tons!”

“The holidays don’t feel the same without you, but I’ll be enjoying all our favorite traditions and thinking of you. Sending hugs, love, and wishes for the best Christmas ever!”

If your relationship with certain family members is complicated, you can still send a message that’s warm but keeps things simple. And if you need help for managing the anxiety that comes with the holidays, here are 10 tips to cope.

“Wishing you a Merry Christmas and a New Year full of happiness. Hope the holidays bring plenty of reasons to smile!”

“Merry Christmas! I hope this season brings you joy, peace, and lots of great food.”

“Thinking of you this Christmas and wishing you all the best. I hope your holidays are full of love and laughter.”

💙 Get in the holiday spirit when you sit down to write by listening to the Holiday Family Reunion playlist.

Whether they’re the ones you’re catching up with over cocoa or the people you’re texting memes to at 2 am, friends add so much to life. Let them know just how much color and joy they bring you, and how much you appreciate them.

For the friends who are practically family, a heartfelt but casual message can show how much you value them.

“Merry Christmas! You’ve been the best part of this year. (Well, you and snacks.) Here’s to more laughs, fewer bad decisions (or maybe more!), and plenty of good times ahead.”

“Happy holidays to my ride-or-die. Thanks for always having my back and knowing exactly how to make me laugh. Hope your Christmas is as awesome as you are!”

“Merry Christmas to the friend who makes life way more fun. I couldn’t have survived this year without you — and I wouldn’t have wanted to, either!”

Even if you’re not super close, a thoughtful holiday message can let casual friends know you’re thinking of them.

“Wishing you a Merry Christmas and a New Year filled with great vibes, good people, and good times.”

Happy holidays! Hope your season is filled with just the right amount of chaos, laughs, and corny holiday sweaters.”

“Merry Christmas! Here’s hoping Santa brings you all the good stuff — and maybe a break from the holiday madness.”

The holidays are a great time to reach out to friends you don’t see as often but still care about. A message like this can help you reconnect.

“It’s been too long! I miss having your vibes in my life. Merry Christmas, and let’s make this the year we actually get to see each other.”

“Thinking of you this Christmas and all the great times we’ve shared. Hope your holidays are as fun and wonderful as you are. Let’s catch up soon!”

“Merry Christmas! Hope your holiday season is full of laughter and good memories. You’ll always hold a special place in my heart.”

“I always think of the most important people in my life at this time of year, and that includes you.  Sending you lots of love and hoping your Christmas is amazing. Let’s talk soon.”

When miles separate you, a thoughtful holiday message can remind your faraway friends that you’re still connected.

“Merry Christmas from across the miles! Missing you tons and raising a glass to all the good times we’ve shared. Can’t wait to catch up soon!”

“Happy holidays to the friend who makes the distance feel smaller. Hope your Christmas is as wonderful as you are, and here’s to making new memories in the new year (even if they’re mostly virtual!)”

“Even though we’re far apart, you’re one of the best gifts in my life. Sending you love, laughter, and this cheesy holiday card.”

If humor is your friendship language, keep your message lighthearted and fun.

“Happy holidays to the friend who always knows how to make me laugh — even when the eggnog is terrible and your Christmas sweater is even uglier than last year. Let’s make 2024 just as ridiculous!”

“Here’s to a Christmas that’s full of laughs and chaos — just like us! Hope your holidays are as fun as that time we [insert your funniest shared memory].”

For the coworkers who turned into your go-to people, a little festive cheer can go a long way.

“Merry Christmas to my favorite office buddy-turned-actual-friend. Thanks for making work (and life) way more fun. Hope your holidays are amazing!”

“Happy holidays! You’ve survived the year with me, so I’m pretty sure you can handle anything. Wishing you the best Christmas ever, [desk-buddy/work-spouse]!”

“Merry Christmas! I’m so glad work gave me at least one good thing this year — our friendship. Hope your holidays are full of laughter and relaxation. Here’s to more office antics in the new year!”

💙 This holiday season, learn to nurture happier and healthier relationships with Tamara Levitt’s Relationship with Others series.

Love has a way of making the holidays feel even more special. Whether you’re celebrating together, apart, or just starting to connect, the right words in a Christmas message can make your special someone feel important.

Your partner is likely at the center of your holiday celebrations, and Christmas is the perfect time to remind them how much you appreciate their love and support. Here are some ideas to inspire your message.

“Christmas wouldn’t be the same without you — and not just because you’re the one who always untangles the lights. Love you lots.”

“You’re still the best gift in my life. Thanks for keeping me sane, laughing at my terrible jokes, and being the amazing person you are. Merry Christmas!”

If your relationship is still in its early stages, a sweet and thoughtful message can show your excitement for the journey ahead without feeling too overwhelming.

“Merry Christmas! I’m so glad you’re part of my life — even if it means pretending I’m good at wrapping presents. Here’s to many more awkward holiday traditions together!”

“Happy holidays! This Christmas, I’m grateful for lots of things — good food, good times, and most importantly, you. Thanks for being amazing and sharing a little festive fun with me.”

“Dating you has been like finding a Christmas movie that's actually good: unexpected, occasionally ridiculous, but kinda magical. Hope your holidays are just as fun as you are.”

If you and your special someone are apart for the holidays, a loving Christmas message can help close the distance so you look forward to seeing each other again soon.

“Even though we’re apart, you’re still the person I think of when I hear corny Christmas songs. Missing you tons — but at least I don’t have to share my chocolate this year. Merry Christmas!”

“Wish you were here so we could argue about whether Die Hard is a Christmas movie again. I miss you, but I’ll settle for sending all my love and saving the debate for next year! (P.S. Die Hard is not a Christmas movie.)”

“Miles apart but always close in my heart (and on my phone screen). Can’t wait to see you IRL soon. Merry Christmas!”

If you’re engaged or recently married, this Christmas marks the start of a new chapter in your journey together. Celebrate it with a message full of love and excitement for the future.

“Our first [engaged/married] Christmas is here, and honestly, I think the biggest gift is that we survived putting up the tree together! Love you, even when we don’t agree on tinsel. Merry Christmas!”

“Merry Christmas to the person who agreed to marry me — proof that miracles really do happen. Let’s make a lifetime of festive memories together!”

“One tree + two Christmas stockings + three arguments about the best way to roast potatoes = our first married Christmas! Love you anyway. Here’s to forever, babe!”

If you’re expressing your feelings to someone you care about but aren’t in a relationship with yet, keep it light while showing your affection.

“Merry Christmas! You’re on my mind this season. I hope your holidays are as fun as you are — and maybe just a little less chaotic.”

“Sending you warm holiday wishes to someone who makes life a little brighter (even from a distance)!”

“Wishing you a Christmas full of good vibes and great food. You out-twinkle my tree lights.”

Coworkers are a big part of our daily lives, so spread a little holiday cheer around the office or your virtual workspace with a card or an email. Christmas greetings are a great way to show appreciation and sprinkle in a little warmth or humor into their day.

When you’re keeping it straightforward and professional, these messages are perfect for any coworker.

“Wishing you a Merry Christmas and a happy new year! Hope you have a relaxing holiday season — you’ve earned it.”

Thank you for all your hard work this year. Wishing you a wonderful holiday season filled with joy.”

“Happy holidays! It’s been great working with you this year. I hope your Christmas is merry and bright. Here's to even more success in the new year.”

For coworkers you know well and think of as friends, a personal touch can go a long way.

“Merry Christmas! Thanks for making work so much more fun. I’m looking forward to another year of laughs and great teamwork.”

“Happy holidays to my favorite teammate! Hope your Christmas is full of good food, great company, and plenty of well-deserved relaxation.”

“Wishing you a fantastic Christmas! Thanks for making the office a better place.”

If your workmates make you laugh, try a playful holiday message.

“Merry Christmas! May your holiday season be as stress-free as a Friday afternoon meeting cancellation.”

“Happy holidays! I hope Santa brings you everything you want this year — especially a new coffee machine for the break room.”

“Merry Christmas! Thanks for surviving another year of office shenanigans with me. Here’s to ignoring all emails over the holidays!”

If your team works across the world and connects virtually, a thoughtful holiday message can remind your coworkers you’re all still a team.

“Wishing you a Merry Christmas from afar! It’s been great working together, and I hope your holidays are full of joy and relaxation. It's time to close the laptop!”

“Happy holidays to one of the best remote teammates out there! Here’s to a new year filled with fewer Zoom glitches and more virtual coffee breaks.”

If you’re writing to your boss or manager, keep it warm, but professional.

“Wishing you a Merry Christmas and a wonderful holiday season! Thank you for your support and guidance this year — I’m looking forward to another exciting year ahead.”

“Happy holidays! I hope you have a relaxing and joyful Christmas. Here’s to a successful year ahead!

“Merry Christmas! Thank you for being such an inspiring boss. Wishing you and your family a season full of love, laughter, and happiness.”

If you want your Christmas greetings to feel more personal, think about what makes your connection with the person you're writing to feel unique.

Mention a shared memory from the year, like that hilarious inside joke from the office party, the big night out, or the epic road trip you took together.

Add a little humor or mention something that makes you both laugh, like their obsession with peppermint mochas or their questionable taste in holiday movies, to make your message stand out. Whether you’re sending a card or a text, writing something beyond “Merry Christmas!” can make it feel special.

If you’re feeling crafty, include a small photo, a doodle, or a festive sticker. These little touches can make your greeting feel more like you.

Writing a Christmas card for work doesn’t have to be stuffy and boring! Keep it polite and respectful, but friendly and positive too — and let your personality shine through. A safe approach is to express gratitude—like thanking your coworker for their teamwork, or your manager for their leadership—and add a kind wish for the holidays.

You could write: “Thank you for your support this year—it’s been a pleasure working together. Wishing you and your family a joyful and relaxing holiday season!”

If your workplace vibe is more relaxed, throw in a little humor: “Here’s to a holiday filled with good food, great company, and zero emails from me. Happy holidays!”

If your friend group loves a good laugh, let your holiday greetings reflect that. Here are some ideas to get you started. Personalize them by  thinking about what always makes your friends laugh, and tie it into the holiday spirit. If you share a favorite show, movie, or meme, reference it — it’ll make your greeting feel uniquely yours.

“Merry Christmas! May your holiday be as magical as finding the last parking spot at the mall on Christmas Eve.”

“Wishing you a Christmas that’s as great as your karaoke version of ‘Jingle Bells’ — so, basically unforgettable.”

The holidays are a time for inclusivity, so tailoring your message to fit the recipient’s traditions is always a thoughtful move.

If you know they celebrate Hanukkah, say “Wishing you a bright and joyous Hanukkah!”

For friends who observe Kwanzaa, “Hope your Kwanzaa is full of light, love, and celebration!” works beautifully.

And if someone isn’t religious, a kind and simple message like “Wishing you a peaceful and joyful holiday season” hits the right note.

If you’re unsure, go with something neutral like “Happy holidays” or “Season’s greetings.”

Digital greetings don’t have to feel impersonal. Start by using the recipient’s name (no “Dear Team” unless it’s unavoidable!) and add something that’s specific to your relationship. For example, mention a funny meme they sent, a virtual coffee chat you enjoyed, or a shared win from the past year.

If it fits your vibe, add a festive emoji, a fun GIF, or a quick voice message to liven it up. Video greetings are great, too — just record yourself wishing them a happy holiday with a little personalized touch. And if you’ve got a photo of a Christmassy experience you’ve enjoyed — like ice skating, mulled wine at a Christmas market, or volunteering at your local soup kitchen, attach it with a message.

Even if it’s short, a thoughtful line or two can go a long way. After all, the effort you put in makes digital greetings just as meaningful as a handwritten note.

The best salutation matches how well you know the person. Use their name when you can. It makes the card feel personal right away.

For family and close friends, try “Dear Mom and Dad,” “To our favorite neighbors,” or “Merry Christmas, Sarah and James.”

For casual notes, “Hi Aunt Lisa” or “Hey Ben, Merry Christmas!” fits well.

For work cards, “Dear Alex” or “Hi Maya and team” keeps the tone friendly and professional.

If you’re writing to a whole household, address everyone, like “To the Garcia family.”

End with a closing line that matches the warmth of your message, then add your name. A kind sign-off can make even a short card feel personal.

For family and close friends, “Love always,” “With love,” or “Big holiday hugs” feels natural.

For casual notes, “Sending love this Christmas” or “Merry Christmas” works.

For coworkers and professional contacts, “Warm wishes,” “Best holiday wishes,” or “With appreciation” keeps things kind without getting too personal.

Keep it warm for loved ones. Keep it friendly and brief for people you don’t know well.

#86. The secret to handling stress better may start at breakfast

Feeling overwhelmed by stress or struggling to adjust when things go wrong? Everyday habits such as eating a nutritious breakfast, getting regular exercise, and sleeping enough may play an important role in how well your mind handles difficult situations.

New research from Binghamton University suggests that these healthy routines are connected to a mental skill called psychological flexibility, which helps people adapt to challenges and recover from stressful experiences.

Psychological flexibility refers to the ability to adjust your thoughts, emotions, and actions as circumstances change. Rather than becoming trapped in negative thinking or overwhelmed by frustration, people with greater psychological flexibility can recognize their emotions, consider their options, and respond in a more productive way.

"You might know someone who stays cool under pressure," said Lina Begdache, an associate professor of health and wellness studies at Binghamton University and lead author of the research. "The kind of person who misses a flight and, instead of panicking, calmly adapts to the situation. This person may still feel stressed, but they're better able to manage it through psychological flexibility."

"People may say that these are resilient people, but they also have what's called psychological flexibility. They're able to change the way they think about the situation and then use brain resources to handle the stress."

How Breakfast, Sleep, and Exercise Relate to Mental Resilience

To explore the relationship between lifestyle choices and emotional resilience, Begdache worked with Jason Cherry, a former Binghamton assistant professor of physical therapy, and former student Alexander J. Talkachov.

The researchers collected anonymous survey responses from approximately 400 college students, gathering information about their diets, sleep patterns, exercise habits, and other lifestyle factors.

Their findings revealed an important connection between healthy routines and the ability to cope with stress. Students who reported healthier habits, including regular physical activity and consistent breakfast consumption, also tended to demonstrate greater psychological flexibility and resilience.

The study identified several notable associations:

The opposite pattern also emerged. Students who reported less healthy behaviors, including frequent fast food consumption and insufficient sleep, tended to show greater psychological rigidity, meaning they had more difficulty adjusting their thoughts and behaviors when circumstances changed.

Because the research relied on survey responses, the results demonstrate associations rather than proving that these habits directly improve psychological flexibility or resilience.

Why Psychological Flexibility Matters for Stress

According to Begdache, psychological flexibility gives people the mental space to recognize what they are experiencing instead of becoming completely absorbed by their stress. This ability to reassess a situation can make it easier to understand difficult emotions and determine how to respond.

She explained that improvements in diet and lifestyle may help support this kind of mental adaptability.

"When we're under stress, we feel like we fuse with the stress. We live the stress. But psychological flexibility is like stepping back and thinking, 'I feel this because of that. What can I do?' Identifying your emotions sometimes helps you find the solution for these emotions," said Begdache.

The findings also build on Begdache's previous research, which linked nutritious diets to greater resilience and poorer dietary habits to reduced resilience.

The latest study offers a possible explanation for that relationship. Rather than influencing resilience alone, diet and lifestyle may support psychological flexibility, which in turn helps people manage stress more effectively.

"The new finding here is that diet and lifestyle don't just make you resilient by themselves. They help you build the psychological flexibility, which, in turn, makes you a resilient person."

The study, "Dietary and lifestyle factors and resilience: the role of psychological flexibility as a mediator," was published in the Journal of American College Health.

Materials provided by Binghamton University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#87. “Rejection Immobilizes Me:” RSD Survey Results

Rejection sensitive dysphoria was called the most impairing aspect of ADHD’s emotional dysregulation by ADDitude readers in a recent survey.

“It feels like a vacuum that physically sucks out every good thought of yourself.” “It is a tightening in my body. A million thoughts at once. A gut punch.” “It is a feeling of being locked in a coffin.”

When adults with ADHD describe the physical and emotional sensations of rejection sensitive dysphoria (RSD), their words are visceral — and sometimes violent. The manifestations of RSD include “intense pain in my stomach,” “a punch to my chest,” and “internal physical discomfort similar to restless leg syndrome but inside my whole body,” according to some of the nearly 3,500 people who answered a recent ADDitude survey on RSD and its impact.

“It almost feels like I’m dying,” wrote one 34-year-old woman. “That’s how horrible it feels. I can’t breathe and I’m all alone because I feel so misunderstood.”

[Free Resource: Understanding Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria]

Though RSD is not an official diagnosis in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5), or considered a core symptom of ADHD, it is experienced by a vast majority of people with the condition. William Dodson, M.D., who coined the term RSD, described it as extreme emotional pain triggered by real or perceived criticism or rejection—and for many, a relentless self-loathing follows.

RSD was called somewhat or very debilitating by 63 percent of ADDitude survey respondents. Two-thirds of them said RSD has a severe impact on their emotional health, and more than half said it is somewhat or very debilitating for their mental health, romantic relationships, and/or career.

“My RSD has resulted in demotions, lost work opportunities, isolation at work, and staying in a romantic relationship that was toxic,” wrote one 58-year-old woman.

“I had a meeting with my boss and all I could hear were the negative words,” wrote another respondent. “When the meeting ended, I went to my car and had to call someone because I was so overwhelmed I couldn’t breathe.”

For 64 percent of respondents, the pain of RSD hits within one minute of encountering a trigger, and it lasts hours or days for most. RSD triggers may include an unanswered text message, a reminder to do a forgotten task, a critique from a loved one, the feeling of being misunderstood or belittled, and even facial expressions or silence during a conversation.

“When I believe I’m being actively judged and found lacking, I am quite simply crushed, gutted, and experiencing an emotional death,” wrote one 74-year-old woman.

“In situations when the content of my character is criticized, my intentions are questioned, or I am misrepresented… RSD causes me the most physical pain and longest-lasting rumination,” wrote another ADDitude reader. “I replay social interactions over and over again in my head, feeling intense anger or anxiety… while picking at my skin.”

Half of survey respondents cited indelible memories of RSD from a very young age, and 79 percent said they remember experiencing RSD before middle school. This suggests that RSD screeners could be used to help detect early signs of ADHD and emotional dysregulation in children with less noticeable symptoms.

“As early as I can remember — and my memories go back to almost 1 year of age — I was quick to appease and ward off any parental reprimands because they hurt too much,” wrote a 68-year-old woman who experiences RSD.

“Two little girls in kindergarten would not let me play with them because I did not know how to tie my shoe,” wrote a 57-year-old woman. “I remember the feeling of rejection to this day.”

“An older neighbor gifted me a weeping teddy bear, saying that since all I seemed to do was cry, it looked just like me,” wrote one 65-year-old woman. “I still have that bear as a reminder of what a ‘terrible’ child I was.”

#88. The Rewards of Slowness

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted September 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

A slower pace of life reduces mental and emotional fatigue. By living slowly, we can find life much less stressful and more fulfilling.

Slowing things down and deliberately paying attention to each aspect of our sensory experience can reveal things that we may have never noticed before. For example, mindless eating is an important reason for overeating. When you eat fast, the body doesn’t get a chance to signal to the brain that you have eaten enough. People often reach for their phone automatically to soothe underlying boredom and stress, or awkwardness. Awareness keeps old habits favored by automatic thoughts from having the final say in our choices.

Going slow is the fastest way to learn a new skill. When you work slowly, things become simpler. Slowness and speed are interdependent. Mastering a subject requires time and patience before speed becomes possible. For example, slow practice is nearly universal in teaching instrumental music. The term “slow practice” can be described as practicing a piece of music, or section of music, at a dramatically slower tempo than that at which it eventually will be performed. The purpose of slow practice is to put ‘thinking space’ between the notes and to allow for awareness of what is being done. As a player, you become aware of what you’re doing while you’re doing it. You hear sounds clearly and monitor your actions precisely.

Slow learning relies heavily on repetition because the brain needs multiple exposures to move facts from short-term to long-term memory. Repetition (doing the same thing repeatedly) is essential for learning and mastering new skills. When an experience is complex, it’s a good idea to repeat it. Whether you’re learning to play an instrument, speak a new language, or excel at a sport, repetition is key for building muscle memory and improving your performance. Every repetition brings you closer to your desired outcome.

You are also far more likely to enjoy something the second time around than you think. We normally miss a substantial part of every new experience. Repetition allows you to dig deeper into a specific experience, such as seeing things that you didn’t see the first time around.

Oscar Wilde once said that “there are two tragedies in life: not getting what you want and getting what you want.” All pleasurable activities (e.g., a cup of coffee in the morning, an afternoon walk) start out very enjoyable, and, within a few minutes, we get used to it. Slowing down and pacing your experience lets your brain savor positive moments. Pacing reward means to scale back (savoring) stimulation deliberately to prolong enjoyment. Savoring describes the ability to appreciate and enhance the positive experiences in one’s life.

Slowing down can help with better listening. To feel more loved requires listening better. However, that kind of genuine, focused listening is rare, although it’s quite powerful. Rather than being good listeners, we tend to impatiently wait our turn to speak or fail to ask follow-up questions. When someone feels deeply understood and valued by you, they become more willing to do the same for you.

Slowing the mind down in favor of slow deliberation takes vigilance, willpower, and training. Pausing is a powerful self-control strategy. Psychologist Rollo May (1981) equated pause with freedom. That is, freedom is the capacity to pause in the face of stimuli from many directions at once and, in this pause, to choose our response. The pause momentarily suspends our automatic reaction, and our responses no longer blindly follow stimulus (e.g., we remark before making an important decision, “Let me sleep on it.”). A pause can be created by a walk or 20 minutes of meditation.

#89. How a Video Game Helped Me Process My Grief

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

In a genre built around sweetness and ease, one “cozy” video game did something far greater: It put me back together after I lost Mary.

Mary was not only my then-boyfriend’s mother, but she also became an important maternal figure when my own family life felt unstable. I accompanied her on weekly grocery store runs that included stops at Marshall’s and Dollar Tree, where I’d watch her study the prices of everything from spices to bath products. When she saw me marveling at her meticulousness, she would share wise tidbits about how she looked for deals.

Our trips often ended with a late-afternoon stop at a Vietnamese restaurant, where she treated me to a warm bowl of beef pho. She’d share what she was excited to make for dinner; I was, of course, welcome to join. In these seemingly mundane afternoons, I felt cared for without the rush of obligations. Mary stopped time for me.

Last November, Mary left behind a world of loved ones after living with cancer for 14 months. From her living room to emergency stays in the hospital, I spent almost every single day of her fight by her side. Yet in my loneliest hours, I agonize over whether I fully cherished our last months together. Did I hug her enough, and did I tell her enough how much she means to me? These questions haunted me in the months afterward.

Funny enough, it wasn’t religion that rescued me; it was Pokémon Pokopia. On the surface, it is a new social simulation game featuring the iconic Japanese creatures who first took the world by storm in 1996. I first heard of its arrival on social media through gamers who raved that it was going to be the best game of the year. I grew up on Pokémon titles, so I recognized it as a distraction from my personal reckoning with abandonment.

But what began as a spur-of-the-moment decision to try what 4 million other gamers were playing turned into a transformative journey exploring what I want my life to mean when it feels as if I have been left behind.

Pokopia falls in the “cozy” game genre, beloved for its warm colors, gentle atmospheres, and easy missions. Released in March, Pokopia stars Ditto, an amorphous purple blob Pokémon that uses its transformative abilities to imitate its human trainer and rebuild a curious post-apocalyptic world devoid of human beings and Pokémon. Ditto first awakens in a cave, and as the story unfolds, the creature looks out at a once-grassy environment of parched earth and litter. It meets the first Pokémon, the hydrophilic Squirtle that teaches Ditto how to spray water across the thirsty soil to bring it back to life; it is also the only other semblance of a survivor in this barren land.

From here the story gains momentum: As Ditto, your mission is to get the environment back to habitable levels and bring back Pokémon creatures that are presumably hiding. Gradually, the unfinished railroad tracks and cracked concrete steps of a staircase stop looking like signs of a catastrophe but rather fixable problems.

I wasn’t alone in trying to find meaning after a loss or trauma. Scholars have explored a variety of constructs around the meaning of life. Psychologists Login S. George and Crystal L. Park articulate a three-part framework in their 2010 article, grounded in comprehension, purpose, and mattering, as a basis for assessing our judgments and feelings as we find meaning after loss.

At first, meaning seemed absent. I sat glued to my Nintendo Switch for three hours on my first day of play. I came up for air only when my console told me that I was low on battery. Yet I did not feel depleted; I had finished restoring the first environment in the Pokopia world to verdant levels with lush berry trees and waterfalls.

As I built new habitats, I met new Pokémon. A Charmander emerged among tall grass. A Cubone spawned from a gravesite surrounded by wildflowers. Every new Pokémon that resurfaced charmed me with their excitement to be back home, scampering across the grass to greet other familiar faces. In my mind, I thanked these creatures for turning to me. Without Ditto’s help—my help—a world of Pokemon creatures ceases to exist, fated to disappear alongside humanity.

After a Pokémon spawns in its revived habitat, it awakens with some surprise. “Huh?” “What?” Some of them startle and put up their defenses in front of Ditto, who then coaxes them into the reality that they are back in a safe, familiar home. Often this realization gives them relief. “Wow, you did all of this? Thank you!”

Some of the Pokémon seem more wistful. They hold on to items or articles of clothing that their trainer used to wear, like the oversized Tangrowth (a large Pokémon with thick, shaggy vines that cover its entire body) that wears a pair of glasses much too small for him that gamers can infer are its trainer’s. Other creatures comment on Ditto’s human-like appearance (“You look like your human!”). These private conversations between Pokémon affirm that Ditto, who is also piecing together where its own trainer has gone, is doing something meaningful.

In 2023, game scholars Karam Eum and Young Yim Doh explored how bereaved adults shaped a meaning-making experience by playing video games with narratives that focus on loss and grief. Subjects spent a week playing two different video games and kept a diary where they shared specific game scenes that were particularly meaningful. While the games did evoke sad memories, participants also recalled positive memories in their pre- and post-loss lives, be it a funny conversation or a serendipitous moment shared with close ones who are still alive.

In the real world, the player behind the console, I, too, wonder where my beloved human has gone. I see Mary in the pink rose bouquets at grocery stores, and I smell her in the fragrant bone broth that wafts from the next-door apartment unit. In some of these most visceral disruptions, I feel my loss painfully.

But even in these heaviest of days, I surrender to the ordinary surprises that come up: a call from an old neighbor asking if I can help make meals for a family in need, or a stray cat mewing at my window to open the building’s front gate. I am startled out of a detached state, and I am moved to help, the way I got to help Mary.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

I associate Mary now with the colorful berry trees in Pokopia. When I come across one that needs tending, I remember how easy it is to water it with my Squirtle-like powers. When I clear a path from blocks of beach sand to make way for a new house for my aquatic Pokémon, I think of Mary’s selfless endeavors to nourish and comfort all of her friends and family.

Despite its sad undertones, Pokopia is full of positive quests, eager to help gamers imbue its universe with the belief that it is worth building a positive world in memory of those who shaped us. Even though our loved ones may “mysteriously” leave us behind, we recreate happiness, redefine ourselves, and choose who and what we live for, even if they do not come back.

It’s curious to me that bereavement can feel so isolating, although it is a human experience universally experienced. It helps to have a video game that reminds me of the actual truth. When I start to catch myself drifting into deeper ends of grief, I have something to divert my attention: I wonder how my Ditto is doing? I pick up my Switch 2 that sits at the foot of my bed, and I make a new home for my Pokémon the way Mary had done for me.

Lisa Kwon is an arts and culture writer based in Los Angeles, CA. She has contributed to The Guardian, Teen Vogue, Vulture, Eater, Prism Reports, Cultured Magazine, National Geographic, and many more.

Body changes or chronic illness can disrupt our sense of meaning and challenge our identity, purpose, and assumptions about the future.

#90. When the Mind Won’t Slow Down, Let the Forest Set the Pace

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

What the Japanese practice of shinrin-yoku ("forest bathing") can teach us about attention, emotional well-being, and finding moments of quiet in a world that rarely stops.

There are days when the body is tired but the mind refuses to follow. We finish work, close the laptop, put away the phone—and yet the conversations continue in our heads. We replay something we said that morning, anticipate tomorrow, remember an email we forgot to send, and move from one thought to the next even after the world around us has become quiet.

Simply telling ourselves to relax may not help. Perhaps that is because relaxation is difficult to achieve when we turn it into another task. There is, however, another possibility: instead of asking the mind to become quiet, we can give it somewhere else to place its attention. A branch moving above us, cool air against the face, rough bark beneath our fingertips, or the sound of a bird somewhere beyond our sight.

Perhaps forest bathing’s greatest gift is not that the forest makes our thoughts disappear, but that for a while they no longer need to occupy the entire landscape of our attention.

This gentle movement of attention—from the thoughts within us toward the living world around us—is at the heart of shinrin-yoku, the Japanese practice widely known as forest bathing. Perhaps its greatest gift is not that the forest makes our thoughts disappear, but that for a while they no longer need to occupy the entire landscape of our attention.

The term shinrin-yoku emerged in Japan in the early 1980s and is commonly translated as “forest bathing” or “taking in the atmosphere of the forest.” The English translation can be misleading: there is no water involved; “bathing” refers instead to immersing oneself in the atmosphere of the forest. At its heart, shinrin-yoku is the practice of entering a forest environment slowly and experiencing it consciously through the senses.

Modern life can easily pull our attention away from the present moment; the forest offers an environment rich enough to hold our attention without constantly demanding it.

This distinguishes it from hiking. When we hike, our attention often has somewhere to go: a route to follow, a distance to cover, or a destination to reach. Forest bathing deliberately loosens those expectations. A session may involve walking, but covering distance isn’t the goal. What matters is not how far we move through the forest, but how deeply we notice where we are.

We might listen to the movement of leaves without trying to identify its source, watch sunlight shifting through the canopy, notice the scent of damp soil after rain, or rest a hand against the trunk of a tree and explore a texture we have passed hundreds of times without touching. These are simple acts, but simplicity is part of their power. Modern life can easily pull our attention away from the present moment; the forest offers an environment rich enough to hold our attention without constantly demanding it.

Consider how many times your attention changes direction during an ordinary hour. A notification appears, a message arrives, another browser tab opens, a headline catches your eye, and you remember something that needs to be done later. This fragmented way of paying attention can begin to feel normal, and we may carry it with us even when the external demands stop.

A tree does not need an immediate response. Birdsong does not require us to formulate an opinion. Clouds moving above the canopy are not asking to be liked, answered, or shared.

Shinrin-yoku creates a deliberate contrast. The forest is full of information, but it is information of a different kind. A tree does not need an immediate response. Birdsong does not require us to formulate an opinion. Clouds moving above the canopy are not asking to be liked, answered, or shared. We can notice them without having to do anything about them, and for a busy mind, that distinction can offer a welcome pause.

The relationship between Forest bathing and psychological well-being has  been studied for its potential mental health benefits. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis by Siah and colleagues, published in the International Journal of Mental Health Nursing examined 36 articles involving more than 3,000 combined participants and found that forest bathing interventions were associated with significant reductions in symptoms of anxiety and depression.

Other systematic reviews have also reported  short-term changes across measures such as anxiety, depression, stress, and anger. At the same time, the evidence requires careful interpretation. Studies vary substantially in design, participant groups, duration, and the activities included under the terms forest bathing and forest therapy, while some studies rely on relatively small samples.

Forest bathing offers a setting and a practice where exploring attention, sensory awareness, and moments of psychological quiet can become easier to access.

Forest bathing should therefore not be presented as a treatment for anxiety or depression, nor as a substitute for appropriate mental health care. Its value may lie somewhere more subtle: it offers a setting and a practice where exploring attention, sensory awareness, and moments of psychological quiet can become easier to access.

Trying to force ourselves to “stop thinking” can quickly become frustrating. The mind thinks; that is what it does. Forest bathing takes a gentler approach. Instead of demanding an empty mind, it invites us to become interested in something beyond our thoughts.

Listen carefully to a forest and another layer of sound may be waiting beneath the first one. At first, perhaps you hear birds. Listen longer and individual calls begin to separate. Beneath them may be leaves moving in the wind, branches rubbing together, or something moving through dry leaf litter. Your thoughts may still be present throughout all of this, but they are no longer alone.

The forest gives us somewhere to return to, again and again.

The aim is not to suppress thought, but to  redirect attention. We do not have to fight every worry that appears. We can notice it and gently return our awareness to what is happening around us. The forest gives us somewhere to return to, again and again.

You do not have to walk into the woods feeling stressed and emerge transformed into a perfectly calm person. You may still be worried, sad, distracted, or impatient. You may spend the first ten minutes thinking about dinner. None of this means that you are doing it wrong.

In forest bathing, the word invitation is often used rather than exercise. This creates space for something easily lost when mindfulness becomes another self-improvement project: kindness toward our own experience.

In forest bathing, the word invitation is often used rather than exercise. An exercise can imply success or failure; an invitation simply offers a direction in which attention might move. This creates space for something easily lost when mindfulness becomes another self-improvement project: kindness toward our own experience. We can arrive exactly as we are. The forest does not require us to be calm before entering it.

Find a quiet woodland or green space and walk slowly until a tree naturally draws your attention. Stand beside it for a moment and notice its shape before touching it. Follow the trunk upward with your eyes, observing where it divides into branches and disappears into the canopy, then notice where it meets the earth.

Place one hand gently against the bark. If moss grows there, notice its texture and color. Close your eyes if that feels comfortable and pay attention to temperature, texture and pressure. Allow your breathing to settle naturally rather than trying to control it.

Now become aware of the ground beneath your feet. Imagine the tree’s roots continuing through the soil below you. As you breathe out, allow one persistent thought to loosen its grip; you do not need to remove it or solve it. As you breathe in, you might imagine the steadiness and strength of the tree and the earth beneath you. Remain there for several minutes. Whenever your thoughts pull you elsewhere, gently return your attention to the sensation beneath your hand, the earth beneath your feet, and the rhythm of your breathing. Before you walk away, spend another moment looking at the tree before walking away. Nothing about it may have changed, yet your experience of standing beside it may have shifted.

You can spend twenty minutes among trees and have nothing tangible to show for it: no distance record, no photograph, and no completed task. Perhaps that is precisely why it matters.

So much of our life is organized around outcomes. We exercise to become fitter, study to learn something, and work to complete tasks. Even rest can become instrumental: we sleep so that we can perform better tomorrow. Forest bathing offers an experience that does not necessarily need to produce anything.

You can spend twenty minutes among trees and have nothing tangible to show for it: no distance record, no photograph and no completed task. Perhaps that is precisely why it matters. There are moments when the mind does not need another achievement; it needs permission to stop achieving.

Find somewhere safe and comfortable to sit for 10 to 15 minutes. Put your phone away and allow your body to settle without immediately searching for anything interesting. Begin with the sounds closest to you, then gradually extend your attention farther away and listen for individual layers of sound: birds calling at different distances, branches moving overhead, wind traveling through the canopy, or something moving quietly through the undergrowth.

After several minutes, allow your attention to move from sound to movement. Rather than constantly looking around, let your eyes rest on one area and wait. Small movements that escaped your attention at first may gradually emerge: an insect crossing a trunk, a bird moving between branches, or light changing across the forest floor.

Whenever your mind returns to plans, worries, or memories, notice without judgment and bring your attention back to a sound or movement. Before leaving, notice whether the place feels different from when you arrived. The forest itself may be unchanged, but you may now be aware of far more of it.

Awe does not necessarily require standing beneath a giant redwood or looking across a vast canyon. It can emerge from paying close enough attention to something ordinary.

Forest bathing can also remind us of an aspect of mental well-being: awe. Awe does not necessarily require standing beneath a giant redwood or looking across a vast canyon. It can emerge from paying close enough attention to something ordinary.

Look closely at moss growing across an old trunk and it begins to resemble a miniature forest. Watch sunlight move through leaves and a familiar woodland can change minute by minute. Consider that an oak beside you may have stood in the same place through thousands of nights, storms, winters, and springs, and your own worries can momentarily take on a different scale. This does not make those worries unimportant; it simply reminds us that they are not the whole world.

A forest bathing guide does not need to create a particular experience for the participant. The task is to create enough time, safety, and attentiveness for people to encounter the forest for themselves.

Forest bathing can sit naturally alongside mindfulness. Both practices invite us away from automatic behavior and toward conscious experience. Both emphasize returning attention gently rather than forcing it. Yet the forest adds something of its own: it reminds us that mindfulness does not have to happen entirely inside our heads. The texture beneath our fingertips, the movement of air, the smell of wet earth, the changing light, and the sound of life around us can all become anchors for attention.

We do not always have to retreat inward to find stillness. Sometimes we can step outside.

Perhaps this is what the practice of shinrin-yoku still has to teach us more than 40 years after the term first emerged. Forest bathing is not about escaping life. Eventually, we leave the trees. The emails remain, tomorrow still arrives, difficult conversations may still need to happen and problems may still need to be solved.

Perhaps, somewhere between the trees, we have experienced a few moments in which we did not need to improve ourselves, explain ourselves, or prepare ourselves for whatever comes next.

But we may return to them differently. For a little while, we have practiced giving our attention to something that did not demand it. We have remembered what damp bark feels like beneath our hand, listened long enough for one sound to become ten, and allowed a thought to exist without immediately following it.

And perhaps, somewhere between the trees, we have experienced a few moments in which we did not need to improve ourselves, explain ourselves, or prepare ourselves for whatever comes next. We were simply present—not perfectly and not permanently, but long enough to remember that we still can be.

If this practice has sparked your curiosity, you can learn more about Forest Bathing and shinrin-yoku at Treeming.org, where we share education and resources designed to help people slow down, reconnect with nature and explore a more attentive relationship with the forest.

Born in Germany and now living in Mexico, Jörg discovered his deep love for nature and the remarkable power of trees at an early age. Throughout his life, forests have been a source of inspiration, inner peace, and connection to the natural world.

Since 2022, Jörg has been working as a Forest Bathing Instructor with the Treeming Organization, sharing his passion for nature-based mindfulness and the transformative experience of reconnecting with the forest.

Jörg believes that the forest is much more than a place to visit—it is a space for reflection, personal growth, and finding balance in an increasingly fast-paced world. Through his work with Treeming, he hopes to make the profound benefits of Forest Bathing accessible to people from all walks of life, encouraging a deeper and more meaningful relationship with nature.
