#91. 22 Christmas party ideas for a cozy, stress-free celebration

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

The moment before guests arrive at your party can be a mixture of excitement and panic. The candles are lit, the food is almost ready, and you’re silently praying nothing burns. You want to create something special for your guests, but the pressure to make it perfect can turn what should be joyful into work.

Christmas parties are meant to bring people closer to enjoy the holiday season, yet they often leave hosts (and sometimes guests) feeling more frazzled than festive. Between elaborate menus, matching place settings, and endless to-do lists, it’s easy to lose sight of what matters most, which is time spent laughing, listening, and feeling genuinely connected to the people you love.

Here are some Christmas party ideas designed to bring calm, warmth, and real connection back to your gatherings. We’ll share a few stress-free ways to celebrate, so you can focus less on playing the perfect host and instead make space for the kind of memories that linger long after the decorations have come down.

Hosting a Christmas party sounds joyful in theory, but in practice, it often feels tense. It’s normal to have a mental checklist of what you “should” do when hosting a party, from having impressive food, sparkling decorations, and ensuring everyone has a great time. Those invisible expectations can pile up fast.

Part of the stress comes from comparison. Social media and glossy magazines make “effortless” gatherings look, well, effortless. But behind those curated scenes are catering teams, stylists, and weeks of prep, which are luxuries most people don’t have. When you try to replicate perfection while juggling work, kids, and life, joy tends to slip through the cracks.

Another culprit is over-commitment. By December, most calendars are overflowing with school concerts, work deadlines, and an abundance of family plans. By the time the party rolls around, you’re running on fumes. Even finding matching napkins can feel monumental when your energy is gone.

And then there’s the emotional side of hosting. It’s normal to want our homes, meals, and families to reflect a version of ourselves that feels “together.” But connection doesn’t come from control — it comes from authenticity. The more you chase a flawless night, the less space there is for genuine warmth and presence.

Related read: How to manage the expectations vs reality trap in 6 steps

When you think about your favorite Christmas gatherings, it’s never the matching tableware that stands out. It’s the moments that feel real, like emotional connection, laughter, and sharing special memories. Here’s what turns a simple evening into something lasting:

Presence over performance: When you stop worrying about appearances, you make room for connection. Dim the lights, play music that feels familiar, and focus on being with people, not impressing them.

Simple structure, open energy: Plan just enough to give the night shape, then let it breathe. A loose rhythm—arrive, eat, pause, chat—creates comfort without rigidity.

Simplicity that invites participation: When guests can contribute to the party by bringing a dish, adding their favorite song to the playlist, or sharing a story, they feel invested. It shifts the mood from host and audience to a more collaborative vibe.

Care over curation: A meaningful party doesn’t come from doing more. It comes from doing less with more care and intention. When the atmosphere feels relaxed and real, people don’t just attend — they belong.

The best Christmas parties aren’t the ones with flawless menus or coordinated tablescapes. They’re the ones where people feel comfortable enough to laugh, linger, and genuinely connect.

These 22 simple, stress-free ideas will help you host a gathering that feels calm, cozy, and full of meaning. And the best part is that they won’t drain your time or energy.

Ask guests to bring a dish that means something to them and share the story behind it. In this way, food becomes a shared memory, and it instantly opens up conversation.

Related read: How to practice mindful cooking

Pick a single idea for the party and turn it into a theme. Perhaps it’s “Candlelight and Comfort,” “Cozy Flannel,” or even “Red and Green Everything.” A loose theme creates focus and atmosphere without requiring Pinterest-level effort. Plus, it’s a great way to spark conversation and connection.

Cook the dishes that are special to you and buy the rest. If it makes you feel better to add a personal touch to store-bought items, like warming rolls and topping with butter and herbs, or making homemade whipped cream for already-baked pie, go that route. No one will know (or care) where it came from.

Instead of opting for a sit-down meal, which can feel formal, try a more casual approach. You could set food out buffet-style and let people eat as they’re hungry, which can keep conversation flowing. Or serve a seated meal family-style so folks get to know each other while passing dishes around.

Fairy lights, candles, or a soft lamp in the corner of your hosting space instantly make your home feel more inviting. Low light hides clutter, calms energy, and adds warmth without costing a cent. Plus, twinkle lights in soft red, green, or white add to the holiday atmosphere.

To reduce overwhelm and keep you from playing bartender all night, consider serving wine and beer as your only alcoholic options. Or if mixology is a passion, offer one signature cocktail and one mocktail.

Make it even easier on yourself by pre-mixing them so they’re batched and ready to drink. Feel free to also include plenty of water, like still and sparkling. You can even toss in some cranberries and citrus to make it festive or quickly warm some cider on the stove.

If you’re operating with limited space, or just want to make your home more comfortable for your guests, feel empowered to rearrange! Move chairs and tables to create cozy clusters where people can chat easily or toss some larger pillows or cushions on the floor for even more seating. Comfort matters more than matching furniture.

If someone asks what they can bring or how they can help, feel free to delegate. Ask guests to help with music, drinks, or clean-up. When people share small roles, they feel more connected. And you’re not stuck running the show alone.

Before buying new decor, take inventory of what you already have on hand. A bowl of ornaments that don’t fit onto the tree, a sprig of rosemary in a cocktail, or a few tea lights placed throughout your home can make the space feel intentional and curated based on your personality instead of the latest trends.

Before guests arrive, take a minute for yourself. Pause for one deep breath, light a candle, or play a calming song that puts you in the headspace to host and have fun. A mindful moment centers you before the night begins and sets the tone for everyone who walks in.

💙 Need some inspiration? Try the Pause to Breathe guided meditation on the Calm app.

Invite each guest to add one song to a collaborative playlist, or bring a record to play if you’re a vinyl-lover. Play it during the night and see who can guess who picked or brought what.

It’s an easy icebreaker that feels effortless and allows for each guest’s personality to shine through.

Related read: 15 ways music can make you feel better in mind and body

Before dessert or during a lull, invite people to share one thing they’re thankful for. This could be something as simple as getting an extra hour of sleep that morning or something more thoughtful like having the opportunity to come together as friends. Keep it optional and lighthearted so no one feels obligated. — it’s about connection, not ceremony.

💙 Need motivation? Press play on our 7 Days of Gratitude series found on the Calm app.

Provide slips of paper and a jar for guests to write down a highlight from the past year or a wish for the next. If guests are comfortable, you could even read a few aloud to end the night on a warm note.

Scatter small cards around your place with pre-written prompts on them. Some favorites to include might be “a tradition you secretly love” or “a funny holiday memory.” They keep conversation flowing naturally and can come in handy if the conversation lulls or your guests meet someone new for the first time.

Depending on the group of people at your gathering, fun games could be a great way to get everyone mixing and mingling. You can play trivia with a holiday twist or something collaborative like charades. Keep it short and silly and have fun with it.

Related read: How to have fun without alcohol? Try these 24 activities

If your party is family-friendly and there are children around, include them by giving them a task. Think passing out napkins, greeting guests, or taking Polaroid pictures. When they have a role, they feel involved (and less likely to throw a tantrum from feeling ignored).

Ask an older guest to share their favorite holiday memory or a tradition they took part in when they were younger. Then, ask the younger ones to teach a new tradition or share their current favorite holiday song or movie. It creates an easy bridge between ages, plus introduces new ideas for ways to enjoy the holiday with all in attendance.

You don’t need props and fancy backdrops to make a photo-worthy spot in your home. Just find an area with good lighting, add in some holiday lights and decor, and encourage guests to take real, candid photos. You can even create a shared album on your phone for guests to upload their snaps from the evening.

If the weather allows, take a short stroll after dinner or dessert to see neighborhood lights or get fresh air together. Movement naturally deepens conversation, plus it’s good for your overall health and mood too. A quick walk can be a nice pause in between dinner and dessert.

As the night winds down, offer tea, cocoa, or a final toast and thank everyone for being there. A soft ending helps everyone leave on a high, calm note and also gives you control over when the festivities end, so you can get the rest you need.

Plus, it’s an opportunity to express your gratitude for the people in your life and having the opportunity to celebrate with them.

If you feel like it, sending your guests home with a memento from the evening is always a nice touch. A Polaroid photo, a handwritten note, or even the shared playlist link from the evening are great options. That said, if you don’t have the bandwidth, sending guests home with a hug and warm smile is enough.

Keep the menu short—one main, one side, one dessert—and let everyone contribute something small. If you have kids around, give them a role like handing out napkins or playing “official photographer.” It helps them feel included and keeps things moving naturally.

Meaning happens in the pauses. If it feels natural, carve out one quiet, intentional moment during your party—before dessert, after dinner, or even at the start—where you invite gratitude or reflection.

You might light a candle and share something you’re thankful for, or go around the room asking guests to recall a small win from the past year. You don’t need to make it formal — it’s the presence, not the presentation, that creates depth.

Start with the feeling you want, not the menu you think you should have. Choose one main dish that feels easy for you and complement it with a few simple sides. You can even skip appetizers altogether and start with drinks and conversation. Lower the lights, put on background music, and use what you already own for décor.

Mindful games are ones that invite more connection than competition. Try “Holiday Bingo” with personal prompts (like “laughed until I cried this year” or “tried something new”), or “Story Circle,” where everyone adds one line to a made-up holiday tale.

You could also play “Name That Nostalgic Song,” using your shared playlist. Keep it loose, short, and optional, as these games work best when they feel like play, not obligation.

Good conversation often needs a nudge. Place a few prompt cards on the table or near drinks with gentle questions: “What’s something you’re proud of from this year?” or “A small joy you’ve discovered recently?”

Also, design the space so guests can naturally break into smaller clusters — people connect more easily in groups of three or four than in one big circle. And don’t overfill the schedule; leave time for quiet, organic conversations.

Try something that creates shared laughter or purpose. You could do a homemade ornament exchange (everyone brings one they made or personalized), a “Secret Compliment Santa” where guests anonymously write kind notes to others, or a group playlist game. Even a simple group walk after dinner or a mini “holiday photo scavenger hunt” keeps people interacting without stress.

Mindfulness isn’t about meditating in silence but about being present for the moments that matter. Before guests arrive, take a breath and remind yourself that this is about connection, not just the photo ops.

Throughout the night, slow down enough to notice the small things, like the sound of laughter, the warmth in the room, or the smell of something delicious. Those moments ground you, and guests pick up on that calm energy. A mindful host creates a mindful space.

Lean into creativity over expense. Use natural elements like branches, pinecones, citrus, or candles to decorate. Borrow serving ware instead of buying new, and plan a potluck-style menu where everyone contributes something.

Free activities like music sharing, memory jars, or story games create connection at no cost. The less you spend trying to impress, the more space you leave for what feels genuine.

Plan less, delegate more, and give yourself permission to step away from the kitchen. The most relaxed hosts are the ones who sit down, eat with their guests, and laugh mid-conversation.

Assign cleanup to a few willing hands or leave dishes for the next day. You deserve to experience the joy you’re creating — not just facilitate it.

“Sometimes one has simply to endure a period of depression for what it may hold of illumination if one can live through it, attentive to what it exposes or demands,” the poet May Sarton wrote as she contemplated the cure for despair amid a dark season of the spirit. But what does it take to perch that precarious if in the direction of the light? When we are in that dark and hollow place, that place of leaden loneliness and isolation, when “the gray drizzle of horror induced by depression takes on the quality of physical pain,” as William Styron wrote in his classic account of the malady — an indiscriminate malady that savaged Keats and savaged Nietzsche and savaged Hansberry — what does it take to live through the horror and the hollowness to the other side, to look back and gasp disbelievingly, with the poet Jane Kenyon: “What hurt me so terribly… until this moment?”

During a recent dark season of the spirit, a dear friend buoyed me with the most wonderful, hope-giving, rehumanizing story: Some years earlier, when a colleague of hers — another physicist — was going through such a season of his own, she gave him an amaryllis bulb in a small pot; the effect it had on him was unexpected and profound, as the effect of uncalculated kindnesses always is — profound and far-reaching, the way a pebble of kindness ripples out widening circles of radiance. As the light slowly returned to his life, he decided to teach a class on the physics of animation. And so it is that one of his students, Emily Johnstone, came to make Bloom — a touching animated short film, drawing from the small personal gesture a universal metaphor for how we survive our densest private darknesses, consonant with Neil Gaiman’s insistence that “sometimes it only takes a stranger, in a dark place… to make us warm in the coldest season.”

Complement with Tim Ferriss on how he survived suicidal depression and Tchaikovsky on depression and finding beauty amid the wreckage of the soul, then revisit “Having It Out with Melancholy” — Jane Kenyon’s stunning poem about life with and after depression.

#94. Scientists uncover a hidden map of the brain with 539 distinct regions

Scientists have spent decades studying the brain's cells, connections, genes, and proteins. Yet another essential part of brain biology has received far less attention: lipids. These fatty molecules make up the membranes surrounding neurons, contribute to the myelin insulation that protects nerve fibers, and play important roles in communication between brain cells.

Although lipids are fundamental to brain function, scientists have struggled to map where different types are located. Conventional imaging techniques cannot easily distinguish individual lipid molecules, leaving a major gap in our understanding of the brain's chemical organization.

"So scientists have had only a blurry picture of how lipids differ from one part of the brain to another," says Giovanni D'Angelo, professor at The Kristian Gerhard Jebsen Foundation Chair in Nutrition and Metabolism at EPFL. "That gap matters, because changes in brain lipids are increasingly linked to conditions from depression to Alzheimer's disease."

Researchers at EPFL have now taken a major step toward filling that gap. A team led by D'Angelo, Luca Fusar Bassini, and Gioele La Manno has created a detailed map showing how lipids are distributed throughout the mouse brain.

Their Lipid Brain Atlas reveals that these molecules are arranged in highly organized patterns. Some match familiar anatomical structures, while others expose chemical boundaries that previous approaches had overlooked. The patterns are so distinctive that researchers could identify where a brain tissue sample originated simply by examining its lipid composition.

Scientists Identify 539 Distinct Chemical Zones in the Brain

To construct the atlas, researchers used mass spectrometry imaging, a technique that allows them to identify lipid molecules across thin sections of brain tissue. A laser scans each slice one location at a time, producing detailed information about which lipids are present and where they are found.

The team examined 172 different lipids in 109 brain slices collected from 11 mice. This generated approximately 7 million measurements, which scientists combined into a comprehensive 3D reconstruction using machine learning tools developed specifically for the project.

The resulting atlas revealed 539 chemically distinct territories, which the researchers named "lipizones." Each has a characteristic combination of lipids, creating a recognizable chemical signature.

Many of these regions correspond to established brain structures and cell types. Others reveal unexpected relationships between groups of nerve cell bodies and distant regions connected by their fibers. Such connections have often been difficult to detect using maps based on gene activity.

"In effect, lipids work like postal codes, giving distant but related parts of the brain the same chemical address," says D'Angelo.

Hidden Chemical Patterns Challenge Previous Brain Maps

The new atlas also uncovered surprising differences within parts of the brain that scientists previously considered relatively uniform.

One striking example is white matter, the tissue containing nerve fibers that connect different brain regions. Rather than having a largely consistent chemical composition, white matter contains numerous distinct lipid zones.

"This shows that the cells which make myelin are far more varied in their chemistry than their genes alone would suggest," says Luca Fusar Bassini.

The researchers also detected previously unrecognized chemical boundaries in the choroid plexus, the structure responsible for producing cerebrospinal fluid, as well as in the tissues lining the brain's internal cavities.

Together, these findings show that lipid mapping can reveal important features of brain organization that are not apparent from anatomy or genetic information alone.

Pregnancy Triggers Widespread Changes in Brain Lipids

Beyond identifying the brain's chemical structure, the atlas offered new insight into how that structure changes during pregnancy.

When researchers examined pregnant mice, they found substantial shifts in lipid composition across numerous brain regions. Overall, these changes were more pronounced than the typical lipid differences observed between male and female mice.

The cortex, which forms the brain's outer layer, showed particularly extensive changes. Meanwhile, levels of galactosyl ceramide, an important component of myelin, increased sharply throughout much of the brain's white matter.

These findings suggest that pregnancy involves significant changes in the brain's chemical makeup, potentially helping its neural connections adapt to the body's changing demands.

"Together, these shifts suggest the brain retunes its own wiring to meet the demands of pregnancy," says Gioele La Manno. "The Atlas reveals that the brain constantly adjusts its lipids to meet the body's changing needs."

A New Tool for Understanding Brain Aging and Disease

The Lipid Brain Atlas is freely available online, allowing scientists worldwide to explore this previously difficult-to-study aspect of brain biology.

By combining lipid information with existing genetic and cellular maps, researchers can gain a more complete understanding of how the brain is organized and how its chemistry changes over time.

The atlas also establishes a detailed reference for healthy mouse brain tissue. Scientists can use it to investigate how disruptions in lipid distribution might contribute to brain development, aging, and disorders such as Alzheimer's disease and depression.

Although the specific mouse brain map cannot be directly applied to humans, the approach used to create it could help researchers uncover comparable patterns in the human brain.

"What transfers to humans isn't the map, it's the method, and the fact that we now know that a healthy brain has a very organized lipid map at all," says Luca Fusar Bassini.

#95. “The Thought Loop That Won’t Close: On Neurodivergence and Perseveration”

“This isn’t occasional overthinking. It can go on for hours, days, sometimes years, and it feels involuntary once it starts.”

We have said goodbye. The conversation is over. Everyone else has moved on. I haven’t.

Since middle school, I’ve experienced a pattern of getting stuck replaying social interactions — a look, a tone, something someone said — analyzing it over and over, trying to figure out what it meant or whether I did something wrong.

This isn’t occasional overthinking. It can go on for hours, days, sometimes years, and it feels involuntary once it starts. It has led me to isolate for long stretches just to avoid triggering it, and now I get anticipatory anxiety before social events too, bracing for the same thing to happen again.

For most of my life, I couldn’t explain this behavior. I just believed something was severely wrong with me.

But there is a word for it: perseveration. For a lot of autistic and ADHD adults like myself, it’s one of the most disruptive, lesser-discussed parts of daily life.

[Read: “A Living Contradiction” – The AuDHD Experience]

Perseveration is the tendency to fixate on particular thoughts or feelings, with real difficulty disengaging from them. Though fixating on a favorite topic or hyperfocusing fall under the umbrella of cognitive perseveration for some, others take perseveration to mean getting stuck on a thought, task, or action long after it is useful, productive, or relevant. (There are other types of perseveration, like verbal and motor.) Perseveration tends to be involuntary, and can cut into sleep, work, and ordinary life.

Perseveration is part and parcel of the inflexible thinking that’s a core trait of autism and found in some other forms of neurodivergence. Emotional and attention regulation issues also play a role in getting stuck on looping thoughts, often of a negative nature. (Rumination is a common form of perseveration.) While it may not seem like it, chewing over the same thought or feeling, even if it’s distressing, can be a form of mental stimulation – another reason the behavior persists.

Cognitive flexibility — the brain’s ability to disengage from one thought and shift to another — is linked to better mental health. That’s why learning to get unstuck matters. Here are a few ways I’ve learned to escape the loop of perseveration:

[Read: “Can’t Stop Worrying? Just Schedule It for Later”]

For many years, the most difficult aspect of perseveration for me wasn’t the loop itself but not knowing that this pattern of behavior has a name, and that other neurodivergent people were experiencing it, too. I had to find my own — often unkind — explanations for being stuck in loops.

While knowing about perseveration doesn’t make it go away, it makes it easier to manage without shame. I now know that something isn’t deeply wrong with me. I simply have a trait that other people have found their way through.

In his wonderful contribution to A Velocity of Being: Letters to a Young Reader, Yo-Yo Ma tells children about how books helped him survive his own childhood, listing King Arthur among his three great heroes; as a young boy born in France to Chinese parents, trying to find his mooring as an immigrant in America, he reaped great consolation and inspiration from the tales of the legendary medieval leader — stories of “adventure, heroism, human frailty and accidental destiny” that emboldened him to believe in the power of the quest for holy grails and improbable dreams — dreams as improbable as a small boy with no homeland growing up to be the world’s greatest cellist.

And, indeed, buried inside the adventure-thrill of these Arthurian tales are treasure troves of wisdom on fortitude, courage, and the art of honorable living, nowhere richer than in the novels by T.H. White (May 29, 1906–January 17, 1964), one particular passage in which offers a meta-testament to the potency of reading in the character-formation of King Arthur himself.

In White’s 1958 Arthurian classic The Once and Future King (public library) — one of Ursula K. Le Guin’s lifelong favorite books — the mystic-magician Merlyn, aware of the young not-yet-king Arthur’s destiny, endeavors to sculpt the boy’s moral fiber and to teach him what it means to be a strong, kindly leader through a series of lessons from the animal kingdom, transforming him by turns into a fish, a hawk, an ant, a goose, and a badger. One day, the young Arthur comes to Merlyn in his ordinary human incarnation, sulking with an ordinary human disappointment — that small, merciless mallet for our fragility. Merlyn offers his advice on the mightiest antidote to disappointment and sorrow:

The best thing for being sad… is to learn something. That is the only thing that never fails. You may grow old and trembling in your anatomies, you may lie awake at night listening to the disorder of your veins, you may miss your only love, you may see the world about you devastated by evil lunatics, or know your honor trampled in the sewers of baser minds. There is only one thing for it then — to learn. Learn why the world wags and what wags it. That is the only thing which the mind can never exhaust, never alienate, never be tortured by, never fear or distrust, and never dream of regretting.

In a sentiment evocative of trailblazing astronomer Maria Mitchell’s observation that “we have a hunger of the mind which asks for knowledge of all around us, and the more we gain, the more is our desire,” Merlyn adds:

Look at what a lot of things there are to learn — pure science, the only purity there is. You can learn astronomy in a lifetime, natural history in three, literature in six. And then, after you have exhausted a million lifetimes in biology and medicine and theocriticism and geography and history and economics — why, you can start to make a cartwheel out of the appropriate wood, or spend fifty years learning to begin to learn to beat your adversary at fencing. After that you can start again on mathematics, until it is time to learn to plough.

Complement with Rebecca Solnit — a modern-day magician of storytelling — on how books solace, empower, and transform us, philosopher Martha Nussbaum on how to live with our human fragility, and poet Mary Oliver on the greatest antidote to sorrow, then revisit Bruce Lee’s philosophy of learning, Lewis Carroll’s four rules of learning, and Albert Einstein’s advice to his own young son on the secret to learning anything.

#98. Does Your Therapy Feel Like Expensive Chit-Chat?

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted September 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

You sit down for therapy fully intending to finally dive deep into your psyche. You have thought about it in the shower, rehearsed what you might say in the car, and perhaps even promised yourself that today you are absolutely going there.

Forty-five minutes later, you have covered your boss’s irritating email, the person who left you on read, and whether you should go to your friend’s birthday party.

As the session winds down, you feel stressed.

Therapy is supposed to be deep, isn’t it? There should be tears, revelations, breakthroughs.

It can be easy to assume that when therapy feels like ordinary conversation, nothing therapeutic is happening. However, some of the most important material in session doesn’t arrive with a drumroll or suspenseful music. Often, awareness emerges through gossip, complaints, dating stories, work drama, and the seemingly insignificant details of your week.

You may think you’re telling your therapist about how your roommate never replaces the toilet paper. However, your therapist may be hearing that you routinely take on more than your share, become resentful, say absolutely nothing, and then insist you’re “fine.”

Everyday interactions contain information about how we handle disappointment, rejection, boundaries, intimacy, anger, and uncertainty.

The incidents you’re recounting in session may not constitute a crisis, but your reactions to them can reveal the narratives you live by. Maybe someone’s irritation means you have done something wrong. Maybe asking for what you need feels demanding, while accommodating everyone else feels perfectly reasonable.

As a therapist, I’m not trying to determine who was right in the argument or whether your friend’s text was objectively rude. I’m listening for what the interaction evoked in you, the meaning you assigned to it, and why the same themes seem to follow you from one relationship to another.

People don’t necessarily walk into therapy and immediately announce their deepest, darkest secrets.

Most sessions begin far less dramatically. You might start with traffic, complain about something that happened at work, or recap the never-ending to-do list. Before you know it, you’re analyzing why your best friend’s thumbs-up emoji felt so hostile, only to realize it reminds you of your mother’s curt responses. Suddenly, what seemed like meaningless chit-chat begins to make sense.

In my sessions, I often see people approach vulnerability gradually. We test the room. We tell funny stories about painful experiences. We talk about music, books, films. Sometimes we spend 20 minutes discussing someone else’s behavior before realizing we’re actually talking about ourselves.

Small talk may be a way of building enough safety to move toward more painful memories. There is no prize for getting to your deepest wound in four sessions. Pacing the work and slowly uncovering what lies beneath are part of the process.

Imagine telling your therapist that someone you’ve been dating hasn’t texted you in three days. You shrug and say, “It’s whatever. I don’t care.”

But you’re sitting on the edge of the couch, twisting your ring around your finger, and your voice changes every time you mention their name.

That discrepancy between what you’re saying and what your body is communicating is information.

Therapists listen to what happened, but we also pay attention to tone of voice, body language, facial expressions, changes in energy, pauses, and moments when your words don’t quite match your demeanor.

I often find one of the most revealing sentences in therapy to be, “Anyway... it’s not a big deal.”

In session, the way you tell me something reveals more than the words themselves.

Therapy isn’t only a place where you talk about your relationships. It is also a relationship in itself. The ways you connect with other people may eventually wander into the therapy room as well.

Maybe you worry about boring your therapist. Maybe you perform being the “good client” who is insightful, self-aware, and conveniently healed by Thursday. Or perhaps you wonder whether your therapist secretly thinks you’re ridiculous for checking the Instagram story of someone you swear you are completely over.

You may apologize for crying or agree with an interpretation you don’t actually agree with because disagreeing feels uncomfortable.

These moments allow you and your therapist to notice how you relate to others while it is actually happening. If you worry about taking up too much space and then apologize to me for “talking too much,” we can become curious about that together, right there in the room.

There is a misconception that good therapy should wreck you. That you should leave emotionally exhausted, choke back tears on the subway ride home, and suddenly understand the origins of your abandonment issues.

Some days, therapy does feel profound. You make a connection you hadn’t made before, finally say something out loud, grieve a loss you have spent years avoiding, or leave with a different understanding of your childhood. Other times, you leave therapy and buy groceries.

A lighter session can help you regulate, reflect, laugh at yourself, or experience being with another person without having to perform, fix, impress, or take care of them.

This is particularly important in relational therapy, where change can happen through the therapeutic relationship itself.

Revealing something you’re ashamed of and being met with curiosity rather than criticism, or expressing anger and discovering that the relationship doesn’t collapse, can offer a different experience of connection.

Taking things slowly and unpacking difficult material gently is one thing. Having the same pleasant conversation every week while avoiding everything you came to therapy to address is another.

If you’re wondering what you’re actually working toward, bring that question into the session.

Advocating for yourself or admitting that something isn’t working can itself become part of the therapeutic process. You can say, “I feel like I keep talking about my week, but I’m not sure we’re getting anywhere.”

A good therapist won’t be threatened by your feedback. In fact, that conversation may take the work deeper. And if advocating for your needs is something you struggle with elsewhere in your life, telling your therapist what you need may itself become the corrective experience you’ve been longing for.

The goal of therapy isn’t to manufacture a breakthrough every 50 minutes. It is to become increasingly curious about your inner landscape and understand why you chase whom you chase, tolerate what you tolerate, and avoid what you avoid.

What feels like chit-chat may also be the unfamiliar ease of connecting with someone who is genuinely interested in you. You may be learning what it feels like to show up as you are and trust that you will be met with curiosity and care. Maybe the conversation you thought was going nowhere is actually what you came to therapy for: the experience of genuine connection.

#99. What is somatic therapy? Plus 5 ways it can support healing

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

The busyness of life can leave you feeling tense from head to toe — jaw clenched, chest tight, stomach in knots, shoulders up to your ears. For many of us, stress creeps up slowly, settling into your body even after your mind has moved on, until tension starts to feel normal.

Somatic therapy works with the mind-body connection directly. It's a body-based approach, most often used to work through chronic stress, anxiety, and trauma. The idea is that tuning into physical sensations can help you process what your mind and body have been holding onto.

Ahead, we’ll break down what somatic therapy involves, what the evidence supports, and a few gentle practices to start noticing what your body’s been carrying.

In somatic therapy, a therapist helps you become aware of physical sensations like tension, breathing, posture, and restlessness. This is often called a "bottom-up" approach. It starts with the body and works toward the mind. Traditional talk therapy tends to move “top-down,” from thoughts toward feelings.

Somatic Experiencing, developed by Peter Levine, is the most studied approach. Others include sensorimotor psychotherapy, which blends talk therapy with movement, and body-focused techniques that are integrated into broader trauma treatment.

Note: Some of the theories behind somatic therapy remain scientifically debated. Polyvagal theory, often used to explain why the nervous system gets "stuck" in a stress state, has been challenged by researchers who argue the evidence doesn’t support its core physiological claims.

In a session, a therapist might open the conversation by asking what you notice physically as feelings and memories come up. For example, if a hard memory makes your chest tighten, they may guide you to gently stay with that sensation, rather than pushing through or ignoring it.

They may draw on a range of tools: breathing exercises, grounding techniques, gentle movement, and sensation tracking. The aim is to help your body and mind feel safe enough to process difficult experiences at a manageable pace.

Related read: What is holistic therapy (and how can it benefit you)?

Somatic therapy is most established as a support for trauma, though it may also be worth exploring if:

you feel stuck in traditional talk therapy

stress tends to show up physically for you

you prefer an approach that involves movement and physical awareness

If you're working through trauma, it’s especially worth finding a licensed professional trained in a somatic approach. This process can bring up intense feelings, and they can help you move at a comfortable pace.

Somatic therapy isn't a fit for everyone, and it’s not a substitute for other evidence-based treatments when those are recommended.

The research here is early but promising. Most studies are small, and somatic therapy hasn't been tested as thoroughly as treatments such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). Here's what the current evidence points to.

1. It may reduce PTSD symptoms: The first randomized controlled trial of Somatic Experiencing found meaningful drops in post-traumatic symptoms and depression in people with PTSD. While the results were positive, researchers noted more study is needed.

2. It may help when talk therapy isn’t working: Some people find it hard to put their trauma into words or haven’t felt any relief from talking about it. A body-based approach offers another path to processing trauma.

3. It may support people with both pain and trauma: One trial looked at a brief Somatic Experiencing intervention for chronic low back pain and PTSD. It found reduced trauma symptoms and less fear of movement, though the overall effect was modest.

4. It can ease the physical side of stress: Stress and anxiety often show up as muscle tension, shallow breathing, or a racing heart. Somatic work targets these physical patterns.

5. It may build body awareness over time: Learning to pick up on early signs of stress, like restlessness or a churning stomach, can help you catch stress before it builds up.

The research above looked at somatic therapy involving trained professionals. These practices below can be done on your own as a complement to everyday self-care — not a trauma treatment. If any of this brings up feelings of distress, it may be useful to reach out to a professional.

A body scan is a mindfulness practice and a foundational way to build physical awareness. You move your attention slowly through your body, noticing where you're holding tension without trying to fix it.

Over time, this makes it easier to recognize tension early, so a tight jaw or clenched shoulders doesn’t turn into a headache or a bad night's sleep.

Try: Sitting or lying down and shifting your focus from your toes to the top of your head, pausing at each area for a breath or two. If you notice tightness, acknowledge it and keep going.

💙 Dive into this Body Scan Meditation on the Calm app.

Tune into your senses to pull your attention back to the present. When your mind races ahead to what might go wrong, or loops back to replay something you said or did, observing what's around you gives it something tangible to hold onto. This works well before a stressful conversation or any time your thoughts start swirling.

Try: Naming five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell, and one you can taste. Take your time to really notice each one. If a sense isn’t accessible to you, swap in something else to focus on, like your breath.

💙 For a guided sensory experience, listen to Tune Into the Senses on Calm.

Slowing your breath tells your nervous system it’s safe to relax. It’s one of the quickest ways to ease a stressful moment, and you can do it anywhere.

Try: Breathing in for a count of four, then out for six. Start with a few rounds, and repeat until you feel settled.

When you’re restless, movement can help you release that energy — in whatever way is comfortable and available to you.

Try: Rolling your shoulders, shaking out your hands, stretching your neck, or gently tensing and releasing different muscle groups for a minute.

Related read: What is progressive muscle relaxation (and how to practice it)

When you name a physical sensation, it turns a vague sense of unease into something concrete: tightness in your chest, buzzing in your hands, a knot in your stomach. That specificity alone can make it feel less overwhelming.

Try: When a strong emotion shows up, pausing and locating it in your body. Just noticing it is often enough to feel more in control.

💙 Practice this skill with Calm’s Labeling meditation.

Somatic therapy works by helping you become aware of and gently process physical sensations linked to trauma.

Instead of only talking through what happened, a trained therapist guides you to track what's happening in your body, pausing whenever a feeling becomes too intense. Research on this approach for PTSD is still early, but the results so far are encouraging.

A body scan is a common example of a somatic practice. You slowly move your attention through your body, checking in on where you’re holding tightness.

Other examples include grounding yourself using your five senses, slowing your breath, and gently moving by either stretching or shaking out your limbs.

When you're stressed, your nervous system reacts as if you're facing a threat, releasing hormones like cortisol and adrenaline and priming your body for action.

Normally, your body relaxes once the moment passes. But ongoing stress can keep those patterns switched on, which is why tension, headaches, or sleep issues can stick around.

Somatic practices, including body scans, grounding, and slow breathing, are safe to try on your own — especially if you don't have a significant trauma history.

If you do have a trauma history, it may be worth exploring deeper body-based work with a therapist instead, since it can bring up strong feelings you may want support to work through.

Somatic therapy provides another way to work through stress or difficult experiences by connecting how you feel physically to how you feel emotionally.

This can be especially useful if talking through things hasn't brought relief, or if certain emotions are hard to put into words. Over time, tuning into your body can also help you catch stress before it accumulates.

EMDR (eye movement desensitization and reprocessing) and somatic therapy are related, but different. EMDR uses guided eye movements or other rhythmic stimulation while you recall a difficult memory, so the memory feels less distressing to recall. Somatic therapy focuses on observing and working with physical sensations as they come up.

EMDR has a larger research base and appears in more clinical guidelines, while the evidence for somatic therapy is still developing. Some therapists draw on both.

Read more: Can EMDR help you better manage your PTSD? 6 things to consider

The main criticism of somatic therapy is that the research is still limited. Some of its underlying theories, such as the polyvagal theory or the idea that trauma is stored in the body, are also scientifically contested. Critics argue that body-based approaches are sometimes marketed as more proven than the evidence supports.

The timeline for somatic therapy depends on what you’re working through. Research trials have generally used treatment courses of several months.

If you're working on everyday stress, you may notice a shift in how you handle pressure fairly quickly, while deeper trauma work usually takes longer. A good therapist will check in on your progress along the way.

#100. 5 Common Prescription Drugs Linked To Memory Loss

Prescription drugs taken by millions of people around the world can affect memory.

Prescription drugs taken by millions of people around the world can affect memory.

Memory loss is not always a result of ageing.

Here are five types of drugs that can affect memory.

The older type of antidepressants — known as tricyclics — have been linked to memory loss.

Around half of people taking them report problems concentrating and one-third say they have memory loss.

Benzodiazepines include drugs marketed under the names Valium, Ativan, Klonopin and Xanax.

These drugs are often prescribed for anxiety and other mental health issues such as OCD, insomnia and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Unfortunately they are also linked to memory loss and even Alzheimer’s.

Dr Helene Alphonso, a psychiatrist and Director of Osteopathic Medical Education at Texas University, said:

“Current research is extremely clear and physicians need to partner with their patients to move them into therapies, like [modern] anti-depressants, that are proven to be safer and more effective.”

Statins are prescribed to many people to keep their cholesterol in a safer range.

The Food and Drug Administration lists memory loss, forgetfulness and confusion as possible side-effects of the drug.

Some people do report memory problems when taking them, but the studies conducted so far are inconclusive.

Beta-blockers slow the heart rate and are used to lower blood pressure.

They are also prescribed to those with congestive heart problems.

Beta-blockers, though, may also cause the loss of emotional memories.

They have even been tested as a way of treating post-traumatic stress disorder because of their ability to block emotional memories.

Again, though, the studies are not conclusive.

People who cannot sleep are sometimes prescribed so-called ‘Z-drugs’.

The ‘Z-drugs’ have been linked to memory loss: especially losing the ability to make new memories.

They have also been reported to cause strange behaviours like driving or cooking with absolutely no memory of the event.

Where possible consider a psychological therapy or applicable alternative to using these drugs.

Naturally, you should always consult your physician before making changes to your medication.

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#101. Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice

What if some of the changes we associate with aging begin with the loss of a single protein deep inside the brain? Scientists investigating that possibility found that restoring a protein called Menin in older mice improved memory, balance, bone mass, and skin thickness in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing the animals with a naturally occurring amino acid improved their learning and memory in only three weeks.

The findings, originally published in March 2023 in PLOS Biology, came from researchers led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in China. Their experiments identified a previously overlooked connection between inflammation, brain chemistry, and aging throughout the body. Although the results were obtained in mice, they raised an intriguing possibility: Some effects of aging may be influenced by biological processes in the brain that scientists could eventually learn to modify.

Research published since then has added evidence that the brain plays an important role in regulating aging. It has also revealed why the seemingly simple supplement findings deserve careful interpretation.

How a Hidden Brain Protein May Influence Aging

At the center of the discovery is the hypothalamus, a small but powerful region near the base of the brain. It helps regulate essential functions such as body temperature, hunger, metabolism, sleep, and hormone production. Because these systems affect nearly every organ, changes in the hypothalamus can have consequences throughout the body.

Scientists have increasingly recognized the hypothalamus as an important player in aging. One possible reason involves neuroinflammation, the brain's inflammatory response. Although inflammation helps protect against infections and injuries, persistent inflammation can interfere with normal cellular function and contribute to age-related deterioration.

Earlier work by Leng and colleagues had identified Menin as a protein that helps restrain inflammation in the hypothalamus. Menin also participates in regulating gene activity, allowing it to influence multiple biological pathways.

The researchers wanted to understand what happens when this protective protein begins to disappear with age.

They discovered that Menin levels gradually declined in certain hypothalamic neurons as mice grew older. Interestingly, the same decrease was not observed in astrocytes or microglia, two other important types of brain cells involved in supporting neurons and managing immune responses.

To investigate whether this decline actually contributed to aging, the team developed genetically modified mice in which Menin could be selectively disabled.

The results were striking. Mice with reduced Menin activity developed greater inflammation in the hypothalamus, thinner skin, reduced bone mass, and worsening cognitive performance. Their lifespans were also modestly shortened.

Rather than simply accompanying aging, the loss of Menin appeared capable of helping drive several of its characteristic changes.

Restoring Menin Reversed Several Signs of Aging in 30 Days

The researchers then asked an even more interesting question: If declining Menin contributes to aging, could restoring the protein reverse some of the damage?

To find out, they used a gene delivery technique to increase Menin production in a specific part of the hypothalamus in older (20-month-old) mice. This region, called the ventromedial hypothalamus, helps coordinate metabolism, energy balance, and other bodily functions.

Just 30 days after treatment, the animals showed measurable improvements.

Their skin became thicker, bone mass increased, and performance improved on tests measuring learning, memory, and balance. Researchers also observed reductions in inflammation and improvements in certain metabolic changes associated with aging.

In a separate survival analysis, mice receiving the Menin treatment also lived longer than untreated controls.

These findings suggested that some biological changes associated with old age could be at least partially reversed by restoring Menin activity in a specific group of brain cells.

But the researchers also uncovered an important clue about how Menin produced these effects.

A Simple Amino Acid Offers a Surprising Clue

When Menin levels declined, the researchers noticed that concentrations of D-serine, an amino acid involved in brain signaling, also fell.

Amino acids are best known as the building blocks of proteins, but some perform other important functions. D-serine helps regulate NMDA receptors, specialized proteins on nerve cells that are essential for communication between neurons, learning, and the formation of memories.

D-serine is closely related to L-serine, an amino acid commonly found in foods such as soybeans, eggs, fish, and nuts. The two forms have different biological roles. Although D-serine is also available as a dietary supplement, consuming ordinary serine-rich foods is not equivalent to taking the form used in the experiments.

Further investigation revealed that Menin helps control the production of PHGDH, an enzyme involved in the biochemical pathway that generates serine (which was in turn regulated by Menin). When Menin activity decreased, this pathway became less active, reducing the amount of D-serine available to the brain.

Restoring Menin increased D-serine levels in the hippocampus, a region especially important for learning and memory.

This connection suggested that the cognitive effects of declining Menin might be partly explained by disruptions in D-serine signaling.

To test the idea directly, the scientists gave older mice D-serine in their drinking water for three weeks.

The supplementation improved their performance on learning and memory tests, even without directly restoring Menin.

However, there was an important distinction. While increasing Menin improved both cognitive function and physical signs of aging, D-serine supplementation primarily improved cognition. It did not restore the age-related losses in bone mass and skin thickness.

That difference suggests Menin influences aging through several biological mechanisms, with D-serine accounting for only part of its effects.

Later Research Strengthens the Link Between the Brain and Aging

Since the original 2023 discovery, additional studies have provided evidence that the hypothalamus helps coordinate aging across the body.

In a 2024 study published in Cell Metabolism, researchers at Washington University School of Medicine identified a different group of hypothalamic neurons that communicates with fat tissue. By maintaining or stimulating this communication pathway, they increased physical activity, improved age-related metabolic function, and extended lifespan in mice.

That work involved a different protein and neural circuit from Menin, but supported the broader idea that signals originating in the hypothalamus can influence how the rest of the body ages.

Another 2024 study in the Journal of Physiology and Biochemistry provided additional insight into Menin itself. Researchers found that increasing Menin helped protect cultured hippocampal cells against inflammation and a form of programmed cell death triggered by exposure to the stress hormone corticosterone. Although these laboratory experiments did not establish an anti-aging effect, they supported the idea that Menin has important protective functions in brain cells.

An even larger picture emerged in January 2025, when scientists published a detailed analysis of approximately 1.2 million mouse brain cells in Nature.

The researchers discovered that some of the brain cells most sensitive to aging were concentrated around the third ventricle, a fluid-filled cavity in the hypothalamus. Many aging cells showed reduced activity in genes involved in normal neuronal function and increased activity in genes associated with inflammation and immune responses.

These findings highlighted the hypothalamus as a potential center of vulnerability during brain aging, although they did not directly test the Menin pathway.

New Findings in 2026 Reveal More Aging Pathways

Research published in 2026 has further strengthened the connection between hypothalamic activity and longevity.

In a study published in Cell, scientists found that strengthening daily biological rhythms in a specific hypothalamic region improved several aging-related measurements and extended lifespan in male mice. The intervention also reduced estimates of biological age based on DNA methylation, chemical modifications to DNA that change with age.

Another 2026 study in Cell Metabolism identified a protein called Mimecan that helps skeletal muscles communicate with the hypothalamus and brown fat, a specialized tissue involved in generating body heat. Restoring circulating Mimecan levels in older mice improved this communication and extended lifespan.

Together, these discoveries suggest that aging involves complex communication between the brain and the rest of the body. Rather than depending on one master switch, multiple neural circuits, hormones, and metabolic signals appear to help determine how age-related changes unfold.

Could D-Serine Supplements Protect the Human Brain?

The possibility of improving memory with a relatively simple amino acid is especially appealing. However, evidence that D-serine can reverse age-related cognitive decline in humans remains limited.

A small randomized clinical trial published in 2016 tested D-serine in 50 healthy older adults. Participants performed better on one assessment of spatial learning and problem-solving after receiving the amino acid, but researchers did not find significant improvements across the other cognitive tests or mood measurements.

More importantly, later research suggests that the effects of D-serine depend on the biological circumstances.

In an April 2025 study published in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences, scientists investigated D-serine in mice genetically engineered to develop features of Alzheimer's disease.

Unlike the Menin experiments, which associated reduced D-serine with age-related memory impairment, this study found that an early increase in D-serine accompanied disruptions in brain signaling. Removing the enzyme responsible for producing D-serine prevented or reduced several later cognitive impairments in those mice.

These findings do not invalidate the earlier results. Instead, they suggest that D-serine signaling is more complicated than simply having too little or too much. Its effects may depend on the condition being studied, the timing of treatment, and how the brain's signaling systems are functioning.

There are also unanswered questions about the long-term safety of D-serine supplementation. High doses have raised kidney safety concerns in animal experiments, and research has not established whether prolonged supplementation is a safe or effective way to prevent age-related memory loss in otherwise healthy people.

For now, D-serine should be considered an experimental approach rather than a proven treatment for brain aging.

Can Scientists Eventually Slow Aging by Targeting the Brain?

Despite the encouraging mouse experiments, researchers still need to answer several fundamental questions.

Why does Menin decline in the hypothalamus as animals age? How many of its effects could be reversed by treatment, and how long would those improvements last? Could restoring Menin influence other biological systems in unexpected ways?

It is also unclear whether treatments targeting Menin or D-serine could reproduce similar results in humans.

Nevertheless, the original researchers believe the pathway deserves further investigation.

"We speculate that the decline of Menin expression in the hypothalamus with age may be one of the driving factors of aging, and Menin may be the key protein connecting the genetic, inflammatory, and metabolic factors of aging. D-serine is a potentially promising therapeutic for cognitive decline," said Leng.

Leng adds, "Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) Menin signaling diminished in aged mice, which contributes to systemic aging phenotypes and cognitive deficits. The effects of Menin on aging are mediated by neuroinflammatory changes and metabolic pathway signaling, accompanied by serine deficiency in VMH, while restoration of Menin in VMH reversed aging-related phenotypes."

The growing body of evidence points toward a potentially important shift in how scientists understand aging. Instead of viewing it only as the gradual deterioration of individual organs, researchers are investigating how specific brain pathways may actively shape the process.

The possibility that restoring those pathways could improve memory, physical function, or longevity remains experimental. But the Menin discovery, together with subsequent findings, offers a compelling reason to explore whether some of the biological changes associated with aging are more reversible than previously thought.

#102. “When Perimenopause, Puberty, and Neurodivergence Clash”

“If another mother is reading this after a sleepless night, after an evening that felt heavier than it had any right to be, I want her to know she isn’t failing. She might just be standing in the middle of two enormous transitions at once.”

There are days when my daughter walks through the front door, drops her bag wherever it lands, and before either of us says a word, I know it’s going to be one of those evenings. She doesn’t always know why she’s overwhelmed. Honestly, some days, neither do I.

She is 12 now. Last year, puberty showed up and brought all its mess with it: the big emotions, the overwhelm, the anxiety, the contradictions that seem to appear overnight. By then, I was already well into my own hormonal transition.

Perimenopause had brought its own collection of restless nights, brain fog, aching joints, changing moods, and the strange feeling that my body no longer recognized the rules it had followed for decades.

My daughter is becoming a woman. I’m becoming a different one.

“Double hormone storm” is how I’ve seen this dynamic described. With more women having children later, a lot of mothers are going through perimenopause just as their daughters hit puberty. Understanding this felt oddly comforting. It didn’t fix anything, but it told me I hadn’t been imagining how hard this stretch of life can be.

[Take This Test: Is It Perimenopause or ADHD?]

Except almost everything I read assumed there were two adults splitting the weight of it. That’s not my house. I’m doing this alone. When we’ve both run out of patience for the day, there’s no one else to hand it off to. If my daughter needs comfort, she comes to me. If I’ve had another broken night’s sleep and feel like I’m running on fumes, I still have to be the calm one. Some days I manage that. Plenty of days I don’t.

There’s another layer to our story. My daughter is neurodivergent — AuDHD. For her, puberty is layered atop a nervous system that already processes the world differently. So when I began to learn about how the menstrual cycle affects ADHD symptoms, I thought: How many evenings had I read wrong? How many hard nights had I understood as simply being about parenting or behavior, when hormonal changes might also have been playing a part?

It made me think about myself, too. Women are finally talking more openly about how fluctuating hormones during perimenopause can affect focus, mood and our ability to cope. Learning this made me look at some of my own difficult days differently, too. We assumed we weren’t trying hard enough. Turns out we might have been carrying a lot more than anyone gave us credit for.

None of this pauses life, though. There are still lunches to pack, laundry piling up, homework to check over her shoulder, bills that don’t care how tired you are, e-mails waiting, work that needs doing, and somewhere underneath all of it, two people trying to make sense of feelings neither of us asked for.

[Read: Let’s Talk About Perimenopause and ADHD]

Dinner has always been our time. We talk about our days, laugh about little things, and I try to be fully present, with my phone nowhere near the table. Sometimes she can’t wait to tell me about the latest adventures of her favorite book character.

Other evenings, words aren’t enough, and what she really needs is to release all the energy she’s been holding in. Then, without much warning, the mood can shift. I might ask her to have a shower before bedtime, while she’s already imagining something completely different, and suddenly we’re standing on opposite sides of an argument neither of us was expecting. Those are the nights I try to remember: connection matters more than getting it perfect.

We’ve built our own small rituals along the way. Long walks, because talking is easier when you don’t have to look at each other. Hot chocolate on rough days. Journals or drawings that say the things our mouths won’t. A dumb joke that somehow cuts through all the tension in the room. And, maybe most of all, letting each other start over after a bad day.

I never like going to bed with things left unresolved between us. Life is uncertain, and tomorrow is never guaranteed. If we’ve had a difficult evening, I try to make sure we’ve found our way back to each other before we fall asleep. Even if we’ve both been tired, overwhelmed or misunderstood, I don’t want the last thing we carry into sleep to be anger. I’d rather it be a cuddle, a smile, an “I love you,” or the quiet certainty that, whatever today looked like, tomorrow we begin again.

I’m not writing this because I’ve cracked the code on raising a daughter through puberty while going through perimenopause myself. I haven’t. Most days I’m just doing the best I can with the woman I am today, hoping I’m becoming the mother I want to be tomorrow. But if another mother is reading this after a sleepless night, or an evening that felt heavier than it had any right to be, I want her to know she isn’t failing. She might simply be standing in the middle of two enormous transitions at once.

My daughter is learning how to inhabit the woman she is becoming. And, unexpectedly, so am I. Because becoming a woman, I’m starting to understand, isn’t something that happens once during puberty. Maybe, in different ways, we keep becoming her throughout our lives.

#103. The Day Dostoyevsky Discovered the Meaning of Life in a Dream

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If it makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider aiding its sustenance with a one-time or loyal donation. Your support makes all the difference.
