#113. Winter solstice celebration: 7 mindful rituals to try

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

During the winter months, evenings rush in earlier, the sun rises later, and if you’re in the northern hemisphere, winter days can become a blur of holiday celebrations and unending to-do lists. For many, this stretch of darkness may bring fatigue, seasonal depression, or a longing to just curl up on the couch until spring arrives. For others, this season brings a type of relief as the extra darkness can give a rare permission to pause and relax.

In that way, the winter solstice—the longest night of the year—marks a time of peak rest. And if you enjoy the cozy, restful vibes, you might opt to honor this time with a winter solstice celebration. Rooted in centuries of ritual and reflection, this time can be an opportunity to honor both the quiet darkness and the slow season. And instead of rushing toward resolutions or year-end checklists, the solstice presents a chance to set a different kind of goal — one that encourages slowing down, breathing, and staying in the moment.

However you honor it, a mindful winter solstice celebration is meant to be about intention and a way to reconnect with your own internal rhythm before stepping into the next chapter. Let’s explore how to plan a mindful winter solstice celebration that can be enjoyed with a group or even by yourself.

The winter solstice marks the exact moment when the hemisphere tilts farthest from the sun, creating the shortest day and longest night of the year. In the Northern Hemisphere, this falls on Dec. 21, while in the Southern Hemisphere, it occurs on June 20. It’s a natural point in the year to stop and pause as the light begins its slow return.

People have honored this shift for thousands of years. Ancient sites like Stonehenge in England and Newgrange in Ireland were built to align with the solstice sunrise, capturing the first light after the longest night. Across various cultures, it’s seen as a time to gather with loved ones around a bonfire, share food, and acknowledge the natural rhythms of the environment.

At its core, the winter solstice celebration has always been about connection to nature, to community, and to something larger than ourselves. In early societies, these gatherings were cornerstones of their culture. Bonfires, feasts, and shared stories offered time for connection, nourishment, and reassurance that the light would soon return.

That impulse to gather and celebrate hasn’t disappeared over the years, even if our celebrations may have evolved since then. While we may not rely on firelight for survival, we still crave the comfort of togetherness, especially during dark or busy seasons of life.

Solstice celebrations today reflect that same human need for connection and meaning. Lighting a candle at dinner, cooking a slow and intentional meal with loved ones, or simply turning off the screens and noticing the quiet of the night.

Psychologically, darkness invites stillness and self-awareness. It gives permission to stop striving and start listening to your own rhythms.

When nights stretch long and energy dips low, it’s natural to turn inward. The winter solstice offers space for reflection — to consider what no longer serves you, what you’re grateful for, and what you’re aiming for in the next season.

Many people mark the solstice by journaling, lighting candles for loved ones, or simply sitting in stillness. Some meditate. Some dance. Some opt for larger gatherings while others prefer alone time.

By acknowledging both the light and dark—within ourselves and in the world—we practice balance. And, in doing so, we prepare ourselves for whatever kind of light comes next.

For many people, the spiritual meaning of the winter solstice is rebirth. The longest night is a turning point, and the days begin to grow longer. Many traditions see that shift as a symbol for life itself: an ending makes room for a new start.

Cultures around the world tell this story in their own ways. Yule traditions in Northern Europe welcomed the sun's return with fire and evergreens. In China, the Dongzhi festival marks the time when yang, the bright and active force in Chinese philosophy, begins to grow again. Families in Iran stay up through Yalda night, reading poetry and eating pomegranates until the sun comes back.

You don't need to follow any one tradition to feel this meaning. A few minutes in a dimly lit room, thinking about what you hope will grow in the next season, can be a spiritual practice on its own.

A winter solstice celebration doesn’t need to be complicated or mystical. What matters most is the intention to pause, acknowledge where you are, and what you’re bringing into your life with the return of the light.

Whether you spend the evening alone, with close friends, or surrounded by family, these rituals offer simple yet meaningful ways to mark the turning of the season.

Lighting candles is one of the oldest ways to honor the solstice, symbolizing hope and the slow return of sunlight. You can make this ritual as simple or symbolic as you like.

If you’re alone, light one candle in a quiet room and take a few deep breaths. As you watch the flame, reflect on what the light represents for you this year. Is it gratitude? Resilience? The will to keep going?

If you’re gathering with others, invite each person to light their own candle and share one thing they’re thankful for. Turn off overhead lights, let the room glow softly, and notice how warmth builds both from the flames and from the presence of others.

Related read: Candle meditation: a step-by-step guide to practice at home

Storytelling has always been a way to pass through the darker times together. It connects people of all backgrounds and ages, offers perspective, and helps us feel seen and heard.

Around a dinner table or fireplace, take turns sharing one memory from the past year or season that felt meaningful or unexpected. It could be a moment of joy, a challenge that you overcame, or something small that shifted your outlook on life.

For a solo version of this exercise, record a voice note or write a letter to yourself about what you’ve learned this year. Maybe you’ll reread it next solstice to see what’s evolved.

The solstice is often seen as a time to release what no longer serves us, from habits to expectations or even emotional clutter that weighs us down. Writing can be a powerful way to do this.

Start by journaling freely about what you’d like to leave behind as the season begins. Then, if it feels right, tear the page as a symbolic act of release. If that feels too ceremonial for you or you’re uncomfortable with the idea, simply close your notebook and take a slow breath to mark the letting go.

Food is a universal language of celebration and togetherness. A solstice feast doesn’t need to be expensive or intricate, because this celebration is about nourishment, not presentation.

Cook something warm and hearty like a soup, roasted vegetables, bread, or anything that brings comfort. Make a table centerpiece with candlelight or a lantern to amp up the cozy vibe. If you’re sharing the meal with others, invite everyone to bring one dish that reminds them of home or brings them comfort.

If you’re celebrating alone, turn it into a sensory ritual by playing soft music, eating slowly and mindfully, and savoring the act of caring for yourself through food and nourishment. It’s a reminder that sustenance—both literal and emotional—comes from simple acts practiced with intention.

Related read: How to practice mindful cooking

Instead of resolutions, which can feel rigid or pressured, set intentions that speak to how you want to feel or move through the year ahead. Or you can reflect on all that you did that felt like enough.

Maybe you choose to reflect on these intentions or actions by candlelight after your meal, using the quiet of the night to imagine how you want those qualities to take root in your life moving forward.

💙 Need help? Join Jay Shetty in this guided meditation on the Calm app about The Power of Reflection.

Connecting with nature during the solstice can deepen your sense of presence and connection to the world around you. Even just a few minutes outdoors can be grounding.

Bundle up and step outside after sunset. Look at the sky and notice the stars, the clouds, or the soft glow of the streetlights, and make a note of how still the world around you feels. Maybe you take a short walk, breathe the fresh air, or simply stand still for a moment.

This practice of stepping outside and noticing the world around you reconnects you with something larger than yourself, which can act as a powerful reminder that even in darkness, there is movement and renewal.

You don’t need to be spiritual to create a small space for gratitude or even to practice it. Gather a few meaningful objects, like candles, flowers, photos, stones, or handwritten notes from loved ones and arrange them in a simple display on your kitchen counter or even your nightstand.

Each item can represent something you’re grateful for or want to honor. You can keep the altar up for a few days or take it down after the solstice as a symbolic release.

The act of intentionally creating a gratitude space or practice during a dark season can help anchor your attention and restore a sense of calm.

Related read: 8 gratitude exercises to cultivate a more grateful mindset

💙 Bring the gratitude into your bedtime routine during this Unwind with Gratitude meditation in the Calm app.

The winter solstice celebrates the shortest day and longest night of the year, marking the turning point toward longer, lighter days.

It’s both an astronomical and symbolic event — a time to recognize the balance between darkness and light and rest and renewal. Across cultures, people have used this moment to honor the cycles of nature and to remind themselves that even the coldest, darkest season carries the promise of light.

Whether you mark it with candlelight, reflection, or a shared meal, the winter solstice is a celebration of hope, endurance, and the quiet strength it takes to move through winter and trust in what comes next.

Mindful intention-setting focuses on how you want to feel or live, not on fixed goals or resolutions.

You might begin by journaling about what brought you peace or growth this year, then write down one or two themes you’d like to carry forward using words like balance, connection, or clarity. Light a candle as you reflect, or keep those words somewhere visible as a reminder.

Intentions are most powerful when they’re simple, personal, and realistic. The solstice is an ideal time to plant them, knowing the light will grow day by day. If it feels like too much to think of more goals, try reflecting on what you’ve already achieved that you’re proud of.

Yes, some of the most meaningful solstice rituals are done solo. If you’re craving solitude, think of the solstice as a built-in permission slip to pause. You could spend the evening journaling, cooking a favorite meal, lighting a single candle, or taking a slow walk under the night sky.

Being alone doesn’t mean being disconnected. It’s a way to reconnect with yourself before the year begins again. The solstice reminds us that stillness is a fertile space for renewal.

Yes. In the Southern Hemisphere, the winter solstice occurs around June 20-21, marking the point in the year when those regions experience their shortest day and longest night.

The meaning of the celebration remains the same: reflection, gratitude, and renewal. While the timing differs, people everywhere can honor the solstice as a moment to slow down, take stock of their lives, and reconnect with the cycles of light and rest that shape us all.

Modern winter solstice celebrations often blend ancient symbolism with everyday mindfulness. There’s no right or wrong way to celebrate. What matters is that it feels authentic and grounding.

Host a candlelit dinner with friends or family

Take part in a lantern walk or nighttime hike

Share gratitude notes or intentions for the coming year

Spend the evening offline, reading or listening to music

Decorate your space with natural elements like pine, citrus, cinnamon, or florals

Absolutely, and many children love the sense of wonder that comes during this time.

You could make paper lanterns together, bake something seasonal, or go outside to look for stars. You might talk about what it means for the days to grow longer and ask what they’re grateful for.

Solstice rituals can help kids understand nature’s cycles and develop gratitude in a way that feels tangible, simple, and joyful.

Related read: 61 fun and simple mindfulness activities for kids to enjoy

Reflection during the solstice mirrors the natural rhythm of rest before renewal.

It’s a moment to look back with honesty and gentleness — to acknowledge what was hard, what brought meaning, and what you want to nurture going forward. In a culture that often pushes constant motion, this quiet reflection is an act of balance.

Taking time to reflect helps you close one chapter and step into the next with clarity, not pressure.

Yes, the winter solstice marks the day when the earth tilts farthest from the sun. In the Northern Hemisphere, this falls on December 21st. In the Southern Hemisphere, this falls on or around June 21st.

After the solstice, daylight gradually increases. This subtle shift reminds us that change doesn’t happen all at once. It begins quietly, almost imperceptibly, and builds with time.

#114. Scientists discover 5 hidden brain patterns behind depression

Two people diagnosed with depression can experience vastly different symptoms. One might struggle with persistent anxiety and repetitive negative thoughts, while another may experience trauma related symptoms or substance abuse. But do these differences also appear in the way their brains function?

Researchers at the University of Helsinki investigated this question and uncovered a striking finding: people with the same depression diagnosis can have dramatically different patterns of brain activity. In some cases, communication between brain regions was unusually strong, while in others, it was weaker than normal.

Depression is a major global health concern. According to the World Health Organization (WHO, 2025), approximately 332 million (5.2%) adults worldwide are affected. In Finland, depression is the leading individual cause of both extended sick leave and disability pensions.

Brain Study Reveals Five Distinct Depression Profiles

To investigate the biological differences associated with depression, researchers examined brain activity in 263 people diagnosed with major depressive disorder and 75 healthy participants who served as a comparison group.

The analysis revealed five distinct groups based on differences in functional connectivity, a measure of how closely activity in different brain regions is coordinated. When two regions show synchronized activity, it suggests they are working together as part of a larger brain network. However, stronger connectivity does not necessarily mean the brain is functioning better.

"What was particularly interesting was the contrasting patterns of brain activity found under the umbrella of the same depression diagnoses. In some individuals, the functional connectivity between brain regions was stronger than usual, while in others it was weaker," says Director Satu Palva of the Neuroscience Center, University of Helsinki.

These differences were also associated with particular symptoms. Participants in one group showed especially strong connections between brain regions, along with more pronounced substance abuse problems. Another group displayed weaker connections and a greater prominence of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms.

The contrasting results could help explain why earlier studies examining the brains of people with depression have sometimes reached conflicting conclusions. If researchers study different combinations of patients, they may observe very different patterns, even though everyone involved has received the same diagnosis.

The findings add to growing evidence that depression may not have a single, consistent biological signature. Instead, the condition could involve several distinct patterns of brain function.

The Five Brain Patterns Linked to Depression

The researchers classified participants with depression into five groups based on how strongly different brain areas communicated and the frequencies at which their activity was coordinated.

Each group had a characteristic pattern of brain connectivity and associated symptoms:

Group 1: Strong connectivity and severe symptoms

Participants generally showed relatively strong connections between brain regions. This profile was associated with more severe symptoms across several areas, including depression, anxiety, rumination, and reduced ability to function in daily life. Rumination refers to repeatedly dwelling on distressing thoughts, worries, or negative experiences.

Group 2: Weaker connectivity and milder depression

This group was characterized by relatively weak communication between brain regions. Compared with the other groups, participants generally experienced milder symptoms.

Group 3: Widespread weak connectivity and trauma symptoms

People in this group showed reduced connectivity across substantial portions of the brain. Symptoms associated with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) were particularly prominent.

Group 4: Mixed connectivity and multiple challenges

This profile combined unusually strong connections in some brain regions with weaker connections in others. Participants tended to experience more severe depression, greater substance abuse problems, and lower overall well-being.

Group 5: The strongest connectivity and substance abuse symptoms

Participants in the fifth group had the strongest connections between brain regions of any group identified in the study. Substance abuse was a particularly prominent issue, while trauma related symptoms were less pronounced than in the other groups.

Importantly, all five groups also showed differences from the healthy participants. These distinctions extended beyond whether brain connections were strong or weak. The groups also differed in which brain regions were involved and the frequencies at which their activity was synchronized.

Together, the patterns suggest that people diagnosed with depression may experience substantially different changes in how their brain networks operate.

Measuring Brain Activity With Millisecond Precision

To capture these differences, the scientists used magnetoencephalography (MEG), a brain imaging technique that detects extremely faint magnetic fields produced by electrical activity in the brain.

Unlike methods that track slower changes associated with brain activity, MEG can follow electrical signals as they unfold over extremely short periods. This makes it particularly useful for investigating the timing and coordination of communication between brain regions.

Using MEG, the researchers recorded brain activity in all 263 participants with depression and the 75 healthy control subjects.

"MEG enabled us to monitor electrical brain activity with millisecond precision, helping us get closer to what actually happens in the brain at any given moment. Previously, depression phenotypes have been studied using methods with slower responses," Palva notes.

This high level of temporal precision allowed the team to examine rapid changes in brain activity that might be difficult to distinguish using slower measurement techniques.

By studying these fast signals, the researchers were able to identify differences not only in the strength of connectivity but also in the frequencies at which brain regions appeared to work together.

Could Brain Activity Lead to More Personalized Depression Treatments?

The discovery raises an important possibility for the future of mental health care: treatments might eventually be selected partly according to a person's individual pattern of brain activity.

Today, finding an effective depression treatment can involve trying different medications or therapies and evaluating how well each works. Because patients can respond differently to the same treatment, identifying the most suitable approach is not always straightforward.

Brain activity measurements could eventually provide additional information to help guide these decisions. However, the researchers emphasize that their findings are not yet ready for clinical use.

"We're not yet at the point where brain measurements can be used to choose the right treatment for patients, but the study does show one possible route," Palva says.

A major long-term goal is to better understand how particular symptoms relate to the way brain networks function. Connecting these biological patterns with patients' experiences could help researchers develop more precise ways to identify and characterize depression.

Eventually, such knowledge might allow doctors to determine which therapies are most likely to help individual patients, potentially reducing the amount of trial and error involved in treatment.

For now, the five brain profiles offer a different way to understand depression. Rather than assuming that one diagnosis corresponds to one underlying pattern of brain activity, the findings suggest that depression can involve markedly different biological changes, sometimes even in opposite directions.

The research was carried out in collaboration with Aalto University and Helsinki and Uusimaa Hospital District (HUS).

#115. The Clothes That Make People Appear More Intelligent

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

Wearing more clothing makes you look more competent, a study finds.

Something as simple as taking off a sweater is enough to make you look less competent, the researchers found.

The finding applies to both men and women, said Dr Kurt Gray, the study’s first author:

“An important thing about our study is that, unlike much previous research, ours applies to both sexes.

It also calls into question the nature of objectification because people without clothes are not seen as mindless objects, but they are instead attributed a different kind of mind.”

The effect occurs because seeing more flesh encourages us to think about a person’s body, rather than their mind.

“We also show that this effect can happen even without the removal of clothes.

Simply focusing on someone’s attractiveness, in essence concentrating on their body rather than their mind, makes you see her or him as less of an agent [someone who acts and plans] more of an experiencer.”

Showing bare skin, though, does have some advantages, explained Dr Gray:

“A focus on the body, and the increased perception of sensitivity and emotion it elicits might be good for lovers in the bedroom.

Others appear to be less inclined to harm people with bare skin and more inclined to protect them.

In one experiment, for example, people viewing male subjects with their shirts off were less inclined to give those subjects uncomfortable electric shocks than when the men had their shirts on.”

“Even more than robbing someone of agency, the increased experience that may accompany body perceptions may lead those who are characterized in terms of their bodies to be seen as more reactive and emotional, traits that may also serve to work against career advancement.”

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Gray et al., 2011).

#116. Do ADHD Meds Stunt Growth? A New Stimulant Study Says No

ADHD stimulants have a negligible effect on adult height, according to a new study that tracked more than 64,000 children for nearly 30 years.

Long-term stimulant use for ADHD negligibly affects adult height, according to a new cohort study published in Pediatric Research that tracked 64,775 children for up to 28 years.1

Parents making ADHD treatment decisions commonly worry that prescription stimulants will stunt their child’s growth. In a 2024 ADDitude survey of 11,000 readers, less than half (42%) of parents chose to medicate their children in the months following an ADHD diagnosis. Those respondents cited side effects like appetite suppression or sleep disruption — both possible impediments to growth — as influences on their decision.

Murky or conflicting findings from previous studies have done little to ease caregivers’ worries.

“Many prior studies either did not follow participants to adult height, so reported effects may reflect delayed maturation rather than true adult height deficits, or they did not account for genetic height potential, which may confound results,” the study’s authors wrote.2, 3

The Pediatric Research study followed a different methodology. It measured the impact of ADHD and stimulant treatment on an individual’s adult height relative to their expected genetic height potential, based on their parents’ heights. Taking an individual-level normalization approach accounted for familial genetic height potential, reducing uncertainty from delayed maturation and group-level bias.

The researchers used health records from a nationwide provider to assemble a retrospective cohort of 17,517 children with treated and untreated ADHD, plus 47,258 in a control group, all born between 1995 and 2003. (Of those with ADHD, 11,846 received stimulant treatment, and 5,671 did not.) They followed the children through 2023 to ensure they reached adult height, defined as at least age 17 for girls and age 19 for boys.

When they compared adult heights across the three groups using an ANOVA (analysis of variance), they found statistically detectable but clinically negligible effect sizes in adult height for girls with ADHD taking stimulant medication and non-significant differences in adult height for boys with ADHD who were treated with stimulants.

“The large sample size increases the likelihood of detecting statistically significant but trivial differences; therefore, effect size analysis is essential for interpreting practical relevance,” the study’s authors wrote.

The effect sizes were consistently very small, and the physical difference measured between the groups was less than a centimeter, which is below the typical range considered clinically meaningful and within the range of routine measurement error.

“Given the very small effect sizes and sub-centimeter absolute differences, clinicians and families can be reassured that decisions regarding stimulant therapy need not be driven primarily by concerns about potential reductions in adult height,” the study’s authors wrote.

1Gabbay, M., Gabbay, U. and Carmi, D. (2026). The impact of ADHD and neurostimulant treatment on normalized height deviance after accounting for genetic height potential. Pediatric Research. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41390-026-04929-1 2Spencer, T.J. et al. (1996). Growth deficits in ADHD children revisited: evidence for disorder-associated growth delays. J. Am. Acad. Child Adolesc. Psychiatry.  https://doi.org/10.1097/00004583-199611000-00014 3Biederman, J. et al. (2003). Growth deficits and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder revisited: impact of gender, development, and treatment. Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.111.5.1010

#117. How to Build a Habit by Starting Ridiculously Small

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

In 75 minutes a week, I can reap the benefits of listening to uplifting music, getting out in nature, and getting morning outdoor light, all while exercising my dogs and getting enough cardio to measurably improve my health, happiness, and longevity.

And at times in my life, I have been a real runner. I ran a marathon in my 20s and a couple of half-marathons in my 30s. In my 40s, I mostly just made spectacular plans every January and September: I’d find exciting destination races to train for, join a gym and a yoga studio, sign up for running challenges, and pick out elaborate training plans. I’d run three or four days a week for a week or two, and then nada. Zippo. Zero runs per week.

Then, in 2020, I got into a real running habit. I’ve told the longer version of this story on a TED stage, so I won’t repeat it here, but suffice it to say that I did it by doing very, very little running. When I started going to Orange Theory classes, I kept running. I sustained this exercise habit for six years, through breast cancer and many other difficult life events.

Then the Orange Theory studio down the street from me closed. I tried other studios, but the classes I like are impossible to get into.

So I embraced working out on my own and getting back to running outside with my dogs. I bought very heavy dumbbells and set up a home gym on our covered porch. I spent an inordinate amount of time choosing a destination race, enlisting my adult children to join me. I set up a training schedule on my Garmin watch, and when I didn’t stick to it, I used Nike Run Club. I made a running playlist. I bought a double running leash.

Friends, I have done four runs in three weeks.

I know what I need to do. It’s so wildly unambitious that I’m embarrassed to tell you. I just need to get dressed to run first thing in the morning, put my dogs on their double leash, put on my playlist, and walk out the door, down the driveway, and to the mailbox. That’s it.

I know that most days, I’ll get a walk in, and once that walk is familiar, I’ll sometimes run a little. Some days I might run more, without even deciding to. But even when I don’t feel like doing more, the morning light I get while retrieving the mail and the walk back up our steep driveway are both good for me and genuinely enjoyable. It’s way better than nothing.

The mistake I make again and again is assuming that the size of my plan and the odds of my success are related: the more inspiring the goal and the more elaborate the plan, the better my results will be.

Ambition and results are related, of course, but not in the direction you think.

Creating a habit takes energy and focus, and we’ve only got so much of either, which is why ambitious plans produce a brilliant week and then…nothing. It takes between 18 and 254 days for a behavior to become automatic, and what predicts faster adoption isn’t ambition, self-discipline, or willpower; it’s repetition.

Repetition in a consistent context drives habit formation. Not just effort, intensity, or how badly someone wants it. Doing the thing, in the same place at about the same time, again and again, has the most impact.

Eli Susman, Ph.D., joins me in a webinar in a few weeks to talk about his book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick

Success is motivating. Doing what you said you’d do, even something absurdly small, builds the belief that you can do it. Failing repeatedly does the opposite; that’s a big part of why I spent my 40s making elaborate plans but not running.

Small behaviors make repetition more likely. What separates an actual habit from a nice couple of weeks is whether it holds up when you’re stressed, tired, busy, or not feeling 100%.

Missing a single day doesn’t meaningfully set most people back. We don’t need to be perfect here, folks. What won’t survive is a plan so ambitious that the off days outnumber the on days.

Micropractices, as researcher Eli Susman calls them, are very small behaviors that also have their own benefits; a tiny practice isn’t just a placeholder for a “real” one. Susman found that 20 seconds of self-compassionate touch (for example, sending kindness to yourself while placing your hand on your heart) per day improved mental health and lowered stress compared with a placebo finger tapping practice.

Across 280,000 meditation sessions in 103 countries, how consistently people meditated predicted their mood and resilience better than how long they sat. Similarly, a meta-analysis combining the results of many studies found that the benefits of practicing breathwork for stress didn’t depend on how long the session were. And breaking up six hours of sitting with brief bouts of walking improves energy, mood, and food cravings more than doing 30 minutes of walking all at once.

I hate the idea of abandoning my big plans. But the truth is that I am not choosing between the ambitious version and the tiny version. I am choosing between the tiny version and nothing.

Break the core behavior central to your habit down into something you can do in under five minutes, start to finish. Under a minute is even better. This isn’t the version that would impress your doctor or your neighbors; it’s the version you can do while exhausted, while traveling, while a little bit sick, and when you want nothing more than to stay on the couch.

Then, check it for resistance. If you feel any reluctance when you imagine doing it, it isn’t small enough yet. Cut it in half. Most people need to start with a micropractice: putting on your walking shoes and stepping out the front door, doing one pushup or 30 seconds of breathing, eating a single leaf of romaine, which, for the record, contains actual fiber and actual nutrients.

Do just that for a while. Resist the urge to do more. This is hard, but the moment you’re no longer willing to be unambitious is the moment you put the whole thing at risk. That’s when difficulty enters, and negotiation with yourself, and the possibility of failure. Your tiny habit doesn’t depend on motivation, which is precisely what makes it survive the days when you have none.

Expand only when you’re itching to, and only in absurdly small increments. Go one more minute, not 10.

Every time you repeat a behavior, your brain physically strengthens the connections that produce it, the way feet crossing a meadow gradually wear a path. Repeat it enough and the path becomes a groove your brain follows on its own, no willpower required. You’re carving a neural pathway for your habit, and everything you want is downstream from that.

At some point, it will become uncomfortable not to do this new behavior. You’ll do it without deciding to, without trying to. That’s the whole goal: repetition until the thing runs itself.

It’s hard to abandon our grand plans and great ambitions for something embarrassingly small. But, paradoxically, it is only in that tiny step that some of our grand plans are truly born.

Join Christine Carter and Eli Susman on Oct. 15 for a free live conversation, with a few tiny habits to try together.

Christine Carter, Ph.D. is a Senior Fellow at the Greater Good Science Center. She is the author of The New Adolescence: Raising Happy and Successful Teens in an Age of Anxiety and Distraction (BenBella, 2020), The Sweet Spot: How to Accomplish More by Doing Less (Ballantine Books, 2015), and Raising Happiness: 10 Simple Steps for More Joyful Kids and Happier Parents (Random House, 2010). A former director of the GGSC, she served for many years as author of its parenting blog, Raising Happiness. Find out more about Christine here.

#118. Bruce Springsteen on Surviving Depression and His Strategy for Living Through the Visitations of the Darkness

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For an act of resistance to the tyranny of algorithms, try the Marginalian newsletter—undistracted notes on the search for meaning, free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human since 2006. (Here is an example.)

It starts with a low hum that adheres itself to the underbelly of the hours like another dimension. Gradually, surreptitiously, the noise swells to a bellowing bass line, until it drowns out the symphony of life.

It can last for days or months or entire seasons of being. It visited Keats frequently in his short life, leaving him with a mind empty of ideas and hands heavy as lead. It rendered Lorraine Hansberry “cold, useless, frustrated, helpless, disillusioned, angry and tired.” It drove Abraham Lincoln to the brink of suicide.

If you are lucky enough, if you have the right aids of science, social support, and chance, one day you look over the shoulder of time and, like the poet Jane Kenyon, gasp in grateful incomprehension: “What hurt me so terribly all my life until this moment?” But until that moment comes, as William Styron so vividly observed in his classic bridge of empathy, “the gray drizzle of horror induced by depression takes on the quality of physical pain.”

Among the legion of us soaked by the drizzle is one of the most beloved artists of our epoch, whose music has made life brighter and more livable for generations.

In his memoir, Born to Run (public library), Bruce Springsteen writes about his father’s “long, drawn-out depressions,” often so debilitating that he could not rise from bed for days, and about his own tumble toward the edge of the abyss quarried by his genetic inheritance and the darknesses of his childhood, and about what kept him from falling. “God help Bruce Springsteen when they decide he’s no longer God,” John Lennon reflected in his most personal interview, but no outside “they” — no critic, no cry from the public — ever measures up to the inner chorus of anguish that most cruelly lowers an artist from the pedestal of their creative power and into the pit of depression.

In a particularly vivid vignette from the period just before he finally sought help, Springsteen writes:

My depression is spewing like an oil spill all over the beautiful turquoise-green gulf of my carefully planned and controlled existence. Its black sludge is threatening to smother every last living part of me.

Even Springsteen’s favorite books reflect this lifelong undertone of black. But it is in his BBC Desert Island Discs appearance that he opens up most candidly about his experience of depression and his life-honed coping mechanisms for it. He reflects:

I’ve developed some skills that help me in dealing with it, but still — it is a powerful, powerful thing that really comes up from things that still remain unexplainable to me.

After noting that much of it is pure biochemistry, and can therefore be greatly salved by biochemical interventions, he considers the psychological skills that have helped him temper the onslaught and offers a Buddhist-like strategy of unresistant presence with the flow of experience on its own terms, laced with a gentle admonition against the trap of blamethirsty projection:

Just naming it [helps]… What most people tend to want to do is, when they feel bad, the first thing you want to do is to name a reason why you feel that way: “I feel bad because…” and you’ll transfer that to someone else “…because Johnny said this to me,” or “this happened.” And, sometimes, that’s true. But a lot of times, you’re simply looking to name something that’s not particularly nameable and if you misname it, it just makes everything that much worse.

So my “skill” is sort of saying, “Okay, it’s not this, it’s not that — it’s just this. This is something that comes; it’s also something that goes — and maybe something I have to live with for a period of time.”

But if you can acknowledge it and you can relax with it a little bit, very often it shortens its duration.

Complement with Bloom — a touching animated short film about depression and what it takes to recover the light of being — and Tim Ferriss on how he survived his suicidal depression, then revisit Robert Burton’s centuries-old salve for melancholy and two centuries of beloved writers — including Keats, Whitman, Hansberry, Carson, and Thoreau — on the mightiest antidote to depression.

#119. When Your Mental Health Career Comes Down to a Test Score

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted September 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

After years of graduate school, clinical training, internship, supervised hours, and countless hours spent learning how to help others, one final hurdle often stands between a mental health professional and independent practice: the licensing exam.

That exam was the Examination for Professional Practice in Psychology.

I knew this exam was important, but I didn’t fully realize its emotional weight until I sat in front of the computer, knowing that years of work came down to a single score. When I didn't pass on my first try or even my second, the experience challenged me in ways that had little to do with my knowledge of psychology.

I joined online forums and study groups for people preparing for the exam, hoping to find information, encouragement, and reassurance that I wasn’t alone. Reading stories from people who hadn’t passed after several attempts made me realize how easily a test score can become intertwined with our professional identity.

I wasn’t the only one struggling with questions that made passing feel like a huge challenge:

Am I good enough?Am I really ready?What does not passing say about me as a clinician?

It’s hard to quiet these questions when so much of your future seems to depend on one exam.

Those questions weren’t just about passing a test. They started to feel like doubts about whether I could really become the psychologist I had worked so hard to be.

Being a high-achieving student and clinician can make failure particularly hard to accept. After many years of training, you may think, After everything I have done to get here, I should be able to do this. That’s when perfectionism and imposter syndrome can begin to creep in. You might wonder if you made it this far by mistake. Maybe you’re not as capable as you thought. Maybe everyone else is ready, and you're the one who isn't. You begin to compare. You watch classmates, colleagues, or people you trained with get licensed while you are still studying, waiting, or trying again. Even if you’re happy for them, it’s hard not to wonder, Why am I still here?

The longer the process drags on, the easier it is to confuse being unlicensed with being unqualified. That distinction matters.

Not passing an exam doesn’t erase your education, training, client relationships, or growth. Still, it’s hard to remember that when your career, finances, and professional future seem to depend on a single score.

Psychologists aren’t the only mental health professionals who experience this. Social workers, marriage and family therapists, and other mental health professionals face their own licensing examinations, along with the uncertainty, pressure, and emotions that come with a high-stakes test.

We can spend years learning to care for other people's emotional well-being while struggling to care for our own, even as our professional future feels uncertain.

The road to licensure can be particularly long for psychologists. After years of education, internships, postdoctoral fellowships, and thousands of supervised hours, often for little or no pay, we keep going because we believe the end is finally in sight.

That meant leaving my home every year, renting a place on top of my mortgage back home, and completing my training away from my family. And after all these years, we finally reach the licensing exam. Strangely for most of us, just one test stands between us and independent practice.

This journey is smooth for some. For others, like me with medical disabilities, it hasn’t been easy. Some exams allow accommodations, which I had, but whether these accommodations level the playing field is another topic.

One of the hardest lessons I learned was that professional competence and test performance aren’t the same thing.

A licensing exam measures what we can demonstrate on a specific day, under particular conditions. It can’t measure every hour spent sitting with clients, the relationships we've helped build, the crisis we've navigated, or the years of growth that have led us here.

Still, when so much depends on licensing exams, it’s hard to keep that in mind.

There’s something ironic about this. As psychologists, we help clients work through self-doubt, perfectionism, and the belief that one outcome doesn’t define them. But when my own future was at stake, I found it much harder to apply those lessons to myself.

I knew intellectually that not passing an exam didn’t mean I wasn't capable. I knew my years of education, training, and experience didn’t disappear because I hadn’t passed. But knowing something and actually believing it when you’re the one facing that score are two very different things.

I spent so much time pushing forward: studying, working, training, and trying again. There wasn't much room to stop and process what this experience was doing to me emotionally, or to my interpersonal relationships. I just kept going because I had to.

When I finally passed the exam on my third attempt, I broke down in tears. I broke, not because I had passed, but because I could finally release everything I’d been carrying—the exhaustion, the emotions I’d set aside, including the grief I had postponed when I lost family members, and the relief of finishing something that made me question myself.

And somewhere in those tears, I realized I wasn’t worthless.

I didn’t suddenly become a competent psychologist just because I passed. I was the same person before that score appeared. The difference was that I could finally stop fighting and allow myself to see it.

The exam changed my professional status, but it didn’t change who I was, what I knew, the clinician I’d become, or the years of work that had brought me here. Maybe that’s something we don't talk about enough with these exams. Sometimes the hardest part isn't just passing; it’s what happens to how you see yourself while you’re waiting to pass.

A licensing exam might decide when we can practice independently, but it doesn’t determine our worth, our potential, or the meaning of everything we’ve already accomplished. A license lets us practice, but it doesn’t create the years of dedication and compassion or the clinical growth that brought us to this moment.

#120. International Men's Day: what it is and how to celebrate

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Every year on November 19, International Men's Day gives the world a chance to pause and think about the issues, challenges, and contributions of men everywhere. It's a global observance that reminds us that men's well-being affects the health and harmony of families, communities, and society as a whole.

Struggles with mental health, suicidal thoughts, and the pressure to conform to narrow ideas of masculinity can leave many men feeling alone and unsure where to turn, which can ripple out into their relationships and physical health too. It's a cycle that needs to change.

Together, we can support the men in our lives—our fathers and father-figures, grandfathers, brothers, partners, friends, sons, and colleagues—by taking action. Below, you'll find what International Men's Day means, why November 19 was chosen, and practical, mindful ways to honor it.

International Men’s Day (IMD) is observed every year on November 19th. This is a day to celebrate men’s positive contributions, while also honoring the tough issues that they face. It’s a time to have open conversations about what masculinity really is, advocate for healthier expressions of what it means to “be a man,” and highlight the positive male role models in our lives.

IMD also complements other important awareness days like International Women’s Day (IWD) in March and Men’s Health Month in June.

The idea of celebrating International Men’s Day dates back to the 1960s, but it wasn’t until 1999 that the day was officially recognized. Dr. Jerome Teelucksingh, a lecturer from Trinidad and Tobago who founded the day, chose November 19 to honor his father’s birthday, who he looked up to for his kindness, resilience, and positive influence.

Since then, the movement has grown, with events now taking place in over 80 countries. While the focus varies from region to region, the overarching goal is to address men’s challenges with togetherness and mutual understanding.

The objectives of International Men’s Day are different depending on your country and culture. There are so many diverse experiences of men across the world and this day aims to celebrate that by encouraging a more inclusive, understanding, and compassionate world.

In all of these communities, the goal is to address the challenges men face in their daily lives. To break it down even further, though, here are six typical key objectives that IMD tries to encourage:

Promote positive male role models: This day aims to celebrate the everyday men who inspire and lead by example.

Celebrate men’s contributions: Men impact communities, families, and the workplace, and this day is a chance to recognize those contributions.

Highlight men’s health: Raising awareness about men’s mental health, physical health, and mental well-being is a key part of celebrating this holiday.

Address discrimination against men: Men face inequality in areas like social services, the law, and overall attitudes and expectations. And this day aims to highlight some of these inequalities.

Improve gender relations: Mutual respect, collaboration, and equality between all genders are among IMD’s main objectives.

Create a safer, better world: Men deserve to live safely and reach their potential by being the fullest versions of themselves. And this holiday helps to remind everyone of that.

International Men’s Day is a great opportunity to honor the men in our lives, and raise awareness about the issues they might face. Here are six mindful and meaningful ways to celebrate and show your support:

Many men feel pressure to shove their emotions down, so creating a safe space for them to share their thoughts and feelings without judgment can be really meaningful. You might go for a walk or ask them to coffee and simply ask, “How are you really feeling?”

If your talk turns to difficult topics and they shut it down — that’s okay. They might not be ready to go there yet. Instead, try gently encouraging them to talk to another loved one like a friend or a family member or just let them know you're available if they do want to talk.

International Men’s Day is a perfect time to remind the men in your life that they need to put themselves first sometimes.

If self-care is new for them, try planning a shared activity, like going to a yoga class together or simply taking a moment to breathe deeply and practice mindfulness. (And if looking inward is really hard for them, here are 20+ self-care practices to get started.) You might even give them a journal as a tool to self-reflect.

💙  Listen to our Radical Self Care series with Lama Rod Owens if the man in your life needs a little push to take care of themselves.

Mark International Men’s Day by contributing to organizations that focus on men’s health. You might volunteer your time, share their message on social media, or donate money to their cause if you’re able. You might consider causes that focus on:

Mental health and suicide prevention: Movember or HeadsUpGuys help reduce the stigma around mental health.

Prostate and testicular cancer research: These common cancers affect men, and increased awareness can save lives.

Homelessness and addiction support: Men often represent a significant portion of the homeless population, and are more likely to struggle with addiction too.

Let the men in your life know how much they mean to you. This can really help show them that you care and make them feel less alone.

While a card is nice, it’s probably unnecessary. Just pull them aside (or send them a text) to say you care.

💙  Listen to the Daily Jay’s Broaden Your Gratitude to help get you feel into all you’re grateful for around the men in your life.

Sometimes, it can mean more to just be together. Organize a friendly game of soccer or any sport that you know the man in your life likes to play. Or keep it more lowkey and invite a group over to your place to have pizza, unwind, and watch a movie.

One way you can really make a difference is to use your voice to let people know what International Men’s Day is actually about. You also could take this day to publicly shout out a specific man you know who has really made a positive impact in your life.

If social media isn’t your thing, maybe consider talking to your boss or school to see if they would recognize the day with an event, workshops, or even a talk.

If you want to honor International Men’s Day, an easy way to do it is by posting about it on your social media or by sharing gratitude for your loved ones in person.

But if you’re looking to raise awareness specifically in the workplace, consider hosting workshops on men’s mental health awareness, stress management, or work-life balance tailored to men’s experiences. You could also invite guest speakers or ask employees to share their stories on topics like emotional resilience.

International Men’s Day and Men’s Health Week are similar celebrations in that they both share a focus on improving men’s lives — but they do so in different ways.

With International Men’s Day, the objective is to raise awareness about a broad range of men’s issues. The day aims to promote positive male role models, address mental health challenges, and improve gender relations. It’s celebrated on November 19.

Men’s Health Week is more focused on encouraging men to take care of their physical and mental health by getting them to work out, eat right, and get regular health screenings. This celebration occurs in June.

Dr. Jerome Teelucksingh of Trinidad and Tobago formalized the observance of International Men’s Day in 1999. He chose November 19th to honor his father’s birthday, as he deeply admired his dad for his kindness and resilience.

But no matter the specific date, the real importance of this day is to celebrate men, raise awareness about the challenges they face, and reflect on the roles men play in our world.

Meditation and mindfulness can be especially beneficial for men who may have been told to suppress their emotions or “tough it out” when things get hard. By practicing mindfulness, men can learn to become more aware of their thoughts and feelings, which can help them feel less stressed, anxious, or overwhelmed.

Mindfulness can also improve emotional regulation, which can make it easier to respond to challenges in healthy and constructive ways. Regular meditation practices have been shown to enhance focus, boost mood, and bring a sense of calm, which can be particularly valuable for men juggling the demands of work, family, and personal responsibilities.

Importantly, mindfulness can also encourage self-compassion, which is important to help men deal with their inner critic and to feel comfortable asking for help when they need it.

To add mindfulness into your daily routine, try a short guided meditation, deep-breathing exercise, or mindful walk (here are 10 more ideas to get you started). With time, these practices can help you improve your mental health and overall well-being.

If you identify as a man and are currently not sure how to bring mindfulness into your daily life, you’re not alone. It can feel really daunting at first to start anything new.

To help you get started, here are five practical and simple activities you could try:

Start the day with intention: Begin each morning with a short moment of reflection. Setting a positive intention can really help frame your day with purpose.

Practice mindful pauses: Consider taking small breaks to check in with yourself throughout your day. It can even be something as brief as a minute of deep breathing.

Enjoy mindful movement: If you like to exercise, try yoga or tai chi. This can help you connect with your body and release your stress.

Practice gratitude: If writing is your thing, consider jotting down three things you’re grateful for at the end of each day. This can help shift your focus away from stressors and into more positivity.

Take a technology detox: Think aboutsetting your phone aside a few minutes each day to disconnect from any screens. This can help you to be more present.

#121. After 30 years, scientists finally have a drug for a deadly brain disease

The FDA has approved the first drug designed to directly treat Alexander disease, an extremely rare neurological disorder that progressively damages the nervous system and can be fatal. The treatment, called Zanvastro, represents a major advance for patients who previously had no options beyond managing their symptoms.

Alexander disease can interfere with movement, thinking, and automatic bodily functions such as breathing and heart rate. Zanvastro is the first and only approved disease-modifying treatment for the condition, meaning it targets an underlying biological process responsible for the disease rather than simply relieving its effects.

The drug emerged from more than three decades of scientific research at the University of Wisconsin-Madison's School of Veterinary Medicine and Waisman Center. Much of that work took place in the laboratory of Albee Messing, professor emeritus of comparative biosciences and former director of the Waisman Center, whose discoveries helped make the treatment possible. Ionis Pharmaceuticals collaborated in developing the drug.

Clinical trials offered encouraging results. Patients receiving Zanvastro generally experienced stabilization of their motor function, and some showed improvements in their ability to move.

"This is a wonderful and long-awaited day for the Alexander disease community," Messing says.

Alexander Disease: A Rare and Devastating Brain Disorder

Alexander disease affects fewer than one in every million people worldwide. Although exceptionally uncommon, its consequences can be severe, with symptoms that gradually interfere with everyday activities and essential bodily functions.

People with the disorder may develop seizures, lose previously acquired developmental abilities, experience increasing difficulty walking or moving, and struggle with speaking or swallowing. Some also develop dangerously elevated pressure inside the brain.

The disease does not follow a single predictable course. Symptoms may first emerge during infancy, childhood, or adulthood, and their severity and progression can differ depending on when the condition begins.

For decades, doctors could offer supportive care and treatments to ease individual symptoms, but they had no approved medication capable of targeting the disease itself.

An Unexpected Discovery Revealed the Genetic Cause

The breakthrough can be traced to research Messing conducted with Michael Brenner, professor emeritus of neurobiology at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. In the late 1990s, their work identified the genetic changes responsible for Alexander disease, providing scientists with a specific biological target for developing treatments.

The discovery began with an unexpected result in laboratory mice.

Messing and Brenner had genetically engineered mice to produce unusually high amounts of a protein known as glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). This protein is normally found in astrocytes, specialized cells that help support and maintain healthy function in the brain and spinal cord.

To the researchers' surprise, the modified mice developed abnormal protein deposits throughout their brains. These deposits appeared inside astrocytes and closely resembled the distinctive abnormalities seen in people with Alexander disease.

"We had, really without intending to, created a mouse that produced these classic lesions of Alexander disease," Messing says.

The abnormal deposits, called Rosenthal fibers, are a defining characteristic of the disorder. Additional genetic studies involving people diagnosed with Alexander disease confirmed that mutations in the gene responsible for producing GFAP were the underlying cause.

"This provided an obvious and specific strategy for therapy -- the GFAP protein," Messing explains.

Identifying the genetic cause also made diagnosing the condition much simpler. Instead of relying on invasive brain biopsies to look for characteristic tissue abnormalities, doctors could use genetic testing from a blood sample to identify the mutations associated with the disease.

Scientists Develop a Drug That Targets Harmful Protein Buildup

Once researchers understood the role of GFAP, their next challenge was finding a way to reduce its production and prevent damaging levels of the protein from accumulating in brain cells.

Messing joined forces with Tracy Hagemann, an associate research professor at the Waisman Center, to create improved rodent models of Alexander disease. These models more closely reproduced important features of the disorder, giving scientists a way to investigate potential treatments before testing them in people.

The team focused on a straightforward idea: If excessive GFAP contributes to the disease, lowering the amount produced might help protect the nervous system.

In collaboration with Ionis Pharmaceuticals, the researchers pursued a technology known as antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs).

These treatments use short, specially designed pieces of genetic material to interfere with instructions that cells use to manufacture particular proteins. Rather than targeting every protein in a cell, an ASO can be designed to reduce production of a specific one.

For Alexander disease, that target was GFAP.

The experimental treatment produced promising results in rodents, supporting the decision to move forward with human testing. A clinical trial began in the summer of 2021.

Zanvastro uses this same targeted strategy. By limiting GFAP production, the drug aims to reduce the buildup of the protein before it can cause additional damage.

Because the treatment needs to reach the central nervous system, it is administered through an injection into the spinal canal. A trained healthcare professional gives the injection once every three months.

Clinical Trials Show Improvements in Walking and Movement

The human trial provided evidence that lowering GFAP could offer meaningful benefits to people living with Alexander disease.

Ionis Pharmaceuticals conducted the international study across 13 clinical sites, enrolling 54 patients to evaluate the treatment's safety and effectiveness.

After receiving Zanvastro for a little more than a year, treated patients demonstrated significantly better walking speeds than patients who had not received the drug.

The results also indicated that treatment could stabilize motor function, an important outcome for a progressive disorder that can steadily undermine a person's ability to move independently. Some participants experienced improvements in motor performance.

These findings helped establish Zanvastro as the first treatment approved to modify the underlying disease process in Alexander disease, rather than focusing exclusively on symptom relief.

The FDA approval covers people with Alexander disease across the full age spectrum, from infancy through adulthood.

Zanvastro is expected to become available in the United States in the weeks following the approval. Outside the United States, access to the drug will be handled through a licensing agreement between Ionis Pharmaceuticals and Recordati, a major pharmaceutical company headquartered in Italy.

A 30-Year Scientific Journey Offers New Hope

For Messing and his colleagues, the approval represents the culmination of more than 30 years of research, beginning with basic investigations into brain cell biology and eventually leading to a treatment for patients.

What started as an unexpected finding in genetically modified mice helped reveal the cause of an extremely rare disease, transformed how doctors diagnose it, and provided the foundation for developing a drug.

The achievement is also an example of translational research, the process of turning discoveries made in laboratories into treatments that can directly benefit patients.

Throughout that journey, individuals living with Alexander disease and their families played an essential role by supporting the research and participating in studies.

"The whole program of research would not have been possible without the support and participation from the patient and family community, to whom we will always be grateful," Messing says.

#122. 17 Ideas From Educators to Start the School Year With Joy

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Joy! What a beautiful way to start the school year, not only because it feels good, but also because science shows that joy is linked closely to learning, as well as individual and collective flourishing.

We asked Greater Good Education newsletter readers to share a favorite strategy for bringing joy into their school or classroom at the beginning of the year. The responses did not disappoint! Here are a few that span ages, time commitments, and subject areas.

Laura M. (Newark, DE): “Dancing it out” is a strategy that has been shown to reduce stress, release held feelings, and encourage kids to be in the moment. Providing time for activities like dancing is often seen as an “extra.” Building this activity into our weekly schedule has become a favorite stress-relieving activity—adding tremendous joy and connection between children and children and children and teachers.

Related Greater Good in Education (GGiE) practices: The World Is a Dance; Getting to Know Each Other Through Dance; We Are Better Dancing Together

Josh (New Haven, CT): Every Monday morning meeting, students greet each other by asking, “What brought you joy (made you smile/laugh) over the weekend?”

Laura H.: At the end of the day, with second graders, we share the activity from our day that brought the most joy. If I wasn’t there for it (i.e., recess, music, art, PE), I ask them to include details.

Related GGiE practices: Noticing Kindness; Giving Thanks; Looking for Gratitude in School; Sharing Gratitude Stories

Emi (Lobitos, Peru): Identifying forms of enchantment—I use this approach in our Women & Water Program. It’s an all-girls (ages 3–16) surf, science, and storytelling program based in Lobitos, a tiny fishing village in Northern Peru. We use “enchantment” as a way for young girls to foster their curiosity, creativity, and care for themselves, peers, community, and the coastal environment. We do this through photography (taking “macro” photos of small, wondrous things found in their environment, like a flower petal, a beetle, etc.). Or we do this in surfing—the girls notice the “awe” of riding the energy of a leftover storm until it crashes into the sand. These girls also made this song after an oil spill that rocked our community about two years ago.

Related GGiE practices: Meaningful Photos for Students; Mindfully Finding Awe in Nature

Angela (Pleasant Hill, CA): I am a school counselor and with my students who experience anxiety we use sidewalk chalk to write positive welcoming messages and pictures in front of our school. It makes others feel welcomed and helps my students feel connected to our school. They even told me it helps get them to school the first couple of days knowing they would see their chalk messages.

Related GGiE practices: Designing the Classroom to Promote Kindness; Kindness Buddy; Awe-Inspiring Affirmations

Lorien (St. Louis, MO): Have a “Would you rather…?” question on the whiteboard at the start of class—the funnier the better. Students put a checkmark next to their choice. It’s a fun way to welcome the “whole student self” into the classroom, not just their “learner selves.” Sometimes we talk about it, but often, we don’t.

Pam (Muscogee County, GA): To kick off the year, my eighth graders design and build a cardboard maze that guides three different rolling spheres from start to finish. Working in teams of four, students sketch a plan, build it with cardboard and hot glue, test it, and revise their design. Nothing works perfectly the first time. Students quickly discover that failure is a useful part of the design process. By the end of the week, teams are cheering when a ping pong ball, golf ball, or rubber ball finally makes it all the way through, and that joy comes from earning it through real trial and error. It sets the tone for the whole year: Engineering is a process of building, testing, and improving.

Kimberly (Williamsport, PA): Something that I introduce during the first week of classes is our 3 Good Things or 3 Little Wins Padlet. Each week students post about three good things or little wins they had during the week. Before the first post, we discuss why it is important to celebrate these things, no matter how small (e.g., a good cup of coffee!). We also discuss the impact that reflecting on these things has on our physical and psychological well-being. Each week I also post my wins for the week and comment on student posts as well. It creates a wonderful community!

Related GGIE practices: Three Good Things for Students; Gratitude Journals

Jonah (Duxbury, VT): As a high school English teacher, the first writing assignment I give to students asks them to choose a (clean) song that represents them and tell me why they feel connected to this song. I then make a playlist including all the students’ songs, and play it during work times or use it to play students’ walk-up song on special days like birthdays.

Related GGiE practices: Creating Musical Playlists for the Classroom; Prosocial Music Hub (13 practices to bring music into the classroom)

Joe (Bridgeport, CT): Students interact with each other as they navigate around the crowded classroom, connected only by cake-pop sticks balanced between each other using only their index finger. Fosters concentration, cooperation, joyful failures, interconnectedness, and intimacy without actually touching one another.

David (San Antonio, TX): For my introductory geology class, I work with the students to develop rules for a “rock-rock-rock” (igneous-sedimentary-metamorphic) version of “rock-paper-scissors.” Students develop the necessary hand signals and the action verbs that say what beats what. Once we have the rules established, the students engage in a best two out of three to crown the class champion. Branded university swag is available for the winners, and everyone gets a candy treat for participating.

Related GGiE practice: Making Science Meaningful

Susan (St. Paul, MN): I ask students to tell the rest of the class their name and a ridiculous lie about themselves—the more absurd the better. There’s always good-natured laughter and encouragement.

Harry (Hailey, ID): I work to end every “session” (class, administration meeting, faculty meeting, etc.) with laughter, whether incited by me or coming from someone else. That moment becomes the punctuation.

Related GGiE practices: Share a Laugh; The SEL 3 Signature Practices

Paige (Seattle, WA): About the second or third week of classes (graduate and undergraduate students) we begin doing this ritual that we do a few times during the semester: “The joy of contribution…I see this in you!” Students take turns identifying something they have genuinely observed in another student in the cohort/class: “One leadership capacity I see developing in you is________, because I watched you ________.” The BECAUSE matters.

Join us in building happier, kinder schools where everyone belongs.

Examples I have heard from pre-certified teachers and principals: “I see courage building in you because I have watched you ask questions the rest of us were afraid to ask.” OR, “I see you really owning belongingness as you consistently notice who is outside the conversation and what is happening around us as you read the room.”

Related GGiE practices: I See You. Everyone Matters; Behind Your Back

Lorien (St. Louis, MO): I use a guided visualization to prompt students to think about what joyful teaching, joyful learning, and joyful interactions look like, sound like, and feel like. It makes what we’re doing much more explicit, and it helps me know what they want from me and vice versa.

Related GGiE practice: Designing the Classroom to Promote Kindness

Angela (McMinnville, OR): A non-dominant hand drawing activity that gets us all out of our “perfection” thinking and into being learners…and laughing.

Related GGiE practice: Drawing as a Way to Manage Emotions

Milton (San Diego, CA): As the associate principal, I stand out in front of the school in the morning with a BIG SMILE sign on and greet the students with a “Good morning & have a great day!” Some students like a fist bump or handshake as well.

Related GGiE practice: Making Families Feel Welcome

Donna (Arkansas): “JOY” is the grounding rhythm that closes every day, honoring the joyful moments that JUST happened, recognizing community attunement through something an OTHER person did, and celebrating internal self-efficacy via something YOU did. Each person is free to select whichever letter resonates with them to share. We pass a rainstick around the circle; once it is turned to let its gentle cascade settle into silence, the person holding it speaks. This tactile ritual and quiet sound not only brings a profound sense of calm to the transition from classroom to home, but it also serves as a gentle reminder to carry those reflections outward.

Related GGiE practices: Inspiring Virtue With Moral Beauty; Stories of Moral Beauty; Noticing Kindness; Nurturing Students’ Wonder and Curiosity

Thank you to all of the educators in the Greater Good community who shared activities for bringing joy into schools and classrooms. We received many, many more than we could share here. Even in the face of incredible challenges, you are bringing so much joy to your students and their families, your colleagues, and yourself. May you all have a joyful start to the new school year!

We look forward to our next post in the From Our Readers series that will focus on building community through connection and belonging. Want to share an activity? Fill out this quick form! Not only will you strengthen our community, you’ll be entered into a drawing for a free self-paced course or a spot in our Flourishing Spring community of practice!

Sarah Bracken is the Education Outreach and Partnerships Manager at Greater Good Science Center. Prior to joining GGSC, Sarah taught in secondary classrooms from Alaska to Virginia and collaborated with educators to co-create communities of practice and other professional learning opportunities focused on belonging and equitable education for students of refugee and immigrant backgrounds. She is a Nationally Board Certified teacher with a B.A. from the University of Virginia and a Master’s in Teaching from The Evergreen State College.

The most reliable way to build a habit that lasts is to make it so small you'd be embarrassed to describe it out loud.

We learned a lot in producing our new documentary series, Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy.

What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.

Dr. David Spiegel leads us in a practice of cyclic sighing, a simple breathing technique that uses slow, extended exhales to calm your nervous system, ease stress and anxiety, and help you feel more relaxed.
