#160. You Might Be Experiencing Rustout, Not Burnout, at Work

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Some forms of distress at work are easy to recognize because they interrupt someone’s daily performance and the work of those around them: For example, a person on your team becomes visibly exhausted, they are irritable, or they’re frequently absent. But other forms of distress are harder to see precisely because the work continues uninterrupted.

It’s common to talk about burnout at work and to recognize it in others and in ourselves. But a new paper of mine with David S. Smith examines a less visible and less understood form of disengagement at work: rustout.

Rustout, as we studied it, often involves being underutilized, intellectually stagnating, and feeling a deep-seated sense of unfulfillment. It can arise when people feel their work no longer offers enough meaning or challenge to keep them intellectually and creatively engaged. But because it’s different from burnout, the solutions are also different—both for individuals and for organizations.

I’ve presented this research at numerous conferences, and each time I have been approached by professionals who say, “That’s what I’ve been going through, but I never had a name for it until now.”

These people, young and older, are committed to their work, they are hardworking, and they haven’t stopped caring. It is often the case that they care very much, and they meet expectations set before them. They are often the ones who are called upon because they are reliable and highly conscientious.

If you look around your workplace, you probably know many people who fit this bill. The problem is not a loss of effort on the part of the individual; it is a breakdown in the relationship between effort and meaningful work. From my study of this topic, rustout is really about the decline in professional vitality, when a person’s capacities are not used in ways that feel meaningful to them.

In our research, participants described experiences shaped by administrative overload, reduced autonomy, and a misalignment between their professional aspirations and assigned tasks. Many people highlighted feeling professionally stuck: “Sadly, the elements I love about the job . . . are often overshadowed by the other administrative aspects of the role,” “I feel like I’m feeding the machine,” and “I’m a square peg in a round hole.”

They highlighted a sense that the work they were doing no longer drew sufficiently on their talents: “The better you are at it, the more of the administrative side of the job you get. It’s lacking opportunities to be creative.”

Rustout can be quite psychologically disorienting. From the outside, a person may appear successful and competent. There is no question about their productivity; they meet set targets, but could do so “with [their] eyes closed.” However, they may feel increasingly detached from the work that once animated them. Their distress isn’t dramatic; it’s a slow process of psychological erosion.

In many ways, rustout overlaps with burnout, but they are not the same. Burnout involves prolonged negative stress that isn’t adequately managed. It’s about too much—working too much, caring too much, too much pressure, and too little time to recuperate. In contrast, rustout is associated with too little positive stress or challenge over time, too little stimulation, and limited opportunities for individual growth.

However, while burnout is part of organizations’ mental health literacy, rustout rarely gets a mention. And this is problematic—both for the individual and the organization. “I often feel I have produced nothing at the end of the week, and there is no sense of development,” one person said.

Some will stay in their roles out of a sense of duty (and for other practical reasons like salary or seniority), but others will choose to leave. Another said, “I am functioning at my job, but I’m not thriving, and I am looking elsewhere.”

Rustout often hides behind competence, and the reliable person is often given more of the same work. The person who does not complain is assumed to be coping and doing OK. The person who stabilizes others and is a good team player is rarely asked whether they themselves feel developed or challenged.

One person said, “I have no experience of ever having a conversation with anyone around it. No line manager ever named it, it has never been mentioned in a communal setting or in a one-to-one setting. . . . No one has ever asked, ‘Do you feel fulfilled or do you feel you have opportunities to use your skills and talents in a meaningful way?’”

It’s easy to see how doing overtime and being dependable can become a trap. Eventually, the employee becomes valued less for what they might become and more for what they can continue to absorb—they won’t “rock the boat” by opening the can of worms that is their dissatisfaction. “You put up, and shut up,” one person said.

Boost satisfaction, engagement, and collaboration with this three-course series

Meanwhile, many workplaces are organized to detect individual or team shortcomings (or failure) more readily than stagnation. If someone stops performing, the problem becomes visible. However, if someone continues to perform while becoming inwardly disengaged, the organization may see no problem at all. And if anyone notices their dissatisfaction, they may not openly discuss it, as another of my interviewees reported. “It suits everyone not to talk about it; when everyone is working and doing their jobs—then don’t disturb anything. Everything is cosy.”

Participants experiencing rustout described barriers that limited their ability to use their strengths or pursue professional growth, which are particularly important for having a sense of meaning and fulfillment at work.

For many people, their working life gives them a sense of identity and purpose, but when work no longer offers that sense of meaning, their relationship with the job can become fractured or feel “off.” In some cases, they can’t put their finger on what is happening, and that might be why I often hear after presentations, “I never had a name for it.”

Naming rustout won’t solve the issue, but it can help the person to understand why they feel underutilized or dissatisfied. Naming rustout can help people understand this isn’t a personal failure but an experience that is shaped by the design or conditions of work (much like burnout). It is also shaped by the culture of work, particularly when there is a resistance to change or a failure to see the value in helping people to flourish.

From my discussions with participants and colleagues about rustout, it is clear that it isn’t a pre-retirement phenomenon. It seems to arise for those who are experienced, perhaps mid-career, and those who have been in their role for a long time.

One participant explained, “I have been doing [this role] for years. There must be better ways to organize things to ensure the expertise of experienced staff is used in more effective ways.” Others said, “It’s the seven-, eight-, nine-year mark when there isn’t an opportunity to be stimulated,” and “It’s the seven-year itch, you’ve been doing something creative and then you reach a point where you are doing the same thing on repeat.”

In such ways, we can’t dismiss rustout as a consequence of aging in the workplace. It can happen whenever people are pigeonholed into a system that no longer offers them meaningful development. Although some repetition and routine are an expected part of every job, there should also be a sense that your abilities and talents matter in your role. That there is a future and something exciting to work toward.

The language of burnout has helped many people name distress that had previously been normalized or dismissed. It has also helped organizations take workplace well-being more seriously. But any dominant mental health vocabulary can become limiting when it starts to stand in for the whole field of experience. If burnout is the only category available for occupational distress, then recovery is often imagined in terms of rest and resilience.

They may be necessary, but they are not always sufficient. A person experiencing rustout may not simply need less work; they may need different work: work that restores their sense of intellectual engagement and curiosity. As Maya Angelou once said, “We aren’t designed to be static”—that could apply to all aspects of life, including the workplace.

If you are experiencing rustout, it would be good to do an inventory of what is happening for you. Do you feel fulfilled in your role? Do you have opportunities to use your talents? Do you gain some sense of meaning from your role? Are there ways to seek renewal in your work? What might this look like, and can you have this conversation with your line manager or boss?

For organizations, the questions are also direct. Look around your team. Are you giving your most dependable employees opportunities for development? Do you continually lean on their “safe pair of hands” because it is easier than asking someone else to learn the ropes? Are you willing to put the conversation about professional dissatisfaction on the table? How can you help your team to flourish?

That is the unsettling truth at the heart of the rustout. A person can be conscientious yet disengaged, reliable yet underused, competent but unfulfilled. They can be good at their job and still feel themselves receding from it. The silence around rustout allows it to thrive, which is why I often hear the same response after conference presentations: “I thought it was just me.” I think there is a particular loneliness in that sentence, the loneliness of continuing to do the work, while privately wondering why it no longer feels like yours.

Sabrina Fitzsimons, Ph.D., is a lecturer at Dublin City University, Ireland. Her research combines expertise in educators’ occupational well-being, mental health, and online environments.

With the rise of AI and multiple global crises, psychologists recommend tending to our bodies, connecting in person, and caring for all humans.

#161. 2 Personality Traits Linked To A Stronger Immune System

Certain personality traits influence the body’s immune system response.

Certain personality traits influence the body’s immune system response.

People with more stable emotions have stronger immune systems, research finds.

People who are emotionally stable usually find it easier to control their urges and are mostly unselfconscious.

Emotional stability is linked to being better at dealing with stress and minor frustrations.

Neuroticism lies at the opposite end of the spectrum from emotional stability.

People who are neurotic typically experience more negative thinking and tend to have worse mental health.

The study included 84 people whose response to a vaccine for hepatitis B was tested.

The results showed that people who were more neurotic — meaning easily stressed, nervous and moody — tended to have weaker immune system responses.

Those who were more emotional stable had a stronger immune response.

Dr Anna L. Marsland,, the study’s first author, said:

“The present findings support a link between trait negative affect and an objective health measure — antibody response to vaccination — raising the possibility that individuals high in trait negative affect or neuroticism may have less protective immune responses.”

In a second part of the study, people were given a stressful task to test their immune function.

The results showed that stress tended to lower people’s immune system response — as previous studies have found.

Along with emotional stability, extraversion has also been linked to a stronger immune system, by a genetic analysis.

Extraverts are typically outgoing, talkative and energetic, meaning they tend to interact with more people.

They are, therefore, exposed to more infections.

A stronger immune response may help to protect extraverts against infectious diseases.

Introverts, meanwhile, tend to have a weaker immune response, as do cautious people.

The study included 121 people who were given personality questionnaires, along with genetic tests and general health screening.

The results showed that extraverts had the highest expression of pro-inflammatory genes.

The effect of these genes is to help fight off infections.

Introverts and cautious conscientious people tended to have a lower inflammatory response.

The study was published in the journal Health Psychology (Marsland et al., 2001).

#162. Children at risk for depression get “stuck” on sad faces

A smile or a frown may reveal more than emotion alone. The faces that capture a child's attention could provide important clues about their mental health and how depression develops.

New research from Binghamton University, State University of New York, suggests that depression may influence how strongly children focus on emotional expressions such as happy or sad faces. The pattern appears to differ depending on whether a child has a family history of depression.

Researchers at the Mood Disorders Institute at Binghamton University study how depression develops in children and adolescents, with particular attention to how family history and emotional experiences may influence vulnerability over time. By identifying these patterns while children are still developing, scientists hope to better understand who may be at greater risk and eventually improve prevention strategies.

"Most of the vulnerabilities that we focus on are still developing during this time period," said Brandon Gibb, director of the Mood Disorders Institute and SUNY distinguished professor of psychology. "You can catch things as they're developing, rather than only studying them once they're already there and pretty stable."

Earlier research has linked depression with greater attention to sad faces. However, those associations have generally been modest, and scientists have not been sure whether biased attention contributes to depression or develops because of it.

The Binghamton study was designed to investigate that question by tracking both depressive symptoms and attention patterns over time. According to the researchers, it is the first study to examine how changes in each may predict later changes in the other among children.

"The real novel piece is that we looked at these transactional relations," said Kelly Gair, a PhD student at Binghamton and lead author of the paper. "Between attentional biases and depressive symptoms, we looked at the way that they were mutually predicting one another across the time points, which is especially novel and hasn't been done before."

The research team, which also included Leslie A. Brick from the University of New Mexico, followed 242 children and their mothers for two years. Participants were assessed every six months.

During each visit, children viewed pairs of faces on a screen. One face showed a neutral expression, while the other displayed an emotion (happy, sad, or angry). Eye tracking technology measured which face held the child's attention and for how long.

Children in the study looked at faces conveying different emotions onscreen, and eye tracking technology recorded where their attention veered. Photo credit: NimStim Set of Facial Expressions (Tottenham et al., 2009).

The results suggest that increasing depressive symptoms do not affect every child's attention in the same way. Family history appeared to play an important role.

Among children whose mothers had a history of major depressive disorder, rising depressive symptoms were associated with greater attention to sad faces. In other words, as these children experienced more symptoms themselves, their attention became increasingly drawn toward expressions of sadness.

"For those who are already at risk, the more these children experience depression themselves, the more they lose their ability to pull their attention away from the sad things around them," Gibb said.

"We know that when you're depressed, it changes what you pay attention to," Gair said. "Our results suggest that these changes may be more long-lasting and may differ depending on family history. One thought is that for children of mothers with depression, who are exposed to more facial displays of sadness from interactions with their mom, these types of facial expressions become even more salient when they experience depression themselves, so their attention becomes increasingly stuck on sad expressions."

A different pattern emerged among children whose mothers had no history of depression.

When depressive symptoms increased in these children, they did not become more focused on sad expressions. Instead, they paid less attention to happy faces.

"In our lower-risk children, what seems to be happening is that experiences of depression are eroding a protective factor, which is how much they pay attention to happy faces," Gibb said.

The distinction suggests that depression may alter emotional attention through different pathways depending on a child's underlying level of familial risk. For some children, sadness may become increasingly difficult to ignore. For others, positive emotional signals may simply become less likely to capture their attention.

The researchers are continuing to follow the children as they enter adolescence, a period when the risk of developing depression increases for many young people. They hope to determine whether these early attention patterns are associated with a greater likelihood of receiving a depression diagnosis later on.

The paper, "Transactional Relations Between Attentional Biases for Affective Stimuli and Depressive Symptoms in Offspring of Mothers With and Without Major Depressive Disorder," was published in the Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science.

Materials provided by Binghamton University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#163. 5 mindfulness tools to support mental well-being for those living with PBC

The realities of living with PBC aren’t always immediately obvious. From the outside, you may seem like you’re managing—balancing your career, caring for children or parents, supporting partners—but behind the scenes, symptoms like chronic itch, fatigue, and brain fog can shape every part of the day.¹˒²

When you’re usually the person that others rely on, needing support yourself can feel strange. Maybe you feel guilty when you have to cancel plans, or if you need time to rest.

It can be difficult to give yourself the same compassion that you would give to someone else. That’s totally normal. But we can help you change that and find ways to approach yourself with kindness and care.

Looking after your health is not always about doing more. Sometimes it’s about giving yourself permission to pause.

That’s why Gilead* and Calm have partnered to offer mindfulness resources for both your body and mind.

Scroll down to explore 5 Calm meditations curated by Gilead to support the mental and emotional well-being of those living with PBC and their caregivers.

While everyone's experience of PBC is different, its impact on your life can be significant — and challenging.

PBC commonly affects women during midlife, often when they’re balancing careers, family responsibilities, and the duties of caring for others.¹ It can also affect men, and there’s increasing prevalence among Black and Asian-American populations in the U.S., with Black and Hispanic patients also experiencing poorer outcomes and reduced access to care.¹

Symptoms such as fatigue, itch, and brain fog can impact everything from getting through the working day to spending time with family and friends.¹˒² Sleep disruption can leave you feeling exhausted before the day has even begun, while the unpredictable and progressive nature of PBC can make it harder to maintain routines, make plans, or feel fully in control of your life.

“There were days when simply getting through daily life felt like climbing a mountain, yet those around me assumed it was just another ordinary day,” shares Carol Roberts, President of PBCers Organization and a person living with PBC.

While maintaining liver health is critical when living with PBC, it's only one part of the picture. Living well with PBC is also about supporting a healthy mind and healthy relationships, because true well-being is measured not only by lab results, but also by how life feels day to day.

Much of life with PBC happens in the moments between appointments. For many people, learning to live with PBC is not about finding ways to do more. It’s about finding sustainable ways to care for yourself while balancing work, family, relationships, and other responsibilities. That might mean adjusting expectations of what you can do on any given day, accepting help when it’s offered, or recognizing when you need to pause and recharge.

The support of partners, family members, friends, and the wider PBC community can also make a meaningful difference and help make living with PBC feel less overwhelming.

Don’t forget that we’re here to give you resources and tools that offer practical coping strategies, emotional support, or moments of comfort throughout the day.

Coping strategies won't remove the challenges of PBC, but they can help create moments of relief throughout the day.

pausing to focus on breathing during an itch flare

turning to a short meditation when feelings of stress or overwhelm begin to build

listening to a Sleep Story when symptoms make it difficult to switch off at night

#164. Five Things Students Taught Us About Connecting Across Differences

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

When I’m producing a documentary, one of my favorite parts of the process is the moment when a bit of our footage sticks to me. Permanently. I never know when it will happen, but it always does. The sticky bit could be a snippet of dialogue or a quote from an interview. After watching the footage over and over again, the bit becomes part of me.

Often it’s a funny line—a perfect, punchy distillation of the truth that gets adopted as an inside joke among the team of producers and editors. We repeat it like a collective spell that buoys us when we’re sinking under the weight of the project’s heavy subject matter. Sometimes the thing that sticks is not funny at all. Sometimes it’s a splinter, a cutting insight that I would have rather avoided. Or it’s a solidly true, heartfelt moment that sits like a smooth stone in my pocket. The touchstone grounds and guides me on the long journey of making a film.

For the better part of the past year, I’ve been working as an executive producer on a series of short documentaries for the Greater Good Science Center called Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy. The series features students at four universities across the country who are attempting to connect in some meaningful way with people who have different life experiences, political beliefs, or visions for the future.

At Iliff School of Theology, master’s and Ph.D. students imagine a version of the United States that embodies their values, and then they share those visions with one another. As they listen to one another’s values, they discover where they align, where they diverge, and where empathy can keep them in relationship with each other even when they disagree.

In a two-part story set at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students from both campuses gather at an event hosted by the schools’ Social Justice Alliance, a first-of-its-kind collaboration between an HBCU (historically Black college or university) and a PWI (predominantly white institution).

At Dickinson College, a deep friendship between the presidents of the Dickinson College Republicans and the Dickinson College Democrats creates the conditions for an unexpectedly collaborative relationship between the two clubs. Members of both clubs gather regularly and listen to each other’s thoughts about complex and often contentious political issues.

Back when we were in the middle of editing these episodes with our collaborators at Anaconda Street Productions, I spent an afternoon reviewing footage from one of the shoots, and then I took my dog for a walk. On the walk, I found myself repeating a line from an interview. It stuck! It’s been one of those smooth stones in my pocket ever since.

Of course, I’m not the only one who was changed by the experience of working on this series. To celebrate the release of Connecting on Campus, I invite you behind the scenes to meet my collaborators as we share some of the many things we learned as we helped tell these stories.

It’s a pretty straightforward message, yet I hear it over and over in my head in the voice of Mrs. Dawn Collins. Your voice matters and everyone has a part to play. Mrs. Collins says these words during an interview in the first of our two episodes about Bowie State University (BSU) and the University of Maryland (UMD). Mrs. Collins and her husband, Mr. Richard Collins Jr., founded the BSU–UMD Social Justice Alliance after their son, Lt. Richard Collins III, a BSU student, was murdered on the UMD campus by a student in 2017. The Alliance brings together faculty, staff, and students to join the Collins’s commitment to “eradicating the ideology of intolerance, while confronting individuals and combatting systems that normalize indifference, justify injustice, perpetuate hate, and inflict violence.”

Mrs. Collins’s words have stuck with me, in part, because they insist on every person’s dignity, power, and responsibility. Our voices matter, and we all have a role to play in eradicating the ideology of intolerance and in combatting systems that perpetuate hate and inflict violence. That’s a strong call to action.

Mrs. Collins’s words have also stuck with me because they clearly articulate the heart of this documentary series. The students featured in this series offer us examples of what happens when people step into their power and accept the responsibility to understand themselves, understand each other (differences and all), and work together to build something new. That new thing could be a collaboration between clubs on campus or a vision for our future as a nation. Either way, these students know their voices matter and they have what it takes to practice doing this work together.

It was so helpful to have Mrs. Collins’s voice in my head, keeping me anchored in this truth as I worked. — Kelly Rafferty

When we first imagined Connecting on Campus, we wanted to find places where students were actually practicing the skills and qualities that make connection across differences possible, and to make those moments visible.

As I spent time with these students and their stories, and as we shaped the episodes in the edit, I found myself thinking more and more about choice. Across the series, you see students staying curious when they could shut down, listening to understand someone else’s experience, sharing their own perspective while making space for someone else’s, or finding the courage to remain in a difficult conversation.

In our Dickinson College episode, that choice shows up in a moment that could have easily passed. Ryan Thies recounts meeting Matthew Craig at a Halloween party during his freshman year. Matthew was dressed as Donald Trump. Ryan could have seen that costume, made an assumption about who Matthew was, and walked away. Instead, he leaned in and got to know him. An unlikely connection became a friendship, and eventually the two chose to become roommates.    Ryan’s choice changed what became possible between them. That choice reflects the kind of empathy we talk about in our Bridging Differences work: the deliberate, and often difficult, choice to engage with someone else’s experience even when it feels unfamiliar or challenges our own worldview.

The choices look different in our Bowie State University and University of Maryland episodes—and the stakes are obviously very different, too. Here, the students and the Collins family are stepping into a history that is devastating: the murder of Lt. Richard Collins III on the University of Maryland campus and the work that emerged from it to confront hatred and bring students from the two campuses together.

Here, courage looks like choosing to show up and engage when discomfort, conflict, and fear might make it easier—and completely understandable—to withdraw. It’s the decision to say: This matters. I’ll attend. I’ll represent. I’ll listen. I’ll do my part.

Practices like “Listen with Empathy,” “Understand Their Values,” “Expand Your Views and Circles,” or “Perspective Giving and Getting” from our Bridging Differences in Higher Education Playbook can be learned.

But the choice to engage is one each of us has to make. My hope is that people watch these stories asking themselves, “What did that person do that made greater understanding possible, and where might I try that myself?”  — Juliana Tafur

I came away thinking that “bridging” is sometimes misunderstood as compromise. Across all four videos, something more interesting emerges: You can build a relationship across a difference without necessarily resolving the difference itself.

At Iliff School of Theology, students imagine very different versions of America without being asked to arrive at one shared vision. At Dickinson, Republicans and Democrats engage seriously with each other without abandoning their political beliefs. And at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students move beyond assumptions, allow themselves to be vulnerable, ask difficult questions, and really listen to people whose backgrounds and experiences differ from their own. The circumstances are very different, but the lesson is consistent: Bridging isn’t about erasing what separates us. It’s about developing the curiosity, trust, and courage to stay connected across those differences.

The series asks a harder and more useful question than “How do we get everyone to agree?” It asks how we live, learn, and build community with people who may never see the world exactly as we do. The answers aren’t presented as a formula. You get to watch people experiment with listening, vulnerability, curiosity, disagreement, and repair, then decide for yourself what actually works. — Omar Lugones

In my own experiences in smaller, more intimate classroom settings, I often observe an echo-chamber effect when opinions are shared, especially when the class is discussing a controversial topic. I have noticed a general apprehension about “going first” or initiating the conversation. Speaking for myself, I am often afraid of offering the “wrong” opinion, meaning a perspective that could be interpreted as supporting a politically or socially unacceptable position and cause my peers to view me as an outsider. I do not necessarily think my peers are experiencing the exact same thought process, but I sense that they are also self-conscious about expressing a conflicting opinion. As a result, people may default to agreeing with whoever offers an opinion first.

I thought it was remarkable that at Iliff School of Theology, Lindsay Ambler and Stephanie Nelson initially disagree with one another, and that moment opens space for others to enter the conversation and offer their own perspectives. By disagreeing respectfully, they demonstrate how disagreement can produce a deeper understanding of an issue than a conversation built only around agreement.

Lindsay takes a strong position on the effects of religion based on her past experiences with Christian institutions. By sharing an extremely vulnerable personal story, she creates the conditions for others to share their experiences and, in turn, promotes a greater sense of empathy within the conversation.

When Stephanie offers her own perspective on whether society can reach a state of perfection and equality, her response conflicts with Lindsay’s position. This point of contention could seemingly disrupt the vulnerable environment Lindsay has created, yet it does not. Instead, Lindsay responds to the challenge by deepening her explanation. In doing so, she creates new points of entry for others to join the conversation and contribute their own experiences.

At the end of the discussion, Stephanie expresses gratitude to those who shared their perspectives and revealed gaps in her own thinking. The conversation demonstrates how respectful disagreement can foster empathy, growth, and greater participation from every member of a group. — Tyler C. Tang

Working on this series, I noticed the relationship between character and discomfort. Courage, empathy, humility, and curiosity all sound admirable in the abstract, but you really discover whether you possess them when another person challenges you. Character in these films often reveals itself in what someone does immediately after hearing something they don’t agree with.

For example, I identified with Josh Perez, a Ph.D. student and teaching assistant at Iliff School of Theology, in particular. I appreciate the way he draws on his own experiences as a second-generation Mexican American while recognizing that other people carry struggles he may never experience himself. His vision isn’t simply about creating a world that works better for people like him. It’s about making room for others to find liberation from their own struggles, as well. That ability to be grounded in your own experience while still making space for the experiences of others is at the heart of bridging differences. — Antonio Carrasco III

If you’re exhausted by watching people argue about politics, identity, and social issues, watch people actually talk to each other instead. The series doesn’t suggest that differences disappear when people sit down together. It shows that disagreement can be productive when people approach each other with curiosity and humility.

Iliff School of Theology student Lindsay Ambler’s story affected me in a way I didn’t expect. It was hard to hear how painful some of her experiences within religious spaces had been. Learning how she was rejected after people discovered she was gay gave me a much deeper understanding of what she carried into the classroom. It reminded me how little we may know about someone until we give them the space to share their story.

Logan Midler from the University of Maryland stands out to me, too. I appreciate how honest she is about not having much interaction with people from different backgrounds and how easy it can be to start those conversations. Her desire to listen, learn, and become a better ally feels like a simple yet powerful example of bridging differences. — Ryan Carrasco

I hope there’s a moment in Connecting on Campus that sticks with you, too. Maybe that memorable line, that bit of dialogue, or that mindful pause will become a touchstone for your own experiments in bridging differences.

As another academic year begins, may the stories in this series also serve as an example of what students are capable of doing when they’re given the space and support to practice connecting with one another. Campuses across the country are facing real challenges—everything from threats of censorship to rising costs and cuts to funding—and these opportunities to practice bridging differences must not be sacrificed along the way. They’re too important to our individual and collective well-being.

Watch Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy.

#165. Handling Dismissive Comments at Work

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted September 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Sometimes dismissive words at work can have a lasting impression and affect long-term career success.

When Marisa was 24 years old, just starting out in her career, she was asked by Phil, a senior executive at work, to go shopping for underwear for his girlfriend. She was taken aback by this request but decided to just go along with it.

On her lunch break, Marisa shopped for the underwear and presented it to him. A few days later, he requested that she shop again, but to make sure to purchase sexy underwear this time. She told Phil that she didn’t feel comfortable shopping again for his girlfriend.

She decided to discuss the situation with her boss as it made her feel uncomfortable around Phil. Her boss just dismissed the incident as silly. Dismissing an incident that makes someone feel uncomfortable as “silly” can lead to an unsafe workplace.

Marisa felt unsupported, and this incident stayed with her throughout her career. She eventually went on to start her own coaching and leadership company in Dubai focused on helping other women achieve success and support when they need it.

Dismissive comments at work undermine confidence, shut down idea creation, and can damage team morale. One way to handle these situations is to repeat back to the person exactly what they just said to you. For instance, Marisa could have said to Phil, “Did you just ask me to go buy sexy underwear for your girlfriend?”

To see how this approach can work, consider this scenario: Barbara, a senior marketing executive in a biotech company, was stating her views strongly in a meeting about the project she was presenting to the team and explaining why she was taking a different approach. John, a colleague, accused her of being mean. In this case, she did his comment back to him, and the entire room went silent. After waiting a few seconds, she continued her presentation.

Would a man ever accuse another man of being mean in a meeting? Not likely.

Often in the workplace, dismissive comments just get brushed aside. Barbara singled out a comment that made her feel and look weak, and simply by repeating it showed the group and the commenter that it was a stupid and damaging thing to say.

Women can take their power back by using this simple technique that gives them respect and enables the other person to see the inappropriateness of their request or comment.

#166. 16 surprising sleep facts that may change how you rest

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

You meant to get to bed early. Then work spilled past dinner, the group chat lit up, your kids were up and down, and the first quiet moment of the day didn't arrive until close to midnight. By then, an extra hour awake felt like the only way to get some time to yourself.

Many of us sacrifice sleep when life gets busy, but that sacrifice may cost you more than you realize. While you rest, your brain and body are hard at work — storing memories, balancing your mood, and supporting your heart and immune system. That’s why getting enough sleep matters.

With that in mind, we're here to give you 16 facts on sleep, ranging from the strange to the surprising. Some are even reassuring, like how dreams (even bad ones) help us sort through our emotions. Together, they explain what your body does while you rest and what the science says about how much sleep you really need.

Sleep may look like downtime, but your brain is actually busy doing some of its most important work while you're catching Zzzs.

Your sleeping brain removes waste that has accumulated during waking hours. This process takes place via the glymphatic system, a network that passes fluid through your brain tissue and removes the byproducts, such as proteins linked to Alzheimer's disease. The system is most active when you’re sleeping, and it’s mostly inactive when you’re awake. A major theory is that this daily cleaning is a principal reason why the body needs sleep at all.

During deep, slow-wave sleep, your brain replays and files away new memories. The hippocampus and the outer brain exchange signals, moving fresh memories into long-term storage. It's one reason a full night of sleep before a test tends to beat an all-nighter of studying.

Read more: Is there a link between sleep deprivation and memory loss?

Your brain isn't the only part of you running maintenance overnight. From your heart to your immune system, a lot of the body's repair work is scheduled for when you're asleep.

Regularly sleeping too little is linked to higher rates of high blood pressure, heart disease, and stroke. Sleep loss ramps up the fight-or-flight side of your nervous system and keeps stress signals elevated, which over time can wear on the heart and blood vessels. One large review tied short sleep to a measurably higher risk of cardiovascular disease.

Related read: Is your sleeping heart rate normal? Here’s how to tell

Sleep helps your immune system do its job, and cutting it short leaves you more open to getting sick. Short sleep is linked to more inflammation in the body and a weaker response when you need to fight off a bug. That's part of why a run of bad nights can end with a cold.

💙 Struggling to shake off every cold that goes around? Tamara Levitt explains how sleep builds your immune system in her Sleep session on Daily Calm.

Sleep helps regulate appetite and how your body handles sugar. When sleep runs short, hunger hormones shift, and the body uses insulin less effectively, which can increase cravings and blood sugar levels. This is part of why ongoing sleep loss is linked to weight gain and type 2 diabetes.

💙 If short nights have you reaching for snacks you don't really want, work through Cravings with Tamara Levitt to meet that pull with a little more awareness.

Sleep isn’t just a long period of being unconscious. Throughout the night, your brain moves through different stages, each with its own purpose.

A night of sleep isn't one steady state. You cycle through light sleep, deep sleep, and REM sleep, with each full cycle lasting around 90 minutes. Most adults run through four to six of these cycles a night. Deep sleep is heaviest early on, and the makeup of each cycle shifts as the night goes on.

Read more: How to optimize your sleep architecture for better rest

If you wake up feeling groggy, that’s called sleep inertia. It’s strongest when you wake from deep sleep instead of a lighter stage. That’s why a short nap of about 20 minutes, or a longer one around 90 minutes, can help you feel more refreshed than a nap that wakes you from deep sleep.

Read more: How to take a nap and wake up feeling refreshed

There's a reason the first night in a hotel or a new apartment often feels restless. Research using brain scans found that on the first night in an unfamiliar place, one half of the brain remains slightly more alert during deep sleep, as if standing guard. Scientists call it the "first-night effect," and it seems to be a built-in way of watching for trouble when your surroundings are new.

💙 Away from home and having a hard time settling in? Let The Country Hotel, narrated by Cat Nguyen, ease you into your unfamiliar surroundings.

You might think you’re in control of your timetable, but your body usually has its own sense of when you should get to bed. Here are two reasons why you get sleepy at certain times and why some people find mornings harder than others.

Deep in the brain sits a cluster of cells called the suprachiasmatic nucleus, your body's master clock. It runs on a roughly 24-hour cycle and signals when to be alert and when to wind down. Morning light resets it each day and keeps it lined up with the outside world. That's part of why bright screens late at night can throw your timing off, and why getting sunlight in the morning helps you shake off grogginess.

Read more: What is circadian rhythm? Plus, why it’s essential for better sleep

Whether you spring up at dawn or come alive after dark isn't only about willpower. Your natural timing, called your chronotype, is partly set by your genes. One study of nearly 700,000 people found hundreds of genetic markers linked to being a morning person. Timing also shifts across your life. Most young kids are morning types, teens' wake-ups often drift much later during puberty, and the pull toward early mornings tends to return as people age.

Read more: What your chronotype says about your sleep patterns, productivity & personality

Missing sleep doesn’t just make you feel tired. Over time, it can affect your mood, focus, and even your long-term health.

You don't need weeks of bad sleep to feel the effects. After even one short night, people tend to be more reactive to stress and more irritable. Drowsy driving is a real danger here, since lack of sleep can make you slower to respond, often without being aware of it.

The good news is that this kind of dip is short-lived. Unlike the ongoing sleep loss further down this list, your body can bounce back from a single rough night after just one or two days of normal sleep.

Read more: What is sleep deprivation? Plus, 11 tips to help you cope

A Saturday lie-in can take the edge off, but it doesn't undo a week of short nights. Studies show that weekend catch-up sleep and naps don't fully reverse the effects of ongoing sleep loss, especially on metabolism. The better fix is keeping to a consistent sleep schedule as much as possible.

Read more: Want to sleep better? These 10 healthy sleep habits can help

REM is the stage most closely associated with vivid dreaming. For years, it puzzled scientists, and what they've learned about it reshapes how we think about why we dream at all.

REM stands for rapid eye movement, the stage when your eyes dart around under closed lids and dreams are most vivid. Early in the night, REM periods are short, sometimes under 10 minutes. By the early morning hours, they can stretch to 40 minutes or more. So the dream you remember most vividly is only a sliver of what your brain was actually doing all night.

Related read: REM sleep vs. deep sleep (and how much do you need of both?)

Dreams may serve a bigger purpose than merely passing the time at night. Research suggests that REM sleep and dreaming help your brain process emotions, making tough memories less painful while keeping their lessons. Studies show that people who miss out on REM sleep are often more emotionally sensitive the next day.

Read more: 22 interesting facts about dreams that might blow your mind

Sleep habits aren’t the same everywhere or in every time period. What seems like the “right” way to sleep often depends on your culture and when you live.

Sleep length differs from country to country, and the gap can exceed an hour a night on average. Work culture, commute times, light, and local habits all play a part. Researchers have even found that the amount of sleep associated with the best health depends on where you live, suggesting that the "right" number of hours may be partly cultural rather than a fixed target for everyone on the planet.

Sleeping straight through the night may be a fairly modern habit. Historical records suggest that before artificial light was common, many people slept in two shifts, a "first sleep" and a "second sleep," with an hour or so of quiet wakefulness in between. Some researchers think waking in the middle of the night isn't always a problem to solve, and may echo this older rhythm. In one lab study, people kept in long nightly darkness gradually drifted back toward that split-sleep pattern.

Read more: Is segmented sleep healthy? How it works and what to expect

During REM sleep, your body is briefly paralyzed while your brain stays nearly as active as when you're awake. This built-in muscle shutdown is called atonia, and it keeps you from acting out your dreams.

It's one of sleep's stranger tricks. REM is when most vivid dreaming happens, and the temporary shutdown means your body stays still while your brain runs wild. When this system misfires, it can lead to sleep paralysis, a brief, unsettling feeling of being awake but unable to move.

A steady sleep routine helps most people, especially keeping consistent sleep and wake times. Sleep responds well to signals of safety and routine, so maintaining the same schedule—even on weekends—helps your body clock stay regulated.

From there, a few habits can help you fall asleep faster:

A wind-down habit tells your brain the day is closing, and some people find that a few minutes of slow breathing or meditation before bed helps quiet a racing mind.

Sleep allows your mind to clear waste from brain tissue and file away the day's memories. It also restores your ability to focus and regulate emotions, so skimping on sleep makes it harder to both learn and manage your mood.

Different sleep stages handle different jobs. Deep sleep drives the cleanup and memory filing, while REM works on emotional processing. Even one short night can leave you foggy and forgetful, and long-term sleep loss is linked to a higher risk of memory problems later in life.

One missed night won't cause lasting harm for most healthy people, but it takes a real toll the next day. After 24 hours awake, attention and judgment drop sharply. Expect slower thinking and reaction times (making work with heavy machinery or driving risky), as well as lower mood.

You'll likely bounce back after a couple of solid nights, though your sleep may feel deeper than usual as your body makes up for lost deep sleep. Repeated all-nighters are harder on the body and worth avoiding.

The common eight-hour number is an average, not a rule. Most adults do best with 7–9 hours, and sleep experts recommend at least seven.

Your ideal amount depends on your age, genes, health, and how you feel and function during the day. A small number of people feel fine on less, but true short sleepers are rare. If you're tired all day despite getting 7-9 hours of sleep, that's worth mentioning to a doctor.

Related read: How many hours of sleep you need based on your age

There's no single agreed-upon answer, but the leading idea is that dreaming helps the brain process emotions and consolidate memories. Most vivid dreams happen during REM sleep.

Research suggests that dreams may help the brain sort through the day's emotional experiences and weave new memories in with old ones. Dreams lean negative more often than positive, which fits the theory that they help you work through stress. Scientists are still debating the details.

Sleep and mental health feed each other. Poor sleep drags your mood down, and a struggling mind can make getting or staying asleep more difficult.

After even a night or two of bad sleep, stress and emotions get harder to manage. When short sleep becomes the norm, it can raise the risk of depression and anxiety while deepening symptoms you already have. The reverse holds too, so better sleep often lifts mood, which is why it's a common focus in mental health care. If sleep trouble and low mood persist, a doctor or therapist can help.

A nap can restore some alertness, but it can't replace the deep, restorative sleep of a full night. Naps ease a rough night, though they can't undo the buildup of ongoing sleep loss, especially its effects on your heart and metabolism.

Related read: Power naps: benefits, length, & how to power nap like a pro

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

#167. 4 Wonderful Signs You Have A High IQ

Four things that indicate high intelligence in a person.

Four things that indicate high intelligence in a person.

Being open to experience, cooperative, happy and having strong perceptual skills are all signs that you have a high IQ, psychological research finds.

Of these, being open to experience is a particularly strong sign…

Insatiable curiosity, an active fantasy life, a sensitivity to emotions and an appreciation of art and beauty are all linked to high IQ.

These are all aspects of the major personality trait called ‘openness to experience’.

People who are open to experience are more interested in things that are complex, new and unconventional.

Being open to experience is so powerful that it is linked to intelligence when measured almost 40 years later.

Children who scored higher on IQ tests at just 11-years-old were more open to experience when they were 50-years-old, the psychologists found.

Intelligent people are better at cooperating with others.

While personality traits like being generous and conscientious have an effect on cooperation, higher IQ is the main factor that encourages people to work well together.

People with higher intelligence use more consistent strategies and consider the consequences of their actions.

That is why people with high IQs are so essential: without them society would not work.

The finding goes against the popular idea that being intelligent somehow predisposes people to unhappiness.

The study looked at happiness in the best-known sense of feeling positive emotions and being satisfied with your life.

The results showed that people with the lowest IQ (70 – 99) were the least happy in comparison to those with the highest IQs (120 – 129).

People with high IQs have stronger basic perceptual skills, research finds.

For example, they can tell which way objects are moving more quickly.

They are also better at blocking out background information to make their judgement.

Imagine a ball thrown at high speed — a more intelligent person can pick up its trajectory faster.

A higher IQ makes the brain faster at a fundamental level.

It helps underline that high IQ is about more than just solving puzzles or making the ‘right’ decision.

#168. Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain

Coffee may affect far more than alertness. New research suggests that both regular and decaffeinated coffee can alter the gut microbiome and may influence mood, stress, memory, and attention through the gut brain connection.

Scientists at APC Microbiome Ireland, a research center at University College Cork, investigated in detail how coffee may influence communication between the digestive system and the brain.

The study published in Nature Communications and sponsored by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), found that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were associated with changes in the gut microbiome as well as differences in mood and stress.

How Coffee May Affect the Gut-Brain Connection

Scientists have long studied coffee for possible effects on digestion, mood, and overall health, but exactly how these effects arise has remained less clear.

The new research focused on the microbiota-gut-brain axis, the two-way communication system linking microorganisms in the digestive tract with the brain. Signals can travel between the gut and brain through immune activity, hormones, nerves, and chemical compounds produced by microbes.

Researchers examined 31 regular coffee drinkers and 31 people who did not normally drink coffee. Participants completed psychological assessments and kept records of caffeine intake and diet. Researchers also collected stool and urine samples to track changes in gut microbes, metabolism, mood, and perceived stress.

For the study, 'Coffee drinkers' were set as those who regularly consume 3-5 cups of coffee a day, defined by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) as a safe and moderate amount for most people.

The regular coffee drinkers first stopped consuming coffee for two weeks. During that period, participants repeatedly completed psychological assessments and provided stool and urine samples.

When coffee drinkers stopped drinking coffee, researchers observed substantial shifts in their gut metabolite profiles compared with people who did not normally consume coffee. Metabolites are small molecules produced or altered during metabolism, including compounds created by gut microbes as they process food and other substances.

Coffee was then reintroduced without participants knowing whether they were receiving caffeinated or decaffeinated coffee. Half received decaf, while the other half received caffeinated coffee.

After coffee returned to their diets, both groups reported lower perceived stress, depression and impulsivity scores. The findings suggest that some of coffee's effects on mood may not depend entirely on caffeine.

Coffee Was Linked to Changes in Gut Bacteria

Researchers also found differences in several types of gut bacteria.

Bacteria, such as 'Eggertella sp.' or 'Cryptobacterium curtum', were more abundant among coffee drinkers than non-coffee drinkers. 'Eggertella sp' is thought to contribute to acid secretion in the stomach and intestines, while 'Cryptobacterium curtum' may participate in bile acid production.

Both processes could potentially help create an intestinal environment that discourages certain harmful bacteria and infections.

Researchers also observed higher levels of 'Firmicutes' bacteria, a broad group of microbes that has previously been associated with positive emotions in females.

Decaf and Caffeinated Coffee Showed Different Effects

One of the most intriguing findings was that caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee did not appear to affect participants in exactly the same way.

Improved learning and memory were observed only among participants drinking decaffeinated coffee. That finding suggests that substances other than caffeine may contribute to some of coffee's effects on cognition.

Coffee contains thousands of chemical compounds, including polyphenols. These plant derived substances can act as antioxidants and can also interact with gut microbes, potentially influencing metabolism and other biological processes.

Caffeinated coffee, meanwhile, was associated with reduced feelings of anxiety as well as improved vigilance and attention. Caffeine was also linked to a reduced risk of inflammation.

Because the study involved a relatively small number of participants, the findings do not establish that coffee directly causes these changes in mood, cognition, or gut health. However, they provide new clues about the biological pathways that could help explain associations reported in earlier coffee research.

Corresponding author of the study, Professor John Cryan, Principal Investigator at APC Microbiome Ireland, University College Cork, commented: "Public interest in gut health has risen hugely. The relationship between digestive and mental health is also increasingly being better understood, but the mechanisms behind coffee's effects on this gut-brain axis have remained unclear.

"Our findings reveal the microbiome and neurological responses to coffee, as well as their potential long-term benefits for a healthier microbiome. Coffee may modify what microbes do collectively, and what metabolites they use. As the public continues to think about dietary changes for the right digestive balance, coffee has the potential to also be harnessed as a further intervention as part of a healthy balanced diet."

The findings add to growing evidence that coffee should not be viewed simply as a source of caffeine. Its many other components may interact with the microbiome, metabolism, and nervous system in different ways.

"Coffee is more than just caffeine -- it's a complex dietary factor that interacts with our gut microbes, our metabolism, and even our emotional well-being," said Professor Cryan. "Our findings suggest that coffee, whether caffeinated or decaffeinated, can influence health in distinct but complementary ways."

Materials provided by University College Cork. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#169. As People Live Longer, How Can We Live Better?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

When the Stanford Center on Longevity launched in 2007, founding director Laura Carstensen spent a lot of time correcting misperceptions. “The initial response people had was, ‘Like the Methuselah Foundation? You are going to extend life?’” Carstensen was clear that the center’s aim was not to increase lifespans—which had nearly doubled during the 20th century—but rather to build societies that accommodated that new and unprecedented reality.

Another persistent misperception was that “longevity” is a euphemism for aging and that the Stanford Center on Longevity was a center on aging. As Carstensen noted often, “Longevity is not synonymous with aging. It is a metric of length.” The center’s interest is in the challenges and opportunities that longer lives present. While the center is keenly interested in older people, in Carstensen’s view, “longer lives have implications for every stage of life, and the roots of many problems faced at advanced ages have their roots much earlier in life.” The center’s mission is to use longer lives to improve quality of life at all ages.

In 2019, under Carstensen’s leadership, the center launched the New Map of Life initiative, designed to rethink the human life course in response to skyrocketing life expectancies, and it has trained nearly 40 postdoctoral fellows, mentored by faculty affiliates spanning multiple disciplines, about the ways in which longevity is transforming societies, cultures, and economies. After nearly 20 years, Carstensen, the Fairleigh S. Dickinson Jr. Professor in Public Policy and a professor of psychology at Stanford, will step down this summer from her role at the Stanford Center on Longevity to pursue a new project alongside her research and teaching.

I spoke with Carstensen about what she’s learned along the way and what’s next. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Karen Breslau: What’s changed since the center’s early days?

Laura Carstensen: I hope it’s clearer that the aging process has not changed much, if any, genetically over the last several thousand years. Rather, longevity—the length of life—increased, and that has enormous implications for nearly all aspects of our lives. The modifiability of aging, on the other hand, is also clear. Even though we’re essentially the same physiological beings that our ancestors were, we changed the world in ways that are allowing us to live healthier and longer. That’s why we are confident that we can build a world where the majority of people live well for a century.

KB: You are on the scientific advisory council to the Health District of Singapore, which is building the Queenstown Health District, a very intentional all-ages community that is incorporating principles from the New Map of Life. What are you seeing?

LC: The Singapore government has given a group of scientists the freedom to design a neighborhood in ways that support long-term health and intergenerational connections, continued financial security, and exercise. They’re thinking about all the factors that contribute to long, healthy, and engaged lives and literally programming them into the community. What’s really cool about the Queenstown Health District is that it can provide a proof of concept that social and physical designs can improve long life.

Already they have built parks and playgrounds with swings for the kids and balance beams for older residents, to provide shared spaces where different ages interact. When we advisers fly in from different countries, we’re starry-eyed at what they can do. Singapore can do things like this in part because they’re smaller, and their government can act quickly. For example, the government recognized about a decade ago that people weren’t saving enough for retirement. So they flipped a switch and said, “OK, everybody’s putting in more money into their retirement account.”

KB: If you had to give a grade to where the U.S. is in implementing the New Map of Life principles, could you take out your red pen?

LC: Compared to some countries, like Singapore, I’d give the U.S. a C-minus, and I am used to grade inflation! The federal government has done little to improve longevity. Unlike the Singapore government, which can require people to save more for retirement, for example, the U.S. cannot quickly implement such programs. On the other hand, in part because the government contributes less, we see a lot of innovation coming from the private sector. We have entire industries offering new products and services. So I’m optimistic about what the U.S. can contribute to longevity. At a global level, it’s fabulous to think about the different approaches that can come from the public and private sectors in a range of countries.

KB: Longevity has gone mainstream and led to billions of dollars in market interest. How has that changed the center’s work?

LC: It’s true that vast investments are going to longevity. Most of these funds are directed at ways that individuals can live longer. There isn’t, in my experience, much philanthropic interest in this space aimed at helping people live better as we live longer lives. I am discouraged that we are sleepwalking through this seismic demographic shift without investing more in the opportunity to rewrite the life scripts that have guided life and imagining ways that we could use them to improve life.

It’s also discouraging that as longevity has entered public consciousness, much of what we hear about are pitches for questionable products that supposedly make people live longer. There are so many snake-oil salesmen in this space that it’s hard for consumers to distinguish what is evidence-based and what is not.

KB: As you often say, transitions are a feature of longer lives. What’s happening next for you?

LC: I’m going to focus more on research and teaching, but first I’m going on sabbatical and look forward to having more time for the things I love—my garden, being at home, sitting in the sun, going for walks. I want to take Pilates lessons. I’m going to take a break in my schedule to say, “How do I create a healthy lifestyle going forward and build the rest around it?”

While I hopefully will have a more relaxed schedule, during my sabbatical I’ll be developing an online course called The Fundamentals of Longevity, which will tell the story of longevity and the potential to live longer, better lives, a change we really need in the world. The course will be accessible far beyond Stanford, so that we can help frame the conversation around longevity and help people appreciate the extraordinary promise of science, technology, and social change to improve life. There is a crisis on the horizon if we don’t change the way we live.

We have the opportunity to change our lives for the better. We have opportunities no previous generation of humans in history has had, and we need to start implementing them.

This story was originally published by Stanford Center on Longevity. Read the original article.

#170. The Hidden Pain of Adoptee Birthdays

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted September 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

For most people, birthday celebrations are filled with cake, candles, and being told, “We’re so happy you were born.” For people, who were adopted, at birth or through foster care, some enjoy celebrating birthdays, others dread them, and for many adoptees, birthdays can feel like an unspeakable loss. As one adoptee said: “When they told me to make a wish before blowing out my candles, I always wished secretly to meet my birth mother.”

As a psychotherapist specializing in adoption and foster care, and as an adoptee myself, I understand that birthdays can carry a double meaning: a celebration of life and a reminder of loss. Both truths exist, and both are hard to carry at once. This day serves as a reminder of the separation from one's birth family, an agony of grief that is real, hidden, and not always recognized, validated, or openly acknowledged by society. Adoptees often keep this loss locked in an internal vault, leaving many holding a vessel of grief that has no clear place to go.

For adoptees, a birthday is not just the beginning of life. It is the day they were separated from their first connection…their birth mother. Even when there is no conscious memory, the body remembers this as separation trauma, as explored in the book The Body Keeps the Score by Bessel van der Kolk. Trauma research shows that early relational breaks are stored as implicit memory in the nervous system. So, while the outside world sings “Happy Birthday,” the inside world is feeling something entirely different, not because something is wrong, but because a profound loss has occurred.

So even if adoptees aren’t actively talking about this, that does not mean they are not actively thinking about this. Some common questions for adoptees on their birthdays are:

What was that day like for my first mother and for me?Who celebrated my birth?Was I held? Did she cry when I left?Am I a memory or a mystery?

Do they think of me on my birthday?Would they recognize me now?What part of me comes from them?

How could any mother give away her baby? Is there something wrong with me?Was I not lovable?Am I not worthy?

These questions live quietly beneath the surface, sometimes acted out as sadness, irritability, withdrawal, or even anger. The family of one child I worked with reported that during his birthday party, he just disappeared. His parents were confused about where he had gone and found him crying alone in his room. He couldn’t put into words what he was feeling in the moment, but when we explored this later in therapy, he said, “Everyone was so happy, and all I felt was alone, like I didn’t exist.” He was experiencing a grief reaction, also called a grief anniversary, the embodied feeling of separation and loss all over again.

One powerful intervention I use with adoptees, especially around birthdays, is a candle ritual. This ritual allows adoptees to honor both parts of their story: the life they are living and the connection they lost. This can be done the day before or on their birthday.

The candle ritual and grief mailbox create something many adoptees never received: permission to feel all of it. This empowers them to feel what interferes with their celebration, have a place to hold questions that don’t have answers, and create a space to honor a part of their story, often coined the "ghost kingdom." The goal is not to take the grief away. The goal is to sit beside it.

For parents, I recommend processing feelings a few days before the birthday, with reflective statements such as:“I wonder if this day brings up a lot for you.”“You can feel happy and sad today.”"I'm so sorry for your loss."“We don’t have to pretend this day is only one thing.”“If you’re thinking about your birth family today, that makes sense.”“You don’t have to carry these feelings alone.”“I can sit with you in whatever comes up.”“There’s room for every part of your story here.”“You can tell me anything you’re feeling; I can handle it.”“This day belongs to you, and we can honor it in whatever way feels right.”

Healing for adoptees does not mean the birthday becomes easy. It means the day becomes integrated. I was born and I was separated. Celebration does not erase the loss, and the loss does not erase the adoptee's worth. This day merits adopting all of their parts, which is essential to developing a true sense of self.

So the next time you think of an adoptee on their birthday, pause and have a moment of compassion to celebrate not just the part that is celebrated, but the part that is remembered.

When the invisible loss is acknowledged, the veil of aloneness begins to lift, the walls protecting pain slowly come down, and the mask concealing questions of one’s identity falls away. And in this newfound space between candlelight and truth, existence is redefined.

I invite you to listen to a poignant song, a moving testimony of what adoptees experience: "Mama Here, Mama Gone," written and performed by folk singer and adoptee Mary Gauthier.

Brodzinsky, D. M., Schecter, M. D., & Henig, R. M. (1993). Being adopted: The lifelong search for self. Anchor.

Lifton, B. J. (2009). Lost & found: The adoption experience. University of Michigan Press.

Van der Kolk, B. (2014). The body keeps the score: Brain, mind, and body in the healing of trauma. Penguin Books.

#171. When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable

Sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense. A shadow can briefly resemble a face, or one object can momentarily be mistaken for another. New research suggests that the brain may resolve these visual conflicts by allowing different regions to compare their interpretations until a more consistent picture emerges.

In a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R. Stebbins Fellow Mitra Javadzadeh and collaborators at the University of Cambridge and University College London examined how two neighboring regions of the visual cortex interact. They found that when activity in the two regions matched, the shared pattern persisted. When the regions produced conflicting patterns, however, the disagreement faded within a fraction of a second.

The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.

How Specialized Brain Regions Work Together

Different parts of the brain are responsible for processing different streams of sensory information, yet our experience of the world usually feels unified rather than fragmented. Understanding how those specialized systems coordinate with one another is a major challenge in neuroscience.

"We are trying to understand how you can have such a high level of specialization between these different blocks, yet always have a consistent holistic outcome," Javadzadeh says.

The researchers focused on two well known visual processing regions in the brain's neocortex: the primary visual cortex (V1) and the lateromedial visual area (LM). Visual processing does not simply move in one direction from one region to the next. Instead, these areas continually exchange information with each other.

Testing What Happens When Visual Areas Disagree

To explore that communication, Javadzadeh and her colleagues trained mice to tell the difference between two visual patterns tilted in opposite directions. The animals received a reward for recognizing only one of the orientations.

During the task, the researchers temporarily silenced either V1 or LM and watched how the remaining region behaved without its usual partner. The team then used those observations to create an artificial neural network model of the V1-LM circuit. With that model, they could test how the system might respond when particular neurons were altered.

The results revealed a striking pattern. Activity that conflicted between the two brain regions quickly disappeared, while activity shared by both areas lasted longer.

"We find that over time, these types of connections between areas implement a mechanism we call consensus building," Javadzadeh explains.

The study examined only two regions involved in vision, but the researchers are now investigating whether the same process may operate more broadly across the neocortex.

"For example, when what you see contradicts with what you hear, do you still use the same kind of mechanisms to reconcile these two?" she wonders.

If dynamic consensus building turns out to be widespread, it could help scientists better understand how the brain combines competing signals into a stable interpretation of the world. It could also shed light on what happens when different brain regions fail to arrive at the same conclusion.

The idea may even have implications beyond neuroscience. Similar principles could help researchers think about how artificial intelligence systems might handle conflicting streams of information and decide which signals to trust.

"While we understand individual building blocks of the brain, what is the glue that puts them together?" Javadzadeh asks. "Knowing that can finally help us understand how the brain works as a whole."

Materials provided by Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
